campaigns.title: Class 1-A — Season 1
campaigns.tone: Primarily lighthearted and fun — dorm life, rivalries, chaos, friendship, competition — with genuine dramatic stakes that escalate through each tier. The comedy and the tragedy earn each other. Season 1 ends with the class intact but the world more complicated than it was.

background.heading: U.A. High School
background.body:
Japan's most prestigious hero-track school, tucked into the quiet residential blocks of Nerima Ward on Tokyo's western edge. Known nationwide for producing top Pro Heroes. Entry is brutally competitive — the entrance exam is genuinely dangerous, and only the top performers earn a spot. Class 1-A is the flagship hero course cohort, the class everyone outside watches and resents a little.

Heights Alliance (the dorms) — The student dormitories. Each student has their own room but shares common spaces — kitchen, living room, laundry. Most of the campaign's downtime drama happens here.

Battle Centres — Numbered training areas (I through VII) with different environments: city block, forest, industrial yard, interior combat. Used for both formal training and exams.

Rankings — Students are ranked internally. This matters more than it probably should to several members of Class 1-A.

background.heading: Tokyo
background.body:
The real city, mostly — busy, dense, and completely used to heroes by now. Hero sightings are a daily occurrence, agency branding is stitched into half the storefronts in Shibuya, and civilians have strong, loud opinions about the Pro Hero rankings. The wards the class actually spends time in each have their own texture.

Shibuya — Downtown commercial core. Agency-sponsored storefronts, the crossing's big public screens running hero ranking updates between ads. Where the class goes on free weekends.

Marunouchi — Glass-and-steel business district where the highest-ranked agencies keep their towers. Looks like money. Feels like a lobby.

Setagaya — Residential sprawl — quiet streets, parks, schools, families. Where most of the class's rescue-and-patrol work happens. Nothing here is glamorous and that's the point.

Kurogane Wharf — A working waterfront pocket on the Koto side of Tokyo Bay — old fish-market blocks, container yards, warehouses that changed hands too many times for anyone to track. Officially still part of the city's shipping backbone. Unofficially, it's Ruin's home turf, and has been for years.

background.heading: Hero Society & the Undertow Problem
background.body:
Mostly functioning and genuinely exciting. Being a hero is cool. Hero rankings are watched like sports. U.A. students are minor celebrities at public events. The world feels alive and worth protecting.

Licensing — Heroes must hold a Hero License to engage in combat. Students operate under provisional licenses before graduating. Unlicensed quirk use in combat is technically criminal, which creates tension during patrol and internship arcs.

Pro Hero Culture — Pro heroes have sponsors, fan rankings, social media followings. Some are genuine legends. Some are PR machines. The class will meet both kinds.

Everyone in Tokyo knows the name Ruin. It's been running out of Kurogane Wharf for years — extortion, quirk-for-hire jobs, black-market support gear, a quiet quirk-research operation hiding behind a tech-consultancy shell. One villain group, six named members, no departments. The Hero Commission's dossier on Ruin is thick, but what it doesn't have is a face for the top of it. Everyone who's ever named a leader has used the same word — Undertow — and nobody official will confirm he exists. Separately, a real anti-licensing movement called Fracture has been getting louder at protests across the city; nobody — not the Commission, not Fracture's own leadership — has connected it to Ruin's money yet. Ruin isn't a mystery. Undertow is.

background.heading: Student Life
background.body:
The backbone of the campaign between dramatic arcs. Cooking arguments, study chaos, dorm drama, class rivalries, gossip about who likes who, culture festival disasters, sports festival tensions. This is as important as the combat.

• Toshida Shogoro's speech bubble head makes doorways a recurring hazard
• Nakaya Emari has accidentally short-circuited several pieces of common room electronics and refuses to apologise
• Masahata Shikoji maintains a printed personal ranking chart on the common room fridge that everyone else ignores
• Kinji Hamakida has the best strategic mind in the class and uses it exclusively to find the optimal napping location

Rivalries — Ando Iorai and Toragi Kayo both think they're the most dangerous person in the room. They are not. The most dangerous person in the room is usually Chozen Tadachi, who is currently staring at a wall.

Friendships — Kibi Kankei and Isokono Yoromu have an unspoken alliance based on being the most laid-back people in a class full of very intense personalities. Yoshibara Hiyoko's chaotic energy pairs oddly well with Nomi Igisa's quietness — they are somehow best friends.

background.heading: Running This Season
background.body:
Class 1-A — Season 1 is written for milestone leveling, not tracked XP: the class starts Season 1 at Level 1 and reaches Level 3 by the end of Chapter 1, then Level 6 by the end of Chapter 2 — the milestone moment is called out at the close of each chapter below. Don't award levels encounter-by-encounter; these are big, ensemble scenes and the pacing is built around chapter breaks, not individual fights.

This campaign assumes a full-ensemble table: most or all twenty named Class 1-A students exist in the fiction, with a handful of players each controlling one PC and the DM running the rest as a live, reactive cast — that's how every chapter's beats are written, named students doing named things whether or not a player happens to be behind them that session. If your table is smaller, let players double up on secondary students in scenes their own PC isn't central to, rather than trimming the roster down. The ensemble texture — Masahata's chart, the 1-A/1-B rivalry, twenty specific people finding out what they're like under pressure — is a deliberate feature of this campaign, not incidental color.

For combat-adjacent encounters (the Entrance Exam's drone boss, the Agency Visit's Ruin Grunts, Convergence's three-way mess), scale enemy count and HP to your actual number of seated players rather than to the fictional headcount of the class — a scene can be narratively full of twenty students in chaos while remaining mechanically sized for four to six PCs at the table.

background.heading: The Season's Throughline
background.body:
Ruin has run Kurogane Wharf for years, comfortably, because nobody with real power has ever needed to look at it closely. Six named members, no departments, and at the top of it a name — Undertow — that the Hero Commission's own dossier can't confirm as more than a rumor repeated by street-level operatives too scared to be specific. That absence of a face is the engine of this whole season: everyone the class meets who works for Ruin is competent, specific, and only loosely coordinated with everyone else who works for Ruin, because Undertow runs it the way water finds the shape of a container — pressure, not structure.

Kuma is the visible edge: loud, physical, a logistics problem the class can actually solve, and by design the season's one clean win. Splice is the quieter problem underneath him — Ruin's research arm, working for a separate interior party (Null) who wants combat and quirk-activation data more than she wants territory, and who has been collecting exactly that data on Class 1-A since the entrance exam's unmarked drone. Neither Kuma nor Splice is working toward the same goal, and neither is fully aware how little the other knows — which is itself the shape of how Undertow prefers to run things.

Fracture is not Ruin, and that distinction matters more than anything else in this season's back half. Shard's grievance is real, and when she makes her case to the class directly in The Fracture Problem, at least two of her specific points should land without a clean rebuttal available. What she doesn't know — and what the class shouldn't be handed outright either — is that a meaningful share of Fracture's operating money traces back to Ruin, laundered clean enough that even Shard's own leadership hasn't connected it. Ruin funds the exact movement that gives it moral cover and political noise to hide inside, and Fracture has no idea it's being used this way. Convergence is the one night all three threads occupy the same physical space — Kuma's operation, Null's extraction, Fracture's own sabotage crew — with no coordination between any of them, which is exactly why it goes as chaotically as it does.

Undertow's single appearance, at the very end of Convergence, is not a fight and was never supposed to be. He is a shape that stands up out of standing water, watches the class for exactly as long as it takes to form an opinion, says four words, and leaves through a drain. Season 1 should end with the class certain they can handle Ruin's people, and considerably less certain what to do about the man running it — or the movement quietly bankrolling itself off his money without knowing it. That uncertainty is the real cliffhanger, not a bigger fight waiting next season.

background.heading: Overview
background.body:
Class 1-A — Season 1 unfolds across two chapters.

In Chapter 1, "Welcome to U.A.," the class survives the entrance exam, moves into Heights Alliance, and takes its first low-stakes field assignment at Patchwork Agency in Kurogane Wharf — where Ruin stops being a name on the news and becomes something they've stood next to. Fracture is present only as texture here: graffiti, a leaflet, a symbol scratched in concrete, never yet a name attached.

In Chapter 2, "Getting Good," the Sports Festival gives the whole class — and the 1-A/1-B rivalry — its first real public stage, before The Fracture Problem forces a harder, less winnable conversation about who the licensing system actually serves. The season closes with Convergence: Ruin's own operation, one of Null's extraction teams, and a Fracture sabotage crew colliding in the same Kurogane Wharf warehouse on the same night, followed by the season's only direct look at Undertow himself — watching, unbothered, gone before anyone can follow.

background.heading: Adventure Hooks
background.body:
Not every table runs Class 1-A — Season 1 with the same students in the spotlight every session. Roll a d8 (or just pick) whenever you want to hand a personal thread to whichever student a player is running that night — new to the table, returning after time away, or simply due for a spotlight beat.

• 1 — Family in Kurogane Wharf. Someone in your family still lives or works near the Wharf. You've told nobody at U.A. this. You notice things there other students don't.
• 2 — You were at the Agency Visit and clocked Splice yourself. You never mentioned it out loud, and you've been quietly watching for the same slim tablet since.
• 3 — Masahata's ranking chart bothers you more than you'll admit. You have a specific, private opinion about where you belong on it, and this arc is a chance to prove it wrong.
• 4 — You've seen the Fracture symbol before U.A. — somewhere in your own neighborhood, years ago, long before it had a name. You've never told anyone.
• 5 — Oshiro pulled you aside once, briefly, and said something that's stuck with you since — vague enough to mean several things, specific enough that you've never forgotten the exact words.
• 6 — You have a sibling, cousin, or childhood friend on a provisional license track at a different school, and you compare notes. They've mentioned hearing the name "Undertow" somewhere you haven't.
• 7 — Something about a classmate's quirk — Kinji's Neutralization, Chozen's Stress, or another — quietly unsettles you, for a personal reason you haven't examined closely. This arc is going to make you examine it.
• 8 — You genuinely believe the ranking chart, the Sports Festival, all of it, is the whole point of being here — being seen, being ranked, being chosen. Convergence is going to complicate that belief badly.

chapters.title: Welcome to U.A.
chapters.intro: Almost entirely fun. This is orientation. The class is meeting each other, figuring out who they are, discovering the school is hard and also ridiculous. Everyone in Tokyo knows the name Ruin — a small, dangerous villain group that's been running Kurogane Wharf for years. Fracture, the anti-licensing movement getting louder across the city, is a completely separate thing — though nobody knows that yet. None of it has touched the class directly, and Undertow himself is still just a name on a rumor. Three sessions of pure orientation and social chaos (Entrance Exam, Dorm Life, first combat class) before the class ever leaves campus, then one low-stakes field trip that quietly puts a face on the villain group everyone's been half-ignoring. Nobody graduates this chapter with a rival, a nemesis, or a wound. They graduate it with roommates, a ranking chart nobody asked for, and a first-hand sense that Kurogane Wharf is a real place with a real problem, not just a line on the evening news.
chapters.dmNote: U.A.'s campus in Tier 1 still feels new — hallways nobody has memorized yet, a dorm kitchen nobody's claimed territory in. The class is twenty strangers figuring out who's actually dangerous and who just looks it. Ruin exists at the edge of things: a name on a news ticker, something Fujisaki mentions and moves past, graffiti near Kurogane Wharf nobody in the class has been to yet. Nobody says the word "Undertow" — it hasn't been said yet, by anyone. When things go wrong here, they go wrong the way a bad dorm fire drill goes wrong: loud, red-faced, survivable. Chozen's Stress spiking during the entrance exam isn't a crisis, it's the first time his classmates see him flinch. Toshida cratering a wall mid-panic gets him a look from Fujisaki, not a lecture. This tier is twenty specific people finding out what they're actually like under pressure. Play tempo matters more than difficulty here — nothing in this chapter should feel like it's testing the party's build, because it isn't; it's testing whether the table can hold twenty personalities in their head at once without losing track of who's who. Lean on running gags (the doorframe, the ranking chart, Kinji's naps) early and often — they're doing the actual work of making the ensemble legible, and every one you plant here pays off bigger later when it resurfaces changed. If a session is dragging, cut toward the next named beat rather than resolving the current one fully; this tier forgives jump-cuts more than any other in the season.

sections.heading: The Entrance Exam
sections.readAloud: A staged disaster scenario in a simulated city block. Students must rescue civilians (actors and prop mannequins) while combat drones provide the villain opposition. No predetermined groupings — everyone is on their own. This is how the class meets each other. Smoke machines, a collapsed pedestrian bridge, and sirens looping on a ten-second delay — none of it is real, and every single person here is about to forget that within about ninety seconds.
sections.body:
• Opening chaos: the exam starts without warning — no countdown, no announcement. Students scatter and self-organise in real time. Ren is simply gone mid-sprint; nobody sees him move.
• Key moments: Toshida shouts a word and levels a wall segment. Nakaya jump-starts a stalled bus's dead battery with a controlled arc to use it as a ramp, then can't get the engine to switch off. Chozen's Stress activates on its own in round one — it doesn't need his permission, and the noise and chaos are enough to trigger a small, unwanted spike before he's decided to fight anything.
• Conflict point: Masahata loudly critiques everyone else's technique mid-exam. He's correct about roughly half of it, which makes it worse.
• Quiet efficiency: Samitsu splits his extra arms without seeming to think about it — one hauling a mannequin clear, one bracing rubble, one flagging down a second victim — and doesn't appear to notice he's doing three things at once until Oshiro's scoring notes flag it afterward.
• Overcorrection: Ichitaka projects a full-scale hologram of himself sprinting toward the drone as a decoy — technically brilliant, and he explains the targeting logic to a bystander mid-exam like it's obvious, which it is, to him.
• Full commitment: Tazato shifts into partial dragon form the moment the first mannequin goes down and doesn't shift back until the exam ends, working through it with the flat, focused calm of someone finally doing something that makes sense to her.
• Drone boss: the final obstacle is a single large combat drone targeting the highest-scoring candidates — it retargets each round toward whoever just did the most visible thing, which punishes showing off and rewards working the crowd instead of the enemy. Students have to cooperate — or use each other as distractions — to bring it down. Setaka's Iron Ball dents its housing without slowing it down at all, which he finds instructive rather than frustrating.
• Resolution: the class passes collectively — nobody is cut, nobody fails alone. Score rankings post that evening. Masahata reads them twice, out loud, to an audience of nobody. The ranking chart era begins before anyone's even unpacked.
• Fujisaki's only announcement, over a crackling PA thirty seconds after the first drone activates: 'No, I'm not going to repeat that.' Nobody asked her to repeat anything. She says it anyway, to nobody in particular, and it becomes the first line anyone quotes back at each other in the dorms that night.
sections.dmNote: The exam starts with no warning and no plan — drones hatch, a wall comes down, civilian actors start shouting, and twenty strangers have to decide in real time whether to work together or not. Oshiro is quietly grading the cooperation instinct. What the table actually gets is better: who reaches for the wall Toshida just leveled, who's already gone before anyone registers Ren moved, whose first instinct under real pressure surprises even them. Run this loose and fast — cut between vignettes rather than resolving one student's beat fully before starting another, the way the exam itself would actually feel from the observation deck. If a player's PC isn't the center of a given beat, that's fine; hand them an NPC classmate's action to narrate instead of skipping it, since half the value of this scene is watching who the class turns out to be before anyone's had a chance to perform it. The drone boss should feel winnable but not tidy — let at least one 'good' plan go sideways (Setaka's Iron Ball doing nothing to the housing is a good place for that) so the eventual win reads as earned improvisation, not a fight the exam handed them.

aside.label: Villain Threads
aside.body:
Fracture — Graffiti on the arena's exterior wall during student arrival: 'HEROES SERVE COMMISSIONS, NOT COMMUNITIES' in the jagged-line Fracture style. Weathered enough to have been there for weeks. Nobody on the exam staff comments on it. A student who lingers on it — no check needed, just idle curiosity — notices it's already been touched up once: a thin, mismatched line of fresh paint over an older, cruder version of the same slogan. Fracture didn't just tag this wall once.

Null Signal — A compact black drone with no UA markings logged the exam from the upper observation tier. The exam team assumed it was another faculty member's equipment. It was not in the manifest. No footage was flagged. Cross-referenced against Hamagawa's file header later in Tier 1, the drone's last transmission timestamp lines up almost exactly with when the exam's official footage review would have started — whoever was watching wanted the same data the exam staff were about to generate anyway.

The Chain — Absent from direct play. A single offhand comment from an agency worker at the venue gates: 'Avoid Kurogane Wharf after dark this week. Ruin's been busy lately.' Said the way you'd mention traffic. Nobody asks a follow-up question. If a player does ask one anyway, the worker doesn't really have an answer — she just shrugs and says everyone says that this time of year, which is true, and also not actually a response. It's the kind of comment that means nothing until it means everything — she won't remember saying it by the time anyone thinks to ask her again.

sections.developments: If the class works the drone boss as a coordinated problem rather than a scramble, note it — this is the first real data point for who instinctively defers to whom under pressure, and it colors how Masahata's ranking chart gets read later. If several students go down before the drone is handled, that's fine too; Recovery Girl handles injuries offscreen and nobody's provisional status is at risk from a rough first day. Either way, the class passes collectively — individual placement only matters socially, not mechanically. Watch specifically for who ends up giving orders without being asked and who ends up taking them without resenting it — that pairing tends to recur all season, usually without either student noticing they've fallen into it again. If a player tries to negotiate with or talk down the drone rather than fight it, let that fail cleanly and quickly — it's a machine, not a villain, and the exam is testing rescue instinct, not diplomacy. Redirect the attempt toward a civilian who does respond to being talked to.
sections.treasure: No physical loot from an exam, but real: provisional standing at U.A., a bunk in Heights Alliance, and the first entry on Masahata's ranking chart — which several students will spend the rest of the season pretending not to care about. One more thing nobody notices as treasure yet: whichever PC clears the entrance exam most quietly — no big moment, no ranking-chart glory — is the one Oshiro's private notes flag as 'worth watching.' He doesn't say so. He just remembers the name.

sections.heading: Dorm Life & Combat Training
sections.tag: Social arc + first formal training encounter · 2 sessions
sections.readAloud: The class moves into Heights Alliance. First week is pure character chaos — personalities collide, routines form, the common room becomes a social ecosystem. Oshiro's opening combat class (Capture the Flag) runs in the second session: two teams, live stakes, no mercy. Twenty teenagers, one kitchen, and a laundry rotation nobody agreed to but somehow everybody's already following by day three.
sections.body:
• The doorframe incident (Toshida, day one): a word escapes him mid-yawn. A panel falls out of the doorframe. He apologises and fixes it. The panel falls again the next morning. He has quietly named the doorframe Hiroshi and considers this an ongoing rivalry.
• The charger incident (Nakaya, day two): she jump-starts Masahata's dead phone charger with a small controlled arc, purely as a favor. It works, technically. It also fuses the charging port shut permanently at roughly double voltage. She considers this an unambiguous success.
• Kitchen diplomacy: Samitsu is discovered, by accident, to be an extraordinary cook — he was just making dinner for himself and got cornered into feeding six people, then twelve. His extra arms multitask without him directing them; he doesn't notice he's stirring, plating, and washing up simultaneously until Isokono points it out and he looks faintly betrayed by his own hands.
• Unsolicited art: Ichitaka's evening habit of projecting small, pointless holograms — a bird, a slow-turning flame, once an entire miniature thunderstorm over the kitchen table — starts as background noise and becomes something people watch for without saying so.
• Efficient kindness: Tazato does the whole floor's dishes on a night she's not on rotation, frames it as "this is faster than watching you all do it badly," and leaves before anyone can thank her properly.
• Correspondence: Setaka starts leaving handwritten thank-you notes under doors after ordinary interactions — helping carry something, a good conversation, a solid training rep. By the end of the tier, most of the class has at least one taped inside a desk drawer they won't admit to keeping.
• Masahata prints and laminates a ranking chart based on exam scores. It appears on the fridge, fully formatted with tier brackets. No one asked him to do this. Kinji stares at it for a long time and says nothing.
• Capture the Flag — Oshiro's opening combat class: team assignments calibrated for discomfort, not balance. Yoshibara immediately doubles herself — Oshiro rules it legal because he didn't say it wasn't. Kinji predicted this exact outcome days ago, told no one, purely to test a hypothesis about whether anyone would believe her if she had. Ando loses to someone he was certain he'd beat and wears his sunglasses for the next 36 hours including during sleep. Samitsu single-handedly holds a chokepoint with a wall of arms until Aikawa gets close enough to work under his reach — the two of them end up trading a grudging, genuine respect neither expected. Ichitaka's hologram of the flag itself sends the opposing team sprinting the wrong way for a full minute; Setaka, on the receiving end of the trick, formally acknowledges it was "well played" before Oshiro's even called the round, then tags Ichitaka out anyway. Kibi treats the whole exercise like a very slow, very patient chess match and is visibly unbothered regardless of the outcome.
• Masahata updates the ranking chart to include 'combat performance (preliminary).' No methodology is explained. It is accurate.
• Cafeteria crossover: Class 1-B eats on the same schedule. First real contact is small and unremarkable — a shared table because the room is full, Matsunami's class visibly running a tighter ship than Oshiro's. No rivalry yet, just the first time 1-A registers there's another class exactly like them, a hallway away. Isokono ends up seated across from a 1-B student she's never spoken to and near-cries at a small unprompted kindness — a napkin passed before she asked for one — which the 1-B student clearly does not know what to do with.
• Oshiro's full debrief after Capture the Flag is five words: 'Some of you can lead.' He doesn't say who. Everyone spends the walk back trying to work out if it was them.
sections.dmNote: This is the class figuring out who's who once the exam adrenaline wears off — burnt rice, a short-circuited toaster nobody will own up to, Masahata's ranking chart appearing on the fridge unasked. Capture the Flag turns that same energy competitive: Oshiro splits teams so nobody fights their obvious counter, and the matchups are where rivalries stop being vibes and start being specific grudges. Nothing here is dangerous. It's just the first time the class looks like a class. Treat this section as a montage you can dip in and out of rather than a scene that has to play out in real time — pick two or three of the beats above per session based on which PCs are actually at the table, and let the rest happen 'offscreen' as things players hear about secondhand. Capture the Flag is the one part worth running in full; it's the tier's only real combat rep before the Agency Visit, and the specific pairings matter more than the final score.

aside.label: Villain Threads
aside.body:
Fracture — A leaflet appears under a dorm door on day three. Black print, spare design, jagged-line symbol. 'Your quirk is yours — not your license.' Someone pushed it through. Nobody saw who. The one handwritten margin note on it — 'ask better questions' — doesn't match any known Fracture printer output on file with the Commission. Someone personalized this particular delivery.

Null Signal — If any student explores Hamagawa's open-door office in the evening, a monitor in standby shows a file header before the screensaver kicks in: 'Provisional License Cohort Data — External Access Request, Ref: SA/7-91.' Requesting party: 'Seika Advanced Systems.' The file is already closed when they look. Hamagawa, if asked directly what it was, says 'paperwork' without looking up — which is either completely true or a very good lie, and he genuinely can't tell which himself. The reference code — SA/7-91 — belongs to the requesting organization, 'Seika Advanced Systems,' whose consulting arm will introduce itself in person at Patchwork Agency, under a slightly different name, in the very next arc.

The Chain — The common room TV runs news in the background one evening. Kurogane Wharf. A small support agency for unlicensed quirk users has closed 'due to changing neighbourhood conditions.' The report is twelve seconds long. The agency's name, if a player pauses the moment or asks the DM to repeat it: Ebisu Mutual Aid. It won't come up again by name for a long time. Worth writing down anyway.

sections.developments: Capture the Flag's final score matters less than who it reveals: track which pairings surprised each other, since Oshiro deliberately built the bracket to manufacture exactly those data points. Whatever the result, this is the session where the class stops being twenty strangers and starts being readable to each other — and to you, as the DM. Samitsu and Aikawa's grudging respect and Ichitaka and Setaka's trick-then-tag-anyway exchange are both worth carrying forward as small, recurring background beats — neither needs to become a plot thread, but both read as real if you let them resurface once or twice more before the season ends. If a table's session runs short, the cafeteria crossover is the safest single beat to cut entirely — nothing forward-facing depends on it happening this tier, and the 1-A/1-B rivalry gets a harder, better-earned start at the Sports Festival regardless.
sections.treasure: A dorm room in Heights Alliance, a place at the common-room table, and — for whoever loses most memorably in Capture the Flag — a nickname that will not go away. Also, quietly, for exactly one person: the first slice of something Samitsu actually put effort into, which is how you find out you've been accepted. And, easy to miss: the same evening the common-room TV runs that story is the same night Nakaya's charger incident happens. Nobody in the room connects a closing charity office to a fused phone port. There's no reason they should — yet.

sections.heading: The Agency Visit
sections.tag: Low-stakes mission / villain seed convergence · 1–2 sessions
sections.readAloud: The class assists at Patchwork Agency in Kurogane Wharf for a day. Filing, crowd management at a public event, basic patrol. Their first taste of actual hero work. Mostly administrative and slightly boring. A minor incident near the end brings the class's first real Ruin encounter — and if students are paying attention, a Ruin researcher and a Fracture marker are also present in the margins. Nothing about the morning suggests any of that is coming.
sections.body:
• Arrival: the agency is underwhelmed by having twenty students in their breakroom simultaneously. They did not fully plan for this.
• Aikawa organises an entire filing system the agency didn't ask for. It is objectively better than what they had. They are mildly resentful.
• Tazato is put on physical setup — barricades, tables, heavy lifting — and is unmistakably the happiest anyone's seen her all week. Efficiency, it turns out, extends to enjoying being useful.
• Setaka introduces himself, by name, individually, to every member of staff at the agency, including the two who are clearly too busy to care. Both remember his name by the end of the day anyway.
• Crowd management at a small community event. Toshida is stationed away from the speakers. This is communicated very clearly. He is stationed near the speakers anyway due to a logistical mix-up.
• The incident: two Ruin Grunts and a Ruin Hardskin are intimidating a shopkeeper in a side street. The class has six seconds before Patchwork arrives. Decision point: wait or intervene. Both choices are defensible. The Hardskin's fear when contained — not of the students, but of being seen by them — is the most important data in the encounter. If Nomi is present and even mildly stressed, loose objects in the alley — a trash can lid, a dropped crate — drift half an inch off the ground without her meaning it to happen; she doesn't notice, but the Hardskin does, and it rattles him more than the actual heroes do.
• Patchwork's debrief: direct, accurate, slightly alarming. She's been watching since they arrived. 'The quiet one — that's not local. You walked into someone's business trip.' She won't say more today. She makes a quiet call after they leave. She also, separately and much more warmly, tells Samitsu the agency's coffee situation has 'measurably improved' since he reorganized the break room, which is the nicest thing anyone at Patchwork says all day.
• A junior agency staffer, overwhelmed, mutters 'I went into filing to get away from this' within earshot of at least one PC, then looks mortified at having said it out loud in front of a student.
sections.dmNote: First time outside the walls without exam conditions telling them what's safe. Patchwork treats the actual villain encounter like a Tuesday; the students don't. Ruin stops being a name on a news ticker and becomes a tag on a warehouse door, a delivery schedule that doesn't add up, a face Hardskin won't explain. Fracture's presence is in the same neighborhood at the same time — a flyer, a chant two streets over — and nothing connects the two out loud. A player who's paying attention notices. Nobody points it out for them. Keep the actual fight short — two Grunts and a Hardskin should not seriously threaten a class this size, and the point isn't difficulty, it's tone. The value of the encounter is entirely in the six seconds of hesitation beforehand and Patchwork's flat, unbothered read of it afterward; don't let mechanics crowd out either of those beats.

aside.label: Villain Threads
aside.body:
The Chain — The Hardskin has a chain-link tattoo visible on DC 15 Perception during the fight, DC 12 on a subdued target. His fear of being identified is disproportionate for a low-level criminal caught by student heroes. That gap is the important data. Patchwork says 'affiliated' once and doesn't elaborate. She later confirms, off the record, that she's seen the same tattoo twice before this year — always on someone who talked less than they should have, given how much trouble they were already in.

Null Signal — Ryo Karashi ('Splice') appears in a corridor inside Patchwork Agency. Visitor badge: 'Seika Consulting — Dr. R. Karashi.' Slim tablet, unhurried, claims wrong floor. If stopped: warm, apologetic, gives nothing away. The tablet, if glimpsed, shows a student photo grid — the class's entrance exam publicity shots. He is gone in thirty seconds. If Ichitaka is the one who clocks him, he recognizes the tablet's interface as bespoke rather than off-the-shelf within about two seconds — the kind of detail nobody asked him to notice and he can't stop noticing anyway. The corridor he claims to have gotten lost in only actually connects two departments: intake processing and the agency's server closet. There's no version of 'wrong floor' that honestly explains both.

Fracture — The Fracture jagged-line symbol is scratched into the concrete of the alley wall behind where the Ruin Hardskin was standing. Old enough to be weathered — months, not weeks. Not a message placed for today. A marker. Someone was using this alley before Ruin was. It's carved at exactly adult eye-level, deliberately, not sprayed hastily at a run. Whoever left it wanted it found by someone specific, not by everyone.

sections.developments: If the class intervenes against the Ruin Grunts and Hardskin immediately, the confrontation resolves faster, with more direct (if brief) villain contact and less time for Splice to linger unnoticed. If they wait for Patchwork, the fight is safer but the Hardskin has more time to consider running, and Patchwork has to explain afterward why she let it develop that far. Either choice is correct and should be validated, not graded. Either way, log whether anyone clocked Splice — it doesn't need to matter yet, but it's worth knowing which PCs already have a face to half-remember when he resurfaces in The Fracture Problem. If nobody clears the DC 18 to spot Splice and nobody clears the DC 15/12 on the Hardskin's tattoo, that's fine — none of tonight's threads require the class to have caught them. Patchwork's line about 'someone's business trip' still lands as the session's one ominous note regardless of what else got noticed.
sections.treasure: Patchwork's private contact number ('for real questions, not homework'), a Kurogane Wharf incident report with the class's name properly logged, and — quietly, unseen by the players until it matters — a line in Ruin's own internal notes confirming Class 1-A now exists on their radar. And, for whoever spent the day on unglamorous setup and paperwork instead of the fight: a specific, sincere thank-you from agency staff who clearly weren't expecting it — the kind of praise that doesn't show up on Masahata's chart and matters more than the kind that does. Quietly filed and easy to forget: Patchwork logs the exact time Splice was seen, cross-referenced against the Hardskin incident sixty feet away. She doesn't say what she thinks the proximity means. She writes it down anyway.

closing.label: Villain Presence — Chapter 1
closing.body: Ruin is background texture in Tier 1. Its street-level side is the most visible — one direct encounter with low-tier operatives, planted through a pro hero's offhand comment. Its research side is glimpsed twice: the unmarked exam drone, Splice's thirty-second corridor appearance. Fracture — a separate movement — is found rather than encountered: graffiti, a leaflet, a symbol scratched in concrete. Nobody from Ruin has spoken to the class directly yet, and Undertow himself hasn't shown his face to anyone — that starts in Tier 2. Nobody in the class could pick Undertow's name out of a lineup of one. That's correct, and it should stay true right up until Convergence — Chapter 1's job is to make Ruin feel local and almost manageable, precisely so the scale of what's actually running it lands as a surprise later, not an inevitability telegraphed too early.

chapters.milestone: Completing Chapter 1 is a story milestone — the class reaches Level 3.

chapters.title: Getting Good
chapters.intro: The Sports Festival is peak chaos and excitement — the class gets to show off and it is almost entirely fun. Then the world gets complicated: Fracture becomes a real moral problem the class can't punch away, and the Convergence finale puts Kuma's logistics run, one of Null's extraction teams, and a Fracture sabotage crew in the same Kurogane Wharf warehouse on the same night — Ruin's own people not coordinating with each other, and Fracture not coordinating with anyone but themselves. Season 1 ends with a win that doesn't feel entirely clean, and Undertow walking out of a fight he was never really in. Three sessions of unambiguous triumph (the Festival) buy exactly enough goodwill for two sessions of real discomfort (The Fracture Problem) before the finale spends all of it at once. Pace this chapter as a rising line, not three equal beats — by the time Convergence starts, the table should feel like they've earned a clean win and are about to not quite get one.
chapters.dmNote: Three arcs, three different colors. The Sports Festival is stadium lights and a live crowd — every match in the bracket below is written as a specific rivalry, not a stat comparison. The Fracture Problem puts Shard in front of the class with real, uncomfortable arguments about the licensing system — she believes every word of it, and has no idea that a chunk of Fracture's funding traces back to Ruin, the group she insists has nothing to do with her movement. Convergence is Ruin's own operation and Fracture's sabotage crew colliding in the same warehouse on the same night, neither side expecting the other. Kuma is the fight the class can't talk their way out of. Splice is the wrinkle nobody predicted. Undertow is a shape in a doorway as everyone else is still catching their breath — seen, not caught. The class walks out having won the room. Season 2 is what happens when they go looking for the man who wasn't in it. If you're running this over multiple months of real time, use the Sports Festival to reset energy after The Fracture Problem's discomfort — but resist smoothing Shard's arguments out of memory once the finale arrives; Convergence works best when at least one player is still visibly unsettled by something she said. Undertow should get less table-clock time than any other named figure in this chapter and more narrative weight than all of them combined — write his one scene tight, rehearse the line if you have to, and don't let a player's action economy turn it into combat.

sections.heading: The Sports Festival
sections.readAloud: U.A.'s annual Sports Festival. Public, broadcast, massive audience. Full tournament structure: obstacle race → cavalry battle → individual brackets with Class 1-B competing alongside Class 1-A. The 1-A vs 1-B rivalry becomes concrete here for the first time. Every seat is full. Somewhere in the stands, a scout from an agency none of them have heard of yet is watching very specifically for one name.
sections.body:
Pre-festival: the class arrives to a stadium already full. Kazama is recognised from the entrance exam footage and loses his composure for about four seconds — long enough for someone to notice his ears go red before the mirror-bright hardening kicks in and hides it. Ichitaka has already mapped the bracket's likely paths on a borrowed tablet and is visibly annoyed nobody asked him to share it.
Obstacle race: Ren places first overall; nobody saw him pass anyone, he was just suddenly at the front. Setaka's iron cannon-balls ricochet through a bottleneck and eliminate four competitors at once, and he apologises to each of them individually afterward. Kinji places top five in a near-sleep state for most of the course. Yamaru Todao (1-B) places third — the class's first look at him in a competitive context. Samitsu clears the rope-bridge section by forming a wall of arms and simply climbing across sideways, which nobody anticipated and several judges have to rule on live. Tazato finishes mid-pack in human form and looks faintly disgusted with herself about it — she's saving her actual advantage for the parts of the tournament that matter.
Cavalry battle: alliances form and collapse. Class 1-B's coordination is visibly drilled and slightly alarming to watch. Yoshibara doubles the wrong person at the wrong moment — an opponent already in the lead. This becomes a permanent campaign reference. Kibi's team wins its bracket almost entirely on patience, letting two more aggressive teams wear each other down before moving in during the last thirty seconds — a strategy Kinji apparently also predicted, unprompted, days in advance. Ichitaka's decoy hologram of an entire second headband prompts a brief booth review over whether holographic decoys count as unsportsmanlike deception; officials rule it legitimate quirk use within about ninety seconds, and he treats the delay as a personal insult.
Broadcast: the commentary team is unprepared for half the quirks on display. One commentator, live, about ninety minutes in: 'I want to stress that I have a script, and none of you are following it.' 'What Is She Doing?' about Kinji trends nationally within twenty minutes. Masahata's ongoing scoring commentary in the waiting room is caught on a spectator's phone and briefly goes viral. The booth review over Ichitaka's decoy gets its own five-minute segment, with a graphics package.
Post-festival: the ranking chart, brought to the festival laminated, doesn't get updated for four days. When asked why: 'The model is broken.' He reprints it anyway.

TOURNAMENT SHAPE — obstacle race → cavalry battle (teams of 4) → 16-competitor single-elimination bracket, mixed 1-A/1-B:
  Seed 1: Ren Suzuki (1-A) — 1st in the obstacle race. The class has been watching him move. Nobody knows what his speed looks like in a direct fight yet — or what Overclock's real cost is, since the bracket hasn't made him pay it yet.
  Seed 2: Yamaru Todao (1-B) — 3rd in the obstacle race. Quiet about being on the fridge chart. Thinking about it too.
  Seed 3: Chozen Tadachi (1-A) — Placed well across both events despite Stress not being a movement quirk — his obstacle finish was pure discipline.
  Seed 4: Kagamo Akake (1-B) — Palm Cannon blasts felt across the arena in the cavalry battle. She was in a different quadrant entirely.

THE FINAL — Toragi Kayo (1-A) vs Chozen Tadachi (1-A). Favored: Toragi — technically superior, has beaten 1-B's seed 2, has a plan for Chozen's escalation curve.
Toragi's plan: end it before he escalates. She lands the cleanest technical strike of the tournament in the opening exchange. It is the worst decision she could have made — Chozen has already fought two escalating rounds today, his damage percentage already elevated before this fight even started, and her perfect hit just adds directly to a total that was never at zero. The fight drags to round 5. Nobody predicted round 5. It ends when his accumulated total exceeds anything her technique can counter.
Winner: Chozen Tadachi. Toragi's plan is visibly correct until the moment the math changes on her. Chozen's win should feel too big for the arena — overwhelming, not triumphant. Give him the quiet moment coming down while the crowd is still loud. Somewhere in the stands, the scout mentioned above writes down exactly one name, and it isn't Toragi's.

Full round-by-round bracket (every match, alternate outcomes, and downstream effects) is written out in the Campaign Overview page — run it live from there.
sections.dmNote: Stadium lights, a real crowd, Masahata's chart getting updated in real time from the stands. Every match in the bracket below is written as two specific people, not two quirks — Yamaru absorbing four clean Impacts from Toragi before he finally goes down, because his whole Quirk is refusing to register how much that should have hurt, Chozen's win feeling too big for the arena because it's damage he can't undo, not a triumphant finish. Play PC fights out in full. NPC fights get one paragraph, read aloud, and then the class's reaction to what they just watched. The obstacle race and cavalry battle are ensemble set pieces — resist the urge to resolve them purely by dice, and instead let two or three named beats per event (drawn from the roster, not just the PCs) stand in for the whole field. The goal is a stadium that feels like it has twenty specific competitors in it, even though you're only narrating six or seven of them in any detail.

aside.label: Villain Threads
aside.body: All Factions — Ruin is watching the Sports Festival broadcast like the rest of Tokyo. Null is collecting comprehensive quirk activation data — better footage than the exam drone captured. Fracture, completely separately, is watching because the festival represents exactly the system they oppose: licensed quirk use as public spectacle. Undertow watches Chozen's final with specific interest — the only person in Tokyo tracking both angles at once. None of this is visible to the class. Splice, watching remotely through the broadcast feed rather than in person, flags three PCs specifically in his notes as 'above baseline' — which three depends entirely on what actually happened at your table. Kuma, separately and for entirely unrelated reasons, is annoyed by the broadcast — his logistics run through Kurogane Wharf that week gets rescheduled twice because half the neighborhood is watching the Festival on break instead of working. He complains about this to nobody who matters.

sections.developments: The full bracket (see the Campaign Overview page) already branches every match with an alternate outcome designed to reroute cleanly into later seeding — use those. The one developmental thread worth tracking regardless of who wins what: how the class reacts to a 1-B upset (Yamaru advancing) versus a clean 1-A sweep. That reaction carries into the rivalry going forward more than the bracket result itself does. The unnamed-student beats above (Samitsu's bridge climb, Kibi's patience play, Ichitaka's booth-review moment) are all safe to cut if the session's running long — none of them feed forward mechanically. Keep them only as much as they're fun in the room. If a PC ends up seeded into the final instead of Toragi or Chozen, keep Chozen's escalation-curve mechanic as the deciding factor either way — Toragi's over-efficient opening exchange is what loses her the fight, not a scripted result, so swap her out for whichever seed actually lands there and let the same dynamic play out honestly.
sections.treasure: Tournament placement (broadcast nationally), a small stipend for top performers, and the single most valuable thing on offer: public visibility. Whatever a PC's placement, professional agencies now know their name — this is what unlocks meaningful internship offers later in the season and beyond. For the students who didn't advance far — which will be most of them — there's a quieter reward worth naming out loud: for the first time, the class watched each other perform under real public pressure, and several private assumptions about who's 'actually' strong get revised that afternoon, chart or no chart. One placement nobody puts on the chart: whichever PC the scout in the stands wrote down gets a plain, unbranded letter at the dorm within the week — no agency name, no logo, just a request to 'keep in touch.' It's real. It's also not explained this season.

sections.heading: The Fracture Problem
sections.readAloud: Fracture stages a large public protest outside a Hero Commission building in Shibuya. Unlicensed quirk users are demanding licensing reform, backed by Fracture cells providing protection. When the protest tips into a confrontation with Commission security, Class 1-A is deployed for crowd management. They meet Shard and Voltage directly. The situation is complicated by the fact that some protesters have genuine grievances, Fracture is genuinely protecting people in this moment, and a Ruin operative is photographing quirk activation patterns from the crowd periphery. Nobody briefed the class on how to feel about any of this, because Oshiro doesn't have a clean answer either.
sections.body:
• Arrival: the protest is peaceful, large, and legally ambiguous. Fracture's jagged-line symbol is everywhere. The students have seen it before — exam graffiti, dorm leaflet, alley concrete. It lands differently at scale.
• Setaka reads the crowd formally, the way he reads everything — he greets the protest marshals by introducing himself and asking, directly, what they need from the class today. It's the single most disarming thing anyone in a uniform does all afternoon.
• Shard approaches the class directly, no aggression. She wants to debate. Her points are specific: the licensing system disadvantages people in communities like Kurogane Wharf. The Commission the class works for actively suppressed investigation into Ruin. Heroes who could have stopped the Wharf problem chose not to. 'I'm not asking you to agree with me. I'm asking you to explain why I'm wrong.' Give her at least two points that land with the players.
• Tazato, stationed near the barricade line, mutters that Shard's point about provisional heroes being treated as disposable is 'not wrong' — loud enough for the PC nearest her to hear, quiet enough that it isn't a scene. She doesn't repeat it.
• The escalation: Commission security physically moves an elderly protester who wasn't causing problems. Voltage intervenes — a burst of Blackout kills the charge in the guard's control baton before it activates, and he positions himself between the guard and the protester. This is a hero move performed by a villain. The class has to decide how to respond.
• Ruin in the margins: Splice is in the crowd, two rows back from the Commission building's west entrance. He's photographing the class — specifically their quirk activation patterns under stress. DC 18 Perception to notice him. If noticed, he's gone by the time anyone looks twice. If Ichitaka is present and within thirty feet of his position, there's a real chance (DC 15 for him specifically) he clocks the tablet's interface a second time and finally places where he's seen it before — Hamagawa's monitor, back in Tier 1.
• Resolution: Shard withdraws the Fracture cells before things become unmanageable. She does not run. She says: 'We'll be back when you've figured out which side you're on.' Voltage leaves last, making sure the elderly protester is clear before he goes. Setaka, unprompted, thanks Shard for 'speaking honestly' as she withdraws. She doesn't quite know what to do with that either.
• A Commission security officer, quietly, to the PC nearest him after Voltage's intervention: 'Off the record? He's not wrong about the batons.' He'll deny saying this if asked again later.
sections.dmNote: Shard stands in front of the class and makes her case without raising her voice, and at least two of her points don't have a clean rebuttal — the licensing system really does work better for people who already have money and connections, and provisional heroes really do get treated as disposable. Nobody throws a punch. The class leaves uncertain, which is the point. Somewhere in the crowd, one of Ruin's people is watching Shard work and taking notes on a movement she doesn't know is bankrolling her — the class walks right past him. Resist the urge to give the class a clean 'win' here, mechanically or morally. If a player tries to out-argue Shard, let them land real points too — she should update, visibly, on at least one thing a sharp PC says — without either side fully convincing the other. The scene succeeds if the table leaves with a mild, unresolved discomfort they're still turning over at the next session.

aside.label: Villain Threads
aside.body:
Fracture — Shard and Voltage are fully visible — named, confronted, argued with. The class knows who they are now. What the class does with Shard's arguments is the open question they carry into the finale. Shard clocks Setaka's introduction, if it happens, and files it away without comment — she's not naive about individual heroes being decent; her argument was always about the system, not the people currently standing in it. Voltage's real name doesn't come up today, and Shard doesn't offer it — but he signs off the retreat with a two-finger tap to his own collarbone, aimed at nobody in particular, that at least one PC clocks as a habit rather than a random gesture.

Null Signal — Splice's photographic operation in the crowd. Ruin now has comprehensive quirk-activation footage of every PC under stress conditions. Whether the class noticed him determines how much warning they have. His footage from today gets filed under a project header the class will never see: 'Cohort — Stress Response, Public Setting.' It's a different category than the entrance exam and Sports Festival files — someone is specifically interested in how they behave when they're uncomfortable, not just when they're fighting.

The Chain — Shard mentions once that the Commission ignored Ruin's Kurogane Wharf operation for eighteen months. She has documentation. She doesn't share it today. She knows the class was at Patchwork Agency — she has sources in the neighbourhood. Her exact phrase — 'eighteen months' — is worth remembering. It's specific enough to be a real number from real documentation, not a rhetorical round figure.

sections.developments: How the class responds to Voltage's intervention — arrest, stand down, argue, or quietly let it go — is this arc's real branch point, and it should follow the party into Convergence: whether Shard considers them worth warning if things go bad on the roof. There's no mechanically "correct" response here; track it as relationship, not score. Tazato's muttered agreement, if it happens, is worth one more quiet beat before the season ends — she's not going to bring it up again unprompted, but she also won't walk it back if a PC does. If a PC tries to physically apprehend Shard or Voltage rather than de-escalate, let it be possible but costly — both are combat-capable and this is a crowd, not an arena; a fight here risks the actual bystanders Fracture is nominally protecting, and Shard will say exactly that out loud before disengaging rather than escalating further herself.
sections.treasure: No loot in the usual sense — the actual reward is information nobody can act on cleanly yet: Shard's name, Voltage's face, and a set of arguments about the licensing system that at least one PC should be quietly unable to fully dismiss going forward. And, less comfortably: the first moment several PCs have to sit with the idea that being a good hero and working inside a fair system might not be the same project. Nobody resolves this today. Nobody's supposed to. The uncomfortable kind of treasure: at least one PC now has Shard's contact information, slipped to them without comment by a protester as the crowd disperses, 'in case you want to actually talk sometime.' Nobody has decided yet whether that's a resource or a liability.

sections.heading: Convergence
sections.readAloud: Acting on information from Oshiro (sourced through Patchwork's contacts), the class intercepts a Ruin logistics operation in a Kurogane Wharf warehouse. Kuma is running it. What they don't know: Splice has identified this operation as a data acquisition target for Null — Kuma is transporting experimental quirk-suppression equipment, and Null wants it, whether or not Kuma's expecting him. Fracture is also here, sabotaging the equipment because Ruin extorts the unlicensed quirk users in their community. Ruin's own people aren't coordinating with each other, Fracture is running its own agenda entirely, and the class has to make decisions in real time. Whatever any of them expected tonight to be, it wasn't three separate plans running into each other by accident.
sections.body:
• Arrival: the warehouse district at night. Signs of Kuma's operation — logistics vehicles, a perimeter. Signs of something else — two Fracture cell members are already inside, cutting equipment cables. Signs of something else entirely — one of Null's technical vans is parked across the street monitoring equipment frequencies. The class has thirty seconds before Kuma notices the Fracture interference.
• Kuma: loud, overconfident, not in on Null's plans or Fracture's presence. 'You're graduating early, students.' He starts Large. He reaches Huge by round 2. His growth is capped at Huge — the warehouse ceiling prevents Gargantuan. Use this. The class should figure out that the architecture is their advantage.
• Ensemble support, if you need it: Ichitaka's hologram of a second entry team peels one or two of Kuma's attention rounds away at a critical moment. Setaka formally announces the class's intent to intervene before anyone throws a punch, which briefly and genuinely confuses Kuma, who was not expecting manners. Tazato, present as backup muscle at Oshiro's discretion, can trade blows with Kuma directly without stealing a PC's spotlight — she's built to hold the line, not to win the fight for the party. Use any, all, or none of these depending on how much help your table's actual roster needs.
• Splice: enters from the north loading door in round 3, after assessing that the fight will compromise the equipment he came for. He does not engage the class unless they block his path to the crates. If the class is occupied with Kuma, he takes what he came for and leaves clean. Either way, Null gets something.
• Shard: she's on the roof of the adjacent building, watching. If the class gets into serious trouble, she could intervene — whether she does depends on how they handled The Fracture Problem. She will not fight the class tonight regardless.
• Undertow: condensation on the warehouse's cold pipes has been gathering and running together across the floor all fight, unnoticed. In the final round, the puddle at the room's edge stands up. He watches Kuma go down. He watches Splice complete or abandon his objective. He looks at each PC for three seconds each — unhurried, interested. Then he says one thing and pours himself down the nearest floor drain: 'Good instincts. Wrong current.' He is gone. Nothing about his appearance should read as combat-imminent — no stance, no telegraphed threat, nothing a player's instincts would flag as 'about to fight.' He's closer to weather arriving than a person entering a room.
• Resolution: Kuma is arrested and in custody. Splice has retreated. Shard is gone. Undertow was never touchable. The class has won the immediate fight. Oshiro arrives — without being called. He reads a single-line report. He puts it down. He says: 'Get some sleep.' The report heading, visible to a sharp-eyed player: 'Undertow — confirmed active, Kurogane Wharf. Status: at large.'
• One of the two Fracture saboteurs, if confronted directly, doesn't fight — she holds up her hands, gestures at the cut cables, and says 'We're not even here for you,' which is, from her perspective, completely true.
sections.dmNote: Ruin's people and Fracture's sabotage crew are both in the warehouse, on the same night, neither side expecting the other — the class walks into a three-way mess nobody planned. They win the fight in front of them. Null still gets her data out. Undertow is a shape leaving through a side door as the dust settles — close enough to be real, gone before anyone can follow. The class ends the night certain Ruin is beatable and completely unsure what to do about Fracture, whose funding they still haven't traced back to the group they just fought. Catching the man behind the name is next season's problem. Pace this as three overlapping problems, not one big fight: Kuma is the mechanical encounter and should get the most table time; Splice is a ticking clock running in parallel, not a second boss fight — track his objective on a plain 3-round counter and resolve it narratively; the Fracture crew barely needs stats at all, they're set dressing for tension until Shard's presence (if she intervenes) turns them into a factor. Undertow closes the session, not the encounter — give the table a beat of quiet before he appears, even if it's just Oshiro's radio going staticky for a second first. If a PC tries to engage Undertow before he speaks, let it fail softly — he simply isn't where the attack lands, without a roll, without drama. This is the one moment all season where the fiction should quietly override the mechanics.

aside.label: Villain Threads
aside.body: All Factions — Ruin and Fracture are both fully present and active in the same warehouse, on the same night, running completely uncoordinated agendas — Kuma doesn't know Splice is here for Null, and neither of them knows Fracture is here at all until the sabotage starts. Kuma is the direct confrontation — arrested. Splice achieves a partial objective for Null regardless of what the class does. Shard is neither defeated nor allied. Undertow's observation and departure is the closing image of Season 1 — the one person in that warehouse who understood everything that happened in it, and the one nobody could touch. If a PC specifically tries to follow him down the drain, into the pipes, or track the water afterward, let them find nothing — not because the fiction is being unfair, but because that's the accurate answer. He doesn't leave a trail this season. He's not supposed to be catchable yet. The Fracture sabotage crew's target list, if recovered from the two saboteurs, names three more Ruin-linked properties in Kurogane Wharf the class has never heard of — real leads, deliberately left dangling into Season 2.

seedsIntoNext.label: Threads Into Season 2
seedsIntoNext.body:
Undertow — At large. 'Wrong current' is not a dismissal — it's an assessment. He's decided the class is interesting. Season 2 opens with Undertow being specifically interested in Class 1-A. Whichever PC(s) held his attention a beat longer during Convergence is the natural thread to pull on first when Season 2 opens.

Null Signal — Whether Splice got the equipment or not, Null has comprehensive combat data on every PC's quirk activation. Her log entry describes the class as 'worth acquiring.' Coming from her, that means something specific.

Fracture — Shard's question — 'which side are you on?' — is unanswered. The class's relationship with Fracture in Season 2 depends entirely on how they handled The Fracture Problem.

Flashpoint (tease) — Among Ruin's seized equipment: an internal memo referencing 'Miruki's job, Wharf side, pending approval.' The name means nothing to the class yet.

Riddle (tease) — One Ruin member being processed says: 'We have a friend who talks to people. He talked to someone you know.' He won't say more. Plant this ambiguously — it could be Riddle, or it could be a bluff.

Null (tease) — Splice's retreating van. A plate number and a logo: 'Seika Advanced Systems.' The same name from Hamagawa's monitor screen in Tier 1, if anyone remembered it.

sections.developments: Whether Splice completes his objective depends on whether the class is occupied with Kuma when he arrives — either way, Null gets something, which shapes how confident her presence feels whenever this campaign continues. Whether Shard intervenes if things go badly depends entirely on how The Fracture Problem resolved. Undertow's appearance is fixed regardless of outcome; he isn't here to fight, he's here to look. Track, quietly, which PC(s) he spends his three seconds on with something other than passing interest — a flicker of actual attention, a half-second longer look. You don't need to decide why yet. That's a Season 2 question with a Season 1 seed planted here. If the class never engages Splice at all — occupied with Kuma and the Fracture crew the whole scene — he simply completes his objective in the background and is gone by the time anyone thinks to look for him. This is the quiet version of the night and is just as valid as a version where they clash with him directly; either way Null's data collection into Season 2 stays intact.
sections.treasure: Kuma's seized equipment (quirk-suppression hardware, real evidence for a future Commission inquiry into Ruin), a formal commendation through Oshiro's chain of command, and the single most valuable and least comfortable item to come out of the night: a case file with Undertow's name finally attached to something official. None of tonight's rewards are unambiguous — the commendation is real, and it's also political cover for the fact that Undertow walked out of a room full of provisional students uncaught. Let that tension sit in the room instead of resolving it. Buried in Kuma's seized paperwork, easy to skim past: a line confirming the warehouse lease is held by a shell company sharing a registered agent with 'Seika Advanced Systems' — the name from Hamagawa's monitor, and from Splice's visitor badge at Patchwork Agency. Nobody at the table has to connect it tonight. The DM should.

closing.label: Villain Presence — Chapter 2
closing.body: Ruin is fully active in Tier 2, and everyone — the class, the Commission, Ruin's own members — knows exactly what it is. What nobody has is a face for Undertow. Kuma is the direct confrontation — a winnable boss fight. Splice, working for Null, is the operationally sophisticated secondary threat who achieves something regardless of how the main fight goes. Fracture (Shard, Voltage) is the moral complication that doesn't resolve cleanly, and is genuinely independent of Ruin — even though Ruin's money is quietly keeping it alive. Undertow's Season 1 closing appearance — watching, commenting, leaving untouched — establishes the scale of the problem the class is not yet equipped to address: not a villain group to defeat, but a man behind it they've barely even seen. The Commission will call Convergence a clean operational success, and by the numbers it is — one arrest, no casualties, seized equipment, a fully documented incident report. Nothing about that paperwork captures what the class actually walked away with: total confidence against Ruin's muscle, and a low, specific unease about everything standing behind it that no incident report has a field for.

chapters.milestone: Completing Chapter 2 closes out Season 1 — the class reaches Level 6, cliffhanger and all.

appendix.heading: Ranking Chart
appendix.body: Masahata's ranking chart on the common room fridge persists through the entire campaign — a habit from a family that ranks things at dinner as a matter of course. Reference it at least once per tier. By Season 1's end it has been annotated, defaced, coffee-stained, and re-laminated over the original lamination. He reprints it every time. This is never commented on directly. Give it a life of its own across the season: a coffee ring from the Dorm Life arc, a torn corner after Capture the Flag, a temporary blackout when Nakaya's static wipes the lamination's static-cling backing right before the Sports Festival (he reprints it in the stadium parking lot, on principle). By Convergence, half the class can recite their own placement from memory and would rather die than admit it.

appendix.heading: Oshiro Arrivals
appendix.body: Whenever things get genuinely serious, Oshiro Daikichi arrives at the scene without being called. No explanation is offered. He just shows up. This should remain unexplained through Season 1. Play the arrival itself the same way every time — no cape flourish, no dramatic entrance, just Oshiro standing where he wasn't a moment ago, already assessing. The gag isn't that it's impossible, it's that nobody's ever caught the part where he got there. Let one sharp-eyed player try to watch for it directly at some point in the season and still miss it.

appendix.heading: Kinji Napping
appendix.body: Kinji Hamakida is asleep somewhere in the background of every session where she is not the primary focus. She is always awake again before it matters. Her eyes flatten to pewter grey for a second whenever Neutralization actually triggers — the class calls this 'turning off.' Track her at least once a session even when she's not in a scene — a line like 'Kinji is asleep against the window' costs nothing and pays for itself every time she wakes up already knowing the answer to whatever the class spent ten minutes arguing about.

appendix.heading: Toshida Head
appendix.body: Toshida's speech bubble head gets stuck in, on, or through something structural at least once per tier — usually the dorm doorframe he's privately named Hiroshi. The scale escalates as his quirk control improves but his spatial awareness does not. Hiroshi should get referenced by name at least once after its introduction in Dorm Life — a repaired panel, a fresh dent, Toshida greeting it under his breath on the way past. By the Sports Festival, at least one classmate should be doing the bit with him unprompted.

appendix.heading: Toragi And Yoshibara
appendix.body: Toragi leaves Yoshibara small, useful, unexplained things — a pencil, a snack — and disappears before she can react. She's started leaving things back. Neither has said a word about it out loud. Let this thread surface once more before Season 1 ends. The exchanges should stay wordless and slightly mismatched in scale — a pencil for a hair tie, a snack for a folded note neither of them mentions again. Resist ever having either of them explain it, even privately to another PC; the thread works because it's the one soft thing in the campaign nobody's turned into dialogue yet.

appendix.heading: Faction Symbol Thread
appendix.body: The Fracture jagged-line symbol appears in each Tier 1 arc (entrance exam wall, dorm leaflet, alley concrete). Everyone knows it's Fracture's mark — it's a public movement. What lands by the time Shard introduces herself in The Fracture Problem is that the class has seen it enough times to feel like it's been following them personally, not just decorating the city. If you're running the season lean and cutting sections, protect this thread specifically — it's the cheapest possible piece of foreshadowing in the whole campaign (one prop, repeated) and it's doing real work making Fracture feel omnipresent before Shard ever says a word.

campaigns.title: Ashfall Hollow
campaigns.tagline: Four provisional heroes, one dying town, and ground that won't stay still.
campaigns.tone: A tight, character-forward campaign built for exactly four people instead of a full class — Ren Suzuki, Kazama Kenji, Chozen Tadachi, and Izuto Kutsu, on a Rural Hero Placement in a struggling mountain town still living in the shadow of a mining disaster. No faction war, no citywide conspiracy — just a small agency, a town with a long memory, and a very human, very sympathetic reason the ground keeps giving way. Quieter and sadder than a Sports-Festival season, and built to let all four of them carry the story personally rather than share it with sixteen classmates.

background.heading: Ashfall Hollow
background.body:
A mountain town of about six thousand people, three train changes and one bad access road from the nearest city, tucked into a valley where the Kessler Mining Company ran ore extraction for sixty years before the seam ran dry. The town kept the name after the Ashfall — the 2019 tunnel collapse and gas ignition that killed eleven miners and opened the first of the sinkholes that still, occasionally, swallow a piece of the town whole. Kessler Mining paid what a settlement required and closed its regional office within the year. Nobody in the Hollow has forgotten either fact.

The ground here is not reliable. Old mine workings honeycomb the bedrock under half the residential district, logged on maps nobody fully trusts and unlogged in places everyone assumes exist anyway. Insurance premiums are the highest in the prefecture. Property values are the lowest. People stay anyway, because it's where they're from, and because leaving costs money nobody has.

background.heading: Tidewell Point Agency
background.body:
The Hollow's only hero agency, run out of a converted hardware store on the town's single commercial street. Two licensed pros on staff: Agency head Renka Amagai ("Groundskeeper" — Quirk: Ballast, lets her anchor herself and one adjacent structure to bedrock for a short duration, functionally useless against a citywide threat and extremely useful against exactly the kind of thing that happens here) and her partner Tobio Sesshin ("Aftercare" — Quirk: Numb Touch, suppresses pain signals on contact, which makes him the most popular person in any triage line and the reason the agency's rescue completion rate looks better on paper than its response time does).

Tidewell Point has never had a provisional intern before this year. It was never going to be able to afford one — the Rural Placement stipend covers it, barely, and only because four came at once instead of one.

There is no other hero presence within forty minutes. When something happens in the Hollow, it is Amagai, Sesshin, and whoever else is standing there. This year, for the first time, that includes four provisional students.

background.heading: The Rural Hero Placement Program
background.body:
A three-year-old Hero Commission initiative responding to a blunt statistic: license-holding heroes cluster in cities, and half the country's small towns have functional coverage only because neighboring cities are close enough to help. The program places small teams of provisional-license students — never a full class, usually three to five — in underserved agencies for an extended field placement, credited as internship hours toward their provisional license upgrade.

Ren Suzuki, Kazama Kenji, Chozen Tadachi, and Izuto Kutsu are this year's Tidewell Point placement. They did not choose each other. The Commission's matching algorithm looked at quirk profiles, ran a compatibility pass against Tidewell Point's stated needs ("structural/rescue-capable, self-sufficient, does not require close supervision"), and produced four names. Amagai got the packet two weeks before they arrived and read it twice, unimpressed by all the parts that weren't the word "self-sufficient."

This is not their class, their school, or their normal support structure. It is the four of them, two overworked pros, and a town that needed help before any of them showed up.

background.heading: The Numbers Nobody's Checked
background.body:
Ground subsidence in the Hollow is real, documented, and — according to every geological survey on file — supposed to be slow. A sinkhole opens every year or two, usually small, usually in the same handful of known soft zones near the old mine workings. This is accounted for. It is priced into the insurance. It is, in the driest possible sense, normal.

This year there have been three incidents in the ten weeks since the placement began. All three are in the survey's "soft zone" list, which makes them technically unremarkable. All three also happened faster, and more completely, than the geology should produce without help. Nobody at Tidewell Point has had the time or staffing to run the comparison. Amagai has noticed the frequency and hasn't said anything out loud yet, mostly because saying it out loud means it's real.

chapters.title: The Assignment
chapters.intro: A small, grounded opening. No factions, no conspiracies yet — just four provisional students, two exhausted pros, and a town whose relationship with disaster is close, personal, and unresolved. The first rescue should feel genuinely good to pull off. The unease comes in quietly, in a detail nobody's had time to check.
chapters.dmNote: Play this tier almost entirely straight. The four of them are good at this, the agency needs them, and the town is grateful in a way U.A.'s campus never quite was — that's a real and earned feeling, let it land before anything complicates it. The sinkhole's clean edges are the only thread pulling forward; everything else is character work and competence porn.

sections.heading: Orientation Day
sections.readAloud: The bus from the last train station lets you off outside a converted hardware store with a hand-painted sign reading TIDEWELL POINT AGENCY — EST. hanging slightly crooked above the door. The street behind you is one block long. It has a noodle shop, a shuttered bank branch, and a memorial plaque bolted to a boulder that you will learn not to ask about on day one.
sections.body:
• Amagai meets you at the door, looks at all four of you for slightly too long, and says "Four. Huh." before showing you the back room that is now your office, equipment locker, and — per the cot in the corner — occasional crash space.
• Sesshin is warmer, immediately curious about all four quirks in a genuinely nerdy way, and asks Izuto detailed questions about Engine's fluid-replenishment math that Izuto is delighted to answer at length.
• Amagai's actual onboarding speech is four sentences long: "Nobody's coming to back you up. Call it in anyway, every time, even when you don't need it, so dispatch has a pattern. Don't be a hero. Be useful." She does not explain further.
• Paperwork, gear checks, and a driving tour of the town's known soft zones — marked on a laminated map that is visibly older than the agency's coffee maker.
