background.heading: The City — the other half of this module
background.body:
This volume is the story: eight chapters, the people in them, and the reference you need to run a session. Everything the class does when nobody is hunting them lives in a companion volume called **After Hours: The City**, on this same page.

WHAT IS OVER THERE — free time and how it works; the side-quest, odd-job, hangout and wandering lists; the whole of Byakko, from the Stripe Law and the Heat track to the middle ranks, the turf economy and the Cage floor by floor; all four Underground factions with their ladders and stat blocks; and the shop.

WHY IT IS SPLIT — because this module got large, and because the two halves are read at different times. You read a chapter before a session. You look up the city during one, when a player says "it's the weekend, what do you do?" Keeping them apart means neither one has to be scrolled through to find the other.

EVERY "SEE X" IN THESE CHAPTERS STILL WORKS. Where a chapter says see "The Four Corners" or see "The Ledger" or see "Free Time — side quests," that is an entry in The City. The names have not changed.

WHAT YOU CAN IGNORE — all of it, for a while. Chapters 1 to 5 can be run start to finish having read nothing in the other volume except "Free Time — How It Works." The city becomes necessary at Chapter 6 and not before.

closing.body: That they got in. That is the entire list. They have not met each other, they have not met a member of staff in the same room, and not one of them has been told what provisional standing does not permit. Somewhere behind all of it, five professional heroes have died in twelve months and it has been on the television for a year without ever becoming a story anybody in this class would have reason to follow.
closing.label: Chapter Note — What the class knows

chapters.intro: The exam is over and nobody knows how they did. Chapter 1 is the six weeks between an entrance exam and a first morning — an envelope that turns out to contain a very small principal, a kit list that gives away more about U.A. than it means to, and twenty fifteen-year-olds each privately convinced they were the admissions mistake. There is no combat in it and no antagonist, and there is not meant to be. Its job is to establish who these people were before U.A. got hold of them, so that the class the campaign spends four chapters assembling has something to have been assembled out of. It ends at a classroom door, on the last morning Class 1-A are twenty separate people.
chapters.milestone: No milestone. The class starts and finishes this chapter at Level 1 — there is nothing here to survive, and the first level-up is earned in Chapter 2 when the bracket reaches the semi-finals.
chapters.title: Provisional
chapters.dmNote:
Play this chapter entirely straight and entirely warm. Nothing in it is a test, nothing in it is a trap, and the only thing that happens outside the PCs' own kitchens is a news item nobody in the room cares about.

Its real work is retroactive. The entrance exam is not played — the module opens the morning after — so this is where you find out what these characters did in it, by asking rather than by rolling. What a player invents about their own exam becomes true, and it is almost always better than anything you would have written for them.

Keep the whole thing at the pace of a conversation. If it runs to twenty minutes and the table is impatient, that is a complete success: go straight into "Ten Names on the Board" and treat the two as one session.

sections.dmNote:
There is no dice roll in this section and there should not be. It is a scene about being told you were chosen, and the only mechanic it needs is going round the table twice.

The two exam questions are the most valuable thing in the chapter. They hand you four pieces of backstory you did not have to invent, in the players' own words, on the first night. Write them on the same sheet as your initiative tracker and keep it for the whole campaign.
sections.tag: Opening session · the letter · no combat
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — the envelope, one player at a time → the disc → Sugitsu runs long → round the table for the room they were standing in → the two exam questions → out.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — the projection once, in full, then both exam questions round the table. Twenty minutes, and it does everything this session needs.

• Open on the letter and play it per-PC rather than as a group scene. This is the last time these four are in four separate buildings, and the contrast is worth buying.
• DO THE PROJECTION ONCE AND PROPERLY, then summarise it for everyone else. It is funny the first time and it is not funny the fourth.
• Play Sugitsu as warm, precise and completely unable to stop talking — a man who is extremely good at his job being asked to perform a small piece of theatre he is not suited to. He is the reason this school is safe. He is also visibly bad at recording a message.
• ASK WHERE THEY WERE. Round the table: what room were you standing in, and who else was in the house? Do not let a player answer "alone" without one follow-up — and do not argue with them if that is genuinely the answer.
• THE EXAM, WITHOUT PLAYING IT. This module opens the morning after, so ask two questions of every player and write both answers down. One: what did you do in that exam that you are proud of? Two: what did you do that you have not told anybody? The second one is a thread — hold it until Chapter 5, when the campaign is asking harder questions and you want a personal lever.
• Whatever a player invents about their own exam is now true, including the parts that make them look bad. Especially those.
• PROVISIONAL IS A REAL WORD and the letter uses it twice. Nobody at the table will care yet, and that is correct — see "Provisional status and what the students can actually do," and let it become a problem in Chapter 4 rather than explaining it here.
sections.heading: The Letter
sections.developments:
• IF A PLAYER ASKS WHAT THEIR SCORE WAS — the letter does not say and the projection does not say. U.A. does not publish them to applicants. This is deliberate on the school's part and it will annoy Masahata Shikoji for an entire term.
• IF A PLAYER WANTS TO HAVE SCRAPED IN — say yes, warmly. Someone who got there on a rescue point rather than a combat point is a more interesting character than someone who topped the exam, and this class contains both.
• IF NOBODY ENGAGES WITH THE HOME SCENE — some tables do not want to play family. Take the letter, take the two exam answers, move on. Nothing is lost.
• IF A PLAYER KEEPS THE DISC — of course they do. Nobody at U.A. ever chases it. Sugitsu mentions it once more, in passing, two chapters later, and does not pursue it.
sections.readAloud:
▶ THE LETTER
HOW TO RUN IT — Read this properly to one player. Summarise it for the rest.

It comes on a Tuesday, and it's heavier than a letter has any business being.

THEY SEE — A stiff cream envelope. The U.A. crest pressed into it, not printed. Their name on the front, handwritten, by somebody who wasn't being careful about it.
INSIDE — One sheet of paper. One flat white disc, about the size of a coaster.

▶ IF SOMEBODY TOUCHES THE DISC

It gets warm. And then there's a man standing over the kitchen table — eighteen inches tall, in a suit, already halfway through a sentence.

"—and if this is playing then it worked, which means congratulations, which I should probably have led with."

He stops. Starts again.

"Sugitsu Jarvichi. Principal. I'm recording twenty of these today and I've been told I can't do them in one take. So if I sound tired, that's why. It's not about you."

▶ THE PART HE READS PROPERLY

"You've been admitted to the Hero Course at U.A. High School on provisional standing. Provisional means you're a student and not a hero, and the difference is legal rather than emotional. Term begins in April. There's a kit list."

A beat.

"Please read the kit list."

▶ AND THEN HE DOESN'T STOP

"I'd like to say something about your exam specifically. But there are twenty of these and I've been asked to keep them general — so I'll say this instead. We weren't looking for the strongest applicant. We have never been looking for the strongest applicant. Anyone who tells you otherwise wasn't sitting on the panel."

He looks off to one side, at somebody out of frame.

"Is that — no. No, I know. Fine."

He turns back.

"Welcome to U.A. Please don't lose the disc. It isn't a keepsake. We'd like it back."

aside.body:
Principal, and the reason U.A. is the safest building in Nerima. His quirk is Search: he scans a one-mile radius as a bonus action and permanently stores ten individuals, and he has known the shape of every person on his campus for years.

None of that is visible here. What the players meet is a small projected man who has already recorded nineteen of these, cannot help going off script, and is being told off by somebody out of frame.

Play the competence later. Play the warmth now. When his quirk is fooled at the festival in Chapter 3, the table should feel it partly because they liked him in a kitchen in February.
aside.label: Sugitsu Jarvichi — first impression

sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — the dead weeks → one home beat per PC → the kit list → the television line, thrown away → out.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — one home beat each and the kit list. Cut the television line; it costs you nothing this early.

• GIVE EVERY PC ONE BEAT AT HOME and keep them short — three or four exchanges each. The question that unlocks it is not "what do you do," it is "who is proudest of you, and who is not saying anything?"
• NOT EVERY FAMILY IS PLEASED. A hero course is a dangerous school and some parents understand that better than others. At least one PC should get a version of this and it should not be resolved in this chapter.
• THE NEIGHBOURHOOD FINDS OUT. This is the specific texture of six weeks of waiting — a neighbour who suddenly knows, a middle-school teacher who writes, somebody who was unkind about the quirk two years ago being extremely warm about it now. Let a player be graceless about that if they want to be.
• THE KIT LIST DOES THE WORLDBUILDING. It is a better introduction to U.A. than any description, because it was written by an institution that learned each line the hard way. The "no irreplaceable items" rule is real and the reason is boring: things get destroyed constantly.
• THE COSTUME ENVELOPE STAYS SEALED. Forge opens that conversation in Chapter 2 and she wants to look at them in person first. If a player opens it anyway, nothing happens — it is a form, and it asks questions they cannot answer yet.
• CLUE ZERO, AND IT IS NOT A CLUE YET. One line of television news about a fifth death in twelve months, delivered flat, in the background of somebody else's scene, and then the channel changes. Do not repeat it. Do not let anyone roll on it. If a player asks directly, the honest answer is that it has been on the news for a year and nobody has explained it.
• The class does not meet in this chapter. They arrive at U.A. as strangers, and that is the entire point of the next section.
sections.treasure: Nothing to find. The kit list, the sealed costume envelope and the disc are all worth having on the table as physical props — see "Props to make before you start" — but none of them is loot.
sections.dmNote:
This is a quiet section in a campaign that gets very loud, and it is doing load-bearing work: everything Chapters 4 and 5 do to these characters costs more if the table has seen where they live.

Resist making the six weeks eventful. Nothing happens. That is the texture — the most exciting thing in your life has already been decided and you are not allowed to start it yet.

The television line is the only forward-facing thing in the chapter and it must be thrown away completely. No music, no lingering, no "roll me a Perception." It is old news to everybody in the room, including the person changing the channel.

aside.label: Where this sits on the Case 9 list
aside.body:
The item on the television is victim five — Ikari Tomonobu, "Backdraft," combustion, found in Ota over the winter. He is already on the list in the appendix before the campaign begins.

The players are not being invited to notice this and there is nothing they can do with it. Its only job is to make the news real before it is relevant, so that when the class opens the archive in Chapter 4 the pattern is something they walked past rather than something the module handed them.

If you would rather keep the chapter completely clean, cut the line. It costs nothing.

sections.developments:
• IF A PLAYER CHASES THE NEWS ITEM — they find twelve months of coverage that says nothing, because there is nothing public to find. No pattern has been published. Give them the frustration honestly: do not reward it with a hint and do not punish it either.
• IF A PLAYER WANTS TO TRAIN THROUGH THE SIX WEEKS — let them, and let it be true. They arrive fitter and slightly overconfident. Do not invent a mechanical benefit; Chapter 3 is where training gets a mechanic, and it is generous when it arrives.
• IF A PLAYER HAS NO FAMILY TO PLAY — plenty of people this age do not. A guardian, a sibling, an empty flat and a landlord are all fine, and an empty flat is a strong choice you should support rather than soften.
• IF THE TABLE WANTS TO SKIP AHEAD — they can. Take one sentence from each player about the six weeks and go straight to First Morning.
sections.readAloud:
▶ THE WAIT

February ends. March happens to somebody else.

You're a U.A. student in every respect except the ones that involve going to U.A. There's a start date on a piece of paper and it is a very long way away. Until then there's nothing to do but be a person in your own house who's been told they're going to be a hero.

▶ THE KIT LIST, WHENEVER SOMEBODY FINALLY READS IT

Two pages, and oddly specific.

THEY SEE — Gym wear. Indoor shoes, outdoor shoes. A sealed envelope marked COSTUME REQUEST — DO NOT COMPLETE YET. Three separate consent forms, one of which uses the word "structural."
AND AT THE BOTTOM — Under OTHER: "Students are asked not to bring valuables or irreplaceable personal items during the first term."

It doesn't say why.

▶ A TELEVISION NOBODY IS WATCHING
HOW TO RUN IT — Say it flatly, over the top of something else, and don't pause.

"— the fifth such case in twelve months, according to the Commission, although a spokesperson declined to confirm any connection between them. In sport, the —"

Somebody in the house changes the channel.

▶ BEFORE THE SESSION ENDS
ASK EVERY PLAYER — What did you do with six weeks of knowing? And who in your house is proud of you?
sections.heading: The Weeks Between

sections.developments:
• IF A PLAYER WANTS TO ARRIVE LATE, EARLY, OR THROUGH A WINDOW — all fine and all characterful. Nobody is taking a register yet.
• IF A PLAYER TAKES THE CHART DOWN — let them, and let Masahata have a second one up by lunchtime. He printed several.
• IF THE TABLE IS ALREADY RESTLESS — they are ready. Go to Forge immediately; this section has done its job the moment the room feels populated.
• IF A PLAYER ASKS WHO THE HOMEROOM TEACHER IS — nobody has told them. The letter did not say. That is normal, and it is also, in retrospect, very Forge.

aside.label: What the players should be able to name by the end of this session
aside.body:
Four things, and no more: that they are provisionally admitted and do not fully know what that limits; that term starts in April; that there are twenty of them; and that the woman in the doorway is eating.

They should not know their homeroom teacher's name, the bracket, the Sports Festival, or anything at all about the news. All of that is Chapter 2's to give away.

sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — the gate → the corridor → the room → three or four first contacts → the door goes → stop, and go straight into "Ten Names on the Board."
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — the corridor and two first contacts. Ten minutes, then Forge.

• THIS SECTION IS A RUN-UP, NOT A SCENE. It exists to put four PCs in a room full of strangers so that the pairing announcement lands on people rather than on names. Keep it moving.
• LET THEM MEET THREE OR FOUR CLASSMATES AND NO MORE. Suggested: Setaka Toko holding the door and apologising for it, Kibi Kankei saying good morning as though this is all perfectly normal, Aikawa Sakume already organising something nobody asked her to organise, and Masahata Shikoji's chart already on the wall. If the room needs noise, add Kinji Hamakida, who has a speaker in his bag, and it is already on.
• MASAHATA'S CHART IS UP BEFORE TERM BEGINS. It moves to the Heights Alliance fridge later and stays there for four chapters. This is its first appearance and nobody should remark on it.
• DO NOT INTRODUCE ALL TWENTY. The next section does that far better, by making the players have opinions about the pairings instead of memorising a list.
• HIRO IS IN THE ROOM AND THE ROOM HAS ALREADY STOPPED STARING. For about the first ninety seconds every student who walks in looks at the seven-foot machine at the back. Then the little screen on his face shows 👋, and that is so disarming that people wave back and stop looking. If a player talks to him he answers in hand signs and one emoji at a time, and he is completely friendly. Nothing about him reads as a mystery today — he is obviously a machine, and obviously nobody minds.
• CHOZEN'S SURNAME ARRIVES BEFORE HE DOES. Everybody in the room knows who Isobar was. Let one classmate — Aikawa, loudly — make the connection out loud, and let Chozen's player decide how that goes. It will not be the last time this term somebody asks him about his father.
• END ON THE DOOR. Forge in the doorway, already eating, is the handoff. Stop the section there and open the next one.

THE HANDOFF — this section and "Ten Names on the Board" are one continuous morning. If you have the time, run them back to back in the same sitting. The chapter break exists for the reader, not for the table.
sections.dmNote:
Twenty strangers in a room is the last moment in this campaign where Class 1-A are twenty individuals, and the next four chapters are entirely about them becoming something else. You do not need to say that out loud. You only need to let the room be slightly awkward before Forge opens the door.

If your table has run other U.A. material, resist the urge to let anyone already know each other. The pairings work because nobody has chosen anything yet.
sections.readAloud:
▶ THE GATE

It's much bigger than it looked in the photographs, and there's no ceremony at it at all. It's a Monday. People are just walking in.

THEY SEE — A sheet of paper taped to the wall inside the entrance. Twenty names in two columns, a room number, and nothing else.

▶ THE CORRIDOR

The 1-A door is at the end, and it's enormous. A good ten feet of it — which is either for somebody specific, or because of something that's already happened.

It's for somebody specific. He's already inside: seven foot two and made of grey metal. He ducks under it anyway, every time, out of what looks like politeness.

Other people are arriving. Nobody's talking much.

A very tall boy holds the door, and then apologises for holding the door. Somebody with vines instead of hair walks past and says good morning like the two of you have already met.

▶ THE ROOM, BEFORE ANYTHING STARTS

Twenty desks. Nineteen strangers — or however many got here first.

Somebody's already pinned a printed sheet to the noticeboard at the back. It's a ranking chart. Term hasn't started.

▶ AND THEN

The door goes.

There's a woman in the doorway with a bento box the size of a briefcase under one arm.

She's already eating.
sections.heading: First Morning
sections.tag: First day · introductions · hands straight off

closing.label: Chapter Note — What the class knows
closing.body: A man came to the gate, asked a classmate a question, and put them on the floor for thirty seconds without touching them. He left before anyone could legally stop him. The principal chose not to pursue and will not say why in a way anyone finds satisfying, and the strictest teacher on staff has been missing lessons since April and arrived at the gate already knowing what he was looking at. Nobody in Class 1-A has connected any of that to the news. Why would they? They have a Sports Festival in six weeks.

chapters.intro: The door opens, and Nobara Forge puts twenty names on a board in ten pairs and refuses to explain herself. Chapter 2 is the 2v2 bracket — full contact, Battle Centre III, a scoreboard, and Aditya Bose shouting at people who have not done anything yet. It is a school story and it is meant to be fun: the class learns to fight as twos, twenty students become twenty legible people, and the fridge in Heights Alliance acquires a printed ranking chart that nobody asked for. In the background, on a television nobody is watching, five professional heroes have been found dead with the tops of their skulls removed, and a teacher who is meant to be officiating the bracket keeps not showing up. The chapter ends at a school open day with a polite man on the public side of the gate asking a student a question.

sections.treasure:
Every pair leaves with a measurement on Forge's list, which becomes a real piece of equipment in "Nobara Forge" later this chapter. Nothing is handed out tonight.

If you want to give something out anyway, give information: Forge will answer one honest question about any student in the class, including the ones the players have not spoken to yet.
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — Forge is eating → the board goes up → read the ten pairs and then stop talking → let the room argue → five minutes per pair → she measures them in twos → out.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — the pairs, the argument, the measuring. Cut the pair-by-pair introductions and give the four that matter one exchange each.

• Open the term with the draw. Read the ten pairs out and let the room react — this is the single best character-introduction device the campaign has, because every player learns nineteen names by having an opinion about who got stuck with whom.
• Forge's stated reason is equipment: gear built for a pair is not gear built for a person, and she has twenty students who all privately believe they are the main character. She says this cheerfully and it lands as an insult on about six of them.
• The pairs are in the appendix. The four that matter most: Ren Suzuki with Kazama Kenji, Kinji Hamakida with Kibi Kankei, Chozen Tadachi with Toragi Kayo, Izuto Kutsu with Isokono Yoromu.
• Masahata Shikoji has already produced a printed ranking chart predicting the bracket and pinned it to the common room fridge. He has himself winning. Ichitaka Shijime, his partner, has annotated it.
• Let each pair have five minutes of first contact. Izuto tries to plan the whole thing alone and present it to Isokono for approval, which is exactly the wrong move and exactly what he would do. Chozen produces a laminated four-page plan inside the hour; Toragi reads all four pages, hands it back, and says "Good," which is the longest review it will ever get. Kinji talks for the full five minutes — last night's television, his shoes, a song Kibi simply has to hear — and Kibi, who has been quietly paying attention to this class since April, listens to every word and then says the one thing nobody else has noticed: "You've never used it. Your quirk. Not once." Kinji laughs a bit too loudly and changes the subject.
• Close on Forge measuring everyone for gear, and on the fact that she measures the pairs together.
• HIRO + RAKUKA RIZO is the tenth pair and the only one nobody has an opinion about, because nobody in the class has ever had a conversation with Hiro. Rakuka is delighted. Rakuka is delighted about most things. Hiro's screen shows 👍 and that is the entire exchange.
• CLUE ONE, and it is the only one this session: when Forge measures the class she measures Hiro without the tape, because she has the numbers already, because she built them. One line, no pause, no reaction shot. If a player asks, Forge says "I've done his," which is true.
• The room's reaction to the board is the session. Masahata will argue his pairing is a tactical error and produce the chart. Ando will claim he wanted Tazato, loudly, in front of Tazato, who says nothing and lets him keep going. Aikawa volunteers to swap with literally anybody. Setaka writes Forge a thank-you note about it, which she finds on the desk the next morning and keeps.
sections.tag: Opening session · the draw · no combat
sections.heading: Ten Names on the Board
sections.dmNote:
This session has no antagonist and does not need one. Its job is to get twenty students legible at the table and to establish the campaign's central mechanical assumption — you fight as two, you plan as two, and the thing that kills you later will be built around separating you.

Play Forge as warm, blunt and slightly overwhelming. She is genuinely trying to help and she is also eating a family-sized katsu curry while telling a student their fighting style is structurally unsound.

Do not foreshadow anything. There is no shadow yet. The only thing that happens outside this room is a line on a news ticker in the common room about a body in Adachi, and nobody in the class looks up at it.
sections.developments:
• IF A PLAYER ARGUES FOR A SWAP — Forge says no, once, and does not get drawn into it. She is not being mysterious for effect; she genuinely will not explain. Let the player be annoyed. Do not soften it, and do not let them win — the pairs are load-bearing for the whole campaign.
• IF A PLAYER ASKS TO BE PAIRED WITH ANOTHER PC — the answer is still no, but tell them they are on Forge's list of people who asked, and have her mention it, once, four sessions later. Wanting something and being told no is a perfectly good character beat.
• IF THE TABLE WANTS TO ROLEPLAY ALL TEN PAIRS MEETING — let them, and cut it off at about twenty minutes. Give each pair one exchange. You do not need to voice sixteen NPCs tonight; you need the players to remember four or five names.
• IF NOBODY ENGAGES AND THE ROOM IS FLAT — skip to Forge measuring them and end the scene. This section is short by design. A quiet opening session is not a failure and the bracket next week will fix it.

aside.label: The fridge chart
aside.body: Masahata's printed bracket prediction stays on the fridge for the whole campaign. Update it between sessions. By Chapter 4 somebody has drawn on it, and by Chapter 5 nobody wants to be the one who takes it down.

sections.readAloud:
▶ OPENING

Forge is eating when you come in. She's always eating — a Creation quirk runs on calories and hers runs on ten pounds a day, so there's a bento the size of a briefcase open on the desk and she's working through it without a flicker of embarrassment.

THEY SEE — Twenty names on the board behind her, already sorted into ten pairs. The handwriting says she did this a while ago and hasn't changed her mind since.

"Right," she says, around a mouthful. "Nobody's swapping. Don't ask."

▶ IF SOMEBODY ASKS WHY THESE PAIRS

"Because gear built for two people isn't gear built for one person. And I can't design for nineteen of you who all think you're the main character."

She says it perfectly pleasantly. About six of them take it personally.

▶ WHEN SHE MEASURES THEM

She works fast — tape measure in one hand, mouthful of rice — and she measures them standing next to each other. Shoulder to shoulder. Reach across. How far apart they stand when they aren't thinking about it.

"Stop moving. I'm not measuring you. I'm measuring the gap."

▶ WHEN SHE GETS TO HIRO
HOW TO RUN IT — Once. Flatly. Don't linger and never repeat it.

She doesn't use the tape.

"You I've got," says Forge, and moves on down the line.

▶ BEFORE YOU SAY ANYTHING ELSE
HOW TO RUN IT — Read the ten pairs, and then stop talking. Let the table react first.

sections.dmNote:
A frame, not a session. Chapter 2's job is to make the class legible and likeable, and the bracket alone will not do it — a bracket makes them competitors. The sofa makes them housemates.

The register here is completely straight. No irony, no winking, no foreshadowing. Teenagers arguing about milk in a kitchen is not a break from the campaign; in Chapter 4 it becomes the campaign, and the DM note for that chapter asks you to play the identical argument in the session after somebody dies. You cannot make that land if you have not made it ordinary first.

Hiro's ground-floor door is planted here and never mentioned again in Chapter 2. Do not weight it. Do not describe it twice. It is a door in a corridor, and its whole job is that a player might, four sessions from now, remember it on their own.
sections.developments:
• IF YOUR TABLE LOVES DOWNTIME — let it run and give it a whole session. It will pay for itself twice over in Chapter 4 and there is nothing in Chapter 2 that is in a hurry.
• IF YOUR TABLE FINDS DORM SCENES SLOW — do not run them as scenes at all. Open each session with sixty seconds of dorm and then go to the bracket. The effect is cumulative and works fine in one-minute doses.
• IF A PLAYER WANTS TO START SOMETHING WITH A CLASSMATE — a rivalry, a friendship, a grudge about the chart — say yes immediately and write the classmate's name on your sheet. That NPC is now load-bearing and you have been handed free material for four chapters.
• IF A PLAYER ASKS ABOUT THE GROUND-FLOOR DOOR — the honest answer is that it is Hiro's room, and there is nothing strange about a student having a room. Give it flatly and do not add anything. It is not a clue yet and pressing on it now will only teach the table that the door is interesting, which is exactly the wrong lesson.
• IF THE CLASS FRAGMENTS INTO CLIQUES — good, and let it. Forge's pairs cut straight across every friendship group in the building, which is the entire reason she did it, and the friction is worth playing.
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — drop into any session with fifteen spare minutes: the common room → one running joke → one PC gets a scene with one classmate → out. Never a whole session on its own.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — one beat. The fridge chart or the milk argument. That is enough to make the dorm real.

• THIS IS NOT A SESSION. It is a frame you drop into any evening in Chapters 2 and 3 when you want the class to be a class. Fifteen minutes, one running joke, one honest conversation, out.
• THE POINT OF IT is that twenty names on a board become twenty people you would be upset about. Everything Chapters 4 and 5 do to this class costs exactly as much as the table invested here and not one yen more.
• THE RUNNING JOKES, and you want all five of them established before Chapter 3 ends — Masahata's laminated chart on the fridge, which gets annotated, then defaced, then defended; Samitsu cooking when something has gone wrong and nobody quite thanking him; whose milk it is; Rakuka announcing his own entrances into rooms that contain two people; and Kinji's speaker, which is always on, and the class's endless negotiation about the volume.
• GIVE EACH PC ONE CLASSMATE. Not a plot, just a person — the classmate they end up sitting next to. Ando needs somebody who does not laugh at the jokes. Nomi Igisa will talk to exactly one person and it will be whoever spoke to her first. Tazato will help a PC with something practical and construct an elaborate reason why it was efficient rather than kind.
• THE GROUND FLOOR is a short corridor with a laundry room, a store cupboard, and one door at the end that stays shut. Nobody has ever remarked on it. If a player asks — and they will not — it is Hiro's room, and everybody has assumed since April that it is where he charges. That is a completely ordinary answer that nobody in the class has ever needed to hear said out loud, because he is upstairs on the sofa with everybody else.
• WHAT THE ADULTS DO NOT DO is come in here. Forge knocks. Bose has never been past the door. This is the students' building and the campaign should protect that, so that the moment in Chapter 4 when a teacher does come in lands like a break in the weather.
sections.heading: Heights Alliance

aside.label: The fridge chart, week by week
aside.body:
Masahata prints it before the draw and it stays on that fridge for the whole campaign. Update it out loud between sessions; it is thirty seconds and it is the best barometer the class has.

Week one — pristine, laminated, Masahata winning.
Week two — annotated in biro by Ichitaka, accurately and without mercy.
Week three — somebody has drawn on it.
After the festival — amended in red, and Masahata has written BROADLY CORRECT across the top.
Chapter 4 — it comes down. Nobody admits to taking it down and nobody asks for it back.
Chapter 5 — it goes back up over the weekend. Nobody says who.

sections.tag: Dorm life · downtime · woven through the chapter
sections.readAloud:
▶ THE COMMON ROOM
HOW TO RUN IT — The first time they come downstairs.

THEY SEE — Two sofas that don't match. A television nobody chose. A kitchen island with nineteen mugs on it and one clean one.
ON THE FRIDGE — A printed chart. Laminated. It predicts the outcome of a tournament that hasn't happened yet, and it has Masahata Shikoji winning.

Somebody's already annotated it in biro.

▶ THE KITCHEN, AFTER A BAD SESSION

Samitsu cooks when things have gone badly. He's never announced this and doesn't seem to have decided it. It's just that at some point in the evening there's food, and it's good, and there's enough of it.

There are three arms growing out of the counter he wiped down earlier — stirring, chopping, tasting. He isn't watching any of them.

Nobody says thank you properly. Everybody eats.

▶ THE ARGUMENT
HOW TO RUN IT — You'll run some version of this about six times.

"That's my milk."

"It's got no name on it."

"It's got no name on it because it's mine, in my fridge, in the house I live in—"

Isokono's tail has wrapped around the nearest available person, which is how everyone knows this has been going a while.

▶ LIGHTS OUT

The corridor light on the ground floor is on a timer. It goes off at eleven, and it clicks when it does.

Everybody in this building could tell you what that click is.
sections.treasure:
Nothing material, and the most valuable section in Chapter 2.

What the players leave with is nineteen classmates they can name without checking. Track which NPCs each PC has actually spoken to; you will want that list in Chapter 4, and the campaign gets significantly crueller if you use it.

sections.readAloud:
▶ BATTLE CENTRE III

A city block nobody has ever lived in. Four storeys, rebar showing where Forge has rebuilt it too many times, and a scoreboard bolted to the shell of what would be a bank.

THEY SEE — Forge up in the booth with a microphone and a second lunch. Bose down on the floor in a tracksuit, shouting at people who haven't done anything yet.

"PAIRS," Bose informs the entire building, at a volume that makes the scoreboard buzz. "YOU FIGHT AS PAIRS. IF I SEE ONE OF YOU FIGHTING AS ONE I WILL COME DOWN THERE."

▶ THE START OF EVERY MATCH

The klaxon's louder than it needs to be. Then there's a full three seconds of nothing, which is somehow the worst part.

Then the scoreboard flicks over, the block is yours, and somewhere in it are two people who've been planning for you all week.

▶ THE FIRST TIME A PAIR COMBINES PROPERLY
HOW TO RUN IT — This is the chapter. Stop and say it.

For a second it doesn't look like two people fighting.

It looks like one thing with four hands.

Up in the booth, Forge stops chewing.

▶ WHEN A MATCH ENDS

Bose is on the floor before the klaxon finishes. He tells the losers exactly what they did wrong — at length, at volume, and with total accuracy.

Then he tells the winners the same thing.
sections.tag: The bracket, first rounds · 1–2 sessions · full contact
sections.heading: Battle Centre III
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — Bose at volume → narrate the two play-ins → play the quarter-finals with a PC in them, in full → Bose comes down there → Forge stops chewing, once → out on the scoreboard.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — one play-in narrated in thirty seconds, then the single quarter-final your PCs are in. Everything else is a line on the board.

• Run the play-in matches fast and narrate them, then play out the quarter-finals the players' characters are in. Full contact, non-lethal, medical on standby, real stakes for pride only.
• REN + KAZAMA vs TAZATO + ANDO — the match where they discover the forge. Battle Centre III is full of exposed rebar, and Kazama's Metal pulls it out of the walls and wears it. Ren's beam does double damage to metal — but held at a careful ten percent, with his veins burning yellow rather than white, it does not cut Kazama's armour. It heats it. Red, then orange. The next thing Kazama hits, he hits with a fist that is glowing. Neither of them planned this. Let a player find it mid-fight and give them the win for it. Tazato's dragon form makes the arena feel small; Ando talks the entire time and is more frightened than he sounds.
• KINJI + KIBI vs YOSHIBARA + NOMI — four bodies and every loose object in the block against a vine user and a boy who will not stop talking. Kibi builds cover across the floor, slowly, the way he does everything, while Kinji closes on foot — shuffling, sandpaper fists, very nice shoes — and does not use his quirk. Not once. Not even when he is losing, and he hates losing, and he loses a round of it loudly. Kinji should win this fight with footwork, not luck, and somebody in the stands should ask out loud what his quirk actually does.
• CHOZEN + TORAGI vs the play-in winner — Chozen freezes for the first round of every fight, standing still and taking hits while he thinks, and Toragi, the moment a fight starts, speaks exclusively in one-liners. Chozen has written their strategy down, laminated it, and given it to Toragi. In the match, Chozen asks him which side to take. Toragi says "Left." There is no left. Then the wind comes up all at once, pins somebody against a wall, and Toragi hits the same spot twice, and nobody can say it was not a plan.
• IZUTO + ISOKONO vs the play-in winner — Izuto tries to carry it, burns two Recipro Bursts doing it, and stalls in the open, rooted to the spot with his calves ticking. Isokono's tail is the only reason they are still standing at the end: she drags him into the bank vault's shade and somebody in the stands throws a water bottle at him. Masahata offers, loudly, to hose him down for a fee. Izuto knows his partner saved the match. He does not say it. Let the table notice that he does not say it.
• Bose comes down there at least twice.
• Rawagi Chiso is meant to be officiating and is not present. Forge covers for him without comment.
• RAKUKA + HIRO vs MASAHATA + ICHITAKA is the play-in worth narrating rather than skipping, because it is the one Masahata loses. He has himself winning the tournament on a laminated chart and he goes out to a theatrical flyer and a seven-foot machine that has never said a word, and Ichitaka says nothing at all on the walk off, which is worse.
• CLUE TWO — Hiro takes a bad hit in that match. A real one, the kind that gets a wince out of the stands. He does not react at all, does not check it, and gets up. Nobody calls medical over. Everybody in the stands puts it down to him being a machine, which is exactly what it looks like and is not what it is.
• THE FLOOR IS A CHARACTER. Battle Centre III is a city block Forge has rebuilt so many times the rebar shows through in places, and she will tell anybody who asks which repairs are hers and roughly what they cost her in rice. Second-storey windows are glassless. The bank shell has a vault door that does not open and that four separate pairs will try to hide behind.
sections.dmNote:
Competence and comedy, played straight. This is the last chapter where a fight is purely a game, so let the table enjoy winning without cost.

Mechanically, 2v2 is a different animal to a party fight and you should lean into it — smaller initiative order, faster rounds, and every action a player takes visibly affecting exactly one ally. Reward genuine combination play with advantage rather than inventing new rules.

Rawagi's absence is the only plot in the session and should get one line of screen time, maximum. He is a strict teacher who believes he has to be, and a strict teacher who has stopped showing up is information the players will file and forget, which is the intention.

aside.body: Someone will ask why the drill sergeant with a rifle in his arm never uses it in training. The answer is that every shot costs him an inch of hair, he has a hundred inches, and it regrows at an inch an hour. He will explain this at length and with visible pride in his ponytail.
aside.label: Bose's ammunition

sections.developments:
• IF A PAIR SPLITS UP AND FIGHTS SOLO — this is the mistake the whole chapter exists to correct, so let it fail. They lose, Bose comes down there, and nobody is hurt. Do not lecture the player; let Bose do it and let it be funny.
• IF A PLAYER INVENTS A COMBO YOU DIDN'T PLAN FOR — say yes. Give it advantage on the roll and describe it working. Rewarding invention in the first fight sets the tone for sixteen sessions, and this is a training exercise where nothing can go permanently wrong.
• IF THE PCs LOSE EARLY — good, and genuinely fine. Losing pairs spend the rest of the bracket in the stands watching everyone else's mechanics, which is exactly what the antagonist is doing, and the parallel is free. Do not fudge dice to keep them in.
• IF A FIGHT DRAGS PAST FORTY MINUTES — end it. Have Forge call the match on points and move on. Nothing in this bracket is worth a slow hour, and a beginner DM should feel actively permitted to cut a fight short.
• IF SOMEONE ASKS ABOUT RAWAGI'S ABSENCE — Forge shrugs and says he is busy. She does not know more than that. There is nothing to find here yet, and that is not a trick.
sections.treasure:
Winning pairs get nothing material — this is a school exercise and the prize is the bracket itself. What they get is standing.

Track it: any pair that reaches the semi-finals is publicly one of the best in the class, which matters at the Sports Festival, and which the class will feel very differently about in Chapter 4.

Each pair gets ONE piece of equipment built for two people. Keep it simple and mechanical — a shared anchor line, a pair of heat-sink gauntlets, a coolant pack one of them carries for the other, a paired comms set.

Write it on both character sheets, not one. The whole point is that neither of them owns it.

aside.body:
One pound of object per pound of food, minimum half a pound per item, and she has to understand the atomic structure of the thing before she can make it. That is the whole economy and it is worth making concrete at the table, once.

Ten pounds a day is not a joke about appetite. It is a professional requirement, it is expensive, and U.A. pays for it as a line item. She eats during lessons because she has to, is completely unembarrassed about it, and gets genuinely irritated with anyone who treats it as a bit.

Her Sweat Conversion Points build as she works — five per level, and then a rank of Queasy. Students who spend real downtime in the lab will watch her hit that ceiling and keep going, and one of them should eventually tell her to stop. She won't.
aside.label: What Creation actually costs her

sections.heading: Nobara Forge
sections.developments:
• IF PLAYERS ASK FOR SOMETHING COMPLICATED — Forge rolls a Technology or Intelligence check against a DC you set by how exotic it is. On a failure she still spends the calories and produces something unstable: halved range, damage dice one step down, advantage on saves against its effects. She shrugs it off and offers to try again tomorrow.
• IF PLAYERS ASK FOR SOMETHING ABSURD — she says the honest thing, which is that she has to understand its atomic structure to build it. She cannot make you a working phone. She can make you a very good crowbar in four seconds.
• IF A PLAYER CHASES THE FALSEWORK LINE — Forge shrugs and says he's probably busy. That is the entire truth as far as she knows it. Do not reward the follow-up with a clue; the line is there so the players remember it in Chapter 4, not so they solve anything now.
• IF NOBODY REACTS TO THE FALSEWORK LINE — perfect. That is the expected outcome and it costs you nothing.
• IF A PLAYER PUSHES BACK ON HER QUESTION TO IZUTO — she drops it immediately and changes the subject. She asks once. That is how every adult in this campaign handles these kids, and it is worth establishing early.
sections.readAloud:
▶ THE SUPPORT LAB

It smells like a canteen.

THEY SEE — Eleven half-finished sets of paired equipment on the benches. A fridge that is entirely full. A whiteboard covered in what appear to be calorie sums.

Forge is sitting on a bench with her legs swinging and a bowl in her lap, looking at a diagram of Kazama's forearm.

"So the problem," she says, "is that your partner's a blowtorch and you're made of the thing blowtorches are for."

▶ WHEN SHE MAKES SOMETHING

She puts the bowl down and holds out her hand.

Nothing happens for about four seconds, and she looks slightly constipated.

Then there's an object in her palm. It's warm, and it's exactly the thing you asked for.

She picks the bowl back up.

▶ IF SHE OVERDOES IT

She goes grey around the mouth, sits down harder than she meant to, and waves you off before you've finished asking.

"Fine. Fine. It's just sugar. Pass me that."

▶ THE FALSEWORK LINE
HOW TO RUN IT — Drop it into the middle of another conversation. Don't land on it.

"— which is what Falsework used to say, actually. Construction bloke, came and talked to my second-years about load paths. Nice man."

She frowns at a bracket.

"He's not answered an email since April. Rude."

▶ THE THING ON THE BENCH
HOW TO RUN IT — Say it once, in passing, and never look at it again.

There's a forearm on the bench by your elbow. Not a gauntlet. A forearm — palm up, unattached, wrist finished, fingers not.

You've been in this room four times and there's always something like this on the bench. This is the support lab, and about a third of what she builds in here is a piece of somebody.

Forge picks it up, sights along it the way you'd sight down a plank, puts it back, and carries on telling you about load paths.
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — the lab smells like a canteen → each pair brings her an idea → she builds one thing per pair, warm, in four seconds → the Falsework line, thrown away mid-sentence → she overdoes it once and waves it off → out.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — go round the pairs, one item each, and drop the Falsework line on whoever is standing closest. Skip the Technology checks and just give them the gear.

• Forge is the class's gear pipeline and the chapter's warmest presence. Creation runs on food — one pound of object per pound eaten, a minimum of half a pound per item, and she must understand the atomic structure of anything she makes. Complex items need a Technology or Intelligence check against a complexity DC, and a failure produces something unstable that still costs the calories.
• She will build for any pair that brings her an idea. Ren and Kazama get a pair of heat-sink gauntlets: one lets Kazama hold the heat Ren puts into him, the other lets Ren dump his recoil into something that is not his own arm. Chozen gets a genuinely excellent binder cover and is delighted out of all proportion — and then tries to pay her for it, in cash, a great deal of cash, and she makes him put it away. Izuto asks for a coolant pack so he can unstall himself mid-fight, and she asks him, mildly, why he wants to carry it instead of asking Isokono to throw water at him, and then drops it.
• IZUTO KNOWS A SUPPORT LAB. His family build support gear for a living and he has been taking things apart since he could hold a screwdriver. Left alone on her bench for ten minutes he will start fixing something of hers. She lets him. She also watches what he is doing very carefully, and once, quietly, corrects him.
• Her Sweat Conversion Points build as she works — five per level and she gains a rank of Queasy. Students who spend enough downtime in the lab will see her hit that ceiling and keep going.
• Use this section as the recurring downtime frame for the whole campaign. Between chapters, each PC can spend a downtime slot in the lab, the gym, the dorm, or the infirmary. Track it.
• Somewhere in this scene, Forge mentions offhand that a pro called Falsework used to come and talk to her students about construction quirks and hasn't answered his email since spring.
• CLUE THREE — a spare forearm on the bench, unattached, wrist finished and fingers not. Nobody asks what it is for, because a third of what Forge builds in this room is a piece of somebody and the class has been walking past prosthetics and support rigs all term. If a player does ask, she says "spare," and it is the truth and it is the whole answer.
• WHAT CREATION FEELS LIKE FROM THE OUTSIDE. Four seconds of nothing while she looks slightly unwell, and then a warm object. The warmth is the detail players remember — it comes out of her at body heat and cools in your hands over about a minute. Say so once and they will bring it up for four chapters.
• SHE ASKS EVERY PAIR THE SAME QUESTION and it is not about gear: "what does he do that you can't?" Most of them answer about quirks. She is asking about reach, footing and where they stand, and she will keep asking until she gets that answer or gets bored.
sections.dmNote:
Forge exists to make the class feel invested in and to make the equipment part of the story rather than a shopping list. Play her as competent, hungry and slightly too honest.

The Falsework line is the campaign's first real thread and it should be delivered with no weight at all — a teacher complaining about an unanswered email. Nothing more. If a player follows up, she shrugs and says he's probably busy.

The Izuto question is the most important line in the section. She asks it once, gets nothing, and never raises it again. That is how the adults in this campaign handle the students: one honest question, then space.

sections.developments:
• IF A PLAYER STOPS AND LISTENS — do not give them more. The report ends, the channel changes, and that is all. Resist the instinct to reward attention with a clue; the horror of this campaign is specifically that the information was public and nobody's business.
• IF A PLAYER ASKS TO RESEARCH CASE 9 — everything in the public record is in the Appendix's victim list, minus the festival connection. It is thin, it is real, and it goes nowhere. Give it to them freely and let it be a dead end.
• IF A PLAYER TRIES TO ROLL TO NOTICE A PATTERN — there is no check here. Tell them so, kindly, out of character if you like. Nothing is hidden and no roll will produce anything.
• IF YOUR TABLE LATCHES ON HARD ANYWAY — that is fine and does not break anything. The campaign does not depend on them being ignorant; it depends on them being unable to act, which is still true. Move the Chapter 4 archive scene earlier if they are impatient.
sections.dmNote:
This is a deliberate anti-hook. Class 1-A are fifteen-year-olds in the best week of their lives and a serial killer on the news is not their business — the campaign only works if the table experiences that indifference honestly first and remembers it later.

Do not let a player roll to notice a pattern. There is no check here. The information is plain, public, and repeated, and the reason nobody acts on it is that nobody in this dorm has any reason to.

In Chapter 4, when the class rewatches their own festival footage, cut back to this room.
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — one line, mid-conversation, flat → do not pause → somebody changes the channel → carry on with whatever the scene actually was.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — this costs you fifteen seconds and is never the reason a session overruns. It is the one thing in Chapter 2 you should never cut, because it costs nothing.

Drop these across the chapter, one per session, always mid-conversation and never as the focus of a scene. Read the line, do not pause, and move on.

• "—identified as Tsuzuri Hane, the professional hero Falsework, whose body was recovered from an Adachi car park in April. Police have not released—"
• "—the fourth such case this year. The Commission has declined to confirm whether the incidents are connected—"
• "—a Commission spokesperson described the profile as 'consistent with a single individual targeting high-classification quirk users'—"
• "—the file number, Case 9, was leaked to press earlier this month. One tabloid has run the name Appetite across—"
• "—confirming that all five victims held Rare classification or above, and that in each case the injuries were confined to the head—"

If a player stops and listens, do not reward them with more. Somebody else changes the channel, or Masahata starts an argument about the fridge chart, or Rakuka does something theatrical. The information is available and the room is louder than it is.
sections.tag: Slow burn · background plot · woven through sessions

aside.label: Why there is no roll here
aside.body:
A player will ask to roll something. Investigation, Insight, History, anything. There is no check, and the kindest thing you can do is say so out of character in one sentence: "there's nothing hidden here, it's just the news."

The instinct behind the request is good and you should not punish it. The reason the answer is no is that this campaign's horror is not that information was concealed. It is that the information was public, repeated, free, and nobody's business. A dice roll would turn a fact about the world into a secret the players failed to find, and that is the opposite of what this scene is doing.

Six sessions later, in a silent common room with the archive open, the players will remember that they heard all of this and changed the channel. That memory is the entire point and it only exists if you let them change the channel.

sections.heading: The Common Room Ticker
sections.readAloud:
▶ THE TICKER
HOW TO RUN IT — One of these per session. Read it flatly, mid-conversation, and do not pause afterwards.

"— identified as Tsuzuri Hane, the professional hero Falsework, whose body was recovered from an Adachi car park in April. Police have not released—"

"— the fourth such case this year. The Commission has declined to confirm whether the incidents are connected—"

"— a Commission spokesperson described the profile as 'consistent with a single individual targeting high-classification quirk users'—"

"— the file number, Case 9, was leaked to press earlier this month. One tabloid has run the name Appetite across—"

"— confirming that all five victims held Rare classification or above, and that in each case the injuries were confined to the head—"

▶ AND THEN, EVERY TIME, IMMEDIATELY

Somebody changes the channel. Or Masahata starts an argument about the fridge chart. Or Rakuka does something theatrical and loud.

The room is louder than the television. It always is.

sections.heading: Free Time — First Weekends
sections.tag: Free time · the first weekends · between bracket sessions
sections.readAloud:
▶ SATURDAY MORNING

Heights Alliance on a Saturday is half empty by nine. Somebody's gone home. Somebody's still asleep. Kinji's speaker is on in the kitchen playing something nobody chose, and he's telling Ando about it.

THEY SEE — The gate is open. The train into the city takes twenty-five minutes. Nobody has told them they can't go.
ASK THEM — It's the weekend. What do you do?

▶ THE FIRST TIME SOMEBODY WANDERS INTO THE BACKSTREETS

Ikebukuro, west side. Two streets off the main road, where the shutters are down even at noon.

THEY SEE — A white tiger sprayed on one of them, mid-stride, about the size of a car. Three lads in matching tracksuits sitting on a crash barrier underneath it.

One of them points at your U.A. bag.

"Hero course? Go on, then. Prove it."

▶ IF THEY DON'T RISE TO IT

"Thought not," says the one in the middle, delighted, and they go back to their cans.

Nobody follows you. On the way out you notice the tiger is on four more shutters — and that one of them has names under it.
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — go round the table, two slots each → resolve each in a sentence or a roll → play the one that turned into something → back to the bracket.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — skip the window entirely, or give each player one slot and one sentence. Nothing is lost.

• THIS IS THE FIRST FREE TIME AND IT SETS THE HABIT. Keep it light and fast, and let the players discover that they can simply go places. The tone is "first weekend away from home" — the city is big, the class are fifteen, and nothing bad is going to happen to them in it yet.
• WHAT IS OPEN — all of Tokyo, every odd job that does not need fame, and the first side quests: "Hiro's Signs," "A Song for Kinji," "Samitsu's Kitchen," "Whose Milk Is It," "Ren's Phone," "Toragi's Gifts," "The Isobar Tapes," and "Nakata's Gym." They are in the appendix with what they pay out.
• THE TWO QUESTS THAT PAY OFF HARDEST LATER are "Hiro's Signs" (it decides who translates in Chapter 4) and "A Song for Kinji" (it decides what plays in Chapter 5). Put both in front of the players in the first window, casually, as things classmates are doing.
• BYAKKO, AT HEAT 0 TO 3 — Strays and Claws, and nothing above. The likeliest first contacts are the three lads on the crash barrier (Strays — they do not count), Hazama Ritsu ("Ricochet"), who will pick the smallest PC, and the Echo Twins, who are the funniest possible mirror of the bracket the class is fighting all week.
• THE LAW THAT BITES — a first-year who uses their quirk in a backstreet scuffle has committed an offence. Byakko know it, and the Strays will try to bait a quirk out of a PC on purpose. If a PC fights with fists, nothing happens. If they use a quirk and somebody films it, Bose finds out by Monday.
• THE UNDERGROUND IS RUMOURS ONLY. If a PC is out after dark somewhere odd, roll a secret d100: on 01–03 they overhear a rumour from the list in the appendix. That is the entire Underground in Chapter 2.
• PAIRS GET A BONUS. If two bracket partners spend a slot together — any slot, a job, a hangout, wandering — they each get a "pair moment": advantage on one roll in their next bracket match. It costs nothing and it nudges the habit the whole campaign wants.
sections.developments:
• IF A PLAYER WANTS TO PICK A FIGHT WITH BYAKKO — let them, at Heat 0 to 3, and play it as the scrappy, slightly ridiculous street brawl it is. Raise Heat by one if they beat anybody with a stripe in front of witnesses. Strays do not count.
• IF A PLAYER USES THEIR QUIRK IN PUBLIC — play the consequence, not a lecture. A phone was out. On Monday, Bose has it. He does not shout. That is worse.
• IF A PLAYER WANTS TO SPEND EVERY SLOT TRAINING — let them. Three training slots buy one named training benefit on the Chapter 3 pattern, and a player who wants to be good at something deserves to be.
• IF NOBODY WANTS FREE TIME — skip it and go to the next bracket session. Free time is a thing you offer, never a thing you insist on.
• IF A PLAYER ASKS ABOUT THE NAMES UNDER THE TIGER — they are local names, Byakko members and people who beat them. None of them are students. Yet.
sections.dmNote:
The first window exists to teach the table that the city is theirs. Keep each slot to a sentence unless it turns into a scene, and do not let free time eat the bracket — the bracket is the chapter.

The three lads on the crash barrier are the most important thing here. They are funny, they are harmless, and they are the first sight of something that is going to come back stronger every time the class meets it. That escalation is the whole design of Byakko, and it starts with a joke.

aside.label: The first Byakko worth naming
aside.body:
Hazama Ritsu, "Ricochet." Sixteen, skinny, one stripe, desperate for a second. He bounces off things — his joints are rubber — and he narrates his own fights out loud, badly, like a commentator who has never seen a fight.

He will pick the smallest-looking PC, lose, and then follow them to the station asking how they did that. If the PC is kind to him, he turns up again in Chapter 3 as a source; if not, he turns up again with his Fang.

sections.treasure:
Yen from odd jobs, the first relationship-tracker entries of the year, and possibly a named training benefit.

And a white tiger on a shutter, which the players will remember.

A trophy that lives in the 1-A classroom for the rest of the campaign, and a photograph that goes up in the corridor.

Both are props. Refer to the photograph in Chapter 4 and again in Chapter 5. It has everybody in it.
sections.readAloud:
▶ THE SEMIS

Four names left on the scoreboard, and the whole class in the stands — which is somehow worse than the whole country would be.

THEY NOTICE — Forge has stopped eating. It's the first time anyone's seen it.
AND — Bose is quiet too. Which is significantly more alarming.

▶ IF FORGE COMMENTATES ON KINJI
HOW TO RUN IT — Admiring, accurate, and completely casual. She has no idea what she's just said in front of everybody.

"— and watch what he does with the gap. He's not using it. Listed quirk, Jackpot Fever, and he hasn't touched it all bracket. That's footwork. All of it."

A pause.

"Those are very nice shoes he's ruining."

▶ FORGE'S CLOSING REMARK
HOW TO RUN IT — Read it whatever the result.

"Right. Well done. That was better than last year and most of you know why."

She picks the bento back up.

"None of you were the best fighter in here today. Two of you were the best pair. That's the only thing I was measuring."

▶ THE PHOTOGRAPH
HOW TO RUN IT — Take your time. You're going to need this twice more.

Somebody from the school office has a real camera and makes everybody get on the steps. It takes four minutes, because it always takes four minutes.

Hiro's at the end of the back row, a full head above everybody, 🙂 on his screen. Bose is on the other end with his arms folded, the only person facing straight forward. Masahata has got himself into the middle. Toragi's at the back and has been asked twice to stop crouching. Ando has his sunglasses on. Kinji is holding his speaker up to the camera. Aikawa has both hands up.

Somebody's eyes are shut and it won't be clear whose until later.

Forge holds the bento out of shot, which is the only concession she makes to a camera all year.

It goes up in the corridor outside the 1-A room on the Monday. In a frame. At the wrong height.
sections.heading: Semis and the Final
sections.dmNote:
Give this session a genuine ending — a trophy, a photograph, an argument about the fridge chart. The class should finish Chapter 2 closer than they started and pleased with themselves, and the campaign needs that to be real rather than ironic.

Carlos Might's appearance is worth exactly one sentence. He does not speak to anyone and does not stay. If a player goes after him he is already gone, and Kinji, who has been training with him privately for two months, does not mention it — which, for a boy who mentions everything, is the strangest thing that happens all day.
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — four names left on the board → semi one → semi two → Forge stops eating → the final → Carlos Might is in the stands, and then is not → the closing remark → trophy, photograph, fridge chart amended in red.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — narrate both semis to their last thirty seconds, play the final, and give Forge her four sentences. The photograph is the part you cannot skip.

• Play the two semi-finals and the final. Whoever the players are, the final should contain at least one PC pair — if the dice have gone otherwise, let a semi-final be the emotional climax instead and give the final to two NPC pairs the class care about.
• The intended shape: Ren and Kazama reach the final having refined the forge into something genuinely dangerous, and meet either Kinji and Kibi or Chozen and Toragi. All three of those matches are good and none of them need a twist.
• If Chozen and Toragi get here, they get here the way they get everywhere: Chozen frozen for a round, taking hits while he thinks, and then the wind comes up all at once and pins somebody to a wall, and Toragi hits the same spot twice. Toragi has said eleven words all match. Four of them were "Wall."
• If Kinji and Kibi get here, the commentary problem arrives early: Forge, on the microphone, points out to forty teenagers that Kinji has not used his quirk once all bracket. It is admiring. It is accurate. It is the first time it has been said out loud in public. File it.
• Whoever wins, Forge's closing remark to the class is four sentences and the last one is: "None of you were the best fighter in here today. Two of you were the best pair. That's the only thing I was measuring."
• Carlos Might is in the stands for the final. Nobody saw him arrive. He is eating something. He leaves before the end.
• THE PHOTOGRAPH IS A PROP AND YOU WILL USE IT TWICE MORE — once in Chapter 4, on the table, after roll call, and once in Chapter 5. Describe it properly now, with four or five students named and doing something specific. It has everybody in it. Hiro is at the end of the back row, a head above everyone, with 🙂 on his screen, and he is the only thing in the photograph that is perfectly in focus.
• THE STANDS ARE THE WHOLE CLASS and the class is loud. Eliminated pairs have spent an afternoon developing opinions and will share them. Masahata provides unsolicited live analysis from the second row. Nomi Igisa, who is terrified of attention, is the one who started the chant.

aside.body: Better, honestly. A pair that goes out in the quarter-finals spends the rest of the chapter in the stands learning everyone else's mechanics, which is exactly what the antagonist is doing, and in Chapter 4 that parallel is available for free.
aside.label: If a PC pair loses early

sections.developments:
• IF NO PC PAIR REACHES THE FINAL — give the emotional climax to whichever PC match went deepest, and hand the final to two NPC pairs the class enjoy. Yoshibara and Nomi winning the whole thing is a great outcome and Nomi will be mortified about it.
• IF A PC PAIR WINS — let them have it completely. Trophy, photograph, the fridge chart amended in red. Do not undercut the victory with a sting; the campaign needs this to be a real, uncomplicated good day.
• IF PLAYERS GO AFTER CARLOS MIGHT — he is already gone. Not mysteriously; they just turn around and he has left. If they persist, someone mentions he does that.
• IF A PLAYER ASKS KINJI ABOUT CARLOS MIGHT — he says Carlos is teaching him to dance, puts a song on, and will talk about the song for as long as you let him. That is not a lie. It is also the only subject in the world on which the loudest boy in the class goes quiet.

sections.heading: A Question at the Gate

aside.label: Who gets asked
aside.body: Pick an NPC classmate rather than a PC, and pick one the class likes without thinking about it — Isokono Yoromu, or Nomi Igisa, or Ando Iorai. They recover fully within the hour. The recovery is complete and the campaign never revisits it, which is what makes it frightening rather than tragic.

sections.treasure:
No reward. This is the first section in the campaign that gives the players nothing at all, and that is deliberate.

What they leave with is a description — tall, thin, white hair, a scar from forehead to chin, no nose, bleeds from the mouth. Write it on an index card for them. It is the only thing they have for two chapters and they will use it in Chapter 4 when Kuma mentions a stain on a carpet.
sections.developments:
• IF THE PLAYERS ATTACK HIM — they are provisional students, on public ground, attacking a man who has committed no visible offence, in front of prospective parents. Let them do it if they insist. He asks a second question of whoever closes first, takes whatever damage lands without commenting on it, and leaves during the confusion. He is not a combat encounter and cannot be beaten into anything useful.
• IF THE PLAYERS DO NOTHING — entirely correct, and they will hate it. Play the constraint honestly. This is the intended outcome.
• IF A PLAYER ANSWERS THE RIDDLE CORRECTLY — the effect ends instantly and they know exactly where he is standing. Give them that. It is a real reward for a real answer, and it still does not help, because knowing where he is and being allowed to touch him are different problems. (The answer, if you need it: the puddles were ice.)
• IF A PC IS THE ONE WHO ANSWERS — allowed, but it is better on an NPC classmate. If a player insists on answering, let them, and give the five rounds to the player rather than skipping past them: ask them to sit out and watch, and let the table feel the length of it.
• IF THE PLAYERS DEMAND SUGITSU CHASE HIM — he refuses and explains why in one sentence: he cannot leave four hundred students undefended to chase one man, and he does not need to move to follow him. He is right. He is also visibly furious about being right.
sections.readAloud:
▶ THE OPEN DAY
HOW TO RUN IT — Spend a real minute here. The contrast is the scene.

THEY SEE — Trestle tables. A banner zip-tied on slightly crooked, which three separate members of staff have decided is not their problem. A queue for the merchandise stall that hasn't moved in twenty minutes.
AND — Prospective students in middle-school uniform, thirteen years old, trying to look like people who belong here. Their parents asking you questions you don't know the answers to. Somebody's little brother has been sick behind the sports hall.
AND — Bose has been on the west gate since seven in the morning, directing pedestrian traffic with the intensity of a man landing aircraft.

It's a nothing day.

Remember that it was a nothing day.

▶ THE MAN AT THE WEST GATE
HOW TO RUN IT — Slow the pace right down.

He's tall and thin, with a scar running straight down from his forehead to his chin — through where a nose ought to be and isn't.

He's standing outside the perimeter, on the public side, doing nothing anybody could ask him to stop doing.

When a student passes close enough, he says, conversationally:

"Can I ask you something?"

▶ THE QUESTION
HOW TO RUN IT — Say it to the table, out loud. Then wait. However long it takes.

"A man is found dead in a locked room. There are forty-eight puddles of water on the floor and nothing else. No weapon, no marks, no way in or out."

He smiles, and it isn't unpleasant, which is the problem.

"How did he die?"

▶ THE MOMENT SOMEBODY ANSWERS

They get about two words out.

Then they stop, mid-syllable. Their eyes stay open. They go down on the paving like a coat sliding off a chair.

They're breathing. They're warm. There's nobody in there.

Somewhere behind you a parent starts screaming.

▶ HE BLEEDS

A thin line of blood comes out of the corner of his mouth and runs down his chin. He doesn't wipe it away, and he doesn't stop watching you.

He isn't looking at the student on the ground.

He's looking at which of you moved first.

▶ WHEN HE LEAVES

He doesn't run. He turns and walks, at the speed of a man who isn't late for anything, and he's across the road and gone before anybody with the authority to stop him arrives.

▶ AFTERWARDS, IN THE HALL
HOW TO RUN IT — Read this, then end the session.

Nobody sends the visitors home. There's no procedure for it, and the thing that happened doesn't have a name yet. The open day carries on for another forty minutes around a taped-off square of paving.

The student wakes up in Help Woman's office inside the hour, completely and unremarkably fine, and asks what everyone's staring at.

Out at the west gate, a member of the ground staff is already washing the paving. Doing it properly. Getting it all.
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — four hours of a nothing open day → the man on the public side of the west gate → the question, asked to the table, and then silence → somebody answers and goes down → the class cannot legally act → Sugitsu in ninety seconds → he lets him go → Rawagi, four minutes late, already knowing.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — do not cut this one. Cut the open day instead — start at the gate, ask the question, and run it from there.

• This is Riddle. He does not enter the campus, does not threaten anybody, and does not touch anyone. He is inside his rights the entire time and he knows exactly where the line is.
• Question One targets one creature within 40 feet who can hear him. Anyone who attempts an answer becomes braindead for five rounds, or until they succeed on a DC 14 Intelligence check. Answering correctly ends it and instantly reveals his location to the answerer. He can only work one target at a time and the question cannot be unanswerable.
• Give him a real question — something mild, almost pleasant, that a polite student would answer without thinking. The horror is entirely in how ordinary the opening is.
• Whoever answers goes down where they stand, eyes open, breathing, gone. Five rounds is a long time in a crowd of parents.
• He bleeds from the mouth afterwards and does not wipe it. He watches the class react. He is not measuring their strength; he is measuring which of them moves first, and toward whom.
• The class cannot legally engage — provisional students, public ground, a man committing no visible offence. Play that constraint honestly and let it be intolerable.
• Sugitsu Jarvichi arrives inside ninety seconds because he scans the campus perimeter as a matter of routine, and Riddle is already walking. Sugitsu does not pursue. He gets between the man and the students and lets him go, and then has to explain that decision to twenty furious teenagers.
• Rawagi Chiso arrives four minutes later, out of breath, and is the only adult present who is not surprised.
• THE OPEN DAY SHOULD BE BORING ON PURPOSE. Give it four minutes of trestle tables, crooked banners, thirteen-year-olds in middle-school uniform, and Class 1-A being polite at strangers for four hours. The scene does not work if the players walk in braced.
• WHAT HE LOOKS LIKE, IN THIS ORDER — tall, thin, white hair. Then the scar: forehead to chin, straight down, through where a nose ought to be and is not. Then that he is standing entirely still on the public pavement, doing nothing anyone could ask him to stop doing. Give them the details one at a time and let the table assemble him.
• HE IS POLITE THROUGHOUT. He says please. He waits to be looked at before he speaks. When the parent starts screaming he glances over, mildly, the way you would at a car alarm, and then goes back to watching which of the students moved first.
• THE PACE IS THE ENCOUNTER. Slow everything down. Ask individual players what their character is doing while the classmate is on the paving. Let a real silence happen before Sugitsu arrives; ninety seconds is a long time and you should let some of it be felt.
sections.dmNote:
The chapter's turn, and it should be sharp. Six sessions of school and competition, and then a man at a gate asks a polite question and a classmate drops.

Do not let this become a fight. If the players force one, Riddle asks a second question of whoever closes first and leaves during the confusion — he is not a combat encounter and losing to him physically would misrepresent what he is.

Sugitsu's non-pursuit is the important beat. He is right: he cannot leave the campus undefended to chase one man, and his quirk means he can follow Riddle across five miles without moving. He is also, visibly, furious about being right. This is the first crack in 'the safest school in Japan' and it is a hairline one.

End the chapter on Rawagi Chiso, who has arrived too late, looking at where the man was standing, and saying — to himself, not to the students — "He's never done one at a school."

chapters.milestone:
LEVEL 2 when the bracket reaches the semi-finals — the class has learned to fight as twos and the mechanic the campaign is built on is now habit.
LEVEL 3 at the end of "A Question at the Gate," whatever the players did or failed to do. They earn this one by standing still while a man walked away, which is the only time in this campaign that doing nothing is worth a level.
chapters.dmNote:
Play this chapter as if it were the whole campaign. No foreshadowing, no ominous music, no rolls to notice a pattern — Class 1-A are fifteen and this is the best week of their lives, and the table needs to feel that unguardedly before anything is taken from it.

The bracket is doing structural work as well as tonal work. Every session your players spend learning how their pair fights is a session invested in the campaign's central mechanic, and the Sports Festival in Chapter 3 runs pairs specifically because this bracket happened. Reward combination play generously here so the habit is set.

The only plot in the chapter is the ticker and Rawagi Chiso's absences, and both should be handled with almost insulting lightness. If a player chases either thread they should find nothing, because there is nothing to find yet — a busy teacher and a news story that has not got anything to do with a school.

The gate scene is the exception and should be played with total control. Slow it down, keep it quiet, and do not roll initiative.
chapters.title: Ten Pairs

sidequests.name: HIRO'S SIGNS
sidequests.hook: Hiro holds up both hands, makes a shape, and waits. The screen says 🙂. He is going to wait as long as it takes.
sidequests.body: Hiro talks in hand signs and nobody in the class can read more than "yes" and "thanks." A PC can learn properly, from Hiro, who is an endlessly patient teacher; the screen shows 🙂 every time they get one right.
sidequests.reward: they can read him, which makes them the translator in "Lockdown." He will remember who bothered.

sidequests.name: A SONG FOR KINJI
sidequests.hook: "Right. Favourite song. Not a safe one — your actual favourite. And I'm going to listen to all of it, so pick carefully."
sidequests.body: Kinji wants everybody's favourite song. He listens to the whole thing with headphones in, in total silence, and then judges it harshly. Ask the player for a real song.
sidequests.reward: if he likes it (CHA DC 14, or you just like the song), it goes on "the playlist," and in Chapter 5 it is what plays. Also, his friendship, which is loud.

sidequests.name: WHOSE MILK IS IT
sidequests.hook: "It's got no name on it because it's MINE." Masahata has a laminated sheet now. "We're doing a stakeout. Two in the morning. Are you in or are you a suspect?"
sidequests.body: The milk argument has an answer. A stakeout finds it at two in the morning: Forge, in the student kitchen, who needs the calories and is too embarrassed to say she has been raiding the fridge.
sidequests.reward: Forge owes the PC one small build, no check. Nobody else ever finds out.

sidequests.name: SAMITSU'S KITCHEN
sidequests.hook: "I need — " Samitsu stops, and starts again, and is clearly furious with himself. "Tsukiji. Five in the morning. Don't ask me why and don't tell anyone."
sidequests.body: He has entered an amateur cooking competition under a fake name and needs a sous-chef at Tsukiji outer market at five in the morning. He will deny all of it.
sidequests.reward: his bento — once per window, whoever eats it starts their next fight with temporary HP equal to their level — and his friendship, which is rarer than it looks.

sidequests.name: REN'S PHONE
