sidequests.hook: Ren is holding his phone at arm's length like it has bitten somebody. The torch is on. It has been on for two days.
sidequests.body: Ren has owned a phone for weeks and uses it as a torch. Teach him. Comic, patient, real.
sidequests.reward: Ren can use a phone, and in "Ikari Tomonobu, Sixth" the PC who taught him is the one who sits beside him at the archive.

sidequests.name: TORAGI'S GIFTS
sidequests.hook: Toragi is standing by the desks with three wrapped boxes in his bag and has been for a fortnight. He says, with enormous difficulty: "I don't know how to do the words part."
sidequests.body: He has three wrapped gifts in his bag — for Yoshibara, Nomi and Setaka — and has carried them for a fortnight. Help him hand one over, in person, with words.
sidequests.reward: in his next fight beside that PC, one of his one-liners lands at exactly the right moment, and the PC gets advantage on one roll.

sidequests.name: THE ISOBAR TAPES
sidequests.hook: "Twenty minutes nobody has ever seen." The collector taps the case. "Before the fight. When his dad already knew. Sixty thousand yen, and I've got someone else coming at four."
sidequests.body: A collector in Akihabara is selling a bootleg VHS of Isobar's last fight with twenty minutes the broadcast never aired: the minutes before, when his father already knew. Chozen has watched every other tape that exists. Buy it (¥60,000, or haggle), take it, or let it go.
sidequests.reward: whatever is on it, decided with Chozen's player. He learned to fight from footage. So did somebody else.

sidequests.name: NAKATA'S GYM
sidequests.hook: "Put it down." Nakata takes the envelope out of your hand, gently. "You're fifteen and you haven't got a licence. If you help me the way you're thinking, you stop being a hero before you start."
sidequests.body: A retired hero runs a boxing gym in Kurogane Wharf and pays Byakko ¥10,000 a month, and will not let students help, because helping would be illegal. The quest is helping legally: witnesses, the police, a quiet word with the right Fang, or — in Chapter 6 — holding the street.
sidequests.reward: one free training slot per window at Nakata's, and a retired hero's respect.

sidequests.name: THE ECHO TWINS
sidequests.hook: The twins arrive together and speak in order. "You're a pair." — "We're a pair." — "Nobody here will fight us as a pair." — "So."
sidequests.body: Byakko's only pair want a 2v2 against "the festival pairs." The rest of Byakko think it is a joke. It is the best fight in Chapter 2 that is not in the bracket.
sidequests.reward: Heat +1, and if the twins lose they ask, very seriously, how U.A. teaches it.

chapters.dmNote:
Run this chapter for joy and do not undercut it. The victory is real, the class earned it, and the campaign's entire second half depends on the table having genuinely enjoyed this week.

The commentary booth is the most important prop you will use all campaign. Write two lines for every notable moment and deliver them in a different voice, warmly and admiringly, always explaining the mechanism and always explaining the limit. Good sports commentary does exactly this. When the class rewatch their own footage in Chapter 4, every one of those lines becomes a page in somebody's file, and you will not have to say so.

Kuma's attack is a genuine boss fight and a genuine distraction, and both halves need to be true. Let them win it properly. Then end on Sugitsu Jarvichi alone in an operations room at eleven at night, running a clean scan for the fourth time, unable to say what is wrong with it.

The class end this chapter ranked, photographed, interviewed, nationally known, and catalogued. Only the last of those is a problem, and none of them can tell which is which.

sections.developments:
• PICK TWO TRAINING FOCUSES PER PC and write the benefit on their sheet by name. Keep them small and concrete — advantage on one kind of check, a once-per-fight reroll, +10 movement, the ability to take an action while grappled. Players should be able to ask for them by name during the festival.
• IF A PLAYER WANTS TO TRAIN WITH A TEACHER NOT LISTED — say yes and invent the benefit on the spot. Every member of staff has something to teach and none of them will refuse a student who asks.
• IF A PLAYER ASKS KINJI DIRECTLY ABOUT CARLOS MIGHT — he says Carlos is teaching him to dance. He is not lying; the footwork is real. Ask what the dice are for and he puts a song on and asks what you think of the bridge.
• IF A PLAYER FOLLOWS CARLOS MIGHT — he is eating. Wherever they follow him to, he is eating, and he is delighted to see them, and he will not discuss the training room.
• IF YOUR TABLE HATES MONTAGE SESSIONS — compress the whole thing to twenty minutes: everyone names two focuses, you name the benefits, done. Then run Day One of the festival in the same sitting.
sections.dmNote:
A pure downtime session, and worth the slot. The festival is three sessions of high-pressure spectacle and the table will play it better having spent an evening choosing what to get good at.

Give every training benefit a name and let players ask for them by name during the festival. Mechanical generosity here costs you nothing and pays off enormously in Chapter 4, when most of these benefits are the only things that still work.

The Carlos Might and Kinji Hamakida thread should be visible and unexplained. Do not have anyone comment on it. If a player asks Kinji directly he deflects into a song, which is the only time all term the loudest boy in the class deflects anything, and which is the clue.
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — Bose has a whistle → each PC picks two training focuses and you name the benefits out loud → one scene each with three different teachers → Forge fits the final gear → somebody walks in on the training room at the wrong hour → out.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — go round the table twice: each player names a focus, you name the benefit, write it on the sheet. Twenty minutes, then start Day One in the same sitting.

• Run this as structured downtime with real mechanical payoff. Each PC picks two training focuses over the six weeks; each gives a concrete, named benefit they can use in the festival. Write the benefit on their sheet.
• BOSE (Rifle) — conditioning and marksmanship. Loud, precise, effective. Despite carrying a rifle in his own arm he mostly teaches people to fight without their quirks at all, which he considers obvious and everyone else finds strange. Nobody yet understands why this matters.
• YANAMI MAHO (Magic) — mobility. Her Energy Rings give flight to people who have none, and half the class have never been airborne. She is a genuinely excellent teacher and she will accept credit afterwards for improvements she had nothing to do with, cheerfully, in front of the people who actually did the work.
• FRED ENTOSS (Fridas, Cement) — terrain and cover. Sarcastic throughout, on their side throughout. Teaches the class to read a battlefield as a set of things that can be made to fall over.
• SAKI HIYORI (Creed, Deathly Endurance) — endurance. His lesson is being hit. He gets visibly more muscular and his hair gets spikier as the session goes on, which the class find hilarious for about twenty minutes and then stop finding hilarious.
• SUPER PANDA — maths. He is not involved in festival preparation in any way and continues to teach maths with total commitment while the entire school ignores him. Give him one scene. He is delighted that Nomi Igisa did the reading.
• FORGE — final gear. Every pair leaves the lab with one piece of equipment built for two people, and she runs a Technology check for anything complicated. A failure produces something unstable that still cost her the calories, and she shrugs it off.
• CARLOS MIGHT — in the training room with Kinji Hamakida, at hours when nobody else books it, with a great many dice. If a PC walks in on this, he stops immediately, says something warm and evasive, and leaves. Kinji, for once in his life, does not brag about something.
• NAME THE BENEFITS OUT LOUD AND WRITE THEM DOWN. "Bose's Fourth Hour" — once per fight, reroll a failed save against being moved, knocked down or restrained. "Yanami's Rings" — you can spend a bonus action to ignore difficult terrain and fall damage for a round. "Entoss's Reading" — advantage on one check per fight to find cover, footing or a way through a wall. Invent freely and generously; a named benefit is a thing a player will ask for by name in a stadium.
• THE SIX WEEKS SHOULD FEEL LIKE SIX WEEKS. Cut between them — week one everybody is enthusiastic, week three everybody is tired and short with each other, week five Bose stops shouting at one specific student and the class notices and finds it more alarming than the shouting, week six nobody can sleep.
• HIRO'S TRAINING, if a player asks, is with nobody. He books the outdoor track at five in the morning and runs the same route, and Bose has watched him do it twice and has said nothing about it, which for Bose is a form of respect so extreme that nobody else recognises it.
• THE WEEKENDS ARE FREE. Six weeks is six weekends, and this is the first real free time the class has had — see "Free Time — How It Works" in the background pages and the side-quest lists in the appendix. If your table wants a slower Chapter 3, this is where to spend it.
sections.heading: Six Weeks
sections.readAloud:
▶ SIX WEEKS OUT

Bose has a whistle now. Nobody knows where he got it and everybody wishes he hadn't.

The gym opens at five in the morning, because Bose opens it at five in the morning. He's already in it. He's already disappointed in you.

"THE COUNTRY," he explains, at a range of four inches, "IS GOING TO WATCH YOU DO THIS."

▶ IF SOMEBODY ASKS WHY EVERY DRILL IS QUIRKLESS

"Because that's the training."

He doesn't elaborate. He blows the whistle instead — directly at them — and moves on down the line.

▶ SAKI HIYORI'S SESSION

The lesson is being hit. That's the whole lesson.

By the second hour his hair's gone from flat to spiked and there's visibly more of him than there was at nine o'clock. The class find this hilarious for about twenty minutes, and then stop finding it hilarious.

▶ IF A PLAYER WALKS IN ON THE TRAINING ROOM AT AN ODD HOUR
HOW TO RUN IT — Completely straight. No music, no weight on it. Then move on and never bring it up again.

THEY SEE — Lights half off. Two people in there: a very large man in a sombrero, and Kinji Hamakida with his music off, which you have never once seen.
AND — Dice all over the floor. A lot of dice. Kinji is making the same small gesture with his hands, over and over. Every time he makes it, Carlos rolls one.

Carlos stops the moment he sees you. He says something warm and completely evasive, and he leaves.

Kinji looks at you for a long second.

Then he says, very loudly, "Did you SEE the thing on telly last night," and doesn't stop talking about it until you leave.
sections.treasure:
Two named training benefits per PC, written on the sheet, usable for the rest of the campaign.

Be generous. Most of these benefits are quirk-independent, and in Chapters 4 and 5 they are frequently the only things still working when a fight goes badly.

aside.label: What Bose is actually teaching
aside.body: Every class he runs is a quirkless class. He never says why. When somebody eventually asks, in Chapter 5, he says that a quirk is a thing you can be separated from and a body isn't, and then he shouts at them for standing badly.

aside.label: How to write a commentary line in ten seconds
aside.body:
You are going to need about thirty of these across the chapter and they are the most important prop in the campaign. There is a formula and it is three parts.

ONE — name the thing warmly. "Now, that's Kutsu's Engine—"
TWO — explain the mechanism in plain words, the way a good pundit does. "—it's a burst, believe it or not, not a cruise."
THREE — name the limit, because that is what real commentary does and it is what makes the line sound authentic. "Every time he goes full throttle he stalls for a few seconds after, rooted to the spot, unless somebody cools him down."

That is it. Warm, accurate, admiring, and it hands a stranger everything they would need.

Deliver them in a different voice from your narration — slightly faster, slightly more pleased. Enjoy them. The players will enjoy them too, which is the trap, because in Chapter 4 you are going to read these exact lines back word for word into a silent room and you will not have to add a thing.

sections.developments:
• WRITE TWO LINES OF COMMENTARY FOR EVERY NOTABLE THING A PC DOES. This is the single most important instruction in the chapter. Be warm, be admiring, be accurate, and always name the weakness — that is what real sports commentary does. You are building the prop that detonates in Chapter 4.
• IF A PLAYER ASKS WHETHER THE BROADCAST IS ARCHIVED — yes. Publicly, free, searchable, indefinitely. Everyone is pleased about this. Say it cheerfully.
• IF A PLAYER DELIBERATELY HIDES THEIR ABILITIES — excellent, and honour it. Note which PC did it. In Chapter 5, Sylar's read on that character is wrong in one specific way, and you should let it save them once.
• IF A PC PLACES BADLY — it does not matter mechanically and the campaign does not punish it. Everyone advances to Day Two in some capacity; the cavalry battle is the real filter.
• IF THE SKILL CHALLENGE STALLS — cut to the next obstacle. Do not roll out four kilometres. Three set pieces and a finish line is the whole event.
sections.treasure:
Placement, publicity, and a place on Day Two. Nothing physical.

Note every PC's finishing position. It feeds the Chapter 3 closing note and the Chapter 4 archive scene, where the top finishers are also the top of two other lists.
sections.readAloud:
▶ THE TUNNEL
HOW TO RUN IT — The biggest moment of these characters' lives so far. Take your time.

Forty thousand people. You can hear them through the concrete before you can see them.

The tunnel out to the start line is about eighty metres long, and about two-thirds of the way down it the noise stops being a sound and becomes a pressure on your chest.

THEY SEE — Above the gate, on a screen the size of a house: their own face. All of their faces. With their quirks written underneath.

▶ THE START

There's no countdown. There's a horn, and forty first-years go through a gate built for about six.

▶ THE COMMENTARY
HOW TO RUN IT — A different, warmer voice. He's good at his job and he likes these kids. And he always explains the limit as well as the trick, because that's what good commentary is.

"Now, Suzuki's beam pierces cover — but watch his veins. Yellow, he's driving it. If they go white, he isn't. Every shot past twenty percent he pays for out of his own body. He's rationing. Every shot is charge he doesn't get back."

"Kutsu's engines give him a burst nobody on this course can live with. But watch what happens after — he stalls. Two, three seconds rooted to the spot, unless somebody throws water on him. Throw water at that lad and you've done him a favour."

▶ CROSSING THE LINE

Their name goes up on the house-sized screen with a number next to it, and forty thousand people make a noise about it.

For a second you can't hear yourself think, and you wouldn't want to.

▶ THE ONE LINE THE BOOTH GIVES HIRO
HOW TO RUN IT — Say it once, all week. Never correct it.

"—and that's Hiro, also of 1-A. Some sort of construct quirk, I'm told. There'll be somebody in there working it, presumably. Not one for the highlights reel, this — but he's still on his feet, which is more than I can say for a dozen of them."

Then the camera cuts away to something more interesting. So does the commentary. So does everybody.
sections.dmNote:
Play the festival for joy. This is the best day of these kids' lives and the campaign has to earn Chapter 4 by making it genuinely good first.

The commentary is a prop with a second function and you should commit to it fully — write the lines, deliver them in a different voice, enjoy them. When the class rewatches this footage in Chapter 4 and hears their own weaknesses explained to a national audience by a friendly professional, the horror is entirely retroactive and entirely free. Do not tip it now.

If a player asks whether the broadcast is archived, the answer is yes, publicly, indefinitely, and everybody is pleased about that.
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — the tunnel and the noise → the horn, no countdown → the bottleneck → Forge's shifting field → the forty-metre drop → the line, and your name on a screen the size of a house.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — three obstacles and a finish line. Do not roll out four kilometres — and do not cut the commentary, which is the only part of this session that matters later.

• Four kilometres, open campus, all forty first-years, top twenty-four advance. Run it as a skill challenge with three or four set-piece obstacles rather than a full initiative track — the point is spectacle and character, not attrition.
• THE BOTTLENECK — the whole field through one gate. Izuto Kutsu is faster than everyone here and should get to be, once, unambiguously. Domoto Fumiju of 1-B is right behind him and delighted about it.
• FORGE'S FIELD — a kilometre of created terrain that shifts. She built it and she is narrating it and she is enjoying herself enormously.
• THE DROP — a forty-metre gap. Fliers cross it. Everyone else negotiates, and forty thousand people find out which of them is willing to jump.
• THE COMMENTARY — this is the mechanically important part of the session and it is not a mechanic. Every time a student does something notable, the booth explains how it works. Write two lines. Be helpful. Be accurate. Explain the limits, because good commentary explains the limits.
• Suggested booth lines to model the register: "Now, Suzuki's beam pierces cover — but watch his veins. Yellow, he's driving it. If they go white, he isn't, and every shot past twenty percent he pays for out of his own body. He's rationing. Every shot is charge he doesn't get back." And: "Kutsu's engines give him a burst nobody on this course can live with — but watch what happens after. He stalls. Two, three seconds rooted to the spot, unless somebody throws water on him. Throw water at that lad and you've done him a favour." And: "Tadachi — yes, that Tadachi, Isobar's lad — freezes for the first few seconds of everything. Have you noticed? He's thinking. Get him in those seconds or don't bother." And: "Kenji's only as armoured as the ground he's stood on. Put him on grass and he's wearing whatever he walked in with." And: "Hamakida — listed quirk Jackpot Fever, which as far as anyone can tell means very loud music and very nice shoes."
• Sugitsu Jarvichi is running surveillance over the entire venue. He tells staff, twice, that the perimeter is clean. Both times he is telling the truth.
• CLUE FOUR — that booth line is the only sentence anyone says about Hiro on national television all week, and it is a guess by a professional who had four seconds and a name. "There'll be somebody in there working it, presumably" is the truest thing said on air all festival. Nobody corrects it. Nobody has any reason to.
• THE TUNNEL IS THE BEST DESCRIPTION IN THE CHAPTER. Eighty metres of concrete, and a point two-thirds along where the crowd stops being a sound and becomes pressure on the chest. Take your time on it. These are fifteen-year-olds and this is the largest thing that has ever happened to any of them.
• BETWEEN OBSTACLES, CUT TO THE STANDS ONCE. Somebody's family with a homemade banner. A row of agency scouts with tablets. The 1-B contingent, who have been told to cheer for their own and are cheering for good moves regardless of whose they are.
• PLACEMENTS TO WRITE DOWN — every PC's finishing position, and the fact that Hiro comes in twenty-second, because he stopped at the drop and carried two General Studies students across it, one under each arm, while the camera was on somebody else. Not last. Not close to it either. Exactly the position that gets no camera time at all.
sections.heading: Day One — The Obstacle Course

sections.dmNote:
The big, loud, joyful set piece. Keep the pace high and let players narrate their own moments.

The single most important instruction in this section is the Moshita Maro commentary. He is a friendly, earnest 1-B student whose quirk is borrowing other people's, and the booth is going to explain exactly how that works to eleven million people. In Chapter 4 he is the student who does not come back. If the table remembers him warmly it is because you spent four segments of commentary here making them.

The man in the stands is one sentence and then never again this session. If a player specifically watches the crowd, they see a tall man in the upper tier reading the screen with a notebook, which is what about four hundred agency scouts are also doing.
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — teams of four, headbands, twelve minutes → phase one → scoreboard → phase two → scoreboard → the last thirty seconds → one sentence about a man in the third tier who is watching the screen instead of the field.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — one phase and a scoreboard. Keep the Moshita Maro commentary in full; it is the reason Chapter 4 hurts.

• Twelve minutes, teams of three or four, top eight advance. This is where 1-A and 1-B mix properly for the first time and where the rivalries in the roster get their airing.
• Run it in three phases of four minutes with a scoreboard between each. Keep the whole field in play — call out what other teams are doing constantly.
• 1-B highlights: Achi Homei echolocating through the scrum and calling positions for his whole team; Hatashi Hamba being consistently, unglamorously better than everyone at everything; Moshita Maro touching an opponent and wearing their quirk for two minutes, which the booth explains in detail and with enthusiasm; Isosato Sari building solid-air platforms that reshape the field twice.
• Kakita Keiko locks on to Ando Iorai early and does not stop. Their rivalry is scales versus a thrown weapon that cannot miss, and she has been studying his exam footage.
• Let the PCs be brilliant here. This is the last unambiguous win in the campaign.
• THE BOOTH keeps working. Moshita Maro's Copy gets four separate explanatory segments because it is the most televisually interesting quirk in the year. Write at least one of those lines out loud, in full, in a warm and admiring voice.
• Between phases, cut once to the stands: a tall thin man in the upper tier, not watching the field. Watching the screen. One sentence. Do not describe his teeth.
• MOSHITA MARO IS THE INVESTMENT AND THIS IS WHERE YOU MAKE IT. He is earnest, he is friendly, he is a bit funny, and he is quietly ashamed that his quirk is other people's. Give him four things across this session: one moment of real skill, one self-deprecating joke about borrowing, one exchange with a PC that ends with him grinning, and the full commentary segment as written. Everything Chapter 4 costs is priced here.
• THE FIELD IS LOUD AND SHOULD BE NARRATED WIDE. Call out what three other teams are doing every round, by name, whether or not it affects the PCs. Achi Homei calling positions through smoke. Hatashi Hamba quietly being better than everybody. Isosato Sari rebuilding the middle of the field out of solid air, twice.
• HIRO AND RAKUKA ARE ON A SCRATCH TEAM with two General Studies students and come nineteenth of twenty-four, and the booth does not mention them once. If a PC is on their team, Rakuka narrates his own manoeuvres continuously and Hiro spends the whole twelve minutes as the horse — seven foot two of it — at the front, taking every hit aimed at the rider, with 😤 on his screen the entire time.
sections.treasure:
A place in the final eight, and — for whoever performs best — the first approach from a professional agency. Play the scout as friendly, slightly slick, and genuinely impressed.

Agency interest is a reward the class will re-evaluate completely in Chapter 4.
sections.developments:
• IF A PLAYER SPECIFICALLY WATCHES THE CROWD — they see a tall man in the upper tier reading the screen and taking notes, which is exactly what about four hundred agency scouts are also doing. Give them that answer flatly and completely. It is true and it is not a clue.
• IF THE PCs END UP ON THE SAME TEAM AS 1-B STUDENTS — encourage it. Achi Homei calling positions through smoke, or Isosato Sari building a platform under a PC, buys you enormous goodwill for Chapter 4.
• IF A PC IS TARGETED BY MOSHITA MARO — let him take their quirk for two minutes and let it be a genuine problem. Then have him grin and thank them for it afterwards. Every minute of screen time he gets here is worth double later.
• IF THE FIGHT SPRAWLS — run it in three four-minute phases with a scoreboard between each, and narrate everything outside the PCs' immediate reach. Do not track twenty-four individual initiatives.
• IF YOU ARE RUNNING SHORT ON TIME — cut this event to a single phase and a scoreboard. Day Three is the one that matters.
sections.readAloud:
▶ THE CAVALRY BATTLE

Teams of four. Headbands worth points. Twelve minutes.

The field is a hundred metres square and contains twenty-four teenagers who have all decided — independently, simultaneously — that this is the most important thing that has ever happened.

Somewhere in the middle of it, Masahata Shikoji is standing on somebody's shoulders shouting about rankings.

▶ MOSHITA MARO
HOW TO RUN IT — In full, warmly, no rush. It matters in nine sessions.

"And there it is — Moshita of 1-B. That's Copy. He touches you, he gets your quirk, two minutes. Two minutes exactly.

"What I love about this lad is that he's never once hidden behind it. Ask him and he'll tell you straight: it's borrowed. All of it, every time. And he still walks into a scrum of eleven people to get a hand on somebody.

"That takes something the quirk doesn't give you."

▶ THE LAST THIRTY SECONDS

The clock's on the big screen. Everyone on the field can see it and nobody's looking at it, because looking at it costs you a second.

▶ BETWEEN PHASES
HOW TO RUN IT — One sentence. Then straight on to something else.

Up in the third tier there's a tall, thin man who isn't watching the field.

He's watching the screen, and writing something down.
sections.heading: Day Two — The Cavalry Battle

aside.body: Agency scouts are everywhere at the festival, openly, with notebooks and tablets, cataloguing quirks and taking notes on weaknesses. This is completely normal, entirely legitimate, and the reason nobody notices one more man doing exactly the same thing.
aside.label: Scouts

sections.developments:
• IF A PC ANSWERS THE INTERVIEW HONESTLY — let it play brilliantly. Compliments, clips, agency interest. Reward it fully and sincerely. Do not hint that it was a mistake.
• IF A PC REFUSES OR DEFLECTS THE INTERVIEW — note it. In Chapter 5, give that character one moment where Sylar has misjudged them and it saves someone. That is the payoff and it should be explicit at the table.
• IF A PC PAIR IS ELIMINATED EARLY — they watch the rest from the competitor's box with 1-B, which is a better scene than winning. Play Yamaru offering commentary and Hatashi Hamba being quietly generous about their performance.
• IF A MATCH RUNS LONG — call it on points. Forge will do it from the booth without ceremony and nobody will consider it unfair.
• IF PLAYERS TRY TO INVESTIGATE THE THIRD-TIER MAN — Sugitsu's Search says the venue is clean, because it is, because the man's biological registration belongs to somebody else. Give them the honest negative result. This is not them failing; it is the quirk working exactly as documented.
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — eight pairs, one arena → two or three matches in full, the rest narrated → the post-match interview, played as the reward it looks like → the podium, with classifications read aloud → a floor manager fixes a badge error → out.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — run the one match with the deepest rivalry in it, then the podium and the interview. The interview is the trap and it is not optional.

• Eight pairs, single elimination, full contact. The format exists because Forge's class bracket impressed the committee, which means Class 1-A are the reason the festival is like this and everybody knows it.
• The 1-A/1-B matchups draw on the existing rivalries — Kakita Keiko against Ando Iorai, Domoto Fumiju against Izuto Kutsu, Yamaru Todao against Kazama Kenji, Tateta Fumira against Ren Suzuki, Hashige Tataka against Setaka Toko, Isosato Sari against Chozen Tadachi, and Moshita Maro against whoever he has already managed to touch.
• YAMARU vs KAZAMA is the match of the tournament: a man who does not stop against a man who is only as armoured as the room. The arena floor is concrete and Entoss's "good fence" is cement, and there is not a bolt of steel on that floor that Kazama did not carry in with him. Every Metal Counter he throws spends armour he cannot replace, and Yamaru simply keeps going. Play the whole thing as a clock, and let Kazama's player count his own metal.
• REN vs TATETA is two precision shooters at range with nowhere to hide, and Kazama standing in the open, glowing, which is a target the size of a man.
• Run two or three matches in full and narrate the rest. Whoever wins, win or lose, the class comes out of this bracket ranked, named and nationally known.
• THE PODIUM — first, second and third are announced with quirk classifications read aloud. Photographs. Interviews. At least one PC is asked, live, to explain their own limits, and the honest answer is the one that makes them look good.
• Somewhere in the last hour, a floor manager notices that a credentialed medical contractor on the third tier is not on the roster she has, decides it is a badge error, and fixes it in the system.
• CLUE FIVE — everybody comes off that arena floor and goes through the medical tent, because full contact means full contact and it is the rule. Hiro waits outside it holding other people's bags. One sentence, once, in passing.
• CLUE SIX — the post-match interviews. The journalist is warm, quick and good at her job, and she works down the line of competitors, and she does not stop at Hiro, because he cannot answer a microphone and everybody knows it, and the producer in her ear has already moved her on. He does not appear to mind. His screen shows 👍 as she passes.
• TWO INTERVIEWS THAT GO STRANGELY. If Toragi is interviewed, his entire answer to "what's the hardest part of your quirk?" is "Hitting it twice." It is the most-clipped moment of the festival and it is, technically, a complete explanation of his mechanism. Kinji gives the longest interview of the week — four minutes on his shoes, his playlist and a show he watched on Tuesday — and at no point says a single word about his quirk. When she asks him directly, he recommends her a song.
• THE PODIUM IS THE PEAK OF THE CAMPAIGN. Names, quirks, classifications read aloud to forty thousand people and eleven million more. Photographs. A medal that is heavier than it looks. Play it entirely straight and let the players have every second of it.
• THE ARENA IS SMALLER THAN THE STANDS SUGGEST and the stands are much higher than they look from the floor. A student standing on that concrete can see individual faces in the first eight rows and nothing at all above that — just a wall of noise going up.
sections.treasure:
Podium places, medals, photographs, and a stack of agency approach letters that arrive at the school over the following week.

Also: a permanent, public, searchable archive entry for every student, with their name, quirk, classification, and eleven hours of footage. Present it as the prize. It is presented as the prize.
sections.heading: Day Three — The Paired Tournament
sections.dmNote:
The peak. Give the players their trophy, their photographs and their moment, and mean it — this is a victory and the campaign is not being sarcastic about it.

The post-match interview is the trap and it should feel like a reward. A journalist asks a PC, warmly, what the hardest thing about their quirk is, and a good answer is candid and self-aware and plays extremely well. Let it play extremely well. Let the player enjoy giving it.

The floor manager's badge correction is a single sentence delivered to nobody. It is the only thing in this session that matters and it should be completely unremarkable.
sections.readAloud:
▶ DAY THREE

Eight pairs. One arena. Medical on standby — which they say every year, and which starts to sound different once you can see how big the arena is.

THEY SEE — Forge in the booth. Bose at the barrier. Entoss has laid a cement perimeter he keeps calling "the good fence." Yanami is in the air above it with three rings turning slowly.

"PAIRS," says the announcer, to a stadium. "For the first time in the history of this competition."

▶ BEFORE A PC MATCH

The arena floor is closer than it looked from the stands, and the stands are much, much higher.

Across from you, two people you've trained with all year are checking each other's straps and not looking over.

▶ THE POST-MATCH INTERVIEW
HOW TO RUN IT — Play this as a reward, because it is one. She's warm, quick and good at her job, and the microphone is already up.

"Brilliant work out there. Tell me honestly — what's the hardest part of your quirk? What do you have to work around?"

She waits. Eleven million people wait with her.

ASK THEM — And the honest, self-aware answer is the one that's going to play beautifully. So: what do they say?

▶ SOMEWHERE IN THE LAST HOUR
HOW TO RUN IT — Throw this away completely. Do not let the table linger on it.

A floor manager frowns at her clipboard. There's a credentialed medical contractor on the third tier who isn't on her roster.

She decides it's a badge error, and fixes it in the system.

▶ THE MEDICAL TENT, BETWEEN ROUNDS
HOW TO RUN IT — Also thrown away. It's warmth, not foreshadowing.

The tent behind the competitors' entrance has eleven beds in it and all of them are full, because full contact means full contact and there are only so many ways a first-year comes off an arena floor.

Everybody gets looked at. That's the rule, and nobody argues with it, not even Bose.

Outside the tent flap, Hiro is holding two people's bags and waiting.

aside.body: Some tables will have clocked the pattern by now and start guarding what they say. Excellent — let them. A PC who refuses to explain their weakness on camera has genuinely made themselves harder to take, and you should honour that in Chapter 4 by making Sylar's read on them wrong in one specific, survivable way.
aside.label: If the players are cautious

sections.tag: Sports Festival · bracket · 1–2 sessions · full contact

sections.readAloud:
▶ THE NORTH CONCOURSE

Four storeys of glass, escalators and food stalls, with about six thousand people trying to get to their seats.

The noise it makes when a nine-foot man starts growing in the middle of it isn't a scream. It's a sort of collective inhale.

And then the escalators stop.

"RIGHT!" says Kuma, delighted, at fifteen feet and rising. "WHO'S IN CHARGE HERE?"

▶ AS HE GROWS

EIGHTEEN FEET — The handrail of the second-floor balcony comes up to his hip. He puts a hand through a shop front without meaning to and looks briefly apologetic about it.
TWENTY-TWO — His shoulders are into the ceiling struts. There's dust coming down in sheets.

▶ WHEN THE CLASS ENGAGES HIM

"Oh, students! Brilliant. No, genuinely — brilliant. I've never done students."

He's enjoying this enormously. That's the horrible part.

▶ THE CLOCK
HOW TO RUN IT — Say a version of this out loud at the top of every round. It is the encounter.

SECOND FLOOR, NORTH SIDE — About eleven hundred people, and the escalator they're standing on isn't moving.
THIRD FLOOR — Worse.
AND — Somebody's grandmother has sat down on the floor because she can't do the stairs. The crowd is going round her. She's completely calm about it, which is somehow the thing you can't stop looking at.

▶ WHEN HE GOES DOWN

He hits the floor at about eleven feet and shrinks the rest of the way on the way down. By the time anyone reaches him he's a very large man lying on a smashed escalator, complaining bitterly.

"Kids. I got done by kids. Don't tell me who you are. I don't want to know."

aside.label: Kuma in custody
aside.body: He talks freely and knows nothing. He was paid, told where to stand and when to start, and given no reason. He is honest about all of it and mildly offended that nobody has asked him about the fight itself. He is a genuinely useful recurring NPC from here — an incarcerated man with no loyalty to anybody who will answer any question he actually knows the answer to, which is almost none of them.

sections.heading: Kuma at the North Concourse
sections.developments:
• THE REAL PROBLEM IS THE CIVILIANS. Put six thousand people on stopped escalators and make it explicit: every round spent fighting is a round not spent evacuating. Track it out loud. A party that solves the crowd and lets the teachers handle Kuma has played this correctly.
• IF PLAYERS TRY TO STOP HIM GROWING — reward it heavily. Anything that denies him room, breaks his footing, or interrupts the growth is worth more than damage. Say yes to improvised ideas here.
• IF THE FIGHT IS GOING BADLY — Entoss and Yanami are on scene and are extremely capable. Have them take pressure off without taking the win. A beginner DM should feel free to use teachers as a difficulty dial in either direction.
• IF THE PLAYERS ASK WHY HE'S HERE — he does not know, and says so, repeatedly, while being restrained. He is not being cagey. He was paid and told where to stand.
• IF THE PLAYERS SUSPECT A DISTRACTION — they are right, and there is nothing they can do about it tonight. Let them be right and let it not help. Sugitsu will confirm the perimeter was clean, honestly, because it was.
sections.dmNote:
The chapter's climax, and it is a lie. Run it as a proper boss fight — big, loud, funny, dangerous — and let the class win it in front of the country.

Then end the session on Sugitsu Jarvichi in an empty operations room at eleven at night, running the scan again. He is not celebrating. He knows exactly how good his quirk is and he knows what a clean sweep costs, and something about the shape of tonight is wrong in a way he cannot yet name.

Do not explain the badge, the contractor, or the biological marker. The players have been given every piece and the arithmetic is theirs to do, in Chapter 4, at the worst possible moment.
sections.treasure:
Public credit, on every channel, that evening. The class beat a named villain in front of the country and nobody died — forty-one injuries, none critical.

And a prisoner. Kuma in custody is the campaign's most useful recurring asset and the players earned him here.
sections.tag: Sports Festival · boss encounter · the distraction
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — six thousand people on stopped escalators → a nine-foot man starts growing → put the civilian clock on the table out loud → the class fights, Entoss routes, Yanami lifts → deny him room and he comes down → then Sugitsu, alone, at eleven at night, running the scan again.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — the concourse, the clock, and the fight. Skip the arrests and go straight to Sugitsu in the operations room, which is the actual end of the chapter.

• Kuma. Gigantification, 9'5" at rest, up to twenty-five feet at peak, with strength, durability and reach scaling as he grows. Overconfident, loud, tactically hopeless, genuinely enjoying himself, and carrying no particular malice — this is a job and he is good at it.
• THE ENCOUNTER'S REAL PROBLEM is not Kuma, it is six thousand civilians on stopped escalators in an enclosed concourse. Every round the class spends fighting is a round they are not evacuating. Make that explicit and put it on a clock.
• DENY HIM ROOM. At full size in an enclosed space he is a natural disaster; the concourse ceiling is his enemy as much as theirs. Smart play is to force him into a stairwell, or bring the ceiling low, or simply not let him finish growing. Reward every attempt to control his size over damaging him.
• FRED ENTOSS arrives fast and turns the concourse into a maze — Cement Wall gives twenty feet of three-quarters cover, and he uses it to route civilians rather than to attack. He is sarcastic the entire time and he is also visibly rationing: his uses are capped by his Constitution modifier and going past them costs him force damage and a level of exhaustion he cannot reduce.
• YANAMI MAHO is overhead moving civilians with Energy Rings, and Momentum Lock stops Kuma's arm mid-swing once, spectacularly, in front of a live camera. She will later describe the whole incident in a way that gives her more of it than she had.
• Kuma loses. He is meant to lose. He is furious and humiliated and says so continuously while being restrained, and complains that he wasn't even told what it was for.
• Nobody dies. Forty-one injuries, none critical. It reads, on every news broadcast that evening, as a triumph.
• SUGITSU JARVICHI was tracking the perimeter, the gates and the service tunnels throughout. He caught Kuma the moment he entered and dispatched staff correctly and quickly. He did not catch the credentialed medical contractor on the third tier, because that man's biological markers were registered to somebody else — a known limit of Search that is written into its own file and that somebody had read.
• PUT A NUMBER ON THE CLOCK AND SAY IT EVERY ROUND. Start at six thousand people in the concourse and take three or four hundred off it for every round the class spends on evacuation, routing or crowd control, and none off it for a round spent doing damage. Say the number out loud. The party will start solving the right problem inside two rounds and they will have worked it out themselves.
• KUMA IS FUNNY AND THAT IS LOAD-BEARING. He apologises for the shop front. He asks a student their name and then says not to tell him. He is having the time of his life and he is standing on an escalator full of civilians, and holding both of those in the same scene is the whole tonal exercise of this campaign in one fight.
• THE CEILING IS HIS ENEMY. Past about twenty feet the struts are on his shoulders and he is fighting the building as much as the class. Any player who works this out and starts forcing him upward instead of hitting him has solved the encounter — reward it heavily and let it be the winning move.
• THE CLASS HAS EXACTLY THE TOOLS FOR THIS, and it is worth reminding yourself before the session. Samitsu can grow an arm forty feet tall out of any surface he has touched, and he has touched the concourse floor. Chozen's wind pushes a growing man into the ceiling struts. Kazama can strip the steel out of a stopped escalator and wear it. Hiro can stand under a falling sign and not notice. Nakaya's lightning loves an escalator. None of these are hints for the players — they are permission for you to say yes.

sections.treasure:
Agency approach letters, a trophy, a corridor photograph, and a national profile.

Every one of these is a genuine reward and every one of them is also a line in somebody's file. Do not tip the second half. The players should re-read this list in Chapter 4 themselves.
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — the archive goes live Monday → a genuinely lovely week, played warm and at length → Okuma arrives and disagrees with Sugitsu, politely → Friday morning, Rawagi asks who gave interviews → "Right" → he teaches the lesson → out on the archive page.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — the good week in five minutes, then Rawagi's question. Do not cut the good week entirely; the question needs something to land on.

• A short session to bank the win and turn the corner. Agency interest, scouting letters, phone calls home, a genuinely lovely week.
• Rawagi Chiso (Instinct) finally becomes a real presence. Dry, poor at conversation, strict because he believes he has to be, and openly bad at hiding which students he prefers. He has been on the Case 9 investigation since April and he has just seen four of five victims' festival footage lined up next to the depth of their post-match interviews.
• He does not tell the class any of that. He asks who gave interviews, notes the answers, and leaves. It is the single most alarming thing an adult has done all year, precisely because he offers no explanation.
• INSPECTOR OKUMA SHIZUKA of the Commission's Serious Incidents division arrives on campus the same week and is politely, immovably at odds with Sugitsu Jarvichi about whether a school is a suitable environment for an active investigation. She thinks it is not. He thinks she is underestimating his quirk. They are both right and neither will move.
• If the players go looking, the Case 9 material is publicly available in outline: five victims, all Rare-class or above, all found with the cranium opened and nothing else disturbed. What is not public, and what Rawagi has, is that four of the five competed in a Sports Festival.
• End on the archive page. Whatever the PCs' placements were, they are on it, with their names, their quirks, their classifications, and eleven hours of searchable footage explaining exactly how they work.
• PLAY THE GOOD WEEK AT LENGTH AND MEAN IT. Letters. Phone calls home, and let players narrate those. A second-year who has never spoken to them says well done in a corridor and keeps walking. Somebody's mother has printed the bracket out and laminated it, which Masahata regards as vindication of a principle.
• AGENCY LETTERS ARRIVE BY NAME. Read two of them out. They are flattering, slightly template, and specific enough about a student's performance to prove somebody watched the footage properly.
• RAWAGI'S QUESTION IS THE HINGE AND IT NEEDS SILENCE. Come in late, do not sit down, ask it flatly, and then actually wait at the table until a player answers. Count the hands. Look at each of them for slightly too long. Say "Right." Then teach the lesson and do not refer to it again.
• HIRO PUTS HIS HAND UP FOR NOTHING, because he gave no interviews and placed nowhere, and Rawagi's eyes go past him the way everyone's do. He is the only student in the room who is not on any of the lists being drawn up that week, and this is the last time that will be a small thing.
• THE OTHER LIST. The same week, somebody spray-paints a white tiger on the wall opposite U.A.'s west gate, with the festival podium names written underneath in the same white paint. It is not Appetite and nobody in this chapter should think it is for long — it is a street gang called Byakko, and it means that the strongest first-years in Japan have just been noticed by people who rank each other by who beat whom. See "Free Time — Famous for a Week."
sections.dmNote:
The turn. Play the whole session warm — this is a good week and the class have earned it — and put the cold at the very end.

Rawagi's question is the hinge of the campaign. He asks it flatly, gets his answer, says "Right," and goes. No explanation, no reassurance, no follow-up. If a player chases him down the corridor he says that he is not able to discuss it and that they should not give any more interviews, which is both entirely correct and completely useless.

The last image of the chapter should be the archive page itself, open on somebody's phone in the common room, with the ticker running in the background.
sections.developments:
• IF PLAYERS CHASE RAWAGI DOWN THE CORRIDOR — he says he is not able to discuss it and that they should not give any more interviews. Both true. Both useless. He will not budge and he is visibly unhappy about not budging.
• IF PLAYERS RESEARCH CASE 9 NOW — give them the public record in full: six victims, all Rare or above, all found with the cranium opened. The festival connection is NOT public. Rawagi has it. Okuma has it. Nobody else does.
• IF YOUR TABLE WORKS IT OUT THIS SESSION — completely fine, and it does not spoil anything. Move the Chapter 4 archive scene forward and let them be the ones who tell the staff. The chapter works just as well with the class ahead of the adults.
• IF NOBODY GAVE AN INTERVIEW — Rawagi asks who placed in the top eight instead, which produces the same list and the same silence.
• END THE SESSION ON THE ARCHIVE PAGE open on somebody's phone, with the ticker running in the background. Then stop. Do not add a sting.

aside.body:
Worth being concrete, because the players are going to re-read this page in Chapter 4 and you want it to have been real.

Every first-year has a page. Name, class, quirk name, classification, height, and eleven hours of indexed footage across three days — every heat, every scrum, every match, with the professional commentary track on by default and a search box that works.

It is free. It requires no account. It is archived indefinitely, as every year's is, because taking it down would be strange and nobody has ever had a reason to want it gone.

The commentary is the part that matters, and it is good commentary, which is exactly the problem. Eleven million people had the mechanism and the limit of forty teenagers explained to them by a professional, warmly, at length, with examples.

Four of the five Case 9 victims are in an archive exactly like this one.
aside.label: What is actually on the archive

sections.readAloud:
▶ MONDAY

The festival archive goes live. Full footage, all three days, every match, with commentary. Searchable by student and by quirk.

By Wednesday, Class 1-A's placements are on the fridge in Heights Alliance, under Masahata's original prediction, which he's annotated with the words "BROADLY CORRECT" in red.

▶ THE GOOD WEEK

Letters. Phone calls home. A second-year you've never spoken to says well done in a corridor and keeps walking. Somebody's mother has printed the bracket out.

It is, without qualification, the best week any of you have ever had.

▶ THE ARCHIVE, THE FIRST TIME SOMEBODY OPENS IT
HOW TO RUN IT — Warmly. This is a good thing, made by people who cared about it.

It's genuinely well made. Somebody's done a proper job.

Every student has a page: name, class, quirk, classification, height. Eleven hours of footage indexed by event and by round, commentary track on by default, and a little search box at the top that works properly.

Masahata has already found his own page and is reading the view count out loud to a room that's asked him twice to stop.

▶ RAWAGI CHISO, FRIDAY MORNING
HOW TO RUN IT — Flat. No preamble, no explanation, and no answer afterwards.

He comes in late, which he never does. He doesn't sit down.

"Before we start. Which of you gave interviews?"

Nobody says anything, so he waits.

ASK THEM — One by one, hands go up. Whose goes up? He looks at each of them for slightly too long.

"Right," he says.

And then he teaches the lesson.
sections.heading: The Results
Free Time — Famous for a Week
sections.tag: Free time · the week after the festival · between sessions
sections.readAloud:
▶ THE FIRST TIME SOMEBODY RECOGNISES YOU

A girl of about twelve on the Yamanote line. Staring. Then whispering to her mother. Then — after a visible struggle — holding out her phone.

"Sorry. Sorry. Are you — from the festival?"

The whole carriage turns round.

▶ THE WEST GATE, TUESDAY MORNING

THEY SEE — A white tiger on the wall opposite U.A.'s west gate that wasn't there on Monday. Beautifully done. Under it, in the same white paint, the names from the festival podium.

Bose is standing in front of it with his arms folded, looking at it the way he looks at a student who has stood badly.

▶ SWING TOWN

A batting centre in the backstreets. Eleven cages, and a vending machine that only sells corn soup.

A very large, gentle young man is showing a nine-year-old how to hold a bat. He looks up, sees the uniforms, and smiles like Christmas has come early.

"Oh, brilliant. You're the festival lot. There's a cage out the back. Friday night."

A pause.

"Bring friends."
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — the good week from "The Results," and in it, one window of two slots each → the class discover they are recognised everywhere → the tiger on the west-gate wall → Byakko come to look → back to the spine for Rawagi's question.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — the tiger on the wall, and one Byakko scene. The fame can be a sentence.

• FAME CHANGES WHAT FREE TIME IS. The class are recognised on trains, in shops and in the street. Odd jobs that trade on a face open up — modelling, an event appearance, a sponsor's photo shoot — and pay well. Wandering unnoticed stops being possible. Every slot spent in public gets a little crowd.
• THE TIGER ON THE WALL is Byakko's answer to the festival, and it is an invitation rather than a threat. The podium names are under it. If a PC is on the podium, their name is on that wall, in white, and the whole school walks past it twice a day.
• BYAKKO COME TO LOOK, at Heat 3 to 5. A Fang comes to see the festival winners: Dōmeki Daigo ("Brick") with an invitation to Friday's Ring at Swing Town, or Saeki Momo ("Hairpin"), who wants to race Izuto and nobody else. If Heat is already high, Ibuki Kōsuke — Three-Stripe Kō — turns up instead, with a notebook, quoting the festival commentary at them word for word. Play that last one lightly: it is a schoolyard echo of the thing that is coming in Chapter 4, and the table should only notice it afterwards.
• THE RING. Friday nights in the cage behind Swing Town: one-on-one, a circle of witnesses, a purse of ¥25,000 to ¥85,000 for a win, and a stripe for anybody who beats a member. It is an unlicensed fight, quirk use in it is an offence, and Bose will find out. It is also the most fun a PC can have in this chapter. Every Ring fight is +2 Heat.
• NEW SIDE QUESTS — "The Agency Letter," "Kazama's Mum," "Izuto's Uncle," "The Byakko Kid," "Yanami's Credit," and "Madame Tsuru's Die." See the appendix.
• THE UNDERGROUND IS STILL RUMOURS ONLY. Fame does produce more of them — people tell famous teenagers strange things. A PC out after dark rolls the secret d100 at 01–05 for a rumour.
• FAME IS DOCUMENTATION. Every photo with a fan, every sponsor shoot, every appearance is one more picture of a student and their quirk on the internet. Do not say this. Chapter 4 will.
sections.developments:
• IF A PC FIGHTS IN THE RING — run it as a proper one-on-one with a crowd, using the Byakko presets. Win or lose, the crowd decides what it was worth: a stripe, a purse, or a story. Raise Heat by two. Then, on Monday, have Bose say one sentence about it and nothing else.
• IF A PC BEATS A FANG IN FRONT OF WITNESSES — under the Stripe Law they now hold two stripes. Byakko treat them as a Fang: free food in Byakko-protected shops, nods in the street, and somebody with one stripe who would like to fight them for it. See "The Rank You Didn't Ask For" in Chapter 6 for where that goes.
• IF THE CLASS WANT THE GRAFFITI GONE — the ground staff paint over it on Wednesday. It is back on Friday, better.
• IF A PLAYER CONNECTS THE TIGER TO APPETITE — let them suspect it for exactly as long as it takes Kuma, Okuma or Rawagi to say flatly that it is a street gang. Do not let the side plot steal the spine's dread.
• IF A PC REFUSES EVERY FAN AND EVERY CAMERA — note it, the same way you noted interview refusals. It is the same instinct and it is worth the same reward in Chapter 5.
sections.dmNote:
This window sits inside "The Results" and should feel like the best week of the class's lives, slightly too much of it. Fame is fun. Byakko are fun. Let both be fun.

The one craft instruction: the cheerful ways the class get documented this week — selfies, shoots, a Stripe with a notebook who has watched their footage — are the comic version of what the archive is about to mean. Play them straight. The table will do the arithmetic in Chapter 4, and it will land harder for having been funny first.

aside.label: Madame Tsuru and the loudest boy in the class
aside.body:
If Kinji is anywhere near the backstreets this week, the old woman who runs the Lucky Seven dice den will spot his shoes from across a street and want to talk to him. She has read his quirk on the festival page — "Jackpot Fever" — and she has a die she would like him to roll.

He will not roll it. Carlos told him not to spin where people can see, and the den is full of people. Watching the most show-off student in the class refuse a gambling grandmother's dare, politely, three times, is one of the best Kinji clues the campaign has.

sections.treasure:
Fame, which is a real reward and a real problem. Yen from better-paying jobs. Possibly a stripe.

And a white tiger on the wall opposite the school, with names under it.

chapters.intro: Six weeks of training and three days of the biggest broadcast in Japan. The obstacle course, the cavalry battle, and — for the first time in the competition's history, because Forge's class bracket impressed the committee — a paired tournament, with every 1-A and 1-B rivalry in the roster getting its match. Forty thousand people in the stands and eleven million watching a professional commentary team explain, helpfully and accurately and at length, exactly how every student's quirk works and exactly where it fails. Halfway through the third day a nine-foot man starts growing in the north concourse and the class beat him in front of the entire country. Nobody dies. It reads as a triumph on every channel that evening. The archive goes live on Monday, searchable, free, and permanent.
chapters.title: The Shortlist
chapters.milestone:
LEVEL 4 at the end of "Six Weeks," so the training benefits and the new tier arrive together and the festival is played by people who feel upgraded.
LEVEL 5 after Kuma goes down in the north concourse. They beat a named villain in front of the country; give it to them on the night, in front of everybody, before the chapter turns cold.

closing.body:
Eleven hours of footage. Forty first-years. Every quirk demonstrated repeatedly, under pressure, at range, against varied opposition, with professional commentary explaining the mechanism and the weakness, because good commentary explains the weakness. Free to watch. Searchable by student and by quirk. Archived indefinitely.

Four of the five Case 9 victims are in an archive exactly like it. Rawagi Chiso worked that out on the Tuesday and has told nobody except Inspector Okuma, who has told nobody at all, because the alternative is telling four hundred students that the most important week of their lives was a shop window.
closing.label: Chapter Note — The archive

sidequests.name: KAZAMA'S MUM
sidequests.hook: Kazama's mother is in the corridor holding a tin of something, and Kazama has gone somewhere else entirely. "I'm sorry — I don't actually know what any of this is. Would you show me round?"
sidequests.body: Mio Kenji visits after the festival. She never wanted this. Kazama is unbearable all day. A classmate shows her round.
sidequests.reward: one honest conversation between mother and son, if his player wants it.

sidequests.name: IZUTO'S UNCLE
sidequests.hook: Izuto has had the sleeve on the bench for three days. "It's fine," he says. "There's a fault and I'll find it." He will not find it.
sidequests.body: His uncle's support company offers a sponsorship if Izuto tests their prototype coolant sleeve. It has a fault Izuto cannot find on his own. The only solution is asking somebody else to look.
sidequests.reward: the Prototype Coolant Sleeve (once per short rest, end your own stall as a bonus action) — but only if somebody else found the fault.

sidequests.name: THE AGENCY LETTER
sidequests.hook: "Blazewatch. Tokyo's number one." The letter is on real paper. "One day, shadowing, Shibuya. We'd love to have you — and there will be photographers, I won't pretend otherwise."
sidequests.body: Tokyo's top-ranked hero wants a PC for a day's shadowing in Shibuya. It is real, it is flattering and there are cameras everywhere.
sidequests.reward: ¥15,000, a contact for life, and one more set of photographs on the internet.

sidequests.name: THE BYAKKO KID
sidequests.hook: He's fourteen and he's been following you for two streets and he finally says it all at once: "How do I get strong? The Cage takes anybody. I asked."
sidequests.body: He saw a PC at the festival and wants to be strong, and the only ladder he can see goes up the Cage. Talk him out of it, take him to Nakata's, or help him prepare for the U.A. exam.
sidequests.reward: a kid who does not climb the Cage. In Chapter 6 he is the one who tells the class where the White Tiger eats.

sidequests.name: YANAMI'S CREDIT
sidequests.hook: On the screen, Yanami Maho is describing your rescue at the north concourse. She is describing it as hers.
sidequests.body: She gave an interview taking credit for a PC's rescue at the concourse. Confront her, or do not. She is lonely and knows it.
sidequests.reward: a private Energy Ring lesson — a training benefit: once per fight, fly 10 feet until the end of your turn.

sidequests.name: MADAME TSURU'S DIE
sidequests.hook: Madame Tsuru puts the die on the table between you. "The loud boy with the shoes. I want to watch him roll it once. You'll ask him for me."
sidequests.body: She wants Kinji to roll her die. He will not. She asks a PC to persuade him; he never agrees before Chapter 5.
sidequests.reward: a Byakko Stripe who will answer questions. After Chapter 5, Kinji goes back and rolls it. Natural twenty.

sidequests.name: ADACHI WANTS IN
sidequests.hook: "I can fold myself through a letterbox," says Adachi Yui, folding herself through something. "General Studies. I want the transfer. Coach me."
sidequests.body: Fold-A-Body; she wants the Hero Course transfer and needs coaching for the practical.
sidequests.reward: if she passes, she can fold herself through a ventilation grille at the Shirahige cold store and open a stairwell door from the inside.

sidequests.name: DOJIMA ON THE ROOF
sidequests.hook: "Shiketsu," he says, from the dorm roof, upside down, about four feet off it. "Zero Gravity. One round. Nobody has to know."
sidequests.body: A Zero Gravity user challenges a PC to an off-the-books spar on the dorm roof. Bose catches them, unless it is spectacular, in which case he watches first.
sidequests.reward: a rival.

sidequests.name: HANA'S LESSONS
sidequests.hook: "Teach me to be a hero." Ryuto Hana is nine. "Not the quirk bit. I know you're not allowed. The other bits."
sidequests.body: A Kurogane Wharf kid wants a hero to teach her. Provisional students cannot train minors in quirk use, so teach her everything else.
sidequests.reward: a friend at the wharf — and later the first person to tell a PC about the grey people at the docks.

sidequests.name: TOBE MIYU'S EXERCISE BOOKS
sidequests.hook: Tobe Miyu has three exercise books held against her chest and one stripe on her forearm, and she is at the U.A. gate at seven in the morning. "Somebody's asking about these. Can I leave them with you? Just for a bit."
sidequests.body: A sixteen-year-old Claw who cannot fight keeps the gang's entire accounts in three exercise books, and somebody has started leaning on her about them. Help her and she gives the class the backstreets' whole economy.
sidequests.reward: everything in "the turf economy," and a Claw who will answer her phone at three in the morning.

sidequests.name: YANAGI'S SECOND ATTEMPT
sidequests.hook: Yanagi stops mid-drill, perfectly still, and then carries on. Later, at the vending machine, he says it to the floor: "I sat it twice. The exam. At fifteen."
sidequests.body: The best technician in two wards failed U.A.'s entrance exam twice at fifteen. He is twenty-one, the general-studies transfer route is still open to him, and he has never once said any of this out loud.
sidequests.reward: if he applies, he gets in, and Byakko lose their teacher, and he will not thank the class for about a year.

closing.label: Chapter Note — What it cost
closing.body:
Powder is dead, properly this time, and the crater in the loading yard will be fenced off for a year. Saki Hiyori is out of hit dice and in a bed he will not stay in. Touch up got away, or didn't, depending on how fast the class worked it out. Three students were taken; one came home and cannot say what happened.

And Moshita Maro is not on the roll. Copy — a quirk that borrowed other people's, belonging to a boy who was quietly ashamed of that and determined not to let it define him. He got four separate segments of admiring commentary during the cavalry battle. It was the best television of the week.

chapters.milestone:
LEVEL 6 after "The Crows" — the chapter's one clean win, and the right place to hand out something good.
LEVEL 7 at the end of "Saki Hiyori Stands in Front of It," and do it quietly. Roll call first. Level after. Do not let a level-up be the thing that closes that session.

sections.heading: Ikari Tomonobu, Sixth
sections.treasure:
Information, and it is the worst kind. The class now have the pattern, and the pattern is a list they are on.

Give them a physical prop: the six victims written out, with festival placements next to five of them. Add their own placements underneath in the same handwriting.
sections.developments:
• LET THE CLASS SOLVE THIS THEMSELVES. Do not have a teacher explain it. The horror is that the shop window was theirs and they built it enthusiastically, and that only lands if they open the archive.
• IF A PLAYER ASKS WHO THE TEN ARE — Sugitsu answers immediately and honestly, and the list is the ten students with the most broadcast footage. Which is the ten who did best. Say it plainly and let the table do the arithmetic.
• IF THE CLASS DEMANDS TO BE LET OUT — no. Sugitsu is immovable and correct. Okuma wants them dispersed off-campus entirely and Sugitsu is refusing that too. Let the players hear the adults disagree in front of them.
• IF A PLAYER SPOTS THE ONDO KASUMI EXCEPTION — victim two never competed. Excellent catch, and there is no answer yet. Rawagi does not have one either and says so. It resolves in Chapter 5: Sylar wanted that quirk enough to do the work without a manual.
• IF YOUR TABLE IS SHAKEN AND WANTS TO STOP — that is a good moment to check in out of character. See the "Safety, and the horror dial" appendix. Nothing in this campaign is worth pushing a table through.
sections.dmNote:
The chapter's opening should be the coldest twenty minutes of the campaign, and almost all of it is a room full of teenagers watching television.

The rule here is that you have already done the work. Every line of commentary you wrote in Chapter 3 is now evidence, and re-reading it verbatim is more effective than any new description you could write. If you skipped the commentary earlier, this is where that decision costs you, so bank it now if you have not.

Do not let an adult solve the puzzle. The class must be the ones to open the archive, because the horror is specifically that the shop window was theirs and they built it enthusiastically.

Sugitsu's ten permanent Search slots is the line to land hardest. He is doing exactly the right thing. He is also a man who has decided which ten children he can guarantee, out of four hundred, and he says it out loud without appearing to notice what he has said.
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — the sixth one is on the news before school → somebody says "wasn't he at ours?" → the class opens the archive themselves → twenty minutes to confirm five of six → then they scroll to this year → read your own Chapter 3 commentary back, word for word → Sugitsu closes the campus that afternoon.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — the news, the archive, and your own commentary read back. That is the whole session and it does not need the rest.

• The class works it out themselves. Do not have an adult explain it. Six victims, and somebody remembers that one of them competed at a Sports Festival, and then somebody opens the archive.
• Within twenty minutes they have five of six confirmed as festival competitors. It takes them another ten to find the commentary segments. It takes Chozen Tadachi about ninety seconds after that to say the thing nobody wants said, because he has been running this arithmetic since Rawagi asked who gave interviews.
• Play the archive scene properly. Put their own footage on. Read back the commentary you wrote in Chapter 3 — the same warm, admiring, accurate lines — in the same voice, in this room, in this silence.
• REN SUZUKI CANNOT WORK THE ARCHIVE. He grew up in the mountains without so much as a television and has owned a phone for eleven weeks. Somebody has to show him how to scroll to his own page, and then sit next to him while it plays. If a PC taught him the phone in free time, it is that PC, and it should be.
• Ondo Kasumi, victim two, is the exception: never competed. This is the hole in the theory and the class will worry at it. The answer, which they will not get until Chapter 5, is that he wanted her quirk badly enough to do the work without a manual.
• RAWAGI CHISO confirms it when asked directly, because lying to them now would be worse. He is not authorised to and does it anyway, and it visibly costs him something. He also tells them the part that matters: the Commission's profile says the killer selects for power, and the profile is wrong, and he has been saying so since June.
• SUGITSU JARVICHI's response is immediate and correct: campus lockdown, no student off-site unaccompanied, his own Search running permanently on every one of them. He stores ten individuals permanently and he uses all ten slots on students. He tells them this. It is meant to be reassuring and it is the most frightening thing they have ever heard a teacher say.
• INSPECTOR OKUMA argues, again, that the students should be moved off-campus and dispersed. Sugitsu refuses. This time the argument happens in front of the class.
• DO NOT LET AN ADULT SOLVE THIS. If the table stalls, have an NPC classmate say the obvious thing — Ichitaka Shijime, who will have got there and be waiting to see whether anyone else does. Never a teacher.
• READ THE COMMENTARY BACK VERBATIM. Find the lines you wrote in Chapter 3 and read them again, in the same warm voice, at the same pace, into this silence. Do not add a sting, do not slow down, do not change a word. If you deliver them exactly as you did when everybody was pleased, the scene works on its own and you can simply stop talking afterwards.
• LET THE AUTOPLAY DO THE WORK. One clip ends and the next one starts by itself, because that is what archives do, and now it is somebody else's turn to have their weakness explained to eleven million people. Nobody in the room reaches for the remote for a while.
• SUGITSU'S ANNOUNCEMENT THAT AFTERNOON is delivered as a comfort and it is the most frightening thing a teacher says all campaign. He is not being ominous. He is a man telling four hundred children that he has personally guaranteed ten of them, and he does not appear to notice what he has said, and no adult in the hall corrects him.
sections.readAloud:
▶ BEFORE SCHOOL

The sixth one is on the news.

A pro called Backdraft. Combustion, Rare, thirty-four. Found in a stairwell in Ota. The report is careful, the photographs aren't shown, and the phrasing is the same phrasing as the other five.

In the common room somebody says, without thinking about it:

"Wasn't he at ours? Like, years ago?"

▶ THE FOUR SECONDS
HOW TO RUN IT — The most important pause in the campaign. Actually take it. Count to four.

They say it and then keep talking, because it was a throwaway remark and they've already moved on.

And then they stop talking, halfway through the next sentence.

It takes about four seconds to go round the room. You can watch it happen.

It gets to Chozen Tadachi first and it gets to him fastest, and he goes completely still — the way he does in the first round of every fight — and stays like that for a minute and a half.

▶ WHAT IT LOOKS LIKE
HOW TO RUN IT — Describe the room, not the screen.

Twenty people around one phone isn't enough, so somebody puts it on the common room television. Which means the archive is now the size of a wall.

Nobody sits down. That's the detail. There are two sofas in this room and everybody is standing.

▶ WHAT THEY FIND

Twenty minutes to confirm five of the six. Another ten to find the commentary segments.

And then somebody scrolls, without really deciding to, to this year.

▶ THEIR OWN COMMENTARY, PLAYED BACK
HOW TO RUN IT — Same warm voice as Chapter 3. Word for word. Do not change a syllable.

"Now, Suzuki's beam pierces cover — but watch his veins. Yellow, he's driving it. If they go white, he isn't. Every shot past twenty percent he pays for out of his own body. He's rationing. Every shot is charge he doesn't get back."

The room doesn't say anything.

The clip autoplays into the next one.

▶ SUGITSU, IN THE HALL, THAT AFTERNOON

"Campus is closed. Nobody off-site unaccompanied. That's not a discussion.

"My quirk holds ten people permanently. Locations, condition, weaknesses — all of it, all the time, no matter where they are. As of this morning I've moved all ten slots onto students."

He means it as a comfort. You can tell he means it as a comfort.

aside.body: If a player asks who the ten are, Sugitsu answers honestly and immediately, and the list is not flattering — it is the ten with the most broadcast footage, which is to say the ten who did best. Winning put them on his list for the same reason it put them on the other one.
aside.label: Which ten

sections.heading: Lockdown
sections.tag: The quiet register · half a session · no combat
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — the gates shut and lessons run anyway → one ordinary domestic scene played entirely straight → 1-B in the corridor → Sugitsu names his ten → somebody counts → a name nobody recognises → out, without resolving it.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — the milk argument and the ten names. Half an hour, and it does more for Chapter 5 than an encounter would.

• RUN THIS DIRECTLY AFTER THE ARCHIVE SESSION, in the same evening or the next one. It is half a session, it has no combat, and it is where the chapter's second register lives — the one the chapter DM note asks for and that the campaign otherwise never writes down.
• THE RULE IS THAT NOTHING IS HEIGHTENED. The lessons happen. The kettle is broken again. Samitsu cooks. Aikawa reorganises the store cupboard nobody asked her to reorganise. Two students have a genuine falling-out about something trivial and it is not a metaphor for anything.
• CLASS 1-B ARE ON THE SAME CAMPUS AND THE TWO CLASSES DO NOT KNOW HOW TO BE AROUND EACH OTHER. Nothing has happened to 1-B yet. That is precisely why it is awkward: everyone can feel that 1-A are the ones on the list and nobody has a way to say so.
• LOCKDOWN AS A SET OF RULES, so the players feel it as a structure rather than a mood — no student off-site unaccompanied; bags checked at the gate; phones on and answered within the hour; a staff member sleeps in the Heights Alliance common room, on the sofa, badly, and it is a different one each night and none of them will admit it is a rota.
• SUGITSU'S TEN. He answers honestly and immediately when asked, and the list is the ten students with the most broadcast footage, which is the ten who did best. Say it plainly and let the table do the arithmetic in front of you.
• AND THEN THE COUNT. Somebody works down the register and finds that Hiro is not on the principal's list, and that a student none of them has ever heard of is. Sugitsu answers the question he was asked, in two flat sentences, and realises about a second and a half too late what he has just told a room of teenagers.
• WHAT ACTUALLY COMES OUT is not that Hiro is a machine. The class has known that since April; it is the first thing anyone ever noticed about him. What comes out is that there is nobody in it — that the body is a frame, that it is driven from a ground-floor room a corridor away by a girl called Otowa Suzume who has never once been in the building, and that not one of them has ever heard her voice, because the frame does not have one.
• PLAY HIM ENTIRELY UNBOTHERED. He does not apologise, does not explain himself unprompted, and is not embarrassed. He answers what he is asked, completely, and stops. "Nobody asked" is signed without any edge on it at all, which is what makes it land.
• THE TRANSLATOR IS THE PAYOFF. If any PC spent free time on "Hiro's Signs," they are the one who reads his answer out to the room, and the table should feel that they earned the job. If an NPC learned them instead — Isokono is the likeliest; she notices people — let it be her, and let the PCs notice it was not them.
• THE NAME IS THE WORST PART. Nobody in Class 1-A knew it. They have lived with him for a term and the register has been sitting in an office the whole time.
• DO NOT RESOLVE IT IN THIS SCENE. Nobody apologises. Nobody makes a speech about having failed to notice her. The class sits with it, badly, and the session ends.
sections.dmNote:
This is the chapter's second register and it is the harder one to run, because nothing happens in it.

The instruction from the appendix applies here more than anywhere: U.A. never stops being funny and Appetite is never funny. The milk argument goes exactly as it always has. Somebody makes a joke and it lands. The maths lesson is good. Play all of it entirely straight and let the contrast do the work — that is what actually happens to people, and a table that has laughed in this session will be in far worse shape for the next one.

The Hiro reveal is the only piece of plot in the scene and it should be delivered as paperwork. Sugitsu is not making a revelation; he is answering a question about slot allocation, and he does not realise what he has said until it is out. Hiro is not making a confession; he is confirming something that has been on a file since April.

The thing to keep hold of is what is actually revealed. Not that he is a machine — the class has always known that, and if you play the scene as though it were that, it will land as nothing. What is revealed is that the machine is empty, that it is driven from a room down the corridor, and that there is a girl in this school whose name none of them has ever heard. The horror is entirely the class's, and it is not about the quirk. It is that they lived with him for a term and nobody thought to ask him anything.

Then let it be unresolved, and end the session. Somebody will want to apologise to her. Do not let them do it well.
sections.developments:
• IF THE PLAYERS WORKED HIRO OUT IN CHAPTER 2 OR 3 — excellent, and it costs the campaign nothing. Skip the reveal and give them the scene instead: they are the ones who tell the rest of the class, or they are the ones who already knew and said nothing, and either is a better version of this beat than the surprise was.
• IF NOBODY EVER ASKS HIM ANYTHING — that is a legitimate and quietly devastating outcome, and you should let it stand. Do not have an NPC ask on the table's behalf. In Chapter 5, when he is the one who cannot come, it will be worth exactly as much as it cost.
• IF A PLAYER ASKS TO SEE THE ROOM — he says yes straight away, without hesitating, because he has never had a reason to say no. Whether you play that scene is your call and the campaign does not need it. If you do: a ground-floor room, a bed, a chair, a window, a great many books, and a girl who looks nothing like the frame, and who has a voice, which nobody in the class has ever heard. It is quieter than they expected. Keep it short and do not make it sad. She is not sad.
