sections.readAloud:
▶ THE COLD STORE
HOW TO RUN IT — Draw ONE floor plan by hand. Give it to them. Tell them it's all eleven.

Eleven storeys of nothing, on the Sumida side, condemned since before any of you were born.

THEY SEE — It was a refrigerated warehouse and the insulation is still in the walls. Every floor is the same floor. Every corridor is the same corridor. No windows above the second storey, because a cold store doesn't need any.
THE LIFTS — Don't work. The stairwells do.

▶ THE SMELL, AND THE FLOOR
HOW TO RUN IT — First thing, before anything happens.

Ammonia, faintly, everywhere — the way it is in a building that held refrigerant for forty years.

The floors are painted concrete with drainage channels cut into them, running to a grate every twenty feet. Because this is a building that was designed to be hosed down.

Everything in here was built to be cleaned easily.

Try not to think about that.

▶ THE SILENCE, THE FIRST TIME SOMEBODY SHOUTS

Nothing comes back. Not an echo, not a muffle — nothing. The insulation takes it out of the air about four feet from your mouth.

Whoever's one floor up didn't hear that.

Whoever's one floor up is not going to hear anything.

▶ THE STAIRWELLS

Four of them, one at each corner. They don't connect to each other at any point.

Whichever one you're in is the one you're committed to. If you want to be in another stairwell, you go back down to the ground floor and walk across the building — in the dark, past every door you haven't opened yet.

▶ ON THE COLD FLOORS

Three, seven and nine still hold temperature, and you feel it in the doorway before you feel it anywhere else.

Izuto's engines notice first. The hum drops a tone and doesn't come back up.

▶ IF REN FIRES IN THE DARK

For a quarter of a second the corridor is the brightest place any of you have ever been, and you can see all the way to the far end of it.

There's nothing there.

Then it's dark again — and everything in the building knows which floor you're on.

▶ SUGITSU, OUTSIDE, ON THE ROAD

"Steel shell, sealed cavity, refrigerant lining. I can see the doors. I cannot see one metre past them, and I haven't been able to for the last forty minutes."

A pause.

"Whoever picked this building knew that before they picked it."
sections.dmNote:
Give the players a floor plan on paper — one floor, hand-drawn, and tell them it is all eleven. The identical-floors gimmick turns a dungeon crawl into an orientation problem and rewards note-taking enormously.

The silence is the most important feature and the easiest to forget. Enforce it every time somebody shouts. A party that gets separated in here is properly separated and the tension of not knowing whether the other half is alive is the whole reason the finale is set here rather than anywhere with windows.

Every environmental detail above is targeted at a specific PC. That is deliberate and it is what a location for a finale should do — Izuto is throttled, Ren is a lighthouse, Kazama is the only thing holding a corridor, and Chozen is, for once, in exactly the kind of problem he has spent four chapters preparing for.
sections.heading: The Shirahige Cold Store

aside.label: Why here
aside.body: If anyone asks how Sylar found an eleven-storey building that defeats the principal's quirk: he did not. Riddle did, by asking somebody who used to work for the Commission a perfectly ordinary question about the limits of Search, and then not letting them remember being asked.

sections.heading: The Question You Don't Answer
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — he has been waiting and he has been practising → question one, given to the table, and then silence for as long as it takes → whatever they do, make the cost explicit → "he's on nine, I'd hurry" → question two if anyone closes → he bleeds out tidily.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — both questions and the choice to walk past. Do not let this become a fight and do not shorten the silence.

• Riddle's last stand and the campaign's final moral beat. He is between the class and Sylar and he knows exactly what he is for.
• QUESTION ONE — 40 feet, must be heard, one target at a time. Anyone who attempts an answer is braindead for five rounds or until they succeed on a DC 14 Intelligence check. Correct answers end it and reveal his location.
• QUESTION TWO — 5 feet. "What would hurt more?" A wrong answer comes true within twenty-four hours. He asks this of whoever reaches him first.
• THE SHAPE OF THE ENCOUNTER: he cannot be beaten quickly and he cannot beat them at all. He is low-HP, has no defences, and every question costs him blood. What he can do is take five rounds off one PC at a time, in a corridor, while something with metal teeth is somewhere ahead of them. He is a delay and he is a very good one.
• THE CORRECT PLAY is still to refuse to engage — but this time refusing means walking past him, leaving him alive and behind you, with a party member down on the floor. Make that cost explicit.
• If a PC answers Question Two wrong, honour it. Within twenty-four hours, the thing they named happens. Do not soften it and do not make it fatal; make it exactly what they said.
• Riddle does not survive the campaign, but the class do not necessarily kill him. He bleeds out from his own quirk if he is made to ask enough questions, which is an ending he seems to have expected and does not appear to mind.
• CHOZEN TADACHI's arc lands here. Every contingency in the binder assumes a problem worth solving. This is a problem whose only correct answer is to walk away from it, and he has never once done that.
• REN SUZUKI MAY BE THE ONE WHO STAYS. His sheet says he wants to forgive people, foes included, and Riddle dying tidily against a wall is the hardest test of that the campaign has. If Ren stays with him, Riddle answers anything Ren asks, and at the very end asks Ren one back — out of habit, not malice. It cannot hurt him now; there is nothing left in Riddle to pay for it. Let Ren's player decide whether to answer anyway.
• THE SILENCE IS THE ENCOUNTER. Ask the question out loud, put your hands down, and wait. Do not fill it. Do not offer a check. However long the table takes is how long the scene is supposed to be, and a minute of five people not speaking is worth more than any amount of damage in this campaign.
• MAKE THE COST OF WALKING PAST EXPLICIT BEFORE THEY CHOOSE. Leaving him alive means leaving him behind them, in a corridor, in a building where sound does not carry, with a classmate on the floor for five rounds and something with metal teeth somewhere ahead. Say all of that, plainly, and then let them decide.
• HE HAS BEEN PRACTISING and it shows. There is blood down his chin and the whole front of his shirt, dried in layers, and he has clearly been asking questions of somebody for some time in order to be ready for this. Do not say who. The players will supply somebody worse than anything you would have named.
• THE END OF HIM IS TIDY AND HE DOES NOT MIND. He asks one too many, it comes out of him all at once, and he sits down against the wall carefully, the way a man does when he has been expecting this and would rather not make a mess of it. If a PC stays with him, he will answer any question they ask, accurately, until he stops.
sections.readAloud:
▶ HE'S WAITING FOR YOU

And he has been for some time. There's blood down his chin and the front of his shirt, because he's been practising.

"You came," he says. "Good. I've got two."

And he smiles, and the scar moves in a way a face should not.

▶ QUESTION ONE
HOW TO RUN IT — Give it to the table. Then wait, however long that takes. Do not help.

"A woman gives birth to two boys. Same hour, same day, same mother, same father."

He tilts his head.

"They are not twins. How?"

▶ IF THEY START TO WALK PAST HIM

"Ah — no, that's clever. That's genuinely clever."

He sounds pleased for them.

Then, to their backs, conversationally: "He's on nine. I'd hurry."

And you will never know whether that was true.

▶ QUESTION TWO
HOW TO RUN IT — Only at five feet. Almost kindly.

He leans in, close enough that you can smell the blood.

"Last one. What would hurt more?"

▶ THE END OF HIM

He asks one too many, and it comes out of him all at once — mouth, nose, the corners of his eyes.

He sits down against the wall quite carefully, as though he'd been expecting this for a while and wanted to do it tidily.

He doesn't seem to mind.
sections.treasure:
If they take him alive, he answers questions honestly and at length, because being asked is the thing he enjoys.

He gives them the ninth floor, the layout, and Sylar's condition. He will not tell them anything about himself and there is nothing to tell.
sections.dmNote:
Structurally this is a puzzle in the shape of a boss fight and you should not let it become a real one. Keep it in a corridor, keep it dark, keep his voice level and conversational.

Give the questions to the players out loud, as questions, and wait. That is the encounter. A table sitting in silence deciding whether to answer a riddle while the clock runs is worth more than any amount of damage.

Make Question Two count. If someone answers it wrong, write down what they said, and use it in the epilogue.
sections.developments:
• THE CORRECT PLAY IS STILL TO WALK PAST — but this time it means leaving him alive behind them, with a party member on the floor, and something with metal teeth somewhere ahead. Make that cost explicit before they choose.
• DO NOT LET THIS BECOME A REAL FIGHT. He is low-HP with no defences. He is a delay, and a very good one: five rounds off one PC at a time while the clock runs.
• IF A PC ANSWERS QUESTION TWO WRONG — write down exactly what they said. It happens within twenty-four hours, precisely as described. Do not soften it, do not make it fatal, and use it in the epilogue.
• IF THE PARTY KILLS HIM OUTRIGHT — fine. He does not resist. But make them spend the actions on it while a PC is down and the clock is running.
• THE "HE'S ON NINE" LINE IS TRUE. Two students are on floor nine. Riddle said it to hurry them into splitting up. Both of those things are true at once and the players should never be certain.
• ANSWER TO QUESTION ONE, if you need it: they are two of a set of triplets.
• IF A PLAYER HAS EARPLUGS IN — it still works, and it is still the best purchase in the campaign. In this building, though, it means they are deaf, in a place where nobody can hear anybody already, with half the party on the other side of a stairwell. Say that out loud before they choose.

aside.body: If Chozen's player refuses both questions and drags the party past him, give it weight — he should be shaking, and he should be no use for the next scene, and it should be the best thing he does in the campaign.
aside.label: Chozen's out

sections.heading: Keepsake

aside.label: If your table would rather not kill him
aside.body: Sylar in custody is a legitimate ending and arguably a worse one for him — a man in permanent pain who cannot stop collecting, in a cell, with nothing new to take. Okuma will prefer this outcome. Rawagi will not say what he prefers.

sections.treasure:
The two students from floor nine, if the party got there. Sylar's collection, ended.

And the thing that is not a reward: they were right about everything and it still cost them a classmate. Let the win be a real win and let the cost stand.
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — he opens with a Copy and it is Moshita's → name every quirk as he uses it → build every ruling around bracket pairs → force him onto the recent ones → Rawagi burns out → a fire door comes off its hinges → beans → and then he points at Kinji.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — the quirk rotation, the pairs rule, and the ending. If the fight is running long, bring Carlos Might in early — he is a difficulty dial as well as a punchline.

• The finale, and the mechanical premise is cruel: Sylar fights the class using their classmates' abilities. Give him three or four in rotation and name every one out loud when he uses it.
• Suggested loadout — Copy (Moshita Maro, 1-B), taken nine days ago and his newest and clumsiest; a construction quirk from Tsuzuri Hane, taken in April and fluent; a perception quirk from Habara Jun; and combustion from Ikari Tomonobu. Plus Maw, always, which is the only thing he is actually good at.
• THE HEADACHE IS THE MECHANIC. Every quirk he holds worsens it. Rule it openly: the recent acquisitions are unreliable — he misjudges ranges, over-commits, and picks the wrong tool. The old ones are lethal. Let the players work out that the way to beat him is to force him to keep switching.
• RAWAGI CHISO burns himself out running Foresight and should be genuinely, visibly ruined by it. Each use is a DC 14 Constitution save or a level of Concussed; he fails several. He keeps doing it. Take him off the board before the end.
• THE PAIRS ARE THE POINT. Every fight in this campaign since session one has been two people covering each other, and the finale should reward that structurally — Sylar's entire method is separating a person from a room. Give mechanical benefit to PCs fighting within reach of their bracket partner, and make Maw's restraint escapable by an ally rather than by the victim.
• REN SUZUKI is the one the campaign has been aiming at. His father taught him a blade and a doctrine, and here is a man who is nothing but other people's quirks. Ren's answer should not be his beam. Give him the moment with the katana and give it to him without comment.
• CARLOS MIGHT arrives. Not at the start — near the end, badly timed, entirely uncoordinated, having found the place by asking in restaurants. Durango Smash does 6d6 and covers everyone present in beans, including the class, including the enemy, including the floor. It is genuinely useful and completely absurd and both of those are true at once.
• ESTADOS UNIDOS DE SMASH — 7d12, and then he points at Kinji Hamakida and says "Ahora es tu turno." Kinji has been training with him privately for two terms, and has never once — not in the bracket, not at the festival, not when he was losing and furious about it — let anybody see his quirk pay out. Sylar's file on him says "novelty quirk, never observed to pay out, low threat," because that is what the booth said.
• THE SPIN, AND HOW TO RUN IT. Jackpot Fever pays out when Kinji rolls the highest face on his current die. A failure steps the die down: d100, d20, d12, d10, d8, d6, d4. Two terms with Carlos have bought him one thing — tonight he starts on the d20, not the d100. Each round he makes the gesture as a bonus action and you roll his die in the open. While he spins, Sylar comes for him, because Sylar is not stupid and he can count. The class's whole job for these rounds is to keep a gambler alive long enough for the odds to come down: somebody between them every round, Kibi first, the pair rule in full effect. If the die reaches d4 and still has not paid, it pays — that is what the training was for. Then three rounds of Jackpot: music pouring out of him, healing instantly from anything, damage and speed multiplied by five. His sandpaper strikes are 1d8+3; five times that, three rounds running, is the end of Sylar.
• THE SONG IS ONE OF THEIRS. If a PC recommended Kinji a song in free time ("A Song for Kinji") and he liked it, that is the track. Say its name out loud when it starts. If nobody did, it is your favourite song, and you should say that out loud too.
• TORAGI SAYS IT. When the die finally lands, it is Toragi Kayo — who has spoken only in one-liners in every fight since April — who says the only word anybody remembers afterwards: "Now."
• ROB JOESTAR is here too and this is where the comedy curdles: he loses his temper properly for the first time on screen, enters the rage, and it is not funny. Acid Pressure builds every time he fires. He does not stop.
• MOSHITA MARO does not come home. Decide before the session whether the class can save the other two, and be honest about it either way.
• BUILD THE RULINGS AROUND PAIRS AND SAY SO AT THE TABLE. Any PC acting within reach of their Chapter 2 bracket partner has advantage on the roll. Maw's restraint is broken by an ALLY, never by the victim. Say both rules out loud at the top of the fight — this is the campaign's thesis and it should be a mechanic the players can see, not a theme they infer.
• THE ROTATION IS THE FIGHT. Give him four abilities, name each one as it comes out, and say how long he has had it. When the class denies him the old fluent ones he is forced onto the nine-day-old Copy and the six-month-old combustion, and he starts getting things wrong — a wall where he wanted a hole, a range misjudged by twenty feet. Let them win by making him reach.
• HIRO, IF HE IS HERE, IS WORTH ONE ENORMOUS MOMENT AND NOT MORE. Maw closes on him and finds nothing, and Sylar loses a full turn to it, and that turn is the party's window. Do not give him the kill and do not give him a speech. His screen shows one emoji the whole time, and the fight carries on.
• CARLOS MIGHT'S ARRIVAL IS BADLY TIMED ON PURPOSE. Not the cavalry — a fire door off its hinges, a man in a sombrero out of breath holding a paper bag, announcing that he asked at four restaurants. The corridor fills with beans. It is absurd and it is genuinely, mechanically effective and both of those are true at the same time.
• AND THEN HE POINTS AT KINJI. Hold it exactly there. No music yet, no slow motion, no speech from anybody. He says four words in Spanish and steps out of the way, and the next sound in the room is a speaker clicking on.
sections.readAloud:
▶ THE FIRST THING HE DOES IS A COPY

He touches Kazama, and for two minutes he's wearing Kazama's Metal — and he uses it badly.

He tears steel out of the cold-store wall in lumps, far too much at once, and it hangs off him like scaffolding. He doesn't notice. He's never seen it done properly. He's only heard it explained.

He's using Moshita Maro's quirk. He learned it nine days ago.

▶ NAME EVERY QUIRK OUT LOUD AS HE USES IT
HOW TO RUN IT — Every single one, as it happens. The naming is the horror.

"That's Falsework. Construction quirk. He's had it since April, and he's very, very good with it."

"That one he's had nine days."

▶ WHEN THE HEADACHE COSTS HIM

He reaches for something and gets the wrong one. A wall goes up where he wanted a wall to come down.

For a second he looks less like a monster and more like a man carrying too much.

Then he shakes it off.

▶ IF HIRO IS IN THE BUILDING
HOW TO RUN IT — The first time Maw closes on him. Let the whole turn pass in silence.

He takes him the way he's taken everybody: down, fast, one hand across the chest. And then the jaw comes open.

And then he stops.

He's knelt over seven feet of grey metal with his teeth through the back of its head, and there's nothing in there. Ceramic. Wiring. A hollow the shape of a thought that was never in it.

He's been doing this for nine years and he has never once been wrong about what he was biting.

He doesn't say anything. He hasn't got anything to say. He just kneels there, for a whole turn, with his mouth full of somebody else's engineering.

▶ AND THE SCREEN

The little LED screen on the front of the frame's head is still on. It's a foot from his face.

It's showing a single emoji, and it's been showing it the whole time.

🙂

▶ CARLOS MIGHT ARRIVES
HOW TO RUN IT — Badly timed, unannounced, absurd. There is no dramatic entrance.

A fire door goes off its hinges, and there's a very large man in a sombrero standing in it, out of breath, holding a paper bag.

"AH! Here! I have found it! I asked at four restaurants!"

▶ DURANGO SMASH

The corridor fills with beans.

All of it. Everyone. Enemy, students, the floor, the ceiling, Rawagi Chiso.

It is, unarguably, extremely effective.

▶ ESTADOS UNIDOS DE SMASH

He hits him hard enough that the sound arrives after the movement.

And then Carlos Might — breathing hard, covered in beans — turns and points across the room at the one student in this class who has never once used his quirk where anybody could see it. The one who's been in an empty training room with him at six in the morning since April, rolling dice.

"¡Ahora es tu turno!"

▶ KINJI HAMAKIDA
HOW TO RUN IT — Hold everything. Give this its own silence. There is no music for this. Not yet.

Kinji Hamakida walks past a teacher covered in beans, and he isn't talking.

Nobody in this class has ever seen him not talking.

He makes the gesture — the small one, the one from the training room — and somewhere on him a speaker clicks on.

▶ THE SPIN
HOW TO RUN IT — Roll it in the open, every round, where everybody can see the die.

"Keep him off me," says Kinji, to nobody in particular, and for once it isn't a joke.

"It comes. It always comes. It just doesn't come first time."

▶ JACKPOT

The song hits the chorus at exactly the wrong volume for a building where sound doesn't carry.

And every one of you can hear it anyway — because it isn't coming out of the speaker any more. It's coming out of him.

He isn't shuffling. He isn't anything you have a word for. He is very fast and he is very loud, and for three rounds nothing in this building can make him stop.
sections.developments:
• BUILD EVERY MECHANIC AROUND PAIRS. Give advantage, a bonus, or a reroll to any PC acting within reach of their Chapter 2 bracket partner, and rule that Maw's restraint is broken by an ALLY rather than by the victim. Sylar's whole method is separating one person from a room; the campaign's answer is that these twenty are components that have finally been assembled.
• FORCE HIM TO SWITCH QUIRKS. Anything that denies him his fluent, old abilities pushes him onto the recent clumsy ones. Reward players who notice and exploit this.
• GIVE KINJI THE FINISHING BLOW. Not a beam, not wind, not metal — a gambler on a hot streak, with a song on, who kept his best card face-down for two terms because a man in a sombrero told him to. Hold the reveal until Carlos Might points at him. If the setup has been played straight since Chapter 2, the table will understand what has been happening in that training room in the same second the music starts.
• AND THEN DO NOT LET ANYONE MAKE A SPEECH ABOUT IT.
• IF THE PARTY WOULD RATHER TAKE HIM ALIVE — a legitimate and arguably worse ending for him: permanent pain, a cell, nothing new to take. Okuma prefers this outcome. Rawagi will not say what he prefers.
• MOSHITA MARO DOES NOT COME HOME. Decide before the session whether the other two students do, and be honest either way. Do not decide it with a die roll at the table.
• IF THE FIGHT IS OVERWHELMING THEM — Rawagi's Foresight, Entoss's walls, and Carlos Might are all difficulty dials. Use them. A beginner DM should feel free to adjust mid-fight and nobody at the table will ever know.
sections.dmNote:
The finale should feel like the 2v2 bracket with the safety off, and every mechanical decision should push toward pairs.

The Kinji Hamakida beat is the campaign's best card and it only works if you have played the setup exactly as written for three chapters: Carlos Might never in the building, always in the training room with him, never explained; Rob Joestar's permission slip as a running joke; and Kinji — who will tell you about his shoes, his playlist and last night's television without being asked — never once using his quirk where anybody could see. If you have done that, the moment Carlos points at him and the speaker clicks on, the whole table realises what has been happening in an empty gym since April, and that is the payoff for the entire campaign.

Give him the kill. Not a beam, not wind, not metal. A fifteen-year-old with a song on and a die coming down, and two terms of private coaching from a man in a sombrero.

And then do not have anyone make a speech about it.

sections.readAloud:
▶ THE INFIRMARY

Six beds, and there are nine of you in it, so three are sitting on the floor against the radiator — which she's already told you not to do twice.

She goes down the line. She doesn't soften anything.

When she gets to the end she stands there for a second with her hands in her cardigan pockets.

"You did what you could. It wasn't enough for everyone. That's usually how it goes."

Which isn't comfort. But it's true, and she has never once said anything to you that wasn't.

▶ THE CORRIDOR

Class 1-B are outside. They have been for a while. Ebina Chikara is with them, and has been for nine days.

ASK THEM — Somebody has to go out there. Who goes?

▶ THE FRIDGE

At some point over the weekend, the chart goes back up.

Nobody says who did it. Nobody takes it down again.

▶ THE LAST BEAT
HOW TO RUN IT — Give it to Masahata and let the room do the rest.

"— which is what I said. Look at it. Look at the original. Broadly correct."

It is not. It's nowhere near correct.

Ichitaka opens his mouth and then closes it again. Aikawa makes a noise into her sleeve. And then the whole room goes, all at once.

It's the first time anybody has laughed in three weeks.

▶ IF HIRO WAS NEVER THERE
HOW TO RUN IT — The morning after. Four lines, and then stop.

The frame's on the sofa in the common room when they come back. It's been there all night. The television has been off the whole time.

It doesn't sign.

Instead the door at the end of the ground-floor corridor is open, and a voice none of you has ever heard says, from inside:

"I couldn't hear anything. That's all. I want you to know it wasn't that I heard it and couldn't do anything. There was just nothing there."

Then she asks who's hurt. And she asks it about each of you separately, by name, in order — which is not something anybody has ever done for her.

▶ AND THEN, MONDAY

Forge is at the board with a marker and a bento the size of a briefcase.

There are twenty names on it. They're already in pairs.

"Right," she says. "Nobody's swapping. Don't ask."

aside.label: The last line
aside.body: Give it to Masahata Shikoji, at the fridge, arguing that his original bracket prediction was broadly correct. He is wrong. Nobody corrects him. It is the first time anyone has laughed in three weeks.

sections.dmNote:
Keep it short and keep it warm. The campaign has been cold for two chapters and the last twenty minutes belong to the school.

The final image is Forge's board. New pairs, no explanation, the same handwriting. Class 1-A go back to being fifteen.

If your table wants a second season, the hook is already in the file and needs no invention: Sylar selected for documentation, and there is nothing about the Sports Festival archive that has changed. It is still free, still searchable, and still up.
sections.heading: Help Woman's Office
sections.treasure:
Whatever the class earned publicly — and it will be considerable, because six professional heroes died before anyone caught this and a first-year class is what caught it.

The real reward is Forge's new board. Same handwriting, twenty names, no explanation. Class 1-A go back to being fifteen.
sections.developments:
• GO ROUND THE TABLE AND GIVE EVERY PC A CLOSING BEAT. Ask each player what their character does in the week afterwards and take whatever they give you as true. This is the last thing that happens; make it theirs.
• IF A PC ANSWERED QUESTION TWO WRONG — this is where it comes true. Exactly as they described it. No worse, no better.
• IF PLAYERS WANT TO VISIT MOSHITA MARO'S FAMILY, OR 1-B, OR KUMA — say yes to all of it and play the scenes. There is no clock any more.
• IF YOUR TABLE WANTS A SECOND SEASON — the hook needs no invention. Sylar selected for documentation, and nothing about the archive has changed. It is still free, still searchable, still up. Next year's first-years would like to watch it.
• KEEP IT SHORT AND WARM. The campaign has been cold for two chapters and the last twenty minutes belong to the school.
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — the infirmary, nine of them in six beds → Help Woman down the line, softening nothing → a closing beat for every PC, round the table → 1-B in the corridor and somebody has to go out → the fridge chart goes back up → Masahata gets the last line → Monday, and a new board.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — the beats round the table and Forge's board. Twenty minutes, warm, and then stop.

• Close in the infirmary. Every chapter has ended here and this one should too.
• HELP WOMAN — straight to the point, tells no lies even where a lie would help. She gives each PC an honest assessment of their injuries and, if asked, an honest assessment of anything else. She is the only adult in the campaign who has never once managed a student's feelings and the class have come to rely on that enormously.
• Go round the table and give every PC a closing beat:

  — REN SUZUKI: the man who was nothing but borrowed quirks is gone, and Ren's own is still the thing his father was afraid of. Nothing resolves. He is calmer about it than he was. If he stayed with Riddle, ask his player what the last question was, and whether he answered it.
  — KAZAMA KENJI: the scar, at last, if his player wants it. He has never refused a direct question and by now somebody has finally asked one. And he rings his mum, who never wanted him to do this, and does not tell her a single thing about the cold store.
  — CHOZEN TADACHI: the binder gets a new page and it is one line long, and it is about walking away. And on the Monday a delivery van arrives at Heights Alliance with something absurdly expensive for every single person in the building, and he cannot explain why, and nobody makes him.
  — IZUTO KUTSU: he stalled, in front of people, and somebody cooled him and somebody carried him. He should say thank you, badly, to exactly one person.

• 1-B are in the corridor. Ebina Chikara is with them and has been for nine days. Somebody has to go out there.
• If a PC answered Question Two wrong, this is where it comes true. Exactly as they described it. No worse and no better.
• The fridge chart goes back up. Somebody puts it back up. Do not say who.
• FORGE has already started on next term's equipment and has a new board with twenty names on it, and she is eating, and she will not explain her pairings.
• GO ROUND THE TABLE AND ASK EACH PLAYER WHAT THEIR CHARACTER DOES IN THE WEEK AFTERWARDS, and take whatever they give you as true without adjusting it. This is the last thing that happens in the campaign and it should belong to them.
• THE NPC CLASSMATES GET ONE LINE EACH and you should give them out loud, quickly, going round the class — Aikawa organising something nobody asked her to organise, Samitsu cooking for a room that is too quiet, Nomi Igisa saying one sentence that stops the room, Tazato helping somebody and constructing a reason it was efficient, Kinji putting a song on at a perfectly reasonable volume — which is how everybody knows he is not all right — and Toragi, in the common room, saying a whole paragraph out loud to nobody in particular, which nobody has ever heard him do. Twenty seconds each. The class survives, and the players should hear all of them survive.
• HIRO gets a beat either way. If he was at the cold store, somebody has to go and collect what is left of him, and Forge does it, and does not want help. If he was not, he is on the sofa in the morning asking who is hurt, by name, one at a time — which is the first time all campaign anyone has done to him what he is doing to them.
• AND IF A PLAYER GOES DOWN THE CORRIDOR AND KNOCKS ON THE GROUND-FLOOR DOOR, give them the scene and keep it to four lines. She is reading. She says come in. She is not sad and you should not play her as sad.
• HELP WOMAN TELLS THE TRUTH ABOUT HOW CLOSE IT WAS, because she tells no lies even where a lie would help, and the class have come to rely on that more than any comfort anyone else has offered them.

closing.label: Chapter Note — What's still up
closing.body:
Sylar is dead or in a cell. Riddle bled out asking questions. Powder is a fenced-off crater and Kuma is doing eleven years and complaining about the food.

The Sports Festival archive is still online. Eleven hours, forty first-years, every quirk demonstrated under pressure with professional commentary explaining the mechanism and the weakness. It has not been taken down, because taking it down would be an admission, and because next year's first-years would like to watch it.

Forge has a new board with twenty names on it and will not explain her pairings.

And on a wall in Ikebukuro, opposite a closed batting centre, somebody has painted a white tiger, and under it the names of every member of Class 1-A who was at the cold store.

sidequests.name: THE SPEAKER
sidequests.slots: 2 slots, and only if somebody knocks
sidequests.hook: Forge has a speaker on the bench, half built, and she has had it there since April. "Third time I've offered. I'm not going to fit it without her saying so. Would you ask her properly?"
sidequests.body: Forge has offered to fit the frame with a speaker twice and Otowa has said she will think about it. A PC can be the person she talks it through with.
sidequests.reward: entirely hers, and if she says yes the class hear her voice for the first time, and the DM should let a player choose what the first thing she says is.

chapters.title: After Hours
chapters.estimate: 4–8 sessions, plus as much free time as the table wants
chapters.intro: Summer term. The man in the Commission jacket has gone from the gate, the fridge chart is back up, and for the first time all year nobody is hunting Class 1-A. They are nationally famous, they are fifteen, and they have weekends. Two kinds of people in Tokyo noticed them at the festival. A street gang called Byakko, who rank each other by who beat whom, have painted every 1-A name on a wall opposite the school as an invitation to climb. And three societies older than quirks — vampires, sun-priests and sorcerers — have been hiding in plain sight for a century, and are about to be found by accident. Chapter 6 is a sandbox with a spine: Byakko's four Corners and the White Tiger herself, one first-contact scene for each Underground faction, and an open city.
chapters.dmNote:
Run this chapter as the summer it is. The horror is over; Appetite is finished and stays finished. What is left is sport, mystery and consequence — Byakko as a tournament with a criminal record, and the Underground as the city's basement.

Ask "it's the weekend, what do you do?" at the top of every session and mean it. Give the players three free-time slots each, resolve them fast, and end each session on one set piece if they reached one. Do not run everything. Pick the Byakko thread and whichever faction surfaced first, and let the rest wait for a second season.

The White Tiger is the chapter's climax and it pays out the campaign's first idea in the side plot: a pair, fighting as one, is something new. If a player remembers Forge on the first morning, let them have the roof.
chapters.milestone:
LEVEL 9 when the class first beat a Corner or first reach Contact with an Underground faction, whichever comes first.
LEVEL 10 at the end of the night on the roof of the Cage — whatever the class chose — or when a faction's Invitation is answered, if they never climb the Cage.

closing.label: Chapter Note — the wall opposite the gate
closing.body:
By the end of the summer the wall opposite U.A.'s west gate has a white tiger on it, and every 1-A name under it, and whatever the class did on the roof of the Cage written in white beside them. Depending on who they met, it may also have a sword through a crown, or a sun.

The ground staff stopped painting over it in August. Sugitsu asked them to. He says it is the most accurate record of the year the school has.

sections.heading: Summer Term
sections.tag: Opening · the sandbox · how to run it
sections.readAloud:
▶ SUMMER TERM

It's a Monday in July. Nobody announced anything — but the man in the Commission jacket isn't at the gate any more.

THEY SEE — The fridge chart's back up. Forge's new board is up. It's thirty-four degrees and the dorm air conditioning has been broken since Thursday.
AND — Samitsu has made cold soba for twenty. Nobody asked him to.

Six weeks of term left, and then the summer.

And for the first time all year, nobody is hunting you.

▶ THE QUESTION
HOW TO RUN IT — Ask it at the top of every single session in this chapter, and mean it.

ASK THEM — It's the weekend. What do you do?
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — open on the dorm → three free-time slots each → resolve them fast → play the one that became something → end each session on one set piece from this chapter, if the players reached one.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — one slot each, then one set piece. This chapter is built to be played in any order and stopped at any point.

• THIS CHAPTER IS A SANDBOX WITH A SPINE, NOT A SPINE WITH A SANDBOX. Nothing in it has to happen. It contains Byakko's top end (the Four Corners and the White Tiger), one first-contact scene for each Underground faction, and an open city. Run what the players reach.
• THREE SLOTS PER WINDOW NOW, and no caps on Heat or the Odd Night table. Everything in the free-time appendix is open, plus the Chapter 6 side quests.
• THE CLASS ARE DIFFERENT PEOPLE. They have buried a classmate's chances, beaten a man who ate brains, and been on the news for both. Play the city noticing: older heroes nod to them, the agency letters are serious, and Byakko's tiger on the west-gate wall now has every 1-A name under it, not just the podium.
• THE SET PIECES — "The Other Shortlist" (Byakko's turf and the Cage), "The Rank You Didn't Ask For" (what happens when a PC holds a stripe), "The Four Corners," "The White Tiger," and the three Underground contacts: "A Party That Ends at Dawn," "Matsu-no-Yu," and "The Thing in the Laundry Room." Each says what reaches it.
• ONE THING PER SESSION. A free-time window and one set piece is a full session. Two set pieces is too many.
• THE SPINE IS FINISHED AND STAYS FINISHED. Do not bring Appetite back. The archive is still online, which is the second-season hook in "The Fourth Door," and nothing more.
sections.developments:
• IF THE PLAYERS WANT TO GO STRAIGHT FOR THE WHITE TIGER — they can try. Heat decides whether she has heard of them; if it is below 8, the Cage's door is shut and Genda Tetsuo is sitting in front of it eating takoyaki. They will have to make her notice them.
• IF THE PLAYERS WANT NOTHING BUT DOWNTIME — that is a legitimate way to play this chapter. Run windows, hangouts and quests, and let the set pieces sit. They keep.
• IF THE PLAYERS WANT A REASON — give them one through somebody they like. Nakata's gym is being squeezed. Ryuto Hana saw something at the wharf. Rob Joestar has stopped coming to class. Somebody is crying in the laundry room at three in the morning and it is not a student.
• IF YOUR TABLE WANTS TO STOP AT CHAPTER 5 — stop. This chapter is dessert.
sections.dmNote:
The hardest thing about a sandbox chapter is the first ten minutes, when the players do not know what is allowed. Answer that by asking the same question at the top of every session — "it's the weekend, what do you do?" — and by having one NPC the players like bring them something small and specific every time they look stuck.

The register is summer: hot, loose, funny, and every so often very strange. The horror is over. Byakko are a sport with consequences. The Underground is a mystery with teeth. Neither of them is Appetite and neither should feel like it.

aside.label: Pacing the chapter
aside.body:
A rough shape, if you want one: two or three sessions of free time in which Byakko escalate and one Underground faction surfaces, then a Corner, then the faction's contact scene, then the White Tiger. Four to eight sessions in all.

Do not run all three factions. Pick the one the dice and the players found first and give it room. The other two are for a second season, or never, and both of those are fine.

sections.treasure: Three free-time slots a window, a city with no caps on it, and nobody hunting them.

sections.heading: The Other Shortlist
sections.readAloud:
▶ THE BACKSTREETS, AFTER DARK

Two streets behind the Ikebukuro west exit. Shutters down, streetlights orange, and every third shutter has a tiger on it.

THEY SEE — The noodle bar's open. The old woman in the window upstairs is shaking dice in a cup.
AND — A boy of about fourteen, no stripes yet, sitting on a crash barrier. He watches you go past the way you'd watch a celebrity. And then, when he thinks you can't see, he practises your stance.

▶ THE CAGE

A batting centre that closed in the nineties and never came down. Six storeys of green netting and floodlight gantries, lit up like a stadium at one in the morning.

You can hear it from three streets away: a crowd, and under the crowd, somebody hitting somebody.

THEY SEE — On the front step, in a folding chair beside a takoyaki cart, the largest man you have ever seen who isn't Kuma. Reading a paperback.

He marks his page with a toothpick and looks up.

"Evening. You'll be the school."
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — the backstreets → the kids who want to be you → the Cage, floodlit → Genda Tetsuo on the step → either they talk their way in, fight their way in, or come back with more Heat.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — the walk, the Cage, Genda. That is the whole location.

• BYAKKO'S TURF is the backstreets of Ikebukuro and the alleys behind the Shinjuku west exit — the west of the city, which is the White Tiger's direction in the old four-guardian scheme, which every member can tell you. It has a noodle bar, Lucky Seven (the dice den), Swing Town (Brick's batting centre), a chop shop, a 24-hour laundrette, and the Cage.
• THE CAGE is Byakko's heart: a dead six-storey batting centre, every floor a ring of green netting under floodlights. Climbing it is the challenge ladder. Ground floor, Claws. First and second, Fangs. Third and fourth, Stripes. Fifth, the Corners when they are home. The roof is the White Tiger's, and she eats ramen up there at one in the morning.
• GENDA TETSUO, the Black Corner, sits on the front step and decides who goes in. He can be beaten — Shell, Immovable, slow — or talked past. He is genuinely interested in Kazama, Setaka and Hiro and will stop a fight to talk about load-bearing with any of them.
• THE CROWD MATTERS. Byakko fights are always witnessed, and the crowd is half the gang and half the neighbourhood. Win cleanly and the crowd decides what it was worth. Cheat — gang up, bring a weapon nobody saw — and the crowd turns on you.
• THE KIDS WITH NO STRIPES ARE THE MORAL CENTRE OF THIS LOCATION. Every fourteen-year-old in these streets wants to be strong, the festival told them the class are the strongest, and the only ladder they can see goes up the Cage. "The Byakko Kid" in the side quests is about one of them.
• HEAT DECIDES WHO IS HOME. At Heat 7 or less, the class can fight their way up to the third floor and no further. At 8 or more, the Corners come down to look. At 10, the roof door is open.
sections.developments:
• IF THE PCs TRY TO CLIMB THE CAGE IN ONE NIGHT — let them try, and run it as a gauntlet: one fight per floor, a short rest's worth of breathing in the stairwell between them, Heat +1 per floor cleared. Nobody has done it in six years. If they reach the roof below Heat 10, she is not there; there is a bowl of ramen, cooling, and a note.
• IF THE PCs BRING THE POLICE OR THE COMMISSION — the Cage is empty by the time anybody arrives and open again on Friday. Byakko have survived worse than a school calling the police.
• IF A PC IS RECOGNISED — they will be. The crowd chants their festival placing. Somebody has printed their archive page.
• IF A PC JUST WANTS TO EAT AT THE NOODLE BAR — the noodles are excellent and nobody bothers them, because the noodle bar is neutral ground under the Law. It is the safest place in the backstreets and the best place to hear things.
sections.dmNote:
This is the location that makes Byakko a place rather than a random encounter. Make it vivid and make it fun: floodlights, netting, a crowd, takoyaki, a paperback, a grandmother with dice.

The kids with no stripes are the part to hold onto. Byakko are criminals, and also the only institution in these streets that tells a teenager they can climb. The class are U.A. students — the other institution that tells teenagers that — and the contrast should be visible without anybody making a speech about it.

aside.label: The Stripe Law, in the gang's own words
aside.body:
Painted on the wall inside the Cage's front door, in white:

ONE. You are what you have beaten.
TWO. Anybody may climb.
THREE. Nobody runs on their own street.
FOUR. Nobody touches the noodle bar.
FIVE. The Tiger is whoever is left.

Under it, smaller, newer, in a different hand: SIX. Nobody fights a kid who hasn't got a stripe yet. The White Tiger added that one.

sections.treasure: A way into the Cage, if they want one. And the noodle bar, which is the best place in the backstreets to hear rumours, Byakko or otherwise.

sections.heading: The Rank You Didn't Ask For
sections.tag: Encounter · Byakko escalation · when a PC holds a stripe
sections.readAloud:
▶ THE MORNING AFTER

There's a box on the Heights Alliance doorstep.

INSIDE IT — A dozen takoyaki, still warm. A bottle of corn soup. And a card with three white stripes painted on it.
THE CARD SAYS — CONGRATULATIONS. THE NORTH ALLEY IS YOURS.

▶ THE CHALLENGER

He's waiting at the station when you come back from your odd job. Two stripes, a cast on one wrist, and a grin.

"Senpai. Sorry. Law's the law."

He shrugs out of his jacket.

"Here, or do you want to pick the street?"

▶ IF THEY WIN AGAIN

He gets up, bows properly, and asks if you're hungry.
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — a PC beats a Stripe or above in front of witnesses → under the Law, they hold that rank → tribute arrives → challengers arrive → the school finds out → the PC decides what to do with a street.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — the box on the doorstep, one challenger, and Sugitsu's office.

• THE RULE — under the Stripe Law, a PC who beats a ranked member in front of witnesses holds that rank, whether they want it or not. Beat Three-Stripe Kō and you hold Ikebukuro North Alley. Beat a Corner and you hold a quarter of the turf. Byakko will treat you accordingly from the next morning onwards.
• WHAT A RANK GIVES — free food in every shop the street protects; the gang's gossip; a dozen teenagers who will run errands for you; and, at Stripe and above, the ability to give orders on your own street. A PC who holds the North Alley can end the protection racket on it with one sentence, and it will stay ended for exactly as long as they hold the rank.
• WHAT A RANK COSTS — challengers from below, under the Law, at a time and place of their choosing. Roll for one every window: a d6, and on a 1 or 2 somebody wants the stripe. They come one at a time, fairly, in front of witnesses. A PC who refuses a challenge on their own street loses the rank on the spot and everything that came with it.
• THE SCHOOL FINDS OUT. A provisional U.A. student holding rank in a criminal gang is a headline waiting to happen. Okuma finds out first and is very calm about it. Sugitsu calls the PC in and asks them one question — "what are you going to do with it?" — and the honest answer decides the scene.
• THE GOOD VERSION OF THIS — a PC who uses a street the way a hero would: ends the racket, gets Nakata's gym left alone, talks the fourteen-year-olds into the noodle bar instead of the Cage. Byakko notice. Some of them like it. The White Tiger hears about it.
• THE BAD VERSION OF THIS — a PC who likes it. Free food, deference, a gang that runs errands. Let it be tempting. Byakko are criminals and a stripe is real power.
• THE NAMED CHALLENGERS, by the rank the PC holds — at Fang, Hazama Ritsu (who has climbed to two stripes and wants his first teacher), or one of the Echo Twins, alone, which is the only time they ever fight alone. At Stripe, Saeki Momo or Brick. At Corner, a Stripe from another street, and then Kōga Rin, who simply wants to know.
sections.developments:
• IF THE PC GIVES THE RANK BACK — there is no mechanism for that under the Law, which is the joke and the point. They can lose it, deliberately, to a challenger of their choosing. Picking who gets the street is a real decision, and a kind PC will pick well.
• IF THE PC STARTS A RACKET OF THEIR OWN — let it happen and let it cost them: Okuma finds out, Bose stops shouting at them, and Rawagi, still half-blind from Chapter 5, asks them in a corridor whether this is what they came here for.
• IF TWO PCs WON THE RANK TOGETHER — under the Law it belongs to whoever landed the last blow. Let them argue about it. Or, if they have read "The White Tiger," let them argue that a pair is one fighter, and see whether the street agrees.
• IF NOBODY EVER BEATS A RANKED MEMBER — this section never happens. Fine.
sections.dmNote:
The best Byakko material in the campaign, because it turns a fight the players won into a problem the players own.

Play the tribute warmly and the challengers fairly. Byakko are not trying to trap anybody. The Law is simply the Law, and it does not care that the person holding the North Alley has a maths test on Monday.

aside.label: Heat while holding a rank
aside.body: A PC who holds a stripe adds 1 to Heat at the start of every window, because the gang is talking about them. Losing the rank drops Heat by 2. Giving a street a good, quiet month — no challenges refused, no rackets, no fights outside the Law — drops it by 1 instead of raising it.

sections.treasure: A street, if they want one. Free takoyaki. Information. A dozen teenagers who think the PC is the coolest person alive, which is a responsibility.

sections.heading: The Four Corners
sections.readAloud:
▶ THE AZURE CORNER
WHERE — A flooded underpass, in the rain.

It's been closed for repairs for a year and it's full of water to the knee. A young man in a swimming parka is standing in the middle of it, perfectly still, while the rain comes down outside.

"Shikoji," says Kuze Asagi, without looking up. "I'd like the one with the water gun, please."

▶ THE VERMILION CORNER
WHERE — A rooftop in Shinjuku, with an audience.

Somebody's run fairy lights round the railings, and there are sixty people on folding chairs.

Hōjō Akane is standing on the parapet in a red coat, on fire.

She's been waiting forty minutes for a dragon.

▶ THE BLACK CORNER
WHERE — The Cage's front door.

Genda Tetsuo closes his paperback and stands up, and the folding chair sighs with relief.

"I've been looking forward to this. Which of you is going to try to move me?"

▶ THE YELLOW CORNER
WHERE — A rail yard, two in the morning.

Overhead lines, wet sleepers, and a woman who is somehow standing on a rail and somewhere else on it at the same time.

"Kutsu," says Kōga Rin. "Forty times. I watched you forty times."

A pause.

"Let's see if they edited it."
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — Heat reaches 8 → the Corners come down → each one asks for somebody specific → play one or two of these four as set pieces, not all four in one session → each Corner beaten moves the class one step from the roof.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — one Corner, chosen by which PC has the best match.

• EACH CORNER IS NAMED FOR ONE OF THE OTHER GUARDIAN BEASTS — azure dragon, vermilion bird, black tortoise, and the yellow beast at the centre — as a boast: Byakko keeps the other gods as doormen. Every member can tell you this.
• EACH ONE ASKS FOR SOMEBODY, and they ask by festival name. Kuze wants Masahata (water against water), and Nakaya should be told, quietly, that lightning in water is very bad news for him. Hōjō wants Tazato (fire against fire) and plays to her rooftop crowd; Rakuka will try to get her autograph. Genda wants whoever hits hardest — Kazama, Setaka or Hiro — and will stop mid-fight to talk about engineering. Kōga wants Izuto and nobody else, and Nakaya is her other natural match.
• THE CLASS DO NOT HAVE TO GIVE THEM WHO THEY ASK FOR. A PC who turns up instead of the requested classmate is accepted under the Law, with visible disappointment.
• THE LAW, AT THIS LEVEL — a Corner will fight one challenger at a time. If a pair engages, the Corner's escort of two Fangs and a Stripe stop watching and join in, and it becomes a proper brawl. Both are good fights; one is a duel and one is a battle, and the players choose.
• USE THE PRESETS. Each Corner has a full stat block in the appendix and in the encounter manager. They are CR 8 to 9, built to be a real fight for two PCs at level 8 or one PC with everything going for them.
• EACH WIN IS PUBLIC. Every Corner fight is witnessed and filmed. The PC who wins holds the Corner — see "The Rank You Didn't Ask For" — and the White Tiger watches the footage that night.
sections.developments:
• IF A PC LOSES TO A CORNER — the Corner helps them up. Byakko do not humiliate a fair loser. Heat drops by 1, and the Corner offers a rematch in a fortnight.
• IF THE CLASS TAKE ALL FOUR — the roof door opens, and the next window starts with a note on the Heights Alliance doormat in white paint: ONE A.M. BRING WHOEVER YOU LIKE. SHE'LL ONLY FIGHT ONE.
• IF THE FIGHT IS GOING BADLY — the crowd is the dial. They can call a fight, and they will if somebody is being badly hurt; Byakko like their fighters coming back.
• IF NAKAYA ZAPS THE FLOODED UNDERPASS — she wins, instantly, and is told off by everybody including Kuze, who is then very impressed and asks her out for noodles.
sections.dmNote:
Four set pieces with four flavours — water, fire, stone, lightning — and four specific matches built off the class's quirks. Pick the ones your table will enjoy most and do not feel obliged to run the others.

Make each one a scene first and a fight second: the underpass in the rain, the rooftop with fairy lights, the takoyaki cart, the rail yard. The Corners are not villains. They are the four best fighters in west Tokyo, and they want the best fight of their lives.

aside.label: Why the Corners are not on the spine
aside.body: Because they are sport. Nobody dies at a Corner fight. Byakko are a gang and they hurt people, but the Corner fights are the part of Byakko that is closest to a tournament, and the campaign plays them as the summer's Sports Festival — witnessed, ranked, and fun.

sections.treasure: A Corner, if they win — a quarter of the turf, and the White Tiger's attention. Level 9 after the first one, if they have not had it already.

sections.heading: The White Tiger
sections.tag: Encounter · Byakko finale · the roof of the Cage · Heat 10
sections.readAloud:
▶ THE ROOF OF THE CAGE
WHERE — One in the morning.

Floodlights. Green netting. Four hundred people on the lower floors, packed against the nets, looking up.

She's sitting cross-legged on an upturned crate, eating ramen out of a takeaway bowl. Very large, very white, black stripes down her arms, gold eyes.

She finishes her noodles before she looks at you. It takes a while.

"Good," says Hakuro Mitsuki. "I've watched your festival nine times. The pairs thing."

She puts the bowl down.

"I thought it was cowardice."

She stands up. She keeps standing up for longer than you expect.

"One of you. Whoever's strongest. That's the Law."

▶ IF TWO OF THEM STEP FORWARD

She steps back. Not afraid. Disappointed.

"Then nobody wins tonight," she says — and four hundred people go quiet.

▶ IF SOMEBODY ARGUES THAT A PAIR IS ONE FIGHTER
HOW TO RUN IT — Only if a player says it themselves. Never suggest it.

She looks at them for a long time.

"Prove it," she says.
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — Heat 10 → the note on the doormat → the roof at one a.m. → she asks for one → the class decide → the fight → whatever they do with a gang.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — the roof, the choice, and the fight. Do not cut the choice; it is the scene.

• HAKURO MITSUKI, BYAKKO. Undefeated for six years. Not a villain — a champion, and the gang's Law in a person. She added the sixth rule herself: nobody fights a kid without a stripe. Play her with total sincerity.
• THE CHOICE IS THE ENCOUNTER, AND THERE ARE THREE WAYS THROUGH IT.
  — ONE ON ONE, UNDER THE LAW. A single PC against a CR 12 heteromorph at level 9 or 10. It is very likely a loss, and a glorious one. She helps them up. She tells the four hundred people on the floors below that U.A. is off limits to Byakko from tonight, because anybody who would climb her roof alone is worth leaving alone. Heat drops to 0 and stays there.
  — AS A PAIR, IGNORING THE LAW. She declares the fight void and walks away, and Byakko splinters: four Corners and a dozen Stripes fighting each other for a title nobody won. The backstreets are worse for a month. Heat stays at 10 and the class have made a war.
  — AS A PAIR, CLAIMING THE LAW. Somebody argues — and it should be a player, out loud — that a pair is one fighter. Forge's whole argument, from the first morning of the year: "for a second it doesn't look like two people. It looks like one thing with four hands." She says "prove it." This is the campaign's thesis, paid out in the side plot.
• HOW TO PROVE IT, MECHANICALLY — the pair fight her together, and every single turn of the fight they must be within reach of each other, with the pair rule in effect. The first time they split — one turn, one PC more than 5 feet from the other at the end of their move — it becomes two fighters, she steps back, and the fight is void. If they never split, it was one fighter, and if they win, the pair hold the title of Byakko together, which has never happened.
• RUN HER FULL STRENGTH. Her stat block is in the appendix and the encounter manager. Apex Read punishes the same PC hitting her twice in a row; Pounce punishes a pair that drifts apart; Undefeated punishes everybody. A pair who stays glued together and trades off who hits her is playing the fight correctly, and you should say so afterwards.
• KŌGA RIN IS HER SECOND and acts right after her if anybody else joins in. Under any of the three outcomes, Rin is the one who tells the floors below what happened.
sections.developments:
• IF THE PAIR WIN — two U.A. first-years hold the White Tiger. Every member of Byakko answers to them. Play the next session as the consequence: what do they do with a gang? Dissolve it (it will not dissolve; it will find a new Tiger by Friday). Reform it (slow, hard, possible). Hand it back (to whom?). Sugitsu asks them the same question he asked about the stripe. Bose says, of the footage, "Good stance."
• IF ONE PC FIGHTS ALONE AND, AGAINST THE ODDS, WINS — they are Byakko. Everything above applies, alone.
• IF THE CLASS REFUSE THE FIGHT — that is allowed and Byakko respect it more than they expect to. She sends them a bowl of ramen. Heat drops to 5.
• IF A PC USES A QUIRK THAT WAS NOT IN THE FESTIVAL ARCHIVE — Kinji's Jackpot, a Sunbreath strike, an Envoy, a Pact — she notices, and grins, because something she did not see coming is the best thing that has happened to her in six years.
sections.dmNote:
This is the Byakko storyline's finale and it should feel like one: floodlights, a crowd, a champion, and a choice that puts the campaign's first idea — that two people fighting as one is something new — against the gang's only idea, which is that strength is singular.

Let the players argue. If nobody thinks of the third option, do not suggest it. A table that fights her alone and loses, or ignores the Law and wins a void, has made a real choice. A table that remembers Forge on the first morning has earned something enormous.

aside.label: What holding the title actually means
aside.body:
Byakko is a few hundred people across two wards: a protection racket, a dice den, a fight club, a chop shop and a lot of teenagers. Holding the title means all of it answers to you, for exactly as long as nobody beats you.

It is a terrible thing for a provisional hero to own, and a fascinating thing to give a group of players in the last chapter of a season. If your table want to keep it into a second season, let them. If they want to end it, the Law offers one clean way: lose, on purpose, to somebody worth giving it to.

sections.treasure: The title of Byakko, or the gang's respect, or a war. Level 10 at the end of the night, whichever it was.

sections.heading: Odd Nights
sections.tag: DM note · how the Underground enters · rare, random, late
sections.readAloud:
▶ THE FIRST TIME AN ODD NIGHT COMES UP
HOW TO RUN IT — Read this and nothing more. Do not point at it. Do not explain it. Move on to something else immediately.

It's nearly midnight and the street is ordinary. A vending machine. A cat. A train going over a bridge somewhere.

And then something about it isn't ordinary — and you couldn't say what — and by the time you've turned round it's gone.
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — a PC spends a slot out after dark somewhere strange → roll a secret d100 → if it hits a faction, give them a trace and nothing else → if they chase it, climb a rung → at Contact, run that faction's scene.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — this is a reference note, not a scene. Read it once before Chapter 4.

• THE ROLL — whenever a PC spends a free-time slot out after dark, somewhere odd, roll a d100 behind the screen. Chapters 2 and 3: 01–03 is a rumour and that is all. Chapter 4 sneak-outs: 01 Legion, 02 Court, 03 Kuroshiki, 04–08 a rumour. Chapter 6: 01–02 Legion, 03–04 Court, 05–06 Kuroshiki, 07–12 a rumour.
• THE HAUNTS — at a faction's haunt its band widens to 01–10. The Legion: Kurogane Wharf, Ginza after midnight, any hospital's back entrance. The Court: Kōenji, any public bathhouse, Byakko turf at Heat 4+ (the stolen arrowhead). Kuroshiki: any Case 9 site, the loading-yard crater, any hospital, and — after Chapter 5 — the Heights Alliance ground floor.
• THE LADDER — every faction sits on five rungs: RUMOUR (somebody says something), TRACE (evidence that does not fit any quirk), WITNESS (they see it happen, and it sees them), CONTACT (a member speaks to them), INVITATION (they are offered something). A PC climbs a rung only by choosing to chase it, with a free-time slot. Nothing ever falls back down a rung; a faction left alone simply waits.
• THE LIMITS — no faction reaches Contact before Chapter 6. Run one faction's contact per window, at most. The class should almost certainly find one faction this season, possibly two, and very probably not all three.
• THE THREE THINGS THE DM MAY PLACE ON PURPOSE, once each — a Legion trace: Alucard Chosoji, glimpsed (see his entry in the supporting cast). A Court trace: Rob Joestar losing his temper, and Whitesnake doing something an acid quirk cannot do. A Kuroshiki trace: the corridor light on the Heights Alliance ground floor clicking off at eleven, and then on, and then off.
• EVERYTHING ELSE IS THE DICE. That is the point. "Incredibly rare to find" means the table might go a whole season without an Odd Night landing, and that is a correct outcome.
sections.developments:
• IF A PLAYER STARTS HUNTING FOR THE SUPERNATURAL ON PURPOSE — let them, and let it be slow. Going to a haunt widens the band; asking at the noodle bar earns a rumour; chasing a rumour earns another roll. Persistence is how a rung is climbed, never a single check.
• IF A PLAYER TELLS A TEACHER — the teacher is kind and does not believe them, with one exception: Rob Joestar, who goes very quiet and changes the subject.
• IF TWO FACTIONS SURFACE AT ONCE — good, especially the Legion and the Court, who have been at war since 1868. Let the class be caught between them. That is a second season.
• IF NO FACTION EVER SURFACES — the city still has a basement and the players never went down. Leave it for next year.
sections.dmNote:
The design brief for the Underground was that the players find it randomly and late, and this note is how that is enforced. Roll in secret, give traces sparingly, and never point. The joy of the Underground is the moment a player says "hang on — that wasn't a quirk," and that moment only exists if the module has not said it first.

When you deliver a trace, deliver it the way the ticker was delivered in Chapter 2: flatly, in passing, as part of something else. Then let the player decide whether to turn round.

aside.label: Why nobody has noticed
aside.body:
Because everybody has a quirk, and anything strange is assumed to be one. A man with a white figure standing behind him has "an acid quirk with a projection component." A woman who can stay underwater for twelve minutes has "something respiratory." A girl who makes lances out of her own blood is "probably Mibu-something, isn't that a quirk family?" The registry is a form, and forms are filled in by people who have stopped wondering.

It is the same blindness as the archive, pointed the other way. Hero society documents everything it can see and assumes it has seen everything.

sections.treasure: Nothing, until a player chooses to turn round.

sections.heading: A Party That Ends at Dawn
sections.readAloud:
▶ THE INVITATION

Heavy cream card, red wax, a seal of a sword through a crown.

Hand-delivered. It was on the inside of the Heights Alliance door, which nobody heard open.

"The Centurion Mina Toda requests the pleasure of the young person who was at the wharf. The Crimson Room, Ginza. Eleven o'clock until dawn. Dress is formal. You may bring one friend."

▶ THE CRIMSON ROOM

Top floor of a Ginza building with no sign on it.

THEY SEE — Red velvet, candlelight, a string quartet. Sixty very beautiful people in evening dress. Every window blacked out.
AND — There's a buffet. It's magnificent. Nobody is eating from it.

▶ MINA TODA

She looks nineteen, and she's holding a glass of something red that she doesn't drink from.

"You came. Good. I'll be honest with you, because it saves time and we have until sunrise."

She smiles, and it doesn't quite get to her eyes, because her eyes are a hundred years old.

"We'd like to talk about your friend with the beam."

▶ AT DAWN
HOW TO RUN IT — Tell them what time it is. Repeatedly, all night.

Somebody pulls the blackout down from the east window.

And the room screams.
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — the Legion reach Contact → an invitation through a door nobody heard open → the Crimson Room, beautiful and wrong → Mina Toda makes an honest offer → something goes wrong, or does not → survive until sunrise → the sun comes in.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — the room, the offer, and dawn.

• THE LEGION REACHED CONTACT because a PC chased a trace: Thralls at Kurogane Wharf, a drained Byakko member in a doorway, a clinic with no night patients and a full blood bank, or a tall pale man who was standing in a crowd and then was not. Somebody saw them. They want to know who.
• THE OFFER IS HONEST, which is the horror. Mina wants three things. One: Ren Suzuki's beam is radiant, and the Legion would like to know whether he knows what that means; they would rather have him as a friend than find out. Two: the class to stop helping Alucard Chosoji, "a deserter, and the worst thing in Tokyo, including us." Three, only if a PC holds Byakko rank: feeding rights. The Legion has been feeding on Byakko because nobody misses them. Now somebody holds a Byakko street. Would that somebody like to negotiate?
• WHAT THE LEGION OFFERS BACK — protection, money, a favour from people who have outlived eleven generations of heroes, and, if anybody asks, eternity. Mina will explain exactly what each costs. Turning a PC is not on the table unless the player wants it to be, and even then it should be a conversation out of character first.
• THE THRESHOLD RULE MATTERS. A Legion vampire cannot enter a private home uninvited. Heights Alliance is a home. If anybody in the class has ever said "come in" to a stranger at the door — a fan, a delivery, a girl from a party — the Legion can come in. Ask the players, casually, early in the chapter, whether anybody has.
• WHAT GOES WRONG — if the PCs refuse, nothing goes wrong; Mina sighs and has them shown out, and Captain Grau follows them home and stands across the road until dawn. If they insult the Legion, threaten Mina, or a Thrall in the service corridor smells somebody's blood, the party turns: Thralls from the kitchens, Legionaries from the dance floor, Grau at the door. The way out is not winning. It is reaching the east window at sunrise.
• ALUCARD CHOSOJI IS HERE THE WHOLE TIME and nobody but the PCs can see him: in a mirror, in a doorway, in the shadow under the piano. He does not help unless it goes badly. If it does, the room's shadows go wrong, and for one round the Legion is fighting something that frightens them.
sections.developments:
• IF THE PCs ACCEPT A DEAL — honour it, and charge for it later. The Legion keep their word to the letter. It is the spirit they have no use for.
• IF REN IS THERE — he is the most important person in the room and does not know it. If he fires, every vampire in the Crimson Room stops. Then they all come for him at once.
• IF A PC TRIES TO FORGIVE THEM — Ren may. Mina is genuinely moved, and genuinely uninterested, which is the saddest thing in the scene.
• IF THE PCs WANT TO WAR WITH THE LEGION — the Astral Court has been at war with them since 1868 and will be very interested to hear that. That is a second season.
• IF NOBODY GOES TO THE PARTY — the Legion take that as an answer. Grau stands across from the west gate for three nights. Then the card comes again, for two.
sections.dmNote:
The Legion is Hellsing: gothic, courteous, monstrous, and very old. Play the room as beautiful first and wrong second — the buffet nobody eats, the windows nobody opens, a string quartet that has not missed a note since 1923.

The scene is a negotiation that can become a siege. The siege has a clock that the players can see coming — dawn — and the way out is the sun, not the sword. Tell them what time it is, every so often.

aside.label: Alucard Chosoji, explained — for the DM only
aside.body:
His registry says Black, a shadow-merging quirk, and the Commission file notes that what he does is well beyond what Black can do. That is because it is not Black. It is not a quirk at all.

Alucard is the oldest vampire in Tokyo, older than the Legate, and a deserter from the Legion since before the war. He hunts them, alone, and has for eighty years. He watched Class 1-A all year because the Legion was watching the festival kids too, the way the Legion watches anything strong. He never says any of this. If a PC asks him directly, he says "Yes," to whichever question they asked, and leaves.

sections.treasure:
An honest offer from something terrible, and the knowledge that Ren Suzuki is a weapon against it.

If Alucard intervened: his card, which is blank and black, and which, if burned at midnight, brings him once.

sections.heading: Matsu-no-Yu
sections.readAloud:
▶ MATSU-NO-YU

A public bathhouse in Kōenji. The old kind, with a painting of Mount Fuji on the wall and a cold plunge pool nobody uses in winter.

Somebody's using it.

THEY SEE — An old woman at the bottom of it, sitting cross-legged on the tiles, eyes closed.

She's been down there since you came in.

▶ WHEN SHE COMES UP

She surfaces without a gasp. Not even a deep breath.

"Twelve minutes," says Grandmother Hinata Sae. "The rumour says ten."

She looks at you.

"Sit down. You breathe like a train. Who taught you to breathe like a train?"

▶ THE BOY AT THE COUNTER

Seventeen, a pompadour you could shelter under, a convenience-store name badge still on from his shift.

And behind him — just for a second, as he turns — there's somebody else standing exactly where he's standing.

Made of folded paper.

▶ ROB JOESTAR, IF SOMEBODY ASKS HIM

He doesn't say anything for a long time.

Then he closes the classroom door.

"It's called Whitesnake. It isn't acid." A pause. "And if Grandmother Hinata sent you, I suppose I owe her a phone call."
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — the Court reached Contact → the bathhouse → the woman at the bottom of the cold pool → a test, not a fight → the boy at the counter and the thing behind him → what the Court needs → Rob Joestar, eventually.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — Hinata surfacing, her test, and the arrowhead.

• THE COURT REACHED CONTACT because a PC chased a trace: Saeki Momo's Envoy at the west gate, a Byakko fighter with a power nobody registered, a teacher whose acid quirk has a man standing behind it, or the rumour about the old woman in the Kōenji cold bath.
• GRANDMOTHER HINATA SAE tests, she does not fight. A slap that stings like sunburn, a question about how they breathe, and then a breathing exercise in the cold pool that every PC fails except, possibly, Chozen, who has read about this. She is eighty-one, kind in a way that hurts, and has buried three students who took an Envoy too young.
• HŌSHŌ KAITO and his Envoy, Paper Planes, are the Court's youngest bearer and the likeliest friend the class make here. He is polite, earnest, works night shifts, and would like very much not to talk about his hair.
• WHAT THE COURT NEEDS — one of their seven arrowheads was stolen in spring by a former Courtier, Saotome Shin. He has been cutting Byakko fighters with it: some die, some wake an Envoy, and all of them climb the Cage faster than they should. The Court cannot walk into Byakko turf; Byakko do not know they exist and would not care. A PC who holds a Byakko rank, or who is known in the backstreets, can.
• ROB JOESTAR was Hinata's student until he was twenty-two, and left because of an Envoy that comes when he is angry. Whitesnake has been standing behind him in plain sight for years, and every person at U.A. assumed it was part of an acid quirk, because everybody assumes. If a PC asks him, he tells them the truth, and asks them not to tell Kinji, because Kinji would never stop asking to see it.
• THE OFFER — Sunbreath. Hinata will teach anybody who passes her test and is willing to come back. Kaito would offer an arrowhead too, if there were one to offer, and Hinata would hit him for suggesting it.
sections.developments:
• IF A PC WANTS TO LEARN SUNBREATH — the Invitation rung, then three free-time training slots at Matsu-no-Yu, each a DC 12 Constitution check in the cold pool. On the third success they have it. See "The Astral Court" for what it does.
• IF A PC WANTS AN ENVOY — the only arrowhead outside the Court's vault is Saotome's. Getting it is a story. Being cut by it is a CON DC 16 save against dropping to 0 HP and dying. Hinata will beg them not to. If a player insists, make it a real choice and a real risk, and if they live, let them name the Envoy after a song.
• IF THE CLASS GO AFTER SAOTOME — he is in Byakko turf, inside an Eclipse that switches off everything the Court taught. Kaito comes. Hinata does not, and stays in the cold pool the whole night, and is there when they get back.
• IF NOBODY EVER ASKS ROB — he keeps it, and nothing breaks. In the epilogue to the season, Kinji sees Whitesnake pick up a pen, and says "Sir, that's not acid," and the bell goes.
sections.dmNote:
The Court is JoJo: a breathing art, a sun war, people with spirits standing behind them named after songs, and a great deal of style. Play Hinata as Lisa Lisa if Lisa Lisa ran a bathhouse, and Kaito as the most polite delinquent in Tokyo.

The scene's job is to connect three threads the players already have: a Byakko fighter with something behind her, a teacher whose quirk never quite added up, and the radiant beam on Ren Suzuki, which Hinata will want to look at very closely.

aside.label: Why Envoys are named after songs
aside.body:
Because the Court is very old, has seen every fashion come and go, and decided some centuries ago that music is the only thing human beings make that is worth naming a soul after. Every bearer names their own. Kaito chose "Paper Planes." Rob Joestar chose "Whitesnake," at twenty, and will tell you he has regretted it ever since and is lying.

If Kinji ever finds out this rule exists, he will not sleep for a week.

sections.treasure: Sunbreath, for anybody who earns it. The Court's gratitude. And a teacher's secret, which is a responsibility.

sections.heading: The Thing in the Laundry Room
sections.readAloud:
▶ ELEVEN O'CLOCK

The corridor light on the ground floor is on a timer and goes off at eleven, and it clicks when it does, and everybody in this building could tell you what that click is.

It clicks off.

It clicks on.

It clicks off.

▶ THREE IN THE MORNING

THEY SEE — Two people in black high-collared uniforms, standing in the ground-floor corridor outside the laundry room. A girl with her sleeve rolled up and a cut on her forearm. A sleepy boy holding his hands together to make a shadow on the wall shaped like a dog.
AND — The dog is moving on its own.

"Go back to bed," says the girl, without turning round. "You can't see it. You'll only get hurt."

▶ THE COUNT
HOW TO RUN IT — Check in with the table before you run this at all. There is a gentler version in the safety note.

Something in the laundry room starts counting. Slowly, out loud.

In a voice you all know. Because it's the voice of whoever started the roll call in the loading yard.

It loses its place.

It starts again.

▶ THE DOOR AT THE END OF THE CORRIDOR

It opens.

A girl none of the sorcerers were expecting is sitting in a chair in the doorway, in pyjamas, looking straight into the laundry room.

"It's been in there since the week after," says Otowa Suzume. "Six weeks."

A pause.

"I didn't know who to tell. Nobody asked."
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — the corridor light clicking → two strangers under a Veil at three a.m. → "go back to bed" → the counting → Otowa, who has seen it every night → the class cannot see it and fight it anyway → the answer is to say your own name.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — the light, the sorcerers, Otowa, and the fight.

• READ THE SAFETY NOTE BELOW FIRST. This is a monster made out of the class's grief for Moshita Maro, and it is the darkest thing in Chapter 6. Check in with the table before you run it. It works just as well as a quieter, stranger scene with the camera pointed away.
• THE KUROSHIKI REACHED CONTACT because a Kegare was born in Heights Alliance. Dread pools where people have been afraid, and a building full of teenagers who lost somebody and did not talk about it is a deep pool. The laundry room is where it settled, three doors down from Otowa Suzume's room.
• MIBU TSUBAKI AND KAGURA ICHIRŌ are Grade Two sorcerers from the Kurama Rite School, a "Shinto seminary" in the hills above Hachiōji, a few miles from U.A. They came under a Veil, expecting a Grade Three. It is a Grade One. They are out of their depth and too proud to say so. Kuroshiki always hunt in pairs — "one to see, one to cut" — and the class should notice that.
• THE CLASS CANNOT SEE IT, at first. Kegare are invisible without Sumi. Ichirō can share his sight for one minute at a time by touching somebody's eyelids with an inked thumb — the Witness rung, in a hurry — and once a PC has seen a Kegare, they can always see them.
• OTOWA CAN SEE IT, because she has been alone in that corridor with it for six weeks, and that is long enough. She has watched it from her doorway every night. She has not told anybody, because the frame does not speak and nobody has knocked. If the class have been visiting her since Chapter 5, she told them a week ago and they thought she was having nightmares. Either way, the fight turns on her: she can see where it is, and she can tell them — out loud, in her own voice.
• THE ROLL CALL — use the Grade One preset. Its weapon is Counting: every round it counts the room, in that voice, loses its place, and frightens everybody who hears it, and it feeds on fear. THE ANSWER IS TO ANSWER IT. Any creature that says its own name out loud when the count reaches it is immune to Counting for the rest of the fight.
