A PC who works that out has solved the encounter, and you should let them say it to the others.
sections.developments:
• IF THE CLASS GO BACK TO BED — the light clicks all night. In the morning Tsubaki and Ichirō are in the infirmary, and Help Woman, who cannot see what did it, says it is the strangest set of injuries she has ever treated. The Kegare is still there. The sorcerers come back with a third, and it is Shirasagi Rei.
• IF A PC ANSWERS THE COUNT WITH MOSHITA'S NAME — that is the best moment in the chapter, if your table can bear it. The thing stops. For one round it does nothing at all. Then it starts again, one higher.
• IF THE CLASS WIN — Tsubaki is furious that a bunch of quirk users did her job, and grateful, and both at full volume. Ichirō thanks Otowa, by name, first.
• THE NEXT DAY, SHIRASAGI REI turns up at the U.A. gate in sunglasses, eats half of Kinji's lunch, takes one look at Kinji's quirk on the registry, and says "huh." That is the Invitation, and also a hook the DM can pick up or leave.
sections.dmNote:
The Kuroshiki are Jujutsu Kaisen: curses born from fear, sorcerers with inherited techniques, barriers nobody outside can see through, and a very strong man in sunglasses who is far too pleased with himself. Their contact scene is the one that comes home, literally, and it should be the most personal of the three.

It is also where Otowa Suzume gets a scene that has nothing to do with the frame. She has been the only witness in the building for six weeks, and the campaign's oldest line — nobody asked — is true one last time. Let a player knock on her door first.

aside.label: Safety, and the horror dial
aside.body:
A monster made out of grief, speaking in a classmate's voice, in the dorm, at three in the morning, is a lot. Before you run this, ask the table the Underground question again: gory, spooky, or Saturday-morning?

For a gentler version, make the voice nobody's — just counting, in a voice like an announcer — and make the fight short. The answer is still to say your own name. The scene still lands. Nobody has to hear a friend's voice come out of a laundry room.

sections.treasure: A building that is theirs again. The ability to see Kegare, permanently, for every PC who looked. Two sorcerers who owe them one. And, from Shirasagi Rei, an invitation to the Kurama Rite School that Sugitsu will absolutely refuse to sign.

sections.heading: The Fourth Door
sections.tag: DM note · room for more · where the next season goes
sections.readAloud:
▶ THE LAST SCENE OF THE SEASON, IF YOU WANT ONE

The last day of term. Forge is at the board with a marker and a bento.

There are twenty names on it. They're already in pairs.

THEY SEE — Behind her, through the window, on the wall opposite the west gate: a white tiger. Next to it, newer, in red, a sword through a crown. And next to that, in a hand nobody recognises, a sun.

There's a fourth space on the wall.

Nothing in it yet.
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — the season ends where it started, at Forge's board → the wall opposite the gate has the year's factions on it → one empty space.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — read the scene and stop.

• THE UNDERGROUND IS BUILT TO GROW. Three factions are written up. A fourth, and a fifth, should be easy to add, and "Room for more" in the appendix has the template and three unclaimed rumours to start from.
• THE ARCHIVE IS STILL UP. Sylar selected for documentation, and nothing about the Sports Festival archive has changed. Next year's first-years would like to watch it. That is the second season's spine, if you want it, and it needs no invention.
• BYAKKO DO NOT GO AWAY. Whoever holds the title, or does not, the backstreets are still there, the Cage is still lit, and there is a new fourteen-year-old on the crash barrier.
• THE QUESTIONS THE SEASON LEFT OPEN, if your table wants threads: what the Legion will do about Ren Suzuki; whether Saotome's arrowhead was the only one that left the vault; why Shirasagi Rei said "huh" at Kinji's registry; whether Rob Joestar ever goes back to the bathhouse; and what Otowa Suzume decides to do about the speaker Forge keeps offering.
• THE FOURTH DOOR IS WRITTEN NOW, IF YOU WANT IT. "The Ledger" in the appendix is a complete fourth faction built on the "Room for more" template — a civil service of death-gods, a writ that is a sword with a name, and a backlog. Its Contact scene is in Chapter 8, so the fourth space on the wall stays empty for the whole of this chapter, and if your table ever finds it the space gets a single black brush-stroke number, and the empty one becomes a fifth. Leave that one empty too.
sections.developments:
• IF YOUR TABLE WANTS TO KEEP PLAYING — the free-time lists keep working, the Heat track keeps working, and the city keeps going. A summer of side quests is a perfectly good season on its own.
• IF YOUR TABLE WANTS TO STOP — stop on Forge's board. It has been the right last image twice already.
sections.dmNote:
The season ends where it began, with twenty names in pairs and no explanation, because that is the campaign's whole argument: these people are components that have finally been assembled, and next year somebody will assemble them differently.

Leave the fourth space on the wall empty. It is the most useful thing in the module.

aside.label: One rule for every faction you add
aside.body: Whatever you add, keep it off the spine. The Underground is the city's basement, not its plot, and the reason it works is that the class find it by accident, late, on their own time. A faction that turns out to be behind everything is a faction that has eaten the campaign.

sections.treasure: Forge's new board. Twenty names. No explanation.

sidequests.name: KUMA'S PAROLE
sidequests.hook: "Character reference," says Kuma, through the glass, embarrassed for the first time in his life. "Parole board. They said it helps if it's someone who fought you."
sidequests.body: He wants a character reference. He is not a good man. Write it, refuse, or write an honest one.
sidequests.reward: an honest one is the only thing he ever thanks anybody for.

sidequests.name: MOSHITA'S NOTEBOOK
sidequests.hook: Hatashi Hamba is holding a notebook and will not look up from it. "Every quirk he ever borrowed. And a thank-you note for each person." He holds it out. "It should be one of yours that takes it."
sidequests.body: Moshita kept a notebook of every quirk he ever borrowed, with a thank-you note for each person. 1-B want somebody from 1-A to take it to his family.
sidequests.reward: none. The scene.

sidequests.name: NEXT YEAR'S CHART
sidequests.hook: "Next year's chart." Masahata has clearly been working on this for weeks. "It's all public data. I need somebody to check the method. Not the conclusions. The method."
sidequests.body: He is already predicting next year and wants help with the data. All of it is public.
sidequests.reward: his thanks, delivered as a correction.

sidequests.name: THE GREY PEOPLE AT THE WHARF
sidequests.hook: "After midnight, down past the container stacks." Okabe Fumi tops up your coffee and doesn't sit down. "Grey people. They walk like they've forgotten how. Don't go."
sidequests.body: A Legion trace quest: slow grey figures at the docks after midnight.
sidequests.reward: the Legion climbs a rung.

sidequests.name: THE OLD WOMAN IN THE COLD BATH
sidequests.hook: "The old girl at Matsu-no-Yu sits at the bottom of the cold pool." Whoever's telling you this thinks it's funny. "Ten minutes. I've timed her."
sidequests.body: An Astral Court trace quest: Matsu-no-Yu, Kōenji.
sidequests.reward: the Court climbs a rung.

sidequests.name: THE STAIRWELL IN OTA
sidequests.hook: "That stairwell in Ota. Where the fire bloke was found." The man says it and then wishes he hadn't. "There's something in it counting. My cousin heard it in the afternoon."
sidequests.body: A Kuroshiki trace quest: the Case 9 stairwell, where a sleepy boy in a black uniform is standing in the middle of the afternoon, looking at nothing.
sidequests.reward: the Kuroshiki climb a rung.

sidequests.name: THE KID WHO DIDN'T CLIMB
sidequests.hook: "February," says Tomo, who is fifteen now and has a folder. "I'm sitting it in February. I've told everyone. So you have to help me now, really."
sidequests.body: Chapter 3's fourteen-year-old is fifteen now and sitting the U.A. entrance exam in February. Coaching is legal.
sidequests.reward: in Chapter 7 he is in the first-year cohort, in the back row, and he has told everybody.

chapters.title: The Teaching Copy
chapters.intro: April. The class are second-years, there are forty new first-years in the building, and the Sports Festival archive is now the syllabus. Somebody in the new cohort has watched a PC's footage four hundred times and built herself out of it, frame by frame, down to the footwork. That is flattering for about a week. Then a company called Clean Read turns out to have been selling quirk teardowns off the back of the same archive for two years — legal, cheap, searchable, and with the class's faces on the thumbnails — and a first-year gets taken apart in a car park in Nerima by a man who paid ¥4,000 to know exactly how. Chapter 7 is the campaign's own idea handed to forty children and a marketplace: everything Sylar did by appetite, done instead by homework, on an invoice.
chapters.dmNote:
This chapter inverts the whole of Season 1 and should be played for that, not for horror. In Chapter 3 the class were catalogued. Now they are the catalogue. Every scene in this chapter is a mirror of one in Chapters 3 and 4, and the table should feel the shape before anybody names it.

Play the first-years with total warmth. They are not sinister. They are fifteen, they are thrilled, and the worst of them is a girl who admires a PC so precisely that she has stopped being anybody else. The horror, such as it is, belongs entirely to the adults' paperwork and to a website with a very good search function.

Clean Read must stay legal all the way through. Nobody there is a villain, the terms of service are fine, the archive is public record, and the Commission signed off on it in 2019. Every time a player goes looking for somebody to punch about it, give them a customer-service email address. Then give them Miyashita Gō, who bought a teardown and used it, and let them punch him.

And put Amano Keita in front of whoever holds a Byakko rank. He is Appetite's method with no teeth in it at all, running up the Stripe Law on a ¥4,000 subscription, and the Law protects him. That fight is this chapter's thesis with a tracksuit on.
chapters.milestone:
LEVEL 11 when the class finish with Miyashita Gō in the Nerima car park, or when they get Clean Read's answer in writing — whichever comes first. Both are the same beat: the moment the class understand that the archive is not going to be taken down.
If your table prefers XP to milestones, hand out a level's worth at that point and stop counting.

closing.label: Chapter Note — the thumbnails
closing.body:
Every Clean Read teardown has a thumbnail, and the thumbnail is a still of the student's face at the moment the commentary explains their weakness. They were chosen by an algorithm for being the frame where the expression changes.

If you want one prop for this chapter, print four of them. Use the PCs. Do not caption them. Put them on the table at the start of the session Clean Read is found, and leave them there.

sections.heading: Second Years
sections.tag: Opening · the new cohort · no combat
sections.readAloud:
▶ SECOND YEARS

April. The corridor outside 2-A smells of new blazers.

Forge is at the board with a marker and a bento. Behind her, through the window, the wall opposite the west gate still has a white tiger on it and twenty names under it. The ground staff stopped painting over it two summers ago.

"Right," she says. "Two things. First: you're second-years, which means you're support staff now. Forty of them arrived this morning and they all think you're on television."

She turns the board round.

"Second: the first-year syllabus this term is the archive. Yours. Three days of it, with the commentary on, in a classroom, every Tuesday."

She eats something.

"Masahata, put your hand down. Yes, all of it."

▶ THE FIRST TUESDAY
HOW TO RUN IT — Do not let any PC watch their own footage in this scene. Through a wall is the whole chapter in ninety seconds.

You're not in the room. You can hear it from the corridor.

"— and this is the moment it goes wrong for him, and if you watch his shoulders you can see he already knows —"

Forty fifteen-year-olds, laughing in the right places.

▶ BEFORE THE SESSION ENDS
HOW TO RUN IT — Write the answers down. Chapter 8 pays every one of them back.

ASK EVERY PLAYER — What does your first-year ask you about, on the first day?
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — the new year at Forge's board → the second-year job → the forty new first-years → the first Tuesday, heard through a wall → the class meet the cohort → one of them has done her homework.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — Forge's board, the corridor outside the classroom, and Tokieda Mei at the end of it.

• THE CLASS ARE SECOND-YEARS AND IT IS A DEMOTION IN EVERY WAY THAT MATTERS TO A FIFTEEN-YEAR-OLD. They are not the newest, most-watched thing in the building any more. They are the ones who carry the cones to Battle Centre III and stand at the back while somebody else is told they might be special.
• THE JOB — each second-year is assigned two first-years to shepherd: timetables, dorm rules, where the good vending machine is, and one afternoon a week of supervised sparring. Hand each PC two of the first-years below. They will keep them all year.
• THE FORTY ARE ONE CLASSROOM TO YOU AND FIVE NAMES. Use these and improvise the rest. TOKIEDA MEI — Replay; small, intense, enormously polite, and has watched one PC's footage four hundred times. ŌGAKI SHUN — Ballast; cheerful, heavy, hero-worships Setaka and writes thank-you notes badly. FUJIMORI NENE — Static; furious at everything including herself, fastest in the cohort, loses on purpose rather than be helped. BABA TOSHIKI — Nine Lives; terrible at the course and will not stop, and everybody already loves him. SHIRAKAWA AOI — Loudspeaker; the cohort's Masahata, already maintaining a chart, which Masahata finds unforgivable.
• THE ARCHIVE IS NOW TEACHING MATERIAL, and that is the chapter. It was always going to be. Forge thinks it is excellent pedagogy and she is right. Sugitsu signed it off and he is right too. Nobody has done anything wrong and the class's worst year is now a Tuesday module with a worksheet.
• LET THEM HEAR IT THROUGH A WALL FIRST. Do not let any PC watch their own footage in this scene. The commentary through a door, in a room full of laughing children, is the whole chapter in ninety seconds.
• ASK EVERY PLAYER ONE QUESTION before the session ends: "What does your first-year ask you about, on the first day?" Write the answers down. Chapter 8 pays them all back.
sections.developments:
• IF A PC WANTS TO SIT IN ON THE TUESDAY CLASS — Forge says yes immediately, and then watches them do it, and then does not mention it again. Run it as a hangout: the PC sits at the back of a classroom while a professional explains their weakness to forty children, and the children take notes.
• IF A PC REFUSES THE FIRST-YEARS — allowed. Forge reassigns them without comment and the two children are told, kindly, that the student is busy. One of them is Baba Toshiki, and he keeps saying hello anyway.
• IF THE PLAYERS ASK WHETHER THEY CAN OPT OUT OF THE ARCHIVE — this is the chapter's first closed door and it should close gently. The footage is public record, the school holds a licence, the licence predates them, and Forge genuinely does not understand the objection until a PC explains it, at which point she stops eating.
• IF THE TABLE TREATS THIS AS A QUIET SESSION AND ENJOYS IT — good. It is one. There is no combat in this section and there should not be.
sections.dmNote:
This is Chapter 2's "Ten Names on the Board" with the camera turned round, and it should be warm, funny and slightly deflating. Second-years carry cones.

The one thing to protect is the corridor. Do not play the commentary as sinister; play it as competent. Good commentary explains the weakness — that is what made it a catalogue in the first place — and a good teacher uses it, and forty children laugh in the right places because the commentator was funny. Nobody in that room is doing anything but their job.

Then let a very polite girl in a new blazer walk up to a PC and get their stance exactly right, and end the session there.

aside.label: What the second-year job is actually for
aside.body:
U.A. puts second-years in front of first-years for the same reason Forge paired the class: it makes the older ones responsible for somebody who is not them.

The mechanical effect is small and worth having. Once per window, a PC can spend a free-time slot on their assigned first-years and gain Inspiration. Once per chapter, a first-year does something useful at exactly the wrong moment, and that is also what they are for.

sections.treasure: Two first-years each, named and written on the sheet. And the question the class have not asked yet, which is what else the archive is being used for.

sections.heading: Tokieda Mei, First Year
sections.tag: NPC · the new cohort · woven through the chapter
sections.readAloud:
▶ THE FIRST TIME

She's very small, she has a new blazer and a notebook, and she's been standing at a polite distance for eleven minutes waiting for a gap in the conversation.

"Excuse me. I'm Tokieda Mei, 1-A." A bow — correct depth, held slightly too long. "I've watched all of your matches."

And then she drops into a stance.

It's your stance. Not an impression of it — the real one. The one you settle into without thinking about it. Including the thing you do with your back foot that nobody has ever mentioned, because nobody has ever noticed.

"Is that right?" she says. "I couldn't tell from the angle."

▶ THE SPARRING HALL

She fights like you.

Badly — she's fifteen and she's had one term — but the shapes are all yours. She has your opening. She has the counter you invented in the semi-final against a boy who isn't here any more.

She doesn't have your quirk. Hers is Replay: she can repeat her own last action perfectly, once, including the parts she doesn't understand.

▶ THE QUESTION FROM THE NOTEBOOK
HOW TO RUN IT — Ask it of the player, in these words, and then say nothing. She has waited all week to ask. She is not being cruel.

She has the notebook out.

ASK THEM — "Can I ask you something? The commentary says you can't keep it up past the fourth round. Is that still true, or did you fix it?"
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — Mei introduces herself with a PC's own stance → she spars like them, badly → she asks about their weakness, from the commentary, in good faith → the PC decides what to do with that → by the end of the chapter she is in danger because of what she copied.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — the stance, and the question from the notebook.

• PICK ONE PC AND MAKE HER THEIRS. Preferably the one whose player most enjoyed the festival, or the one who gave the honest interview in Chapter 3. Tokieda Mei is that PC's reflection, and the chapter needs her to belong to somebody specific.
• WHAT SHE IS — a fifteen-year-old who got into U.A. on a sixth-place entrance exam and a year of footage. She watched the archive the way Chozen watched his father's tapes: as the only available teacher. She is polite, relentless, entirely without guile, and has no idea that any of this is strange.
• WHAT SHE IS NOT — a spy, a plant, a Sylar, or anybody's agent. She has no connection to Clean Read and will be upset to learn it exists. Resist every temptation to make her sinister; the chapter is much better if she never is.
• HER QUIRK IS THE JOKE AND THE TRAGEDY — Replay repeats her own last action exactly once, perfectly, including the parts she does not understand. She has built a fighting style entirely out of a style that was built for somebody else's body, and it will never fit her, and she has not worked that out yet. The commentary never explained why the PC does what they do. Only what.
• THE QUESTION FROM THE NOTEBOOK IS THE SCENE. "The commentary says you can't keep it up past the fourth round — is that still true, or did you fix it?" Ask it of the player, in those words, and then say nothing. Every answer is a good answer. Lying to her is a good answer. Telling her the truth is a good answer and has consequences in "The Man Who Bought a Read."
• SHE HAS A NOTEBOOK AND IT IS FORTY PAGES LONG, all on one student. If a PC asks to see it, let them read it. It is accurate, affectionate, and includes two weaknesses the PC did not know the commentary had identified.
• WHERE SHE ENDS UP — Mei is the first-year in the Nerima car park. Miyashita Gō bought a Clean Read teardown of a U.A. first-year who fights exactly like a famous second-year, and the teardown works on her, because she copied the style and not the body.
sections.developments:
• IF THE PC TELLS HER TO STOP COPYING THEM — she stops instantly, apologises properly, and is quietly devastated, and then turns up a fortnight later having built something of her own that is worse and hers. This is the best outcome and the PC should never be told so.
• IF THE PC TEACHES HER PROPERLY — three free-time slots. She gets good fast, and in Chapter 8 she is the first-year who stands up in the hearing.
• IF THE PC IS FLATTERED AND LEANS INTO IT — also fine, and funnier, and it costs more later. She will be in the car park with a copy of a style she cannot carry.
• IF A PLAYER ASKS WHETHER SHE IS DANGEROUS — she is not. Say so plainly through an NPC if the table starts building a conspiracy. Forge: "She's a first-year with a notebook. You were worse."
• IF SHE SEES A PC USE SOMETHING THAT IS NOT IN THE ARCHIVE — Kinji's Jackpot, a Pact, Sunbreath, an Envoy, a Mark — she goes completely silent, and then asks, with enormous care, why it is not in the footage. She is the first person all season to ask that question out loud.
sections.dmNote:
Tokieda Mei exists so that the archive has a face that loves it.

Every other objection in this chapter is institutional — a licence, a syllabus, a terms-of-service page. Mei is the argument for the archive, standing in front of the person it catalogued, bowing slightly too long. She is a better hero for having watched it. She is also forty pages of somebody else's weaknesses, carried around in a satchel by a child.

Play her warm, play her small, and never play her as a threat. The chapter's pivot is that she gets hurt by the same document that made her, and it lands only if the table likes her first.

aside.label: Running a first-year who copies a PC
aside.body:
Mechanically: she uses the PC's signature move at a fraction of the power and with none of the judgement. Narratively: she does it at the wrong moment.

The useful trick is to let her copy a decision, not a technique. In the sparring hall, give her the PC's actual opening from Chapter 3's tournament, and let the player recognise it before the DM names it. Then let her lose, badly, because the opening was built for someone with a different body, and let the PC watch that happen.

sections.treasure: A forty-page notebook about one PC, written with great affection, containing two weaknesses they did not know were on the record.

sections.heading: Clean Read
sections.readAloud:
▶ HOW IT TURNS UP

It's a first-year who shows you, because to a first-year it isn't news.

"Oh — everyone uses it. It's four thousand yen a month."

Ōgaki Shun turns his phone round, cheerfully, the way you'd show somebody a train timetable.

THEY SEE — cleanread.jp. A search box. A grid of thumbnails.
AND — The thumbnails are faces. Some of them are yours.

▶ YOUR PAGE

Eleven minutes long. Clean titles, clean edit, no music. A calm man's voice.

"— so what we're actually looking at here is a hard ceiling, and the commentary team flag it at four minutes forty in the Day Three broadcast, which you can hear for yourself —"

And then the broadcast audio. Unedited. The original commentator saying the thing he said in front of forty thousand people.

"— and from there it's just arithmetic. Three recommended approaches. One of them you can do with a van."

Timestamps down the side. A comments section, closed. A rating: 4.6.

▶ THE BOTTOM OF THE PAGE
HOW TO RUN IT — This is the chapter's closed door. Read it flatly. It is all true.

"All footage used under the Sports Festival Public Broadcast Licence (2019 revision). Clean Read does not film, interview, or contact any athlete."

And under that, smaller: Sources. Four hundred and six of them. Every one a public link.

▶ THE SEARCH BOX
HOW TO RUN IT — Hand it to a player and let them type at the table. This is the session.

ASK THEM — What do you look up?

Saki Hiyori's page is forty minutes long and has 2.3 million views.

Moshita Maro's page is still up. It has a comment section, and the comment section is closed, and the top of the page says MEMORIAL in small grey letters — because somebody at Clean Read thought that was the decent thing to do.
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — a first-year shows them the site, casually → a PC reads their own page → the class work out how big it is → every door they push is open and legal → they get an answer in writing, and the answer is no.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — the phone, the eleven-minute video, and the licence line at the bottom of the page.

• WHAT CLEAN READ IS — a two-year-old subscription site with four employees and about ninety thousand subscribers, which sells quirk teardowns: calm, well-made, eleven-minute breakdowns of a named quirk user's mechanism, limit and weakness, assembled entirely from public broadcast footage and professional commentary. Sports Festival pages are the back catalogue. Pro-hero pages are the business. ¥4,000 a month, cancel any time.
• IT IS ENTIRELY LEGAL AND THAT IS THE POINT. The footage is public record under a licence the Commission revised in 2019. They never contact a subject. They have never been sued. They have a press page and a customer-service email and a politely worded takedown policy that applies to copyrighted material and not to facts.
• WHO IS BEHIND IT — Kirishita Noe, thirty-one, a former broadcast researcher who worked on the festival commentary team for four years and left to do this. She will answer an email within a day, in person if asked, and she is not sorry, and she is not a monster. She thinks she is doing journalism and she can argue it well. Let her.
• THE SEARCH BOX IS THE SCARIEST OBJECT IN THE CHAPTER. Let a player type things into it at the table. Their own name. A classmate's. A teacher's — Saki Hiyori's page is forty minutes long and has 2.3 million views. Moshita Maro's page is still up, and it has a comment section, and the comment section is closed, and the top of the page says MEMORIAL in small grey letters because somebody at Clean Read thought that was the decent thing to do.
• WHAT THE CLASS CAN ACTUALLY DO, AND WHAT EACH COSTS — email the company (they get a polite, prompt, immovable reply); ask Forge (she goes to the staff room and comes back angrier than they have ever seen her, and with nothing); ask Sugitsu (he already knows, has known for two years, and will tell them exactly how many times he has raised it: four); ask the Commission (a form); ask Inspector Okuma (she tells them the truth, which is that it is lawful and that she has used it); go to the press (Yanami Maho will take the story and it will make the site more popular); break something (see Developments, and do not let them get away with it cleanly).
• EVERY DOOR IS OPEN AND NONE OF THEM LEADS ANYWHERE. Play that straight. This is Chapter 4's investigation structure — the class find out everything and can do nothing with it — and the class will recognise the shape, and somebody at the table should say so out loud.
sections.developments:
• IF A PC ASKS WHETHER SYLAR USED IT — the honest answer is that he did not need to; he had the broadcast. But Kirishita Noe was on the commentary team for the festival that catalogued Habara Jun, and she knows which lines were hers, and if a PC asks her that question directly she stops being able to argue for about ten seconds. Then she answers it anyway, and her answer is good.
• IF THE CLASS TRY TO GET THE ARCHIVE ITSELF TAKEN DOWN — that is Chapter 8. Write the request down and let them draft it.
• IF A PC BUYS A SUBSCRIPTION — let them. ¥4,000 a month. It is extremely useful: a teardown gives advantage on the first attack against any quirk user with a Clean Read page, once per fight, for anyone who has watched it. Half the table will want to cancel it afterwards and one player will not, and that is a better character beat than anything the DM could write.
• IF SOMEBODY HACKS OR VANDALISES CLEAN READ — four employees in a rented office in Nakano. Breaking it is easy, illegal, and provisional-licence-ending; the site is back up in nine days on a new host with a crowdfunded legal fund and twice the subscribers. Make the consequence administrative, not violent: Sugitsu in an office, very quietly disappointed.
• IF A PLAYER WANTS TO MAKE THEIR OWN PAGE, ON PURPOSE, WITH THE TRUTH IN IT — remember this. It is the ending of Chapter 8.
sections.dmNote:
This is the chapter's engine and it is an investigation with no antagonist at the end of it, which is unusual and worth committing to.

The rule is: nobody involved in Clean Read does anything wrong at any point. Kirishita Noe is courteous, prompt, honest and correct about the law. Her product is a weapon and she did not make the weapon; she published the manual the broadcaster already wrote, and the broadcaster wrote it because explaining the weakness is what good commentary is.

Give the players the search box early and let them use it in character. Let them look up people they love. That is the session. The fight is next week and it is a man in a car park who paid four thousand yen, and he will be a relief.

aside.label: If your table wants somebody to blame
aside.body:
They will, and the honest answer is the Commission's 2019 licence revision, which was a transparency measure. It was passed after a scandal about agencies hiding hero injury records, it is a good law, and it is the reason the archive is searchable and the teardowns are lawful.

The class can read the committee minutes. Three of the signatures on them belong to people the class have met. None of them is a villain. One of them, in Chapter 8, will be in the room.

sections.treasure: A written answer from a company that has done nothing wrong, and a search box the players will keep thinking about. And, if they want it, a ¥4,000-a-month subscription that works.

sections.heading: The Man Who Bought a Read
sections.readAloud:
▶ THE CALL

Ten past nine on a Thursday. Ōgaki Shun is on the phone and he's trying very hard to be calm.

"She didn't come back. Mei. We had sparring and she said she'd walk, and — there's a man. He's been at the gate twice this week. He asked which one of us was the one who fights like —"

He says the PC's name.

▶ THE CAR PARK, NERIMA
HOW TO RUN IT — The same kind of car park as Chapter 4. Do not point at it. Describe the strip lights and the ramp and move on.

THEY SEE — Level three. Strip lights. A van parked badly. A girl's satchel on the ground with forty pages of notebook spilling out of it.
AND — Tokieda Mei is up, and bleeding, and still going. Because she copied somebody who doesn't stop.

The man facing her is about fifty, in a quilted jacket, and he isn't in a hurry. There's a phone clipped to his jacket at chest height, playing — quietly — an eleven-minute video he's watched eleven times.

"Fourth round," he says, to nobody. "Here we go."

▶ WHEN THE CLASS ARRIVE

He looks at them for a moment. And then he laughs.

It's the worst sound in the chapter, because it's relieved.

"Oh, thank God. I've got yours too."

▶ READ AHEAD
HOW TO RUN IT — Once a round, open the PC's sheet, find the limitation the Chapter 3 commentary flagged, and have him say it out loud. Accurately. The first time you do this the table will go very quiet.
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — a first-year does not come back → the car park in Nerima → Mei, up and losing → Miyashita Gō, who has watched the video → he has a teardown for every PC who walks in → the fight → what the class do with a man who did his homework.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — the phone call, the car park, the fight. Cut the aftermath to one line from Okuma.

• MIYASHITA GŌ, "TENPIN" — fifty-one, a C-rank villain with nine previous convictions and a kinetic quirk that puts a standing target down and keeps it down. He is not clever, he is not connected, and he has never beaten anybody good in his life. He subscribed to Clean Read in February. He has beaten four licensed heroes since.
• THE SET PIECE IS THAT HE KNOWS. Use the preset, and use READ AHEAD: once per round, he names a thing a PC's quirk cannot do — out loud, from the video, accurately — and gains advantage on his next attack roll against them. Say the actual limitation. Read it off the PC's own sheet. The first time you do this the table will go very quiet.
• IT IS A CAR PARK IN NERIMA ON LEVEL THREE, and the campaign has been in a car park before, and everybody at the table knows it. Do not point at it. Describe the strip lights and the ramp and move on.
• MEI IS IN THE FIGHT AND SHOULD STAY IN IT. She has 9 HP, she will not go down, and she will use the PC's own signature opening at the worst possible moment with Replay stacked on it. A PC who tells her to get out has to actually make her. A PC who lets her stay has to cover her.
• HE IS NOT STRONG. He is CR 7 against a party at level 10, and the fight is short and ugly. The encounter is not the challenge; the encounter is hearing your own weakness read aloud by a man who paid four thousand yen for it while a child you are supposed to be shepherding bleeds on the concrete.
• HE SURRENDERS THE MOMENT IT GOES BADLY, and he is talkative, and what he has to say is the worst part. He will explain the business to them: which pages are worth buying, which heroes are easy now, that there is a man in Shinjuku who will buy a Read for you and tell you who to use it on, and that everybody does this. The man in Shinjuku is Ebata Kyōsuke, and this is how the class get his name.
• THE QUESTION THE CHAPTER ASKS HERE — he bought a public document for four thousand yen and used it on a fifteen-year-old. Which of those steps was the crime? Okuma will charge him with the last one. The class will want her to charge him with all of them.
sections.developments:
• IF A PC LOSES THEIR TEMPER — likely, and it should cost. Provisional licences are a term away; second-years can act in a declared emergency and this is one, but Okuma's report has a line in it about proportionality, and Sugitsu reads every report.
• IF THE CLASS GET THERE LATE — let them get there late if the dice say so. Mei survives either way. She is in the infirmary for a week and she apologises, repeatedly, for having been difficult to find.
• IF A PC ASKS WHY HE PICKED MEI — because she was the cheapest way to a famous student's style, and because there is no teardown of a first-year, so he reasoned that a first-year who fights like a second-year is a second-year with less HP. He says this plainly. He thinks it was smart. It was.
• IF THE PLAYERS WANT TO KNOW WHETHER HE HAS DONE IT BEFORE — four licensed heroes since February, all of them mid-ranked, all of them with long Clean Read pages. One of them is Natsuki Kaori's agency colleague. Blazewatch will want a word.
• IF SOMEBODY TAKES HIS PHONE — eleven videos in the watch history. Four are PCs. One is Moshita Maro's, and it is the memorial page, and he watched it in March, and there is no good reason for that and he does not have one.
sections.dmNote:
This is the chapter's fight and it is a deliberately small one. Season 1's monster could not be reasoned with and could not be beaten by homework. This one is a middle-aged man with a phone clipped to his jacket who has done exactly what the document invited anybody to do.

Read the PCs' real limitations out loud. Open their sheets, find the line the Chapter 3 commentary flagged, and have him say it. That is the whole design of the encounter, it costs nothing mechanically beyond advantage, and it will be the thing the table remembers from Chapter 7.

Then let them win quickly, and let him talk, and give them Ebata Kyōsuke's name from the mouth of a man who thinks he is being helpful.

aside.label: Safety note
aside.body:
A child hurt in a car park, in the same shape as Chapter 4, is a deliberate echo and it will land harder than it looks on the page — particularly if your table had a bad time with Case 9.

Check in before you run it. The gentler version: the class arrive before he touches her, and the fight is over the satchel rather than over Mei. Everything in the section still works, including the laugh and the line about having theirs too.

sections.treasure: Miyashita Gō in custody, a phone with eleven videos on it, and a name: Ebata Kyōsuke, who works out of a karaoke booth in Shinjuku and sells people a way to beat a U.A. student.

sections.heading: A Challenge, Bought and Paid For
sections.tag: Encounter · Byakko · the Stripe Law against homework · 1 session
sections.readAloud:
▶ THE NOTE

White paint on the Heights Alliance doormat, which has happened before and means something different every time.

"FRIDAY. THE CAGE. THIRD FLOOR. HE'S BEEN SAYING YOUR NAME ALL WEEK AND WE CAN'T STOP HIM. — K.R."

Kōga Rin does not write notes.

That's the alarming part.

▶ THE THIRD FLOOR

Green netting, floodlights, and a crowd that isn't enjoying itself.

THEY SEE — The young man in the middle of the ring is nineteen. Average height, average build, tracksuit. And four white stripes on the inside of his left forearm — which is one more than Three-Stripe Kō, who is standing at the netting with his notebook closed.

"Amano Keita," he says. "Hello. I've beaten six people this year."

He takes out a phone and props it on a crate, screen up, playing something eleven minutes long with the sound off.

"I've never won a fight I didn't watch first."

He rolls his shoulder. It's nobody's stance. He hasn't got one.

"The Law says I can climb. So."

▶ GENDA, FROM THE STAIRWELL

"He's not cheating."

The Black Corner sounds tired in a way nobody's heard before.

"That's the problem. Read the wall."

▶ HOW HE LOSES
HOW TO RUN IT — Do not tell the players this. Let them find it, and say so out loud afterwards when they do.

Anything that has never been filmed strips him completely. A die nobody has watched pay out. A restriction declared at three in the morning in a laundry room. A combination they worked out last term with a partner.

He has nothing for that. He's only ever done the homework.
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — Rin's note → the third floor of the Cage → Amano Keita, four stripes, no quirk worth mentioning → he has a Clean Read page open on a crate → the fight → and then what Byakko do about a man the Law protects.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — the note, Amano's introduction, the fight. Genda's line can go last instead of first.

• AMANO KEITA, "FOOTNOTE" — nineteen, a Stray eight months ago, and now four stripes up the Law. His quirk is Second Wind: he can stand up once. That is all it does. He has beaten a Claw, two Fangs, Three-Stripe Kō and Saeki Momo, in front of witnesses, every time by knowing precisely what the other person cannot do — because he watched the festival archive, then subscribed to Clean Read, and then started doing teardowns of Byakko fighters himself, off phone footage of Ring nights, in a notebook.
• HE IS BYAKKO'S VERSION OF THE WHOLE CAMPAIGN and he should be played completely without malice. He is polite, slightly apologetic, and genuinely puzzled that anybody minds. He did not break the Law. He read it. You are what you have beaten, and he has beaten six people.
• THE FIGHT — use the preset. PREPARED FOR YOU: he has a teardown of every PC with a Clean Read page, and once per round he may name one thing their quirk cannot do and gain advantage. SECOND WIND: the first time he drops to 0 HP he stands back up with 25. FOOTWORK, NOTHING ELSE: he has no signature move at all, and if a PC does something that is not in any footage anywhere, he has nothing — see below.
• THE WAY TO BEAT HIM IS THE THING THAT IS NOT ON THE RECORD. Any PC who uses a technique, a trained benefit or a borrowed Underground gift that has never been filmed — Kinji's Jackpot, a Pact, Sunbreath, an Envoy, a Mark, a training benefit invented in free time, or simply a combination they worked out last term with a partner — strips Prepared For You for the rest of the fight. Do not tell the players this. Let them find it, and when they do, say so out loud afterwards.
• HE IS AT THE CAGE BECAUSE OF THE CLASS. The festival made Byakko interested in U.A.; Clean Read made U.A. legible to anybody with four thousand yen; and Amano is the first person to point that machinery at the gang itself. Byakko do not have a rule for this. Several of them have asked the White Tiger — or whoever holds the title now, which may be a PC — to make one.
• IF A PC HOLDS A BYAKKO RANK, HE IS HERE FOR THEM SPECIFICALLY, and this is the best version of the scene. The Law they inherited in Chapter 6 now protects somebody using the class's own worst year as a manual. They can fight him under it, or they can change it, and changing the Law of a gang you nominally run is a Chapter 8 problem with a Chapter 7 fight in front of it.
sections.developments:
• IF THE CLASS BEAT HIM — he gets up, because he always gets up, and then he loses, and he takes it extremely well, and he asks for the fight to be described to him properly so he can write it down. He is the first person in the backstreets to say thank you for a beating since Hazama Ritsu.
• IF HE BEATS A PC — he does not gloat and he does not take anything. He says "four minutes forty" and helps them up, and the clip is on Byakko's group chat by morning, and a fortnight later it is on Clean Read as a source link.
• IF THE CLASS TRY TO HAVE HIM THROWN OUT OF BYAKKO — the Law has no mechanism for it and the Corners will say so, uncomfortably. Genda offers the only honest answer: somebody has to beat him, in front of witnesses, and then the Law will have decided.
• IF A PC SUGGESTS A SEVENTH RULE — write it down. If a PC holds the title, they can simply declare it, and the backstreets will argue about it for a month, and some of them will leave. Suggested wording from Madame Tsuru, who has been waiting all year to be asked: "Seven. You climb with what's yours."
• IF THE CLASS FEEL SORRY FOR HIM — they should. He is a nineteen-year-old with a useless quirk who found the only ladder that would take him and climbed it with a library card. Nakata's Gym would have him tomorrow.
sections.dmNote:
Amano Keita is the chapter's argument with no villainy attached, and he belongs to the Byakko storyline because the Stripe Law is the only institution in this campaign honest enough to have no answer for him.

Play him quiet. He does not posture, he does not threaten, and he is never cruel. He props a phone on a crate, watches eleven minutes with the sound off, and then beats somebody better than him, and he is correct that he has done nothing wrong.

The payoff is the thing that is not on the record. Every table that reaches Chapter 7 has a season's worth of material no camera ever saw — a combination invented in the bracket, a die nobody has ever watched pay out, a restriction declared out loud at three in the morning in a laundry room. This fight is where that stops being flavour and starts being the win condition.

aside.label: Where this leaves Byakko
aside.body:
Amano is not an isolated case by the end of the chapter. Two more Strays turn up with notebooks, and a Fang quietly cancels her own Ring nights because somebody has footage of her.

The gang's whole structure assumes that strength is a property of a person. Clean Read assumes it is a property of a document. One of those is going to lose, and it is not the document. Byakko have about a year.

If your table holds the title, that is their problem now.

sections.treasure: A fight won by something nobody filmed. And, if they want it, a seventh rule on the wall inside the Cage's front door, in their own handwriting.

sections.heading: Free Time — Second Years
sections.tag: Free time · the new year · three slots each
sections.readAloud:
▶ AT THE TOP OF EVERY SESSION IN THIS CHAPTER

ASK THEM — It's the weekend. You've got two first-years, a city, and a subscription you keep meaning to cancel. What do you do?
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — three slots each, as in Chapter 6 → the new side quests are open → so is everything from the Chapter 6 lists → Heat carries over from wherever the class left it → Odd Night bands are at their widest now, and there are four of them.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — one slot each, and one scene with a first-year.

• THREE SLOTS EACH, NO CAPS. Everything in the free-time appendices is open, including the second forty of little things and the second block of side quests, which are written for Chapters 7 and 8.
• THE NEW THING THIS CHAPTER IS THE FIRST-YEARS. A slot spent on an assigned first-year is the cheapest Inspiration in the campaign and the easiest scene to improvise: a timetable, a bad sparring session, a vending machine, a question nobody has ever asked the PC before.
• ODD NIGHTS NOW HAVE FOUR FACTIONS. Chapter 7 bands: 01–02 Legion, 03–04 Court, 05–06 Kuroshiki, 07–08 the Ledger, 09–14 a rumour. The Ledger's haunts are Yanaka, any hospital, any level crossing after midnight, and every Case 9 site — which means it shares haunts with the Kuroshiki, which is the whole reason those two hate each other. See "The Ledger."
• A SECOND FACTION IS VERY LIKELY THIS CHAPTER. Chapter 6 probably gave the table one. Two seasons of slots, four factions and no caps make a second one close to inevitable, and two factions in the same city is where a season's best scenes come from. Let the Legion and the Court find out about each other.
• TRAINING STILL WORKS, and at second-year level a training benefit should be one of the most useful things on a sheet. Three slots, one named benefit, a teacher who says yes. And anything learned in free time is, by definition, not in the archive.
• MONEY — second-years can take paid civilian work without the paperwork being a problem, and the odd jobs list has a second block. The Ring still pays better and is still illegal.
sections.developments:
• IF A PLAYER SPENDS EVERY SLOT ON THEIR FIRST-YEARS — give them the best material in the chapter. Baba Toshiki cannot pass the obstacle course and will not stop; Fujimori Nene loses on purpose rather than accept help, which is Izuto's arc wearing a different blazer; Shirakawa Aoi has built a chart and wants a quote.
• IF A PLAYER SPENDS EVERY SLOT ON CLEAN READ — they will find the whole of "The Market" early. Let them. Chapter 8 is improved by a table that walked into it already angry.
• IF NOBODY WANTS FREE TIME THIS CHAPTER — run one window, offer the first-years, and move to the car park. Chapter 7 holds together as four sessions with no free time at all.
• IF HEAT IS AT 0 BECAUSE OF WHAT HAPPENED ON THE ROOF — then Byakko come to them instead, politely, because of Amano Keita. Heat is not the only reason the backstreets call.
sections.dmNote:
The free-time structure does not change in Chapter 7; the list does. Use this section to put the new side quests in front of the players and to establish the first-years as a standing part of the week rather than a plot device.

The one thing worth protecting: do not let free time solve Clean Read. The site cannot be investigated into submission, and a Saturday spent trying is a Saturday spent reading terms of service, which the Developments box in "Clean Read" already covers. Byakko and the Ledger are what Saturdays are for.

aside.label: The second-year slot, in one line
aside.body:
Once per window, a PC who spends a slot on their assigned first-years gets Inspiration, and the DM gets to ask the player one question about their character that a fifteen-year-old would ask.

Those questions have been the best thing in several tables' second seasons. Write the answers on the sheet.

sections.treasure: Whatever they spend it on. And a first-year who starts turning up uninvited, which is the point.

sections.heading: What the Archive Is For
sections.tag: DM note · the chapter in one page · read before session one
sections.readAloud:
▶ IF YOU WANT TO END THE CHAPTER ON A SCENE

The Tuesday class, the last one of the term. The commentary is still playing.

A PC is at the back of the room this time, because they asked to be, and nobody made anything of it.

On the screen, a fifteen-year-old who isn't here any more borrows somebody's quirk in a cavalry battle and gives it straight back — and the commentator says the thing he said about him, warmly, in front of forty thousand people.

Forty first-years write it down.
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — this is a reference note, not a scene. Read it before session one and use the closing read-aloud if you want an ending.

• THE CHAPTER'S ARGUMENT, IN ONE SENTENCE — the catalogue that got five people killed is also the best teaching resource in the country, and both of those are true at the same time, and nobody gets to pick one.
• WHAT EACH SECTION IS FOR. "Second Years" turns the class from the subject of the archive into its staff. "Tokieda Mei" gives the archive a face that loves it. "Clean Read" is Chapter 4's investigation with no monster at the end. "The Man Who Bought a Read" is the bill. "A Challenge, Bought and Paid For" is the same bill handed to Byakko, who have no idea what to do with it. Free time is where the class find out what else is in the city now.
• THE THREE ECHOES, AND HOW HARD TO LEAN ON THEM. A car park in Nerima (Chapter 4's Adachi). A document that explains a weakness (Chapter 3's commentary). A child who has studied somebody to the frame (Chozen and his father's tapes). Set each one up and then say nothing. Let a player point at it.
• WHAT THIS CHAPTER MUST NOT DO — it must not make Clean Read evil, it must not make Tokieda Mei sinister, and it must not produce a second Sylar. The whole value of a second season built on this spine is that the threat is structural and the people are ordinary. If your table wants a monster, the Underground has four of them and none of them are on the spine.
• WHERE IT GOES — Chapter 8 is the class asking, formally, for the record to be changed, and finding out what it costs to be in a catalogue on purpose. Keep Ebata Kyōsuke's name, the draft of whatever the class wrote to Clean Read, and the answers to "what does your first-year ask you about?"
• IF YOU ARE RUNNING THIS AS A STANDALONE SECOND SEASON for a new table, Chapter 7 works from a cold start: hand the players the four PCs, say that last year a man read the Sports Festival archive and ate five people, and begin at Forge's board.
sections.developments:
• IF THE TABLE WANTS TO SKIP CHAPTER 8 AND STAY IN THE SANDBOX — Chapter 7 ends cleanly on the Tuesday classroom, and the free-time lists, the Heat track and four factions will carry a table for a long time. Nothing is lost.
• IF THE TABLE WANTS THE HEARING IMMEDIATELY — run "A Letter from the Commission" the week after the car park. Chapter 8 does not need the Byakko thread finished first.
• IF A PLAYER ASKS THE QUESTION THE CHAPTER IS BUILT AROUND — "would you take it down, if you could?" — do not answer it as the DM. Write it on a card, put it in the middle of the table, and let Chapter 8 be about it.
sections.dmNote:
Season 1 asked what happens when somebody reads the catalogue with an appetite. Season 2 asks what the catalogue is for, which is a harder question and a better school story, because the answer involves a girl with a notebook who is going to be a very good hero because of it.

The campaign's position, for what it is worth: the archive should exist, the commentary should explain the weakness, Clean Read should probably be legal, and all of that is still a bill that gets paid by fifteen-year-olds who did not vote on any of it. Hold both ends. Do not resolve it in Chapter 7, and be careful about resolving it in Chapter 8 either — "On the Record" is written to let the class answer it with an action rather than a verdict.

And keep the tone where Chapter 6 left it. There is a panda in the staff room. Kinji has a new pair of shoes. The archive is a Tuesday module. This is a school.

aside.label: One rule for the second season
aside.body:
The same rule as the Underground, pointed at the spine: nothing in Chapters 7 and 8 is allowed to retroactively change what happened in Chapters 1 to 5.

Sylar was not working for anybody. Clean Read did not help him. Nobody planned the archive as a trap. The second season is a consequence, not a revelation, and the moment it becomes a revelation it eats the first one.

sections.treasure: Nothing. It is a note.

sidequests.name: MEI'S NOTEBOOK
sidequests.hook: Mei puts the notebook on the table and opens it at the first page and turns it round to face you. Forty pages. All of them about one person.
sidequests.body: Forty pages about one PC, offered freely. Reading it is one slot. Correcting it is another. Teaching her properly is three.
sidequests.reward: whichever the PC chose, and a first-year who stands up in the hearing in Chapter 8.

sidequests.name: BABA TOSHIKI AND THE OBSTACLE COURSE
sidequests.hook: Ōgaki finds you at lunch. "He's done it ten times. Baba. The course. He's not passed it once and he won't stop and I don't know whether I'm supposed to tell a teacher."
sidequests.body: He cannot pass it. He will not stop. Nobody has asked him to.
sidequests.reward: on the eleventh attempt he finishes, and the only person who sees it is whoever was assigned to him.

sidequests.name: FUJIMORI NENE WILL NOT BE HELPED
sidequests.hook: Fujimori Nene is fastest in the cohort by four seconds and she has just thrown a sparring match on purpose rather than take a hand up off the mat. She sees you see it.
sidequests.body: The fastest first-year loses on purpose rather than accept a hand, which is Izuto's arc in a smaller blazer, and the PC who shares it is the one who can reach her.
sidequests.reward: she accepts help once, badly, in public, and hates it, and does it again a week later.

sidequests.name: SHIRAKAWA'S CHART
sidequests.hook: "A quote." Shirakawa Aoi has a chart, a pen, and the complete confidence of a fifteen-year-old with a deadline. "Two sentences. On the record. About where you expect to place."
sidequests.body: The first-year cohort's Masahata wants a quote for her ranking chart. Masahata considers the whole enterprise an act of war.
sidequests.reward: comedy, a quote in print, and Masahata speaking to a first-year for the first time.

sidequests.name: CANCEL THE SUBSCRIPTION
sidequests.slots: 1 slot, and it is not a joke
sidequests.hook: The Clean Read account page is open on your phone. The cancel button is at the bottom. Nobody else is in the room, and the subscription is genuinely useful.
sidequests.body: A PC who bought Clean Read in Chapter 7 has to decide whether to keep it. Play the scene: the account page, the button, the thing it is useful for.
sidequests.reward: either way, one honest moment with themselves. Nobody else ever knows.

chapters.title: Right of Reply
chapters.intro: The class ask, formally and in writing, for the record to be changed — and get a hearing, in a committee room in Kasumigaseki, in front of three people who signed the 2019 licence and one who did not. Meanwhile a man in a karaoke booth in Shinjuku has been selling a way to beat a U.A. student to anybody with a grudge and four thousand yen, and his customers arrive over a fortnight in ascending order of how much they paid. And at a level crossing in Yanaka, two people in black who have been filing paperwork on this city since before the registry existed finally have a reason to speak to Class 2-A, because something at one of the Case 9 sites is nine months overdue and nobody will sign for it. The chapter ends with the class choosing, on purpose, in front of cameras, to put something in the archive.
chapters.dmNote:
Chapter 8 has one job: let the class answer Chapter 7's question with an action instead of a verdict.

So do not let the hearing be the climax. The hearing is session two, it is excellent, it is largely talking, and the class lose it — not because the committee are fools, but because they are right about the law and the class are right about the cost, and those are not the same argument. Then give the table a fortnight of fights they can actually win, and then let them decide what goes on the record.

Play the committee as competent adults. Councillor Minagawa is the campaign's last and best version of Sugitsu's position: sincere, informed, and immovable for good reasons. Hanazawa is the one who did not sign, and she is not a hero either; she wants the archive sealed because sealed records suit her department.

And run "On the Record" as the finale it is. Season 1 ended with a pair fighting as one thing with four hands, in a cold store, with nobody watching. This one ends with the same idea on television, chosen, with the commentary on.
chapters.milestone:
LEVEL 12 at the end of the hearing, win or lose — the class need it for the fortnight that follows, and "The Market" is not a place to be doing arithmetic.
There is no level after this one in this module. If your table carries on, Chapter 6's free-time structure and four factions will hold a third season without any more levels.

closing.label: Chapter Note — what the wall says at the end
closing.body:
The wall opposite the west gate, by the end of the second season: a white tiger with twenty names under it. A sword through a crown. A sun. A single black brush-stroke number, if the class ever found the Ledger.

And, new, in the fourth space or the fifth, whatever the class put there themselves — because somebody in Class 2-A painted on that wall this year on purpose, and Sugitsu asked the ground staff to leave it, again.

There is still one empty space. There is always one empty space.

sections.heading: A Letter from the Commission
sections.tag: Opening · the request is accepted · no combat
sections.readAloud:
▶ THE LETTER

It arrives in the pigeonholes, which is itself strange, because nothing arrives in the pigeonholes.

A cream envelope. The Commission's crest. Inside, four paragraphs of extremely polite Japanese that take three readings to parse — and then one sentence that's perfectly clear.

"Your application for amendment of the Public Broadcast Record (Sports Festival, Class 1-A, last year) has been listed for oral submission before the Standing Committee on Records and Licensing on the fourteenth, at ten o'clock. Kasumigaseki, Room 4."

And under it:

"Submissions are limited to twenty minutes. Two students may speak."

▶ WHAT FORGE SAYS

She reads it twice, puts it down, and doesn't eat anything for nearly a minute — which is the most alarming thing that's happened all term.

"They've never listed one of these before," she says. "Not from a school."

She picks the letter up again.

"Two of you."

▶ SUGITSU, LATER, IN HIS OFFICE
HOW TO RUN IT — Not scolding, not bitter. He is genuinely glad, and he is right, and he says it in one sentence.

"I have raised this four times and been refused four times."

He isn't smiling, and he isn't being unkind.

"They've listed you in nine days. Do you know why?"

He waits. Properly. For an answer.

"Because you're famous. Which is the thing you're complaining about."

▶ THE CHOICE
HOW TO RUN IT — Let the table argue. The correct dramatic answer is almost never the most articulate PC.

ASK THEM — Twenty minutes, and two of you can speak. Who stands up?
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — the letter → Forge not eating → Sugitsu's office and the thing he says → the class have nine days and twenty minutes → they choose two speakers → they prepare, and preparation is the session.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — the letter, Sugitsu's line, and the choice of who speaks.

• THE REQUEST THEY FILED IS WHATEVER THEY DRAFTED IN CHAPTER 7. If they never drafted one, Forge did, in February, and did not tell them, and she will hand it over looking slightly ashamed of herself. Read their own words back to them if you have them.
• TWENTY MINUTES AND TWO SPEAKERS. This is the session's engine. The class have to decide who speaks, and the correct dramatic answer is almost never the most articulate PC. Let the table argue. Let the quiet one volunteer.
• NINE DAYS OF PREPARATION, AND IT IS WORTH PLAYING. Each PC gets two slots; what they spend them on changes the hearing. Ask Okuma what the committee responds to (she tells them: numbers, not feelings). Read the 2019 minutes properly (INT DC 15 finds Councillor Minagawa's actual reasoning, which is good). Get a letter from a victim's family (Ikari Tomonobu's widow will write one; Meguro Sanae's brother will refuse, politely, and his reason is devastating). Ask Kirishita Noe for her view (she gives it, honestly, and it does not help them). Ask a first-year to come (Tokieda Mei will say yes before the sentence is finished).
• EVERY PREPARATION SLOT BECOMES A CONCRETE THING IN THE HEARING — a document, a name, a number, a person in the public gallery. Write them on a list in front of the players. The hearing scene uses the list.
• WHAT THEY ARE ACTUALLY ASKING FOR, and they need to decide: the archive taken down (will not happen); the commentary audio stripped from the public copy (possible, and the one real win available); the archive restricted to licensed professionals (the committee's own compromise, and it has a price); a right of reply — an annotation, by the subject, attached to their own footage (nobody has ever asked for this, and it is the thing the chapter is named after).
• DO NOT TELL THE PLAYERS WHICH ONE IS WINNABLE. Let them pick. A table that asks for the whole archive to come down and gets nothing has had a better session than a table the DM steered.
sections.developments:
• IF THE CLASS WANT ALL TWENTY TO SPEAK — not permitted, and Forge will not fight it, and twenty second-years in a public gallery is permitted and is worth more than they think.
• IF A PC WANTS TO LEAK SOMETHING TO THE PRESS BEFOREHAND — Yanami Maho will run it, the committee will note it, and the twenty minutes becomes fifteen. A real cost for a real gain; let them weigh it.
• IF NOBODY WANTS TO SPEAK — Forge speaks, badly, with her whole heart, and it is the worst submission the committee hears all year, and three members remember it for the rest of their careers. This is a legitimate and quite beautiful outcome.
• IF A PLAYER ASKS WHETHER THIS IS REALLY WORTH A SESSION — yes, and say so out loud at the table if you need to. This is the chapter where the class do the thing adults do, with paper, and win something small. Pitch it as that and every player will find something to want.
• IF THE CLASS SPEND THE NINE DAYS FIGHTING INSTEAD — "The Market" is already running. Ebata's customers do not wait for the hearing.
sections.dmNote:
This section exists to make the hearing a scene the players have equipped themselves for. Nine days, two slots each, and a list on the table of everything they gathered.

Sugitsu's line is the one to get right. He is not scolding them and he is not being bitter; he has been refused four times, he is genuinely glad they have been listed, and he is pointing out — accurately, kindly, in one sentence — that the only reason the door opened is the thing they are there to complain about. He has been the adult who is right more often than the class wants all campaign. Let him be right one more time.

And put the choice of speakers in the players' hands early, so they have nine days to be nervous about it.

aside.label: The four things they can ask for
aside.body:
Pin these up where the players can see them, and let them pick one as their primary ask and one as a fallback. The committee will ask which is which.

1. TAKE IT DOWN. Refused. Public record.
2. STRIP THE COMMENTARY from the public copy; keep it in the licensed professional copy. Winnable, and it is what Clean Read is built from.
3. RESTRICT ACCESS to licence-holders. The committee's own preference, and it quietly hands the archive to agencies and the Commission alone.
4. A RIGHT OF REPLY — the subject may attach their own annotation to their own footage, permanently, and it plays first.

Number four has never been asked for by anybody. That is why it is the chapter's title.

sections.treasure: A hearing date, twenty minutes, two speakers, and a list of everything nine days of work got them.

sections.heading: The Hearing
sections.tag: Location · Kasumigaseki, Room 4 · 1 session · no combat
sections.readAloud:
▶ ROOM 4

THEY SEE — Strip lighting. A horseshoe table. Carafes of water. A clock on the wall behind the committee that everybody in the room can see except the committee.
AND — Five members. Name cards. A clerk with a laptop. Nineteen second-years in a public gallery built for forty. And one first-year in a blazer that's still slightly too big, sitting bolt upright.

The chair, Councillor Minagawa Kōtarō, sixty-four, is reading your submission. He's read it before. He's annotated it.

"Twenty minutes," he says, and looks up — and he looks genuinely interested, which is somehow worse. "Please don't use them on an introduction. I know who you are. Everyone in this building knows who you are."

A pause.

"Begin."

▶ THE FOUR QUESTIONS
HOW TO RUN IT — Ask them of the players, in character, and wait. They are all fair, all answerable, and none of them has a clean answer.

MINAGAWA — "If the commentary hadn't explained Habara Jun's limitation, would he be alive?"
ŌKURA — "If the archive had been sealed last year, how would you have identified the pattern in time to save Ikari Tomonobu?"
TATEISHI — "Your classmate borrowed a quirk in a cavalry battle and gave it back. Forty first-years watched that on Tuesday. Should they not have?"
MINAGAWA, AGAIN — "You're asking me to make the country's heroes harder to study. Who benefits from that, in your view? Be specific."

▶ HANAZAWA, WHO DIDN'T SIGN IN 2019
HOW TO RUN IT — Pleasantly. She is helping them, and it is the worst thing that happens in the room.

"I'll support you," she says, halfway through. "Sealed is cleaner. Sealed is always cleaner."

And two of the class work out at the same moment what that means.

▶ THE RESULT
HOW TO RUN IT — Minagawa offers this himself, unprompted. He has had nine days with their submission. Let him be the best adult in the campaign for ninety seconds.

Takedown is refused. Unanimously, with reasons.

And then Minagawa puts his pen down.

"Nobody has ever asked for this, so I had to go and look it up. Any subject of the public record may attach an annotation to their own footage. It plays first. It cannot be edited by anybody else."

He looks at the clerk.

"It's going to be an administrative nightmare."
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — Room 4, the clock, the gallery → twenty minutes, two speakers → four questions from four members → Hanazawa's support, which is poison → the vote → they lose the big ask and win the small one.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — the opening, two of the four questions, Hanazawa, and the result.

• HOW TO RUN TWENTY MINUTES OF TALKING AS A SESSION: use the list from the nine days. Each item on it is an asset the speakers can spend — a document, a number, a name, a person in the gallery. Let the players decide what to deploy and when, the way they would spend resources in a fight. Checks are CHA (Persuasion) or INT (History/Investigation) at DC 15, and every asset they gathered gives advantage or a flat +2 on one specific question.
• THE FIVE MEMBERS. MINAGAWA KŌTARŌ (chair, signed in 2019) — the transparency measure was his, it was passed after agencies were caught hiding hero injury records, and he is proud of it and should be. ŌKURA (signed) — bored, and the easiest vote in the room; he responds to numbers and nothing else. TATEISHI (signed) — a former pro, forty-one, and the only member who knows what the class are actually describing; she is winnable and she is ashamed of the vote she is about to cast. KISHI (abstained in 2019) — will abstain again; a PC who makes him choose has done something no lobbyist has managed. HANAZAWA (did not sign) — Internal Affairs, wants the archive sealed because sealed records cannot be used against her department, and she will vote with the class for exactly that reason.
• THE FOUR QUESTIONS ARE THE ENCOUNTER. Ask them of the players, in character, and wait. They are all fair, all answerable, and none of them has a clean answer. The best one is the third — Moshita Maro borrowed a quirk and gave it back, forty first-years watched it on Tuesday, and should they not have? Nobody at the table will want to answer that and somebody will have to.
• HANAZAWA'S SUPPORT IS A TRAP AND THE PLAYERS SHOULD BE ALLOWED TO TAKE IT. If they accept her help, the vote goes 3–2 their way and the archive is sealed to licence-holders — which means Clean Read dies, and so does the Tuesday class, and so does any chance of a civilian ever checking what a hero did. Tateishi will tell them, in the corridor afterwards, exactly what they have done. If they refuse it, in the room, out loud, they have done the hardest thing in the chapter.
• THE RESULT, HOWEVER IT GOES. The committee refuses takedown (unanimously, with reasons). It refuses restriction if the class refused Hanazawa. And then Minagawa, who has had nine days with their submission and has annotated it, grants the thing nobody asked for before: a right of reply. Any subject of the public archive may attach an annotation of their own to their own footage. It plays first. It cannot be edited by anybody else. It is, he observes drily, going to be an administrative nightmare.
• IF THE CLASS NEVER ASKED FOR A RIGHT OF REPLY, Minagawa asks whether they would accept one, because he thought of it himself while reading them. Let him. He is allowed to be the best adult in the campaign for ninety seconds.
sections.developments:
• IF THE SPEAKERS ROLL BADLY THROUGHOUT — they still get the right of reply, and Minagawa says why: "Your submission was better than your submission." The paperwork won it. The nine days won it. Say that plainly.
• IF A PC LOSES THEIR TEMPER IN ROOM 4 — Minagawa lets them finish, entirely without reacting, and then thanks them, and the clerk types it all down, and it is in the minutes forever. No sanction. Nothing is more chilling.
• IF TOKIEDA MEI IS IN THE GALLERY AND SOMEBODY ASKS HER TO SPEAK — she is not permitted to, and she stands up anyway, and the chair allows it because he is curious, and she says one sentence about having learned to fight from a dead man's footage, and sits down. If a PC taught her in Chapter 7, give the player the line.
• IF THE CLASS ACCEPT HANAZAWA AND SEAL THE ARCHIVE — a legitimate ending, and a darker season. Clean Read closes in a month. The Tuesday class is cancelled. Yanami Maho cannot check a hero's record any more and says so on television. Run "On the Record" anyway; it is sharper when the archive is sealed and the class choose to put something into it regardless.
• IF SOMEBODY ASKS WHETHER THE COMMITTEE EVER READ CASE 9 — all five did. Tateishi has it in her folder. Minagawa says, without being asked, that he reads the five names before every licensing session and has done since February, and then he moves to the next question, and nobody follows up.
sections.dmNote:
A session of talking in a strip-lit room is a hard sell and it is one of the best sessions in this module if you commit to the structure: assets gathered in advance, spent against four questions, in front of five people with real positions.

Nobody in Room 4 is a villain, including Hanazawa, who is merely self-interested in a direction that happens to align with the class. The committee's questions are the strongest arguments against the class's own position, and the class should lose the big ask on the merits.

And the right of reply must come from Minagawa, unprompted, because the chapter's point is that the class's twenty minutes changed a sixty-four-year-old's mind about something narrow and real. That is what the process is for. It is not a triumph. It is a procedural footnote that will matter to four thousand people, and the class earned it with paper.

aside.label: Why the class should lose the big ask
aside.body:
Because the committee is right. The 2019 revision was passed because agencies were hiding the records of heroes who hurt people, and sealing the archive hands that power back. Every argument for taking the catalogue down is also an argument for letting the strong go unwatched.

The campaign has never once pretended that the adults in the room are cowards or fools, and this is the last and biggest version of that. Sugitsu was right about staying on campus. Minagawa is right about the record.

What the class win is the right to speak first about themselves. That is all. It is not nothing.

sections.treasure: A right of reply: any subject of the public archive may attach their own annotation to their own footage, permanently, and it plays first. Nobody has ever used it. There are four thousand people who can.

sections.heading: Nobody Signed For It
sections.tag: Encounter · the Ledger · Contact · a level crossing in Yanaka
sections.readAloud:
▶ THE CROSSING

Half past midnight in Yanaka, where the cemetery runs right up to the railway and the barriers come down every four minutes for a train that isn't carrying anybody.

THEY SEE — Two people standing on the wrong side of the barrier, in black. They aren't waiting for the train.
ONE — A girl of about fifteen with a satchel and a bicycle, licking the end of a pencil.
THE OTHER — Very tall, very still, with a sword. It's the only thing either of them is wearing that doesn't look like a uniform from a company that files things.

"Twelve," says the girl, writing. "No — thirteen. Hello. You can see us."

She doesn't sound surprised. She sounds relieved to have somebody to talk to.

"That's going to be paperwork."

▶ THE THING UNDER THE CROSSING

It was a person. It's been nine months since it was a person and it's got very bad at it.

It's standing in the four inches of space under the barrier arm. It isn't hiding. It's waiting — the way a thing waits when it's been told to be somewhere and nobody has come.

▶ WHAT THE TALL ONE SAYS
HOW TO RUN IT — The only thing he says. He has not moved.

"It is nine months in arrears." A pause. "It is also, by the Rite's reckoning, a Kegare. The Kuroshiki will not release it to us and we will not sign for theirs. So it stands here."

A train goes over. The barriers go up.

Nobody crosses.

▶ THE NOTEBOOK
HOW TO RUN IT — Deliver it flatly. Then say nothing at all and let a player speak first. Check in with the table before you run this scene.

Somebody will ask about Case 9. They always do.

"Oh — yes, I did four of those."

Hibino Asa turns a page back, finds it, and turns it round so they can see. Five names. Five dates. A column of ticks.

"All on time."

She closes the notebook.

"Was there a problem with it?"
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — a PC spends a slot out after midnight in Yanaka, or at a Case 9 site, or at a hospital → the crossing → two wardens who cannot act → the thing in arrears → the class can see it and they can hit it → Asa's notebook, and the five ticks → what that does to a table.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — the crossing, the thing, the fight, and the notebook at the end. The notebook is the scene.

• READ "THE LEDGER" IN THE APPENDIX FIRST. The fourth faction is a civil service of death-gods who have been filing this city since before the registry, and their whole character is procedure. This is their Contact scene and it should be polite, dry, and absolutely devastating in one specific place.
• WHY CONTACT HAPPENS HERE — because the thing under the barrier has been stuck for nine months between two jurisdictions, and a warden who cannot act gets bored, and Hibino Asa has been looking for somebody to talk to about it since March. A PC who can see her is the first person in nine months who can be told.
• THE TWO WARDENS. HIBINO ASA, Runner of the Ninth Round — fifteen, has been fifteen since 1998, does a notice round on a bicycle, cheerful, chatty, and keeps immaculate records. KAJIURA, Hand of the Fourth Desk — enormous, silent, carries a writ called a sword, and will not draw it without a countersignature, and does not have one. Use the presets.
• THE FIGHT — the ARREAR, NINE MONTHS OVERDUE. It is CR 8 and the class are level 11 or 12, so it is not a hard fight; it is a strange one. OVERDUE means quirk damage is halved against it, exactly as with a Kegare — and it means the thing cannot leave the spot it was told to wait in, so the encounter is a fight against something that will not chase and will not stop. Radiant and Sumi hurt it fully. So does a writ, and Kajiura cannot use his.
• THE CLASS CAN ACT AND THE WARDENS CANNOT, and that is the whole scene. Asa will not stop them, will not help, and will narrate helpfully from the other side of the barrier. Kajiura will say one sentence, once, if a PC is about to die, and it is a procedural observation and it saves their life.
• THE NOTEBOOK IS THE POINT OF THE FACTION. When a PC asks about Case 9 — and they will, immediately — Asa has it. Four of the five, done personally, on time, correctly filed, with ticks. She is not being cruel; she has no idea what those names mean to anybody. The worst year of the class's life was administratively unremarkable, and the people who would know have already closed the file. Deliver it flatly and then let the table sit in it.
• WHAT CONTACT GETS THEM — the Invitation rung, if they chase it: Shirouzu Genbei's sweet shop three streets away, a Mark, and eventually a question answered truthfully by the First Desk, at a price. See "The Ledger."
sections.developments:
• IF A PC DEMANDS TO KNOW WHY THE LEDGER DID NOT STOP SYLAR — Asa does not understand the question, and then does, and is briefly embarrassed on the class's behalf. The Ledger does not prevent. It collects. There is no clause about how somebody died and there never has been, and she will show them the form, which has no field for it. This is the faction's single hardest line and it should never be apologised for.
• IF THE CLASS TRY TO GET KAJIURA A COUNTERSIGNATURE — excellent, and it is the Ledger's whole storyline in one errand. It needs a Desk, and the nearest Desk is unavailable, and the struck-off warden in Yanaka who sells sweets will forge one for a price that is not money.
• IF THE KUROSHIKI TURN UP — they will if the class call them, and Mibu Tsubaki and Kajiura have met before and it was awful. Two Grade Twos and two wardens arguing about jurisdiction across a level crossing while something waits under the barrier is the funniest and most characteristic scene the Underground has.
• IF A PC OFFERS TO SIGN FOR IT THEMSELVES — the single best outcome, and the Ledger has a form for it, because the Ledger has a form for everything. It costs a page with their name on it. Asa will warn them, properly and clearly, before she hands over the pencil. See "The Ledger" for what a page means.
