• IF THE CLASS WALK AWAY — the barriers keep going up and down. Asa waves. It is still there in a third season.
sections.dmNote:
The Ledger is the fourth faction and this is its first scene, so pitch everything in it as administration: a notice round on a bicycle, a satchel, a pencil, a form with no field for how somebody died.

The horror is not that they are cruel. The Legion are cruel. The Ledger are punctual. Four of the five Case 9 victims were collected on time by a cheerful fifteen-year-old who has never heard of Appetite and would not consider it relevant, and the file is closed, and she wants to know whether there was a problem with it.

Play that line exactly as written and then say nothing at all. Let a player speak first.

aside.label: Safety, and the horror dial
aside.body:
This scene puts the five Case 9 names back on the table, in a ticked column, nine chapters after the class buried somebody. That is a deliberate and heavy beat.

Check in with the table. The gentler version: Asa has the four names but does not show the notebook, and the information arrives as her mentioning in passing that it was a quiet winter. Everything else in the scene works untouched.

And if your table's season ended with Moshita Maro, consider whether his name is in that notebook. The Ledger's answer is that of course it is. Whether you say so is yours.

sections.treasure: Contact with the Ledger, a thing under a barrier finally dealt with, and four ticks in a notebook. If a PC signed for it, they have a page.

sections.heading: The Market
sections.tag: Encounter · a fortnight of bought fights · 1–2 sessions · full contact
sections.readAloud:
▶ THE FIRST ONE, ON A TUESDAY
HOW TO RUN IT — Say the price out loud. Every customer, every time. ¥4,000.

She's waiting outside the west gate at four in the afternoon in a cardigan, and she has a printout.

"Are you —" She checks the printout. "Yes. Sorry. This is going to sound mad."

She's paid eighteen thousand yen for nine pages about a sixteen-year-old. She's going to try. She isn't going to come close.

She's doing it because a hero she won't name ruined her brother's life and nobody listened.

▶ THE FOURTH ONE, ON A SATURDAY
PRICE — ¥60,000. A package.

Three of them, in a stairwell at Nakano station. They've co-ordinated, because the plan needs a corridor.

"Four minutes forty," says the one at the top. "We just have to get to four minutes forty."

▶ THE LAST ONE
PRICE — ¥400,000.

The last customer didn't buy a teardown of a student.

She bought one of Saki Hiyori.

"Forty minutes long," she says, conversationally, taking her coat off in the middle of the road outside the Kurogane Wharf gate. "Two point three million views."

She folds the coat over her arm.

"Do you know what she costs an hour?"
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — a fortnight, run in whatever order the table's week allows → one customer per window, escalating → each one arrives with a printout and a grievance → the class work backwards to the man who sold them → the last customer is not after a student at all.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — two customers and the clue chain. The ladder works at any length.

• THE STRUCTURE IS A LADDER OF FIVE, in ascending order of how much the customer paid, and they are deliberately not all villains. Use as many as your fortnight has room for.
  — ¥4,000. YUKA ŌBA, thirty-eight, a cardigan and a printout, no combat training, a real grievance about a real hero, and she will try anyway. CR 1 and the hardest fight in the chapter, because hitting her is monstrous and she will not stop.
  — ¥9,000. A SEVENTEEN-YEAR-OLD FROM A GENERAL STUDIES COURSE at another school who wanted to know if he could, and can nearly, and is appalled at himself afterwards. CR 4.
  — ¥18,000. HAZAMA RITSU, "RICOCHET," if Byakko are in play — he bought one, of a PC, with eight months of Ring purses, because he has wanted a rematch since Chapter 2 and this is the only way he can imagine getting one. CR 1, plays like CR 6 with nine pages of homework, and it should be the funniest and most affecting fight in the chapter.
  — ¥60,000. THREE OF THEM, A PACKAGE, co-ordinated, in a stairwell at Nakano. CR 5 each, and they have a plan built around a real limitation and they get to four minutes forty.
  — ¥400,000. THE LAST CUSTOMER bought a teardown of a pro: forty minutes on Saki Hiyori, 2.3 million views. She is CR 10, she is a professional, and she is not interested in the class at all except as the people standing in her way.
• EVERY CUSTOMER ARRIVES WITH A PRINTOUT and every customer says one line off it. That is the motif of the fortnight: a stranger quoting the class's own commentary at them in the street, badly, from paper.
• THE CLUE CHAIN BACKWARDS IS TRIVIAL AND SHOULD BE. Every customer will say where they got it, because none of them thinks it is a secret: a man in a karaoke booth in Shinjuku, Room 9, after eight, who takes cash, buys the Clean Read page for you, and tells you which approach to use. The class have had Ebata Kyōsuke's name since Chapter 7. The investigation is not the obstacle.
• ESCALATE THE STAKES, NOT THE SPECTACLE. Customer one is a woman in a cardigan and she is the moral centre of the chapter. Customer five is a professional with a grudge against a teacher. The class will be far more frightened by the cardigan a week later, when they realise they have no idea what to do about ninety thousand subscribers.
• USE THE FIRST-YEARS. Each customer is a chance for an assigned first-year to be in the wrong place. Use it at most twice, and never fatally; this chapter has already had its car park.
sections.developments:
• IF THE CLASS HURT YUKA ŌBA — Okuma charges her, the class are cleared, Yanami Maho runs the footage, and the comments are not on the class's side. The chapter's single most uncomfortable outcome and entirely fair.
• IF THE CLASS TALK HER OUT OF IT — possible, hard, and worth more than any fight in the chapter. Her grievance is real and checkable, and a PC who follows it up finds that she is right about the hero and that nobody did listen. That thread can run into a third season.
• IF HAZAMA RITSU WINS — he will not know what to do with himself. He gives the printout back and asks to be taught properly instead, and if a PC says yes he turns up at Nakata's Gym on Monday and stays.
• IF THE CLASS GO TO ROOM 9 EARLY — fine, and Chapter 8 is improved by it. Ebata is not hiding and never has been. Skip to his section and let the fortnight's remaining customers arrive afterwards, already paid for, which is worse.
• IF THE LAST CUSTOMER IS GOING TO KILL SOMEBODY — she might. She is a professional at CR 10 against a party at 12, she has forty minutes of teardown on Saki Hiyori, and she is not expecting four second-years to be in the road. Let Creed arrive at the end of round three if the table needs her, and let her be absolutely furious about the whole business.
sections.dmNote:
This is the chapter's fighting, and the design brief is that each fight is cheaper or dearer than the last and the prices are visible to the players. Say the amount out loud every time. ¥4,000. ¥9,000. ¥18,000. ¥60,000. ¥400,000.

By the third customer the table will have stopped asking who these people are and started asking how many there are, and that is the correct question and it has no answer, which is what makes Ebata Kyōsuke worth meeting rather than punching.

Keep the woman in the cardigan first and keep her harmless. Everything the chapter has to say about the market is in a thirty-eight-year-old with a printout who paid four thousand yen because nobody listened to her, and who is, as it happens, right.

aside.label: Running the printout
aside.body:
Make a prop. One sheet of A4: the PC's name, a thumbnail, three bullet points in plain language about what their quirk cannot do, and a price in the corner.

Hand it to the player at the end of the fight. Do not say anything about it. Several tables have reported that this is the moment the second season landed.

sections.treasure: Five customers dealt with, a woman in a cardigan who may now have an advocate, and the certainty that Room 9 is the only address worth going to.

sections.heading: Ebata Kyōsuke
sections.tag: NPC · Room 9, after eight · half a session · no combat if he can help it
sections.readAloud:
▶ ROOM 9

A karaoke place off Shinjuku's east exit, third floor. Room 9 is the small one at the end with a broken remote.

THEY SEE — A man of about forty-five in a good coat, eating the free pickles. A laptop on the table and a second phone face-down beside it. The screen on the wall is showing a muted music video from 2004.

"Four of you," says Ebata Kyōsuke, and he moves his bag off the bench so they can sit down. "Sit down. I'll order tea."

He eats a pickle.

"I've been expecting someone since February. I thought it'd be the police."

▶ WHAT HE DOES FOR A LIVING
HOW TO RUN IT — Courteous and unhurried. He is not a sophist and he is genuinely willing to be argued with.

"I buy a public video for four thousand yen. I read it — because most people can't, not really, not the technical parts. I write a page of plain Japanese. I charge between eight and four hundred thousand depending on who it's about and how much the customer's got."

He eats another pickle.

"You tell me which part of that I should stop doing and I'll consider it. I'm not being clever. I'll actually consider it."

▶ THE THING THAT ENDS THE SCENE

"You want me gone. Fine — I'm one man in a karaoke booth. You could have me gone by Friday."

He turns the laptop round. A browser. A search box. A grid of thumbnails.

"There are four of these now. One's in Osaka and one's in Korean. I was the first because I used to do fight analysis for a living and I'm good at it."

He closes the lid.

"The video's free. I'm the easy part."

▶ WHAT HE GIVES THEM ON HIS WAY OUT
HOW TO RUN IT — This is the handover into the finale, and it should come from him.

"If you lot ever get to say something first — over the top of your own footage — say the thing the commentary got wrong."

He puts his coat on.

"Not the weakness. The reason. Nobody's ever put a reason in the archive."
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — Room 9, after eight → he orders tea for them → he explains the business without being asked → he is not frightened, not armed, and not sorry → the class decide what to do with somebody who cannot be punched out of existence → he gives them one thing on his way out.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — the pickles, the explanation, and the laptop turned round.

• WHO HE IS — forty-five, a former fight analyst for a broadcaster's sports desk, made redundant in 2021 when the desk was cut, and currently earning more than he ever did. One man, a laptop, a karaoke booth, and no employees. He has never used a quirk on anybody and has never been in a fight. His quirk is Legible: he reads footage faster than a person should. It is registered. It is on a form. Nobody has ever thought about it.
• HE IS NOT A VILLAIN AND HE IS NOT A SOPHIST. He is a middle-aged man doing lawful work that hurts children, and he knows the second half of that sentence and has decided it is not his half. He is courteous, unhurried, and genuinely willing to be argued with. A PC who makes a good argument will get a real answer, and sometimes a concession.
• WHAT HE WILL ACTUALLY AGREE TO, if the class find the right pressure: he will stop selling pages on anybody under eighteen (he agrees to this immediately if asked directly, and is faintly insulted nobody asked in February). He will hand over his customer list (for immunity, or for a favour, or for free if a PC is honest with him about Tokieda Mei). He will not stop trading in pro-hero pages, and he will explain why, at length, and his reason is Yuka Ōba.
• HE KNOWS ABOUT YUKA ŌBA. He sold her nine pages for eighteen thousand yen and he remembers her, and he will tell the class what her brother's hero did, and he will say — accurately — that nobody in the Commission, the press or the agency would look at it and that she came to a karaoke booth because it was the only door that opened. This is the chapter's hardest conversation and he is not wrong.
• THE FOUR COMPETITORS ARE THE POINT OF THE SCENE. Removing Ebata does not remove the market. Say it with the laptop: four sites, one in Osaka, one in Korean, and the archive is free and public and will be either way. The class cannot win this by finding a person, and the scene exists to make that physical.
• WHAT HE GIVES THEM ON HIS WAY OUT — the one thing he has that nobody else does: he knows exactly what a right of reply would be worth. "If you lot ever get to say something first, over the top of your own footage — say the thing the commentary got wrong. Not the weakness. The reason. Nobody's ever put a reason in the archive." That is the handover into "On the Record," and it should come from him, because the chapter is better if the man who monetised the class is also the man who tells them how to answer it.
sections.developments:
• IF THE CLASS ATTACK HIM — he does not fight, he does not run, and he lets them, and it is the single worst thing the class do all season. He presses charges. Second-years with provisional status assaulting an unarmed civilian in a karaoke booth is the end of somebody's licence, and Sugitsu will not be able to fix it, and will say so with enormous sadness.
• IF THE CLASS TURN HIM IN — Okuma takes the file, reads it, and tells them the truth: there is nothing to charge. She will go and talk to him anyway, because she is who she is, and she will come back having got the under-eighteens concession in writing, which the class could have got for free by asking.
• IF A PC ASKS WHETHER HE WATCHED MOSHITA MARO'S PAGE — he did not make it and will not discuss whether he has watched it, and his refusal is the only moment in the scene where he is not completely at ease.
• IF THE CLASS WANT TO HIRE HIM — several tables have. He is for hire. For ¥400,000 he will read anybody, including the White Tiger, including Amano Keita, including a PC's own footage, and tell them what the commentary missed. That is a legitimate and interesting thing to own, and he does good work.
• IF A PLAYER SIMPLY ASKS HIM TO STOP — he says no, and then thinks about it for the rest of the conversation, and at the door he says the under-eighteens thing without being asked again. People do move, slightly, and the campaign has never pretended otherwise.
sections.dmNote:
Ebata Kyōsuke is the second season's closest thing to an antagonist and he must never be a fight. The whole architecture of Chapters 7 and 8 is that the thing hurting the class is a structure, and a structure cannot be beaten at the end of a boss fight — so the man at the centre of it is a polite analyst in a karaoke booth who orders them tea and offers to be argued with.

Give him the dignity of a real position. He is better at reading fights than anybody the class have met, he was made redundant by the industry he is now feeding on, and he is the only person in two chapters who has done something for Yuka Ōba.

Then let him hand them the ending. "Nobody's ever put a reason in the archive." The class spent nine days and twenty minutes winning the right to say something first, and the man who sells their weaknesses is the one who tells them what to say. Chapter 8 is built to arrive exactly there.

aside.label: If your table needs to hit something
aside.body:
They may, and the chapter should not punish a table for wanting a fight. "The Market" has five, the Byakko thread has as many as anybody wants, and the Underground has four factions in it.

What the chapter will not provide is a fight that fixes the problem, and it is worth saying so out loud at the table if the players start hunting for one. "There isn't a guy. That's the chapter." Most tables find that more interesting than a guy, once they believe it.

sections.treasure: A customer list, a written concession about under-eighteens, four competitors' names, and one sentence about what to put in the archive.

sections.heading: On the Record
sections.tag: Final encounter · chosen, broadcast, with the commentary on · 1–2 sessions
sections.readAloud:
▶ WHAT THEY'RE OFFERED

The festival committee needs a demonstration match for the first-years' opening ceremony. Second-years, two pairs, Battle Centre III. Cameras, commentary, and the whole thing archived under the same licence as everything else.

Forge brings it to them with her mouth full and no opinion at all, which is how everybody knows it matters.

"It goes in," she says. "Same archive. Same commentary team. Same everything. You've got a right of reply now, so you'd be the first people in the country to use one."

She swallows.

"You can say no. I'd back you."

▶ THE ANNOTATION
HOW TO RUN IT — This is the finale. Before anybody rolls a die. Give the table five real minutes of quiet and write down exactly what they say, word for word.

The form is two pages. The field is called SUBJECT'S STATEMENT and it has no character limit, which means nobody has ever filled it in.

It plays first. Over the top of their own footage. Before the commentary. Permanently.

ASK EVERY PLAYER — What does your character write in it?

▶ THE MATCH

Floodlights in Battle Centre III, which the class haven't fought in since they were fifteen.

THEY SEE — Forty first-years in the stands, one of them with a notebook. Nineteen classmates. A commentary box with the same two voices in it. Four cameras, and a red light on each.
AND — On the screen above the gate, before anything happens: white text on black. Somebody's own words.

▶ THE LAST ROUND
HOW TO RUN IT — The commentary team say the thing about the weakness, warmly, live, in front of everybody. The class knew it was coming and signed the form anyway. That is the point of the chapter.

And then, somewhere in the last round, the pair do the thing. The combination invented in free time. The Pact declared out loud. The die nobody has ever seen pay out. A frame that finally has a speaker in it.

The commentary box goes quiet.

And then one of them says, honestly:

"I don't know what that was."
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — the demonstration match is offered → the class decide whether to be filmed on purpose → each PC writes an annotation → the match, run full strength in pairs → the commentary, live, in front of them → the thing they show that the commentary cannot explain.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — the annotations and the last round of the match. The annotations are the finale; the match is the celebration.

• THIS IS THE FINALE AND IT IS A SPORTS MATCH, ON PURPOSE. Season 1's climax was a cold store with the safety off and nobody watching. Season 2's is a floodlit demonstration bout that the class chose to have filmed, catalogued and commentated, which is the bravest thing anybody in this campaign has done with a camera.
• THE ANNOTATION IS THE SCENE. Go round the table and ask each player what their character puts in SUBJECT'S STATEMENT. There is no wrong answer and no mechanical effect. Write them down verbatim; they are the campaign's last words about itself. Ebata's advice, if the class got it, is to put the reason in — the thing the commentary never explains, because commentary explains what, not why.
• THE MATCH — two PC pairs against each other, or both pairs against a staff pair (Bose and Help Woman will do it and it will be humiliating and hilarious), at full strength, with the pair rules from Chapter 2 in force and every training benefit, Underground gift and free-time invention on the table. Run it as a real fight. Four rounds, floodlights, commentary.
• THE COMMENTARY TEAM ARE THE SAME TWO PEOPLE and they are good at their job, which means they will explain a weakness live, warmly, in front of forty thousand viewers and forty first-years, the way they did two years ago. Do it. Say the line. The class knew it was coming and signed the form anyway, and that is the entire point of the chapter.
• AND THEN THE THING THE COMMENTARY CANNOT EXPLAIN. Somewhere in the last round, let the pair do the thing: the combination invented in free time, the Pact declared out loud, the die that nobody has ever seen pay out, a frame that finally has a speaker in it. The commentary box goes quiet, and then one of them says, honestly, "I don't know what that was." That sentence is the campaign's answer to its own thesis and it should be the last thing said before the horn.
• WHAT IT CHANGES, CONCRETELY — within a month, four thousand people have filed annotations. Clean Read starts playing them, because it has to. Ebata reads them and says they are mostly badly written and one of them is the best thing in the archive. Tokieda Mei files one on her own entrance-exam footage and it is four words long.
• IF THE CLASS SAY NO TO THE MATCH — a completely legitimate ending, and Forge meant it when she said she would back them. Run "The Last Roll Call" straight after, and let the annotations be filed on the old footage instead. The scene still works: four people writing over the top of the worst year of their lives, in their own words, permanently.
sections.developments:
• IF A PLAYER WRITES SOMETHING FUNNY IN THE ANNOTATION — let them, and let it be the one Ebata says is the best thing in the archive. Kinji's would be funny. Kinji's would also be about a song.
• IF A PLAYER WRITES MOSHITA MARO'S NAME IN IT — stop, let the table sit, and then carry on exactly as written. It plays first. It plays before the commentary. Forever.
• IF THE CLASS WANT A FIRST-YEAR IN THE MATCH — not permitted, and Tokieda Mei will ask anyway, and the right answer is to put her in the commentary box, where she is extremely good.
• IF THE PAIR SPLIT UP IN THE LAST ROUND — no mechanical penalty here; this is not the roof of the Cage. But the commentary will notice, out loud, and say the thing about two people instead of one, and that is penalty enough.
• IF BYAKKO TURN UP — four hundred people from the backstreets in the public stands at a U.A. demonstration match, having queued, is a wonderful image and entirely plausible by this point in the campaign. Hakuro Mitsuki watches from the back. Genda brings the cart. Amano Keita takes notes and is not thrown out, because nobody can think of a rule he has broken.
sections.dmNote:
Everything in the second season points here, and the finale is a form with a text field on it.

Get the order right: the offer, then the annotations, then the match. The annotations must be written before anybody rolls dice, because the match is the celebration and the form is the decision. Ask the question properly, give the table silence, and write down what they say word for word.

Then run a genuinely good fight — floodlights, pairs, four rounds, the commentary team being excellent at the thing that hurt them — and let the last round contain something that has never been filmed. The commentator saying "I don't know what that was" is the sentence the whole campaign has been building towards since Forge put twenty names on a board and refused to explain why.

And then go to the infirmary, or the sofa, or the roof, and finish small.

aside.label: The annotation form, as a prop
aside.body:
One sheet per player. At the top: SUBJECT'S STATEMENT — Public Broadcast Record (Amendment) Form 4B. Underneath, the student's name and the match reference. Then the rest of the page blank.

Hand them out, give the table five real minutes of quiet, and collect them in. Keep them. If your table ever plays a third season, put them on the table in session one.

sections.treasure: Four annotations, in the players' own words, permanently attached to the front of their own footage. And a commentator saying, live, that he does not know what he just saw.

sections.heading: The Last Roll Call
sections.tag: Epilogue · 1 short session · keep it under half an hour
sections.readAloud:
▶ THE SOFA

Heights Alliance, the evening after, and the air conditioning is broken again.

THEY SEE — Samitsu has made something for twenty-four, because there are first-years in the building now and he's counted them.
AND — Masahata has a new chart. It's a chart of the annotations, ranked by quality, and he's put his own fourth — which is the most honest thing he has ever done.

▶ ROUND THE TABLE
HOW TO RUN IT — Ask every player, one at a time, in their own words. Read all four annotations out loud. This is the ending and the players wrote it.

ASK THEM — What did you write?
AND THEN — Who's going to read it?

▶ AND THEN, OUTSIDE

The wall opposite the west gate. A white tiger with twenty names. A sword through a crown, if they met the Legion. A sun, if they met the Court. A black brush-stroke number, if the Ledger ever signed anything of theirs.

And a space, which there always is.

THEY SEE — Somebody from the first-year class standing in front of it with a tin of paint, trying to work out whether she's allowed.

▶ THE ANSWER IS YES
HOW TO RUN IT — If a PC is the one who tells her so, that is the end of the campaign.
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — the dorm, the evening after → the class's own people, one line each → the annotations read out loud round the table → the wall → a first-year with a tin of paint → stop.
IF YOU ONLY HAVE AN HOUR — you only need twenty minutes. Do not pad this.

• ONE BEAT FOR EVERY PC, ROUND THE TABLE, in the players' own words. The campaign has ended this way twice; do it a third time and do not change the format.
• ONE LINE FOR EVERY NPC WHO EARNED ONE THIS SEASON. Tokieda Mei, who has filed a four-word annotation on her own entrance-exam footage. Baba Toshiki, who finished the obstacle course on the eleventh attempt and nobody saw it except whoever was assigned to him. Fujimori Nene, who accepted help once. Ōgaki Shun's thank-you note, which is badly written and six pages long. Amano Keita at Nakata's Gym on a Monday. Yuka Ōba, if anybody took up her brother's case. Hibino Asa, who sent a notice to the dorm by bicycle, correctly addressed, to a PC who signed for something.
• FORGE GETS THE SECOND-TO-LAST WORD and she should be eating when she says it.
• AND GIVE THE LAST WORD TO A FIRST-YEAR, not to the class. That is the difference between this epilogue and Chapter 5's. The class are second-years; the building is full of people who arrived after the worst of it; and the last image is somebody younger, in front of a wall, with a tin of paint, trying to work out whether she is allowed.
• THE ANSWER IS YES. Sugitsu asked the ground staff to leave the wall alone two summers ago and he has not changed his mind. If a PC is the one who tells her so, that is the end of the campaign.
sections.developments:
• IF THE TABLE WANTS TO KEEP PLAYING — they can, indefinitely. Three slots a window, four factions, a Heat track, a gang that may belong to them, a market that is still trading, and forty first-years. "The Fifth Door" has the threads.
• IF THE TABLE WANTS TO STOP — stop on the paint. It is the right last image and it is the one the module is built to end on.
• IF A PLAYER ASKS WHAT HAPPENED TO EVERYBODY — answer generously and in one sentence each. This is not the place for ambiguity.
• IF SOMEBODY ASKS ABOUT THE FOUR THINGS ON THE WALL — nobody at U.A. knows what three of them mean and the class will never be believed about any of it, which is correct and which the Underground has been telling them for two seasons.
sections.dmNote:
Short, warm, and absolutely not a twist. The second season ends on a sofa and a wall, the way the first one ended in Help Woman's office.

The structural job of this epilogue is to hand the campaign to somebody else. Season 1 was about twenty components being assembled. Season 2 was about what happens when the assembly is written down and handed to children. So end on a child, holding a tin of paint, in front of the record.

And read the annotations out loud. All four. That is the campaign's ending and the players wrote it.

aside.label: If you want one last prop
aside.body:
Put the four annotation sheets in the middle of the table, face up, for the whole of this session.

Nobody needs to say anything about them. They are the last thing the players made and the first thing anybody watching their footage will ever see.

sections.treasure: Nothing, and everything. Four annotations, read out loud, and a first-year who is allowed.

sections.heading: The Fifth Door
sections.tag: DM note · where a third season goes · the threads left open
sections.readAloud:
▶ ONE LAST SCENE AFTER THE LAST SCENE

Yanaka, a level crossing, half past midnight.

The barriers come down for a train that isn't carrying anybody. There's nothing standing under the arm any more.

On the other side, a girl of about fifteen with a bicycle and a satchel is licking the end of a pencil. She has four names in her notebook with ticks against them — and a fifth with no date, because somebody signed for something and the form has a field for that.

She looks up. Waves.

And gets on the bicycle.
sections.body:
RUNNING ORDER — a reference note. Read it when the table asks what happens next.

• THE MARKET IS STILL TRADING. Ebata Kyōsuke is one of four and the smallest. The archive is still public, the commentary still explains the weakness, and four thousand annotations are now attached to the front of it. A third season about what people write in those fields is a genuinely strange and good campaign and needs no invention.
• THE UNDERGROUND HAS FOUR DOORS AND A FIFTH SPACE. The Legion, the Court, the Kuroshiki and the Ledger are written up. "Room for more" still has the template and one unclaimed rumour — the teahouse in Yanaka where you can buy a dream, and the price is one of yours — and the Ledger's own haunt is three streets from it, which is not a coincidence if you want it not to be.
• THE FACTIONS NOW HAVE A GRIEVANCE EACH. The Legion and the Court have been at war since 1868. The Kuroshiki and the Ledger will not sign for each other's work and there are things standing in the gaps all over the city. And every vampire in Ginza is four hundred years in arrears, and the First Desk has one page with no date on it, and it is hers.
• BYAKKO ARE A YEAR FROM AN ANSWER. The Stripe Law assumes strength belongs to a person; Clean Read proved it belongs to a document. Amano Keita was the first and will not be the last, and if the class hold the title it is their problem, and if they do not then the next White Tiger will be whoever reads fastest.
• THE QUESTIONS THIS SEASON LEFT OPEN — whether Hanazawa gets her sealed records some other way; what Tateishi does with the vote she is ashamed of; whether anybody takes up Yuka Ōba's brother's case; what Tokieda Mei's four words were; which hero Yuka Ōba would not name; and whose name is on the page a PC signed.
• AND THE OLD ONES ARE STILL OPEN. What the Legion will do about Ren Suzuki. Whether Saotome's arrowhead was the only one that left the vault. Why Shirasagi Rei said "huh." Whether Rob Joestar ever goes back to the bathhouse. And what Otowa Suzume decided about the speaker Forge keeps offering — which, after two seasons, she may simply have accepted, and the first thing the class hear her say out loud is a thing the DM should let a player choose.
sections.developments:
• IF YOUR TABLE WANTS A THIRD SEASON WITH A SPINE — the annotations are the best one available: four thousand people have been given a text field on the front of their own public record, and some of them have written things that are not true. Nobody has ever had to check the archive before.
• IF YOUR TABLE WANTS A THIRD SEASON WITHOUT ONE — the city is a sandbox with four factions, a gang, a market and forty first-years, and the free-time lists keep working at any level.
• IF YOUR TABLE WANTS TO STOP — stop at the tin of paint. The module has now ended twice on Forge's board and once on a wall, and all three are correct.
• IF YOUR TABLE WANTS TO START AGAIN WITH NEW CHARACTERS — run the first-years. Tokieda Mei, Ōgaki Shun, Fujimori Nene and Baba Toshiki are a party, their homeroom teacher is still Forge, and the archive they learned from is the old party's. That is the cleanest third season in the module and it costs nothing to set up.
sections.dmNote:
Leave the fifth space on the wall empty, for the same reason the fourth was left empty: it is the most useful thing in the module.

The second season's argument was that a catalogue is not a villain and cannot be defeated, only answered — and the class answered it with a form, in their own words, in public, on purpose. That is a finished thought. Anything a third season does should start from the annotations rather than reopening the archive.

And whatever you add, the rule has not changed since Chapter 6. Keep it off the spine. The Underground is the city's basement, the market is its ground floor, and the school is still a school with a panda in it.

aside.label: One rule for every faction you add
aside.body:
Unchanged, and worth repeating at the end of two seasons: a faction that turns out to be behind everything is a faction that has eaten the campaign.

Four doors are painted. The fifth is not. There is one unclaimed rumour left in the appendix and a template to build it with, and the best version of it is the one the DM thought of in the car.

sections.treasure: Nothing. It is a note. The fifth space is the treasure.

sidequests.name: YUKA ŌBA'S BROTHER
sidequests.hook: "Nobody looked at it." Yuka Ōba has the whole thing in a supermarket bag — three years of letters, in order. "I went to the agency, the Commission, two newspapers. So then I went to a karaoke booth in Shinjuku."
sidequests.body: The woman in the cardigan paid eighteen thousand yen because nobody would look at what a hero did to her brother. Somebody could look.
sidequests.reward: the file is real, the hero is still working, and the complaint is three years out of time — and Okuma knows a way round that, and it will take the rest of the season.

sidequests.name: WHAT KAJIURA CANNOT DO
sidequests.hook: Kajiura has not moved in eleven minutes. "I require a countersignature," he says, to the barrier. "There is no Desk above me to provide one. There has not been since 1945."
sidequests.body: A Hand with a writ he will not draw because his Desk has been vacant since 1945. The countersignature exists; it is in a sweet shop in Yanaka and the price is not money.
sidequests.reward: the best ally in the Underground, and a favour owed to a man who was struck off.

sidequests.name: A PAGE WITH YOUR NAME ON IT
sidequests.hook: "One question," says Tōno Shigemori, who has an appointment at eleven. "Answered truthfully. The price is a page with your name on it, and I will not show you the date."
sidequests.body: The First Desk will answer one question truthfully. Any question. He will tell them the price before they ask, which is a page with their name on it and a date he will not show them.
sidequests.reward: one true answer, and a thing the player now carries. Let them choose the question out loud at the table.

sidequests.name: THE ANNOTATION
sidequests.hook: Form 4B. SUBJECT'S STATEMENT. No character limit. Four thousand people can file one now, and most of them don't know how to start.
sidequests.body: Four thousand people can now write on the front of their own footage. A PC who wants to help somebody else write theirs — a classmate, a first-year, Nakata Isamu, Saki Hiyori, a dead boy's family — spends a slot on it.
sidequests.reward: the best use of a free-time slot in the module. Read out what they wrote.

appendix.heading: Your First Session, Step By Step
appendix.body:
If you have never done this before, run session one exactly like this.

BEFORE — read Chapter 1. All three sections, start to finish; it is the shortest chapter in the module and it has no combat, no dice and no antagonist. Write the four PC names down the side of a piece of paper. That is your notes page. Total prep: fifteen minutes.

AT THE TABLE

• Ask each player to say their character's name, quirk, and one thing they are like. Two minutes each, no more.
• Read the ▶ OPENING block of "The Letter" to one player, properly, in full. Then summarise it for the others — it is funnier once.
• Go round the table: what room were you standing in when it arrived, and who else was in the house?
• Ask the two exam questions. What did you do that you are proud of, and what did you do that you have not told anybody? Write down both answers for all four players. Do not skip this; it is the most useful twenty minutes in the campaign.
• Give each PC one short scene at home during the six weeks, then read the kit list.
• Finish with First Morning — the gate, the corridor, three classmates, and a woman in the doorway eating.

THAT IS A FULL SESSION. It has no combat and no dice, and it is the right way to start this campaign.

IF YOU FINISH EARLY — go straight into "Ten Names on the Board" in Chapter 2. The two are one continuous morning and were written to be run back to back. If you run out of time — stop anyway; the board keeps.

AFTERWARDS, ASK ONE QUESTION: "anything you want more of next time?" Then give them that. It is the single most useful thing a new DM can do and it takes thirty seconds.

appendix.heading: Running A Fight Without Panicking
appendix.body:
Combat is where new DMs freeze. Here is the minimum that works.

THE LOOP — go round the table in initiative order. On each turn ask "what do you do?", let them do one thing and move, roll to see if it lands, describe the result in one sentence, next person. That is combat.

IF YOU DO NOT KNOW WHETHER SOMETHING WORKS — pick a number between 10 and 18, ask for a d20 roll plus whatever ability seems right, and go with it. Nobody will check. Consistency matters more than correctness.

2v2 IS DIFFERENT AND EASIER. Fewer combatants, faster rounds, and every action visibly affects one specific ally. Lean into it: ask players to describe what their partner is doing while they act.

REWARD COMBINATION PLAY WITH ADVANTAGE. When two players coordinate, give the roll advantage rather than inventing a new rule. This is the whole mechanical spine of the campaign and advantage is enough to carry it.

END FIGHTS EARLY. When the outcome is obvious, narrate the last thirty seconds and stop rolling. A fight that has been decided but is still being rolled out is the most common way a good session goes flat.

IF THE PARTY IS LOSING AND YOU DID NOT MEAN THEM TO — a teacher arrives. This campaign has eleven of them and several are explicitly written as difficulty dials. Nobody at the table will ever know you adjusted it.

IF THE PARTY IS WINNING TOO EASILY — do not add hit points mid-fight. Add a complication instead: a civilian in the way, a floor giving, a second thing happening elsewhere.

appendix.heading: When The Players Go Somewhere You Didn't Prepare
appendix.body:
They will. Every time. It is not a problem and it is not your fault.

THE FOUR-STEP FIX
1. Say "give me a second" out loud. Genuinely. Take the second.
2. Ask them what they are hoping to find. Their answer is usually a better idea than yours would have been.
3. Give them a version of it, plus one complication.
4. Steer back by having something happen — Ame-style: a phone call, a teacher looking for them, a classmate at the door.

WHAT THIS CAMPAIGN GUARANTEES — no scene is load-bearing. If the players skip the archive, Rawagi tells them. If they skip Kuma's interview, Okuma raises the carpet detail. If they never fight Powder in Chapter 4, he is at the cold store in Chapter 5. Every thread has at least two ways to reach the players and the Developments boxes list them.

IF THEY WANT TO INVESTIGATE SOMETHING THAT ISN'T THERE — say so, gently, in the fiction. A dead end that is confirmed as a dead end costs five minutes. A dead end you improvise into a plot costs you three sessions.

IF THEY SOLVE THE MYSTERY EARLY — let them, and skip forward. This campaign is not damaged by players being ahead of it; the threat does not depend on secrecy. Move the Chapter 4 archive scene up and carry on.

appendix.heading: Pacing — What To Cut And When
appendix.body:
Seventeen to nineteen sessions for the spine, plus Chapter 6 and as much free time as your table wants, is a guideline, not a target. Here is where the slack is.

FREE TIME IS ALWAYS OPTIONAL. It is the thing you add when the table wants it, never the thing the story needs. A table that never takes a weekend off loses Byakko and the Underground and nothing else.

SAFE TO CUT ENTIRELY

• The Common Room Ticker as its own scene — fold the lines into other sessions.
• Day Two of the festival, down to a single phase and a scoreboard.
• Kuma's interview, if Okuma delivers the carpet detail in a briefing instead.
• Any bracket match with no PC in it.

SAFE TO COMPRESS

• Chapter 1 entire — take one sentence per PC about the exam and the wait, then open at the classroom door.
• Six Weeks — twenty minutes of everyone naming two training focuses.
• The obstacle course — three obstacles and a finish line.
• Nine Days — a single scene with Rawagi, then straight to the cold store.

DO NOT CUT

• A Question at the Gate.
• The archive scene in Ikari Tomonobu, Sixth.
• Saki Hiyori Stands in Front of It.
• The Kinji Hamakida moment in Keepsake.

These four are the campaign. Everything else is support — and everything in Chapter 6 is dessert.

SIGNS A SCENE HAS GONE ON TOO LONG — players checking phones, the same suggestion being made twice, or you narrating for more than about ninety seconds without a question. Cut to the next named beat. You do not have to resolve the current one.

A SHORT CAMPAIGN VERSION exists if you want one: compress Chapter 1 into the first twenty minutes of session one; run Chapter 2 sections 1, 2 and 6; all of Chapter 3; Chapter 4 sections 1, 3 and 6; and all of Chapter 5. That is roughly ten sessions and loses nothing structural.

appendix.heading: Safety, And The Horror Dial
appendix.body:
This campaign contains a man who eats brains, a student who does not come home, and a suicide detonation. It is also a school story with a panda in it. Both need managing.

BEFORE SESSION ONE, say this or something like it: "This one gets darker as it goes — there's body horror and characters we like get hurt. If anything lands badly, say so and we'll move past it, no explanation needed. That goes for me too." Thirty seconds, once, and it makes the rest of the campaign easier to run.

GIVE EVERYONE A WAY TO STOP A SCENE. The simplest version: anybody at the table can say "let's cut away from this" and you cut, immediately, without discussion or negotiation. Use it yourself early on so it is clearly not a big deal.

THE DIAL IS THE DESCRIPTION, NOT THE PLOT. Every beat in this campaign works with the camera pointed away. Sylar's method can be a closed door and a Commission report rather than anything on screen. Riddle's victims can go quiet rather than anything worse. Powder's self-mutilation can be entirely off-camera. None of that changes a single event.

THE ONE THING NOT TO SOFTEN is the cost. Moshita Maro not being at roll call is the campaign's spine. You can make it bloodless. Do not make it reversible.

IF A PLAYER IS UPSET RATHER THAN THRILLED — take a break, out of character, and ask. Being frightened by a story you chose is fun; being upset is not, and the difference is not always visible from the DM's chair.

THE UNDERGROUND IS A THIRD REGISTER and it needs its own check-in. Vampires that feed, things born out of human dread, and a gang that settles rank with fists are all darker than a school story and lighter than Appetite. Before the first Odd Night, ask the table one question out of character: "there's some supernatural stuff hidden in this city — do you want it gory, spooky, or Saturday-morning?" Then pitch every faction scene to the answer.

You will need a person or a monster you have not prepared. Here is the fast version.

A PERSON — a job, a want, and one physical detail. "Floor manager, wants her shift to end, keeps losing her pen." That is a complete NPC and it will hold up for an entire scene.

A VOICE — you do not need to act. Change one thing: speak slower, speak quieter, be blunter, use shorter sentences. Rawagi is short sentences. Kuma is too many. Help Woman never softens anything. Toragi, mid-fight, is one-liners and nothing else. Kinji is a song recommendation. That is enough to tell people apart.

A STAT BLOCK — pick a difficulty and use these:

• Minor threat: AC 13, 25 HP, +4 to hit, 2d6 damage.
• Real threat: AC 15, 60 HP, +6 to hit, 3d8 damage.
• Serious threat: AC 17, 120 HP, +8 to hit, 4d10 damage, one special move.

Give it one interesting thing it can do and nothing else. Nobody needs a full sheet.

A QUIRK ON THE SPOT — name it, say what it does in one sentence, and say what it cannot do. The limit is what makes it feel real. Every quirk in this campaign is written that way and players will match the pattern without being asked.

IF A PLAYER ASKS SOMETHING ABOUT THE WORLD YOU HAVE NOT DECIDED — the honest answer, "I don't know yet, what do you think?", works far more often than it has any right to.
appendix.heading: Improvising An NPC Or A Stat Block In Thirty Seconds

appendix.body:
Ten pairs, assigned by Forge, no substitutions, no negotiation. Two play-in matches cut the field to eight, then quarters, semis, final — nine matches in total. Play three or four at the table and narrate the rest.

PLAY-IN
· Aikawa Sakume + Samitsu Hinsei  vs  Setaka Toko + Nakaya Emari
· Rakuka Rizo + Hiro  vs  Masahata Shikoji + Ichitaka Shijime

QUARTER-FINALS
· Ren Suzuki + Kazama Kenji  vs  Tazato Tadamaki + Ando Iorai
· Kinji Hamakida + Kibi Kankei  vs  Yoshibara Hiyoko + Nomi Igisa
· Chozen Tadachi + Toragi Kayo  vs  second play-in winner
· Izuto Kutsu + Isokono Yoromu  vs  first play-in winner

WHY THESE PAIRS
Ren + Kazama — a beam that does double damage to metal, paired with a boy who wears it. Held at ten percent the beam does not cut Kazama's armour; it heats it, and the next thing he hits, he hits glowing. They find "the forge" in round one and spend the rest of the bracket learning exactly how much heat is too much.
Kinji + Kibi — the loudest student in the class and the most relaxed one. Kibi is the only person in 1-A who does not find Kinji tiring, and the only one who had noticed, before the draw, that Kinji has never used his quirk. In a format where a partner covers your reach, a boy who will not spin needs somebody patient behind him, and that is the whole of Kibi.
Chozen + Toragi — an overthinker who freezes in the first round of every fight while he works out a plan, and a boy who, the moment a fight starts, speaks only in one-liners. Chozen's wind pins people to walls. Toragi needs a target that stays still long enough to be hit twice. Enormous ceiling, catastrophic communication.
Izuto + Isokono — speed and grapple. Izuto stalls after every burst and is rooted to the spot until somebody cools him; Isokono's tail can drag him out of the way, and she will, and he will not thank her. Izuto cannot win this alone and the whole exercise knows it.
Masahata + Ichitaka — the two most arrogant people in the class, who are also, infuriatingly, effective together. Being made to fight a play-in when his own laminated chart has him winning the tournament is the funniest thing that happens to Masahata all term, and he does not find it funny.
Yoshibara + Nomi — best friends. A clone and a poltergeist is four bodies and every loose object in the arena.
Setaka + Nakaya — iron balls and lightning, and Setaka's skin is metal panelling. Conductive artillery, and a genuine safety briefing beforehand.
Tazato + Ando — a cranky dragon and a lizard who is far more frightened than he admits.
Aikawa + Samitsu — a loud striker behind a wall of arms that grow out of anything Samitsu has touched.
Rakuka + Hiro — a boy who announces every move to a crowd, and a seven-foot machine that has never said a word. Rakuka treats the whole bracket as theatre and Hiro lets him, and somewhere in round one they find out that a partner willing to stand in the worst place on the floor is worth more than either of them expected. Forge will not say what she was thinking. Forge never does.
appendix.heading: The 2v2 bracket — Class 1-A
Sports Festival — event format
appendix.body:
DAY ONE · THE OBSTACLE COURSE — all forty first-years, four kilometres, open campus. Top twenty-four advance. Terrain is Forge's and it is unkind. Run as a skill challenge with three or four set-piece obstacles rather than a full initiative track.

DAY TWO · CAVALRY BATTLE — teams of three or four, headbands worth points, twelve minutes. Top eight teams advance. This is where 1-A and 1-B genuinely mix, and where the commentary booth starts explaining everyone's mechanics to a national audience in helpful, ruinous detail.

DAY THREE · THE PAIRED TOURNAMENT — eight pairs, single elimination, full contact, medical on standby. The format that exists only because Forge's bracket impressed the committee.

1-A versus 1-B matchups, drawn from the existing rivalries — Kakita Keiko against Ando Iorai, Domoto Fumiju against Izuto Kutsu, Moshita Maro against whichever 1-A student he has already touched, Yamaru Todao against Kazama Kenji, Tateta Fumira against Ren Suzuki, Hashige Tataka against Setaka Toko, Isosato Sari against Chozen Tadachi.

THE COMMENTARY — write two or three lines of broadcast commentary for every match you run. It is the single most important prop in the campaign. Every line that explains how a quirk works is a line Sylar is listening to, and when the class rewatches the footage in Chapter 4 they should recognise their own highlights.

SYLAR (Ken Reed) — Transfer. Never opens a fight and never fights fair. Maw is a melee attack that on a hit grabs the target, forces them prone and begins working through the skull; the target is restrained and Sylar must make a DC 12 check each turn to maintain it. Keepsake is passive — a consumed brain gives him the quirk permanently. Play him as patient, quiet and appallingly fast, and have him disengage the moment a fight becomes a fight. His weakness is the collection: every quirk he holds worsens a permanent headache, and by Chapter 5 he is in constant pain and increasingly imprecise with abilities he has not practised.

RIDDLE (Makochi Clue) — Question One targets one creature within 40 feet who can hear him; anyone who attempts an answer is braindead for five rounds or until they pass a DC 14 Intelligence check, and on answering correctly they instantly know where he is. Question Two, at 5 feet, asks 'what would hurt more?' — a wrong answer comes true within twenty-four hours. He bleeds from the mouth after every question and never hides it. One target at a time; the questions cannot be unanswerable. Play him as cruel and unhurried. He does not want to win, he wants you to participate.

POWDER (Yutaki Yusuzen) — Destruction lets him tear off parts of his own body and detonate them at 30 feet for 4d6, which he does constantly and cheerfully. Burst is the endgame: 15d12 plus his current hit points, force or fire, in a 100-foot radius, Strength save at disadvantage, five ranks of bleed, five ranks of concussed, knockback to the edge. It kills him. It has killed him before. A third party can trigger it if he is incapacitated, which is the detail that should make the table stop breathing.

TOUCH UP (Fuchiguchi Yuko) — the reason Powder is a recurring enemy instead of a one-off. Healing Touch mends 3d6 and repairs specific limbs; Regenerative Kiss grants 5 HP a round for a minute and strips ranks of bleeding, queasy and concussed. Heal a target five times in a minute and they gain exhaustion, which is the only clock the class has against her. She is the correct target and it takes the class an embarrassingly long time to work that out.

KUMA — Gigantification, 9'5" at rest, up to 25 feet at peak, strength and reach scaling with size. Overconfident, loud, no strategy, and no particular malice — this is a job and he is good at it. Deny him room to grow and he is manageable; give him a stadium concourse and he is a natural disaster. Getting beaten by a class of first-years is going to be very embarrassing for him, and he will say so, at length, while it happens.
appendix.heading: Appetite — tactics
The staff, and what each is for
appendix.body:
NOBARA FORGE (Creation) — 1-A homeroom. Builds the class's paired gear out of her own caloric budget. Ten pounds of food a day, minimum, and she will eat during a lesson without apologising. Chapter 2 is hers.

SUGITSU JARVICHI (Search) — Principal. Scans a one-mile radius as a bonus action, tracks up to a hundred targets across five miles by 5th level, and permanently stores ten individuals. Strict, funny once you know him, avoids combat and flees after hitting. He is the reason the school is safe and the reason the failure at the festival is unbearable — his quirk can be fooled by presented biological material, and someone knew that.

RAWAGI CHISO, Instinct (Foresight) — seconded to the Case 9 investigation and visibly worse at his job for it. Foresight makes visible creatures declare movement, action and reaction in advance and gives him their HP, AC and initiative. Dry, poor at conversation, denies having favourites while obviously having them. He is the only person who can make Sylar predictable, and it costs him a level of Concussed every time.

SAKI HIYORI, Creed (Deathly Endurance) — Constitution up to 24, and Death's Standing lets him spend hit dice at 0 HP to stand back up as long as he has dice left. Extreme passion for teaching, and does not hold back when someone gets between him and his students. He is the answer to Powder and the campaign's best single image.

CARLOS MIGHT (Calos over wall) — barely attends. Turns up in the canteen eating Mexican food, or in the training room with Kinji Hamakida and a great many dice, and nowhere else. Durango Smash does 6d6 and covers everyone present in beans. Estados Unidos de Smash does 7d12 and ends with him pointing at Kinji and saying 'Ahora es tu turno.' Play the absence as a running joke for three chapters and then do not play it as a joke.

ROB JOESTAR (Acid) — English. Chill until he isn't; short temper, and at full wind-up he enters the rage and summons Whitesnake. Strict, gets the lesson done, and holds a written permission slip to beat Kinji and only Kinji if he is naughty, which he waves at people, and which Kinji has framed. (If you are running the Underground: read "The Astral Court" before you describe Whitesnake. It is not part of his quirk.) Acid Pressure Points accumulate every time he fires and reset on a rest.

ADITYA BOSE, Bad Touch Bose (Rifle) — drill sergeant, always precisely on time, shouts at minor inconveniences. Standard Shot is 4d12 piercing at 120 feet and ignores resistance; ammunition costs an inch of his own hair, one hundred inches maximum, regrowing an inch an hour. Despite the range he prefers to close and beat people with no quirk at all. Festival training is his.

FRED ENTOSS, Fridas (Cement) — sarcastic, enjoys banter, on the students' side. Cement Wall builds twenty feet of three-quarters cover or a fifteen-foot restraining trap; Cement Spike Rush is 4d10 in a cone. Limited uses, and going past them costs him force damage and exhaustion. Stadium containment is his.

YANAMI MAHO (Magic) — rescue specialist. Energy Rings grant flight or halve movement; Momentum Lock freezes a creature mid-air as a reaction. Concentration-dependent, useless above 500 pounds. Enjoys being alone, and accepts the majority of the credit for things she did not do — play this honestly, it is funny and then it is a little sad.

SUPER PANDA, pasta man (Anivoice) — maths, passionately, and nothing else. Talks to and commands animals within 120 feet; Hitchcock Birds blinds a cone and restrains. Happy, sleepy, never angry. In Chapter 4 he finds three missing students by asking the crows, and it is the least funny thing that happens that session.

HELP WOMAN (Heal) — school nurse. Short, hunched, grey. Straight to the point and tells no lies, including the ones that would help. Every chapter ends in her office.

appendix.heading: Case 9 — the victim list
appendix.body:
Kept as a physical prop. Add to it in front of the players.

1 · Tsuzuri Hane, 'Falsework' — Rare, construction. Adachi car park, spring. Competed in the Sports Festival, eleven years ago, placed fourth.
2 · Ondo Kasumi, 'Kelvin' — Very Rare, thermal. Nerima, summer. Never competed. The outlier, and the one that made the Commission's power-based profile look right for a while.
3 · Habara Jun, 'Sightline' — Rare, perception. Itabashi, autumn. Competed. Placed second. Extensive broadcast commentary explaining exactly how his quirk was limited.
4 · Meguro Sanae, 'Trellis' — Rare, growth. Suginami, autumn. Competed, placed sixth, and gave a post-match interview about her own weakness because she was proud of having worked around it.
5 · Ikari Tomonobu, 'Backdraft' — Rare, combustion. Ota, winter. Competed. Placed ninth.

The pattern the Commission missed and Rawagi did not: four of five have festival footage, and the depth of the commentary tracks with how cleanly they were taken. Ondo Kasumi is the exception — a quirk he wanted enough to work for without a manual.

REN SUZUKI — Charge. Raised in the mountains by a father who taught him a blade and the doctrine that a quirk is the thing evil grows from, then disowned the day a beam of rage came out of his eyes and cut the house in two. Ren forgives people — foes included — and means it, and he has never once started a conversation he did not have to. Sylar is a man who is nothing but other people's quirks, worn badly; Ren is the only student in the class who looks at him and understands what he is looking at. His beam is radiant, which will matter enormously if the class ever meets something that hates the sun. He only eats traditional food and has owned a phone for eleven weeks.

KAZAMA KENJI — Metal. Absorbs up to half a ton of metal a turn and wears it as armour, strikes with it, and can dump all of it into one counter-punch, after which he is wearing nothing. He is only as armoured as the room — on grass he has what he walked in with. Kind or cruel depending on the day, straight to the point, close to a mother who never wanted him to do this and a father who thought ambition was for other people. His sheet says the scar is a story about a moment he did not act, or could not, or chose wrong. Chapter 4 offers that moment again, in almost the same shape.

CHOZEN TADACHI — Whirlwind, and the son of Isobar, the most famous retired hero in the country, which every single person he meets already knows. An anxious overthinker who freezes in the first round of every fight while the plan assembles itself, then ends it fast. His wind runs on how wound-up he is; calm takes the edge off it, and after a long fight he crashes. Rich, raised mostly by the mansion staff, learned to fight from VHS tapes of a father he barely saw, and gives enormous gifts on holidays that do not involve gifts. Riddle is written for him specifically: a threat that punishes preparation. His growth is learning to walk away from a problem, which he has never once done.

IZUTO KUTSU — Engine. The fastest thing in the class for five rounds at a time, and then stalled, rooted to the spot, until he rests or somebody cools him with water or ice. Grew up in a family of support-gear engineers and taught himself everything alone, which is exactly the problem: his growth arc is accepting help, and the 2v2 format is that arc rendered as a rule. Give him a Chapter 4 sequence where he stalls in the open and has to be carried, in front of people, and let him hate it.

SEASON TWO, FOR EACH OF THEM — one thread per PC for Chapters 7 and 8, built off the first season's.

REN SUZUKI — he is the only one of them who ever looked at Sylar and understood what he was looking at, and Chapter 7 hands him the same thing without the teeth: a document that turns a person into a list of components, sold for four thousand yen, and nobody to forgive for it. He forgives people. There is no person here. Give him Ebata Kyōsuke in Room 9 and let him try. And remember his beam is radiant, which the Ledger will notice, because radiant is one of three things that hurt an Arrear and they are chronically short of all three.

KAZAMA KENJI — the scar is a story about a moment he did not act. Chapter 4 offered him that moment again. Chapter 7 offers it a third time, in a car park in Nerima, with a fifteen-year-old in it who copied somebody else's style — and this time he arrives in time, or does not, on the dice. He is also only as armoured as the room, which is a thing the commentary explained in detail on national television, and Miyashita Gō has read it.

CHOZEN TADACHI — he learned to fight from VHS tapes of a father he barely saw, and Tokieda Mei learned to fight from eleven hours of broadcast footage of people she has never met. He is the only PC who already knows exactly what she is and exactly what it costs. His first-season growth was learning to walk away from a problem; his second is being the one who tells somebody else to.

IZUTO KUTSU — his arc was accepting help and the 2v2 format was that arc as a rule. Fujimori Nene, first year, Static, fastest in the cohort, loses on purpose rather than take a hand. Give her to him. And give him the fact that his stall is on page one of his own teardown, in plain Japanese, with three recommended approaches, one of which you can do with a van.
appendix.heading: Per-PC threads

appendix.body:
The tonal risk is obvious: a maths teacher who is a panda, and a man who eats brains. The two have to live in the same campaign for sixteen sessions.

The rule that makes it work is that Appetite is never funny and U.A. never stops being funny. Do not have Rob Joestar make a joke about Case 9. Do not have Riddle say anything wry. Keep the two registers in separate scenes and let the contrast do the work — the dorm kitchen argument about whose milk it is should be played completely straight, in the session after somebody dies, because that is what actually happens to people.

Second rule: Appetite is quiet. No monologues, no theatrics, no announcements. Sylar has nothing to say to the class. Riddle only ever asks. The loudest thing any of them do is Kuma, and Kuma is a decoy.

Third rule: nobody dies off-screen to make a point. If a named student is taken, the table sees the room afterwards.

Fourth rule, for this edition: Byakko are allowed to be funny and the Underground is allowed to be strange, but neither of them is allowed into an Appetite scene. If the class is being hunted, the backstreets are quiet. The city waits.
appendix.heading: Running the horror without breaking the school
Two new faces
appendix.body:
TSUZURI HANE, 'Falsework' — the first victim, and the campaign's only ghost. A mid-ranked pro with a construction quirk and a genuinely nice reputation, twenty-nine, eleven years on the boards, a fourth place at his own Sports Festival that he never stopped mentioning. He appears only in archive footage, in a commentary clip, and in the fact that Rawagi Chiso knew him.

INSPECTOR OKUMA SHIZUKA — Hero Public Safety Commission, Serious Incidents. Forties, unhurried, entirely without warmth and entirely without malice. She thinks a school is the worst possible place to run an investigation and she is correct. She and Sugitsu Jarvichi disagree in a formal, polite, escalating way across three chapters, and neither of them is wrong.

Numbers for the five members of Appetite, pitched at the level the party will be when they meet them. They use the same three-tier scale as "Improvising An NPC Or A Stat Block In Thirty Seconds" above, so the two agree; adjust anything freely and nothing here will break.

RIDDLE (Makochi Clue) — Chapters 2, 4 and 5 · not a fight
AC 12 · HP 30 · Speed 30 ft · Initiative +2 · Quirk save DC 14
STR 8 · DEX 14 · CON 10 · INT 16 · WIS 14 · CHA 12
Unarmed +2, 1d4 bludgeoning. That is his entire offensive capability and it is not a mistake.
· QUESTION ONE (Action) — one creature within 40 feet who can hear him. The target chooses whether to attempt an answer; a creature that does not attempt one is entirely unaffected. A creature that does is braindead for 5 rounds, or until it succeeds on a DC 14 Intelligence check at the end of each of its turns. A correct answer ends the effect instantly and the answerer knows exactly where he is standing. One target at a time. The question cannot be unanswerable.
· QUESTION TWO (Action) — 5 feet, and only against a creature currently engaged with Question One. 2d6 psychic. "What would hurt more?" A wrong answer comes true within 24 hours, exactly as described.
· HAEMORRHAGE (Passive) — every question costs him 3 hit points, ignoring everything. He does not stop asking. Ten questions kills him and he knows the number.
· HOW TO RUN HIM — he never raises his voice, never gloats, never fights back, and leaves when he is finished rather than when he is losing. If the party attacks, he lets them, and keeps talking. He is a delay, and the delay is measured in five-round blocks off one PC at a time.

KUMA — Chapter 3 · a genuine boss fight
AC 15 · HP 160 · Speed 40 ft · Initiative +2 · Quirk save DC 15
STR 20 · DEX 10 · CON 18 · INT 8 · WIS 10 · CHA 14
· GIGANTIFICATION (Bonus action) — one size step per round, from 9'5" to 15 feet to 25 feet. He starts small and grows, and the fight is a race against that clock.
· AT 9'5" — +6 to hit, 2d10+5 bludgeoning, reach 10 ft.
· AT 15 FEET — +7 to hit, 3d10+6, reach 15 ft, advantage on Strength checks and saves.
· AT 25 FEET — +8 to hit, 4d10+7, reach 20 ft. In any enclosed space he takes 2d6 at the start of each of his turns from the structure he is wearing, and attacks at disadvantage against anything smaller than a car.
· HE IS RUBBISH ON THE FLOOR and says so afterwards. Prone, he cannot grow, attacks at disadvantage, and needs his whole movement to stand. Anything that takes his footing is worth more than damage and the encounter is built to be won that way.
· NOT A KILLER. He has no interest in casualties and will not pursue a fleeing civilian. The danger in this fight is the building and the six thousand people in it.

POWDER (Yutaki Yusuzen) — Chapter 4
AC 14 · HP 75 · Speed 30 ft · Initiative +3 · Quirk save DC 15
STR 12 · DEX 16 · CON 16 · INT 12 · WIS 10 · CHA 14
· DESTRUCTION (Action) — tears off a part of himself and detonates it at 30 feet. 4d6 fire, DC 15 Dexterity save for half. He takes 1d6 doing it and does not appear to notice.
· LEFT HAND, THUMB, TWO FINGERS (Trap) — he sets pieces of himself around the ground before the party arrives. 4d6 in a 10-foot radius, DC 15 Dexterity for half, triggered when he chooses. Three of them, and using one in the first round establishes that the street is his.
· BURST (Action or Reaction, once, and it kills him) — 15d12 plus his current hit points, force or fire, 100-foot radius. Strength save at disadvantage against DC 15 or full damage, 5 ranks of bleed, 5 ranks of Concussed, and knocked back to the edge of the radius; success is half damage, no knockback and half the conditions. Ignores resistance, treats immunity as resistance, ignores all damage reduction. Collapses structures and leaves a crater. A third party can trigger it if he is incapacitated.
· DO NOT USE BURST IN HIS FIRST APPEARANCE. He threatens it, enjoys threatening it, and does up his shirt button again.

TOUCH UP (Fuchiguchi Yuko) — Chapter 4 · the actual problem
AC 12 · HP 40 · Speed 30 ft · Initiative +1 · Quirk save DC 13
STR 8 · DEX 12 · CON 14 · INT 12 · WIS 16 · CHA 10
· HEALING TOUCH (Action) — 5 feet, restores 3d6 and mends a named limb, fracture or burn. Cannot regrow what is missing.
· REGENERATIVE KISS (Action, 3/long rest) — 5 hit points at the start of each of the target's turns for 1 minute, and strips a rank of Bleeding, Queasy and Concussed each turn.
· CELLULAR FATIGUE — this is the encounter. Heal a creature 5 times within one minute and it gains a rank of exhaustion, plus one more for every 2 further uses, to a maximum of 5. Powder is being healed constantly. Count it out loud once the players start watching her.
· SHE DOES NOT FIGHT, does not speak, and does not look at the students. She is more frightening as a function than as a person and her sheet should stay this empty.

SYLAR (Ken Reed) — Chapter 5
AC 17 · HP 190 · Speed 40 ft · Initiative +5 · Quirk save DC 16
STR 18 · DEX 16 · CON 18 · INT 14 · WIS 12 · CHA 6
· MAW (Action, melee +9) — 3d12 slashing. On a hit the target is grabbed, forced prone and restrained, and he begins working through the skull. At the start of each of his turns he must succeed on a DC 12 check to maintain it; while maintained the target takes 2d12 at the start of each of his turns. THE RESTRAINT IS BROKEN BY AN ALLY, not by the victim — DC 16 Strength or Dexterity check by any creature within 5 feet. This is the campaign's whole argument expressed as a rule and you should say it out loud at the table.
· KEEPSAKE (Passive) — a consumed brain gives him that quirk, permanently.
· BORROWED QUIRKS — give him three or four, name each one aloud, and say how long he has had it. Old acquisitions (Falsework's construction quirk, April) attack at +9 and roll full damage. Recent ones (Moshita Maro's Copy, nine days) attack at +5, roll half the damage dice rounded down, and on an attack roll of 5 or less he has reached for the wrong one entirely — describe the mistake and lose him the action.
· THE HEADACHE (Passive) — the first time he drops below half hit points he stops, puts the heel of his hand against his temple, and loses his entire turn. Once per fight, free, and the players should see it happen.
· HE DISENGAGES the moment a fight becomes a fight. He does not pursue committed opposition; he goes and finds somebody on their own instead.
appendix.heading: Stat blocks — Appetite
Stat blocks — the staff, as difficulty dials
appendix.body:
You will need numbers for teachers twice: when the party is losing and you want to take pressure off, and when a teacher is the scene. Keep them vague in play and precise on your own sheet.

SAKI HIYORI, Creed (Deathly Endurance) — the answer to Powder
AC 16 · HP 140 · Speed 30 ft · Initiative +1 · CON 24 (+7)
· DEATH'S STANDING — at 0 hit points he may spend hit dice to stabilise and regain consciousness, and may keep doing it as long as he has dice left. He has 12d12. Spend them out loud, one at a time, and say the number remaining each time he stands up. When they are gone, he stays down.
· Unarmed +8, 2d8+7. He is not there to deal damage.

FRED ENTOSS, Fridas (Cement) — containment, and rationed
· CEMENT WALL (Action) — 20 feet of three-quarters cover, or a 15-foot restraining trap, DC 15 Strength to break out. Uses equal to his Constitution modifier (4) per day.
· CEMENT SPIKE RUSH (Action) — 4d10 in a 30-foot cone, DC 15 Dexterity for half.
· PAST HIS USES he can keep going, and each further use costs him 3d6 force damage and a level of exhaustion he cannot reduce. He will do this. He will be sarcastic about it.

RAWAGI CHISO, Instinct (Foresight) — the only thing that makes Sylar legible
· FORESIGHT (Action, concentration) — one visible creature must declare its movement, action and reaction in advance, and Rawagi learns its current hit points, AC and initiative. Requires uninterrupted vision.
· THE COST — after every use, DC 14 Constitution save or a level of Concussed, and at the start of each of his turns a DC 13 Perception check or he cannot use it again for 3 rounds.
· He will burn himself past the point of sense. Take him off the board before the end of the finale and let the party watch it happen.

SUGITSU JARVICHI (Search) — never in a fight
· Scans a one-mile radius as a bonus action; tracks up to a hundred targets across five miles; stores ten individuals permanently, wherever they are.
· DEFEATED BY presented biological material — blood or tissue belonging to somebody else — and by sealed refrigerated structures. Both limits are written in his own quirk file, and somebody has read it.
· He avoids combat and withdraws after striking. He is the reason the school is safe and the reason the failure is unbearable.

YANAMI MAHO (Magic) — rescue
· ENERGY RINGS — grant flight, or halve a creature's movement. Concentration. Useless above 500 pounds.
· MOMENTUM LOCK (Reaction) — freeze one creature mid-air. Once, spectacularly, and she will accept the credit for rather more than that.

ADITYA BOSE (Rifle) · ROB JOESTAR (Acid) · CARLOS MIGHT (Calos over wall)
· Bose: Standard Shot 4d12 piercing at 120 feet, ignores resistance, ammunition costs an inch of his own hair from a hundred, regrowing an inch an hour. He would rather close and hit you.
· Joestar: Acid Pressure Points accumulate on every shot and reset on a rest. At full wind-up he enters the rage and summons Whitesnake, and in Chapter 5 that stops being funny.
· Carlos Might: Durango Smash 6d6 and everyone present is covered in beans. Estados Unidos de Smash 7d12. Two moves, no defence worth writing down, and he is a plot device with a sombrero — use him exactly once.

Everything you need to voice the class without opening another page. Bracket partner in brackets. Full sheets are on the characters page.

THE FOUR PLAYER CHARACTERS
· REN SUZUKI — Charge (Rare). [Kazama Kenji] Extremely respectful, forgives everybody, never starts a conversation. Fires a beam that pierces cover, does double damage to metal, and burns radiant; every shot past ten percent costs him in recoil. Carries a katana. Disowned by a father who thought quirks were the root of evil. Only eats traditional food; cannot work a phone.
· KAZAMA KENJI — Metal (Rare). [Ren Suzuki] Kind or cruel depending on the day, straight to the point, does not care what you think of him, and is never seen untidy. Pulls metal out of his surroundings and wears it; only as armoured as the room. The scar on his left cheek is from before U.A. and he has never refused a direct question about it. Nobody has asked one.
· CHOZEN TADACHI — Whirlwind (Uncommon). [Toragi Kayo] Isobar's son, which everybody knows. Anxious overthinker with forty contingencies laminated, stutters when surprised, freezes in round one of every fight and then ends it. Fitness-obsessed. Gives gifts nobody can afford to reciprocate.
· IZUTO KUTSU — Engine (Rare). [Isokono Yoromu] Intelligent, self-reliant, terrible at accepting help, builds and upgrades his own gear. Recipro bursts are devastating; afterwards he stalls, unable to move, until he rests or somebody cools him with water or ice.

THE CLASS
· AIKAWA SAKUME — Iron Claws. [Samitsu Hinsei] Loud, proud, first to volunteer, organises things nobody asked her to organise. Gets in close and applies bleed.
· ANDO IORAI — Scales. [Tazato Tadamaki] Cocky, jokes constantly, far more frightened than he admits; he and Kinji are a double act nobody asked for. The sunglasses come off only when he is genuinely shaken, which is rare.
· HIRO — ??? [Rakuka Rizo] Seven foot two, grey metal panels, hydraulic fists, a pill-shaped head with an LED screen that shows one emoji at a time. Never speaks; talks in hand signs. Always present and never eating. The whole class knows he is a machine and nobody finds it remarkable. There is a second thing about him and it does not come out before Chapter 4; see "Hiro — the clues, in order."
· ICHITAKA SHIJIME — Hologram. [Masahata Shikoji] From one of the richest families in Japan and moulded for it from birth. Genius, knows it, mildly superior to everyone equally. Creates false targets and splits attention. Gets to the answer first and waits to see if anybody else does.
· ISOKONO YOROMU — Tail. [Izuto Kutsu] Shy in groups, fiercely loyal, cries easily and does not hide it. Grapples one enemy and holds them where the heavy hitters can reach.
· KIBI KANKEI — Vines. [Kinji Hamakida] The most relaxed person in the class, and the only one who never finds Kinji tiring. Builds cover and chokepoints. His vine-hair flowers when he is content and he will not discuss this.
· MASAHATA SHIKOJI — Water Gun. [Ichitaka Shijime] Arrogant, loud, maintains the laminated ranking chart on the fridge. Annoying, and correct more often than is fair.
· NAKAYA EMARI — Element (Lightning). [Setaka Toko] Giggly, delighted by everything, no charge is too much charge. Chains current between conductive points.
· NOMI IGISA — Poltergeist. [Yoshibara Hiyoko] Timid, quiet, speaks perhaps twice a term and the room listens when she does. Moves enemies into bad positions.
· RAKUKA RIZO — Dying Flight. [Hiro] Theatrical, warm, announces every move and cannot stop. Flies in, gets somebody out, flies off.
· SAMITSU HINSEI — Arms. [Aikawa Sakume] Cool exterior, easily offended, genuinely nice, extraordinary cook. Grows arms — up to forty feet tall — out of any surface he has touched within eighty feet; they vanish the moment they take damage. In the kitchen they come up out of the counter.
· SETAKA TOKO — Iron Ball. [Nakaya Emari] Respectful and honourable, writes actual thank-you notes, the tallest person in the class at six foot eight (Hiro is taller and does not count, and has signed that he would like that noted). Skin of matte aqua metal panelling. The class's moral north.
· KINJI HAMAKIDA — Jackpot Fever. [Kibi Kankei] Loud, cocky, music-obsessed, talks about last night's television whether or not anybody asked, a catastrophic loser who wants applause even when he lost. Best mates with Ando. Pink hair, expensive shoes he ruins shuffling. Fights with abrasive, sandpaper-rough strikes and footwork. His quirk is a gamble — a song, a die, and three rounds of being unstoppable when it pays out — and he has never once used it where anybody could see, because Carlos Might told him not to.
· TAZATO TADAMAKI — Dragon. [Ando Iorai] Cranky as a resting state, not a bad mood. Helps people and constructs an efficiency-based reason for it every time.
· TORAGI KAYO — Twin Impact. [Chozen Tadachi] Intimidating, awkward, leaves small useful gifts on people's desks with no note. Can hit the same spot twice. Out of a fight he apologises for interrupting; in one, he speaks only in one-liners, which makes him spectacularly unhelpful to whoever he is working with.
· YOSHIBARA HIYOKO — Double. [Nomi Igisa] Funny and friendly, then suddenly and completely furious, then fine. Her clone is exactly as much of all of that.

VOICES, IF YOU NEED THEM QUICKLY — Rakuka announces. Masahata ranks. Tazato is blunt and it is kindness. Setaka is formal. Ando jokes over the top of everything, and Kinji jokes over the top of Ando. Nomi says one sentence. Toragi, in a fight, says one line. Chozen starts a sentence twice. Ren waits to be spoken to. Hiro signs, and the screen does the rest.
appendix.heading: Class 1-A — twenty students at a glance
Class 1-B — the ones this campaign uses
appendix.body:
Ebina Chikara's class, twenty of them, and the campaign leans on nine. They are not the enemy; they are the other half of a year group, and by Chapter 5 they are in a corridor waiting for news.

· MOSHITA MARO — Copy. Touch someone, wear their quirk for two minutes exactly. Earnest, friendly, quietly ashamed that everything he has is borrowed, and he still walks into a scrum of eleven people to get a hand on somebody. He gets four separate segments of admiring commentary in the cavalry battle because his is the most televisually interesting quirk in the year. He is the student who does not come back. Every minute of screen time you give him in Chapter 3 is worth double in Chapter 4.
