· YAMARU TODAO — Deathly Endurance. A man who does not stop, against Kazama Kenji, who has a hard cap on what he can absorb. The match of the tournament and you should run it as a clock.
· KAKITA KEIKO — Homing. A thrown weapon that cannot miss, locked onto Ando Iorai early and permanently. She has studied his exam footage.
· DOMOTO FUMIJU — Rabbit. Right behind Izuto Kutsu at the bottleneck and delighted about it.
· TATETA FUMIRA — Bullet Laser. Two precision shooters at range with nowhere to hide, against Ren Suzuki, with Kazama standing in the open, glowing.
· HASHIGE TATAKA — Metal Manipulation. Against Setaka Toko, whose entire quirk is iron.
· ISOSATO SARI — Solid Air. Builds platforms that reshape the field twice in one event. Put one under a PC and you buy enormous goodwill for Chapter 4.
· ACHI HOMEI — Voice. Echolocates through a scrum and calls positions for his whole team.
· HATASHI HAMBA — High Specs. Consistently, unglamorously better than everyone at everything. Keeps a notebook of exact numbers.

THE OTHER ELEVEN — Naza Keiseki (Dark Shadow), Mawa Hisaya (Fire skin), Koto Kohomi (Gyrate), Chisano Tomose (Wave Motion), Asabira Magi (Weather Manipulation), Zabata Haho (Elasticity), Kagamo Akake (Air Cannon), Detsu Narumitsu (Beast Creation), Kukino Kaino (Clean Bubbler), Detsami Doki (Frog), Hama Kokao (Search). Use them as scenery, as cavalry-battle opposition, and as the faces in the corridor at the end.

EBINA CHIKARA brings his class in every morning for nine days after Moshita is taken, because the alternative is them sitting at home. He is in the corridor in the epilogue and he has been there the whole time.

Forty-two sections across about twenty-two to thirty sessions, plus as much free time as your table wants. Prep is what you actually need to read beforehand; the one thing is what the session fails without. Free-time windows are marked ✦ and are never required.

CHAPTER 1 — PROVISIONAL · Level 1
1 · The Letter + The Weeks Between + First Morning — prep 15 min. THE ONE THING: both exam questions, asked of every player, written down. Cut: the six weeks, to one sentence each.

CHAPTER 2 — TEN PAIRS · Levels 1-3
2 · Ten Names on the Board — prep 20 min. THE ONE THING: read the ten pairs and then stop talking. Cut: the pair-by-pair introductions.
3 · Battle Centre III, first half — prep 15 min. THE ONE THING: a PC pair discovers a combination nobody planned. Cut: every match with no PC in it.
✦ Free Time — First Weekends — prep 10 min. THE ONE THING: put "Hiro's Signs" and "A Song for Kinji" in front of the players.
4 · Battle Centre III, second half + Nobara Forge — prep 15 min. THE ONE THING: each pair leaves the lab with one item written on both sheets. Cut: the Technology checks.
5 · Semis and the Final — prep 10 min. THE ONE THING: the photograph. Cut: one of the two semi-finals.
6 · A Question at the Gate — prep 25 min. THE ONE THING: the class cannot legally act and has to stand there. Cut: nothing.
Heights Alliance and The Common Room Ticker are woven through all five and cost no session.

CHAPTER 3 — THE SHORTLIST · Levels 3-5
7 · Six Weeks — prep 15 min. THE ONE THING: two named training benefits per PC, written on the sheet. Cut: to twenty minutes and run Day One after it.
8 · Day One, the Obstacle Course — prep 20 min. THE ONE THING: the commentary. Cut: the fourth obstacle.
9 · Day Two, the Cavalry Battle — prep 20 min. THE ONE THING: the Moshita Maro segment, in full, warmly. Cut: to one phase and a scoreboard.
10 · Day Three, the Paired Tournament — prep 25 min. THE ONE THING: a PC answers the interview honestly and it plays beautifully. Cut: to two matches and the podium.
11 · Kuma at the North Concourse — prep 30 min. THE ONE THING: six thousand civilians on a clock you say out loud. Cut: nothing; this is the chapter's climax.
12 · The Results — prep 10 min, short session. THE ONE THING: "Which of you gave interviews?" Cut: run it as the last twenty minutes of session 11.
✦ Free Time — Famous for a Week — prep 15 min. THE ONE THING: the tiger on the wall opposite the west gate.

CHAPTER 4 — QUESTION ONE · Levels 5-7
13 · Ikari Tomonobu, Sixth — prep 20 min, and re-read your own Chapter 3 commentary. THE ONE THING: the class opens the archive without adult help. Cut: nothing.
14 · Lockdown — prep 10 min, half a session. THE ONE THING: Sugitsu's ten names, and then somebody counts, and then somebody translates. Cut: to the kitchen and the ten names, fifteen minutes.
15 · Riddle at the Perimeter — prep 20 min. THE ONE THING: give the question to the player and wait. Cut: run it straight after session 14, same evening.
✦ Free Time — Inside the Fence — prep 10 min. THE ONE THING: sneaking out is a real choice with a real cost.
16 · Powder and Touch up — prep 30 min, may run to two. THE ONE THING: somebody says "kill the healer." Cut: the trap phase.
17 · The Crows — prep 20 min. THE ONE THING: they find the girl alive. Cut: two of the three parallel searches.
18 · Kuma, Interviewed — prep 10 min, half a session. THE ONE THING: the carpet line, thrown away. Cut: entirely — Okuma delivers it in a briefing.
19 · Saki Hiyori Stands in Front of It — prep 30 min. THE ONE THING: roll 15d12 in the open, then roll call. Cut: nothing.

CHAPTER 5 — KEEPSAKE · Levels 7-8 · no free time
20 · Nine Days — prep 20 min. THE ONE THING: Rawagi's eleven seconds, and the class being told they are not part of what happens next. Cut: keep it short on purpose.
21 · The Shirahige Cold Store — prep 30 min, plus drawing one floor plan. THE ONE THING: enforce the silence the first time somebody shouts. Cut: floors, freely — eleven is a feeling, not a count.
22 · The Question You Don't Answer — prep 15 min. THE ONE THING: the silence while they decide. Cut: nothing; it is twenty minutes long.
23 · Keepsake — prep 40 min, likely two sessions. THE ONE THING: Carlos Might points at Kinji Hamakida, and the dice come down in the open. Cut: two of Sylar's borrowed quirks.
24 · Help Woman's Office — prep 5 min, short session. THE ONE THING: a closing beat for every PC, round the table. Cut: nothing, and keep it under half an hour.

CHAPTER 6 — AFTER HOURS · Levels 8-10 · run in any order
25 · Summer Term — prep 10 min. THE ONE THING: "it's the weekend — what do you do?" Every session opens with it.
26 · The Other Shortlist — prep 15 min. THE ONE THING: the Cage, floodlit, and Genda on the step.
27 · The Rank You Didn't Ask For — prep 10 min, only if a PC holds a stripe. THE ONE THING: Sugitsu asks what they are going to do with it.
28 · The Four Corners — prep 20 min per Corner. THE ONE THING: each one asks for somebody by name. Cut: to the one best match.
29 · The White Tiger — prep 30 min. THE ONE THING: the choice — alone, as a pair against the Law, or as a pair that is one fighter. Cut: nothing.
30 · Odd Nights — reference, read once before Chapter 4.
31 · A Party That Ends at Dawn — prep 25 min, only if the Legion reach Contact. THE ONE THING: tell them what time it is.
32 · Matsu-no-Yu — prep 20 min, only if the Court reach Contact. THE ONE THING: twelve minutes underwater.
33 · The Thing in the Laundry Room — prep 25 min, only if the Kuroshiki reach Contact, and check in with the table first. THE ONE THING: say your own name.
34 · The Fourth Door — prep 5 min. THE ONE THING: Forge's board, and an empty space on the wall.

THE SHORT VERSION, if you want ten sessions: 1, 2, 3, 6, then all of Chapter 3, then 13, 15, 19, then all of Chapter 5. Nothing structural is lost, and none of the free time or Chapter 6 is required.

CHAPTER 7 — THE TEACHING COPY · Levels 10-11
35 · Second Years — prep 15 min. THE ONE THING: the commentary heard through a classroom wall, and forty first-years laughing in the right places. Cut: the pair-by-pair assignment of first-years.
36 · Tokieda Mei, First Year — prep 10 min; woven through, costs no session of its own. THE ONE THING: the question from the notebook, asked of the player, and then silence.
37 · Clean Read — prep 20 min. THE ONE THING: hand a player the search box and let them type their own name. Cut: two of the six doors they can push.
✦ Free Time — Second Years — prep 10 min. THE ONE THING: a slot spent on an assigned first-year, and the question a fifteen-year-old asks.
38 · The Man Who Bought a Read — prep 25 min. THE ONE THING: read the PC's real limitation off their sheet, out loud, in his voice. Cut: the aftermath, to one line from Okuma.
39 · A Challenge, Bought and Paid For — prep 20 min, only if Byakko are in play. THE ONE THING: the fight is won by something nobody filmed. Cut: nothing; it is one scene.
40 · What the Archive Is For — reference, read before session one.

CHAPTER 8 — RIGHT OF REPLY · Levels 11-12
41 · A Letter from the Commission — prep 15 min. THE ONE THING: two speakers, chosen by the players, out loud. Cut: the nine days, to one slot each.
42 · The Hearing — prep 30 min, and write the five members' names on cards. THE ONE THING: the third question — Moshita Maro borrowed a quirk and gave it back, and forty first-years watched it on Tuesday, and should they not have? Cut: two of the four questions.
43 · Nobody Signed For It — prep 25 min, only if the Ledger reached Contact, and check in with the table first. THE ONE THING: the notebook, four names, four ticks, "was there a problem with it?"
44 · The Market — prep 25 min, may run to two sessions. THE ONE THING: say the price out loud every single time. Cut: any two of the five customers.
45 · Ebata Kyōsuke — prep 15 min, half a session. THE ONE THING: the laptop turned round, and four competitors.
46 · On the Record — prep 30 min, likely two sessions. THE ONE THING: every player writes an annotation before anybody rolls a die, and you write down exactly what they said. Cut: nothing.
47 · The Last Roll Call — prep 5 min, short session. THE ONE THING: read all four annotations out loud, and give the last word to a first-year. Cut: nothing, and keep it under half an hour.
48 · The Fifth Door — prep 5 min. THE ONE THING: the fifth space on the wall stays empty.

THE SHORT VERSION OF THE SECOND SEASON, if you want six sessions: 35, 37, 38, 41, 42, 46. Nothing structural is lost, and none of the Byakko thread, the Ledger or the free time is required.
appendix.heading: The session-by-session run sheet
The table cheat sheet
appendix.body:
One page, for during play. Everything here is stated somewhere in the module; this is where you look when somebody is waiting for an answer.

THE PAIR RULE — the campaign's spine and the only house rule it needs. A PC acting within reach of their Chapter 2 bracket partner has advantage on the roll. Say it out loud in the first fight and use it in every fight after. In the finale it is the difference between winning and not.

RECURRING DCs
· Riddle's Question One — DC 14 Intelligence to break out, at the end of each of the target's turns. 5 rounds otherwise.
· Sylar's Maw — DC 12 for him to maintain the grab; DC 16 Strength or Dexterity for an ALLY to break it. The victim cannot.
· Touch up's exhaustion clock — 5 heals on one creature in a minute is a rank of exhaustion, plus one per 2 further uses, maximum 5.
· Powder's Burst — Strength save at disadvantage vs DC 15.
· Rawagi's Foresight — DC 14 Constitution or a level of Concussed, every single use.
· Forge building something complicated — Technology or Intelligence vs a DC you set. A failure still costs her the calories and makes something unstable: halved range, damage dice one step down, advantage on saves against it.

THE PCs' OWN CLOCKS — hold these honestly and the campaign runs itself
· Kazama's Metal: up to 1,000 lb of metal a turn, from whatever is in reach, worn as armour. Metal Counter dumps all of it into one strike and leaves him with nothing. On grass, concrete or a cement arena he has only what he carried in.
· Izuto's Engine: Recipro Burst (proficiency bonus uses per short rest) doubles his speed and gives advantage for 5 rounds; afterwards his speed is 0 for 2 rounds, or until somebody cools him with water or ice (an action, from an ally — the pair rule in miniature). Cold slows his start and lowers his top tier.
· Chozen's Whirlwind: Gale Blast 3d8 and a 20-foot shove; Cyclone Reaction when something closes on him. He freezes in round one of every fight, by temperament not by rule — let him take hits while he plans. His output follows how wound-up he is, and after a long, high-pressure fight he crashes: disadvantage on checks until a short rest.
· Ren's Charge: charge points equal CON × 2 + level × 3. Laser Beam is 1d12 radiant, pierces cover, double damage to metal. Every 10% of output past the first costs him 2 true damage in recoil and more the higher he goes; his maximum output is 20% until level 4, then rises by 20% at 4, 6, 8 and 12. Yellow veins mean control; white means rage.
· Toragi's Twin Impact needs two hits on the same target in the same round, and has a 2-turn cooldown after it fires. Also: one-liners only, in any fight, always.
· Kinji's Jackpot Fever (finale only, unless you choose otherwise): roll the highest face on the current die to pay out — d100, d20, d12, d10, d8, d6, d4, one step down per failure. Three rounds of immortality, five times the damage and speed.

TRAINING BENEFITS — two per PC from Chapter 3, named, written on the sheet, and usable for the rest of the campaign. Be generous. In Chapters 4 and 5 these are frequently the only things still working.

WHEN YOU DO NOT KNOW — pick a number between 10 and 18, ask for a d20 plus whatever ability sounds right, and go. Consistency beats correctness and nobody will check.

WHEN THE PARTY IS LOSING AND YOU DID NOT MEAN IT — a teacher arrives. There are eleven of them and several are written as dials. Nobody at the table will ever know.

WHEN THE PARTY IS WINNING TOO EASILY — never add hit points mid-fight. Add a civilian, a floor giving way, or a second thing happening somewhere else.

THE NEW CLOCKS, for free time and Chapter 6
· Byakko Heat — 0 to 10. +1 every time the class beats a Byakko member in front of witnesses, +2 for a Ring fight, −1 for every free-time window with no contact. The chapter caps it: 3 in Chapter 2, 5 in Chapter 3, 7 in Chapters 4–5, and nothing in Chapter 6. Heat decides who shows up next.
· Odd Night — a secret d100 when a PC is out after dark somewhere strange. See "The Underground — Odd Nights and the discovery ladder."
· Free time — two slots per PC per window, three in Chapter 6.

The class knows Hiro is a machine. What comes out in Chapter 4 is that there is nobody in it. Everything before that is fair play: each of these is literally true, none is a trick, and all of them re-read cleanly afterwards. Plant three or four. Do not press any of them.

CHAPTER 2
1 · Forge measures the whole class for gear and does not use the tape on Hiro. "You I've got." She has the numbers because she built them.
2 · In the play-in he takes a hit that gets a wince out of the stands, does not react, does not check it, and gets up. Nobody calls medical over. This reads as him being a machine, and it is not quite that.
3 · A forearm on a bench in the support lab, unattached, wrist finished and fingers not, in the same grey panelling. A third of what Forge builds in that room is a piece of somebody, so it is unremarkable. If asked, she says "spare."
4 · A ground-floor corridor in Heights Alliance with a laundry, a store cupboard and one door at the end. It is Hiro's room, and everybody assumes it is where he charges. He is upstairs on the sofa.
5 · The emoji is always half a second late. Somebody says something funny, the room laughs, and then the screen shows 😂 — a beat behind, every time, like the far end of a video call. Mention it once, as a thing everybody finds endearing.

CHAPTER 3
6 · The booth gives him one line all week — "some sort of construct quirk, I'm told — there'll be somebody in there working it, presumably" — and it is a guess, and nobody corrects it.
7 · Everybody goes through the medical tent after full contact, because that is the rule. He waits outside it, holding other people's bags.
8 · The journalist works down the line of competitors after the tournament and does not stop at him, because he cannot answer a microphone and everybody knows it.
9 · He is at every meal, at the table, holding a cup, and has never once been seen to drink from it. This has been true since April.

THE ONE THAT IS NOT ABOUT HIM AT ALL
10 · Nobody in Class 1-A knows his family name, and nobody has ever needed to. It is not on the fridge chart, which lists him as "HIRO" in a column of nineteen full names, and Masahata — who is meticulous about this sort of thing — has simply never got round to asking.

CHAPTER 4 — the reveal, in "Lockdown"
11 · Sugitsu names his ten permanent Search slots. Somebody counts, works down the register, and finds that Hiro is not on the list and a student none of them has ever heard of is. He explains why in two flat sentences, in front of him, and Hiro answers in signs — and the room finds out who can read them.

IF THEY WORK IT OUT EARLY — let them, immediately, and give them the credit. The campaign loses nothing; the Chapter 5 payoff is entirely unaffected. A table that spotted it will be far more invested in him than a table that was surprised.

IF THEY NEVER ASK HIM ANYTHING — that is a real outcome and you should let it stand. It is the whole point of the character and the campaign is willing to charge for it in Chapter 5.

WHAT IS SAFE TO SHOW THEM — his character sheet, all of it. It says he is a machine, gives his quirk as "???", and says nothing else, and every word on it is true.
appendix.heading: Hiro — the clues, in order

appendix.body:
Five things, all of them paper, none of them taking more than ten minutes. This campaign is about documentation and it works considerably better when there is some on the table.

1 · THE CASE 9 VICTIM LIST — an index card or a sheet of A4 with five names, quirks, wards and dates. Add to it in front of the players when the sixth arrives. In Chapter 4, write the class's own festival placements underneath in the same handwriting and slide it across. That is the single most effective prop in the module and it costs one pen.

2 · THE FRIDGE CHART — Masahata's laminated bracket prediction, with himself winning. Print it, actually laminate it if you are that sort of person, and update it between sessions: annotated in week two, drawn on in week three, amended in red after the festival, gone in Chapter 4, back up in Chapter 5. Nobody says who put it back.

3 · RIDDLE'S INDEX CARD — after "A Question at the Gate," hand the players a card that says: tall, thin, white hair, scar forehead to chin, no nose, bleeds from the mouth. That is everything they have for two chapters, and they will produce it themselves in Chapter 4 when Kuma complains about a stain on his carpet.

4 · ONE FLOOR OF THE COLD STORE — hand-drawn, deliberately plain, on a sheet of paper. Give it to them at the door and tell them it is all eleven floors. Give them a pencil. Let them mark what they have cleared, and when they come out of a stairwell onto a floor they have already been on, say nothing and let them find it on their own map.

5 · THE CLASS PHOTOGRAPH — you do not need an image. You need four or five sentences describing it, written down and read out identically all three times you use it: on the steps in Chapter 2, on the table after roll call in Chapter 4, and in the epilogue. Same words every time. It has everybody in it.

AND ONE THING THAT IS NOT A PROP — the commentary. Write your lines down as you invent them in Chapter 3 and keep the sheet, because in Chapter 4 you are going to read them back word for word and there is no substitute for having actually said them when everyone was happy.

AND THREE MORE FOR THIS EDITION

6 · THE BYAKKO HEAT TRACK — a strip of paper numbered 0 to 10 and a paperclip. Move the clip where the players can see it, and never explain what the numbers mean. They will work out quickly that the higher it goes the worse the people who turn up, and that is exactly the right amount for them to know.

7 · THE RUMOUR BOARD — an index card per rumour the class has heard, pinned in a corner of the table. True and false ones go up the same way, in the same handwriting. When a rumour turns out to be true, do not take it down. Just put a second card next to it.

8 · KINJI'S DICE — a d100, a d20, a d12, a d10, a d8, a d6 and a d4, in a row, kept somewhere visible from Chapter 2 onwards with no explanation. If anybody asks, say they are Kinji's. In the finale, pick them up one at a time.
appendix.heading: Props to make before you start
Table traits — the class, in a fight and out of one
appendix.body:
Some traits are on the sheets. Some were improvised at the table and turned out to be better than anything written down. This page holds both, so they get used.

TORAGI KAYO — IN A FIGHT, ONLY ONE-LINERS. Improvised at the table and now canon. Out of a fight Toragi is awkward, apologetic and kind, and will say sorry for a full minute for interrupting you. The moment a fight starts he speaks exclusively in one short line at a time, and nothing else, which makes him spectacularly unhelpful to whoever is working with him — usually Chozen, who wants to discuss the plan.
· THE RULE — one line per round, four words or fewer. If a PC asks him something mid-fight, the answer is technically correct and practically useless.
· THE PAYOFF — once per session, at most, the DM may have one of his lines land at exactly the right moment; his partner gets advantage on one roll. In the Chapter 5 finale, his line is "Now." In the epilogue, he says a whole paragraph in the common room, and nobody has ever heard him say so much.
· LINES TO STEAL — "Hit him." "Twice." "Left." "Not yet." "Noted." "Wall." "Duck." "He's big." "Now." "Mm." "Later." "Good." "Again." "Fine." "Behind you." "Bad idea." "Yes." "No." "That's a wall." "Run."

THE REST OF THE CLASS, FROM THEIR SHEETS
· KINJI — talks about last night's television whether or not anybody asked; wants applause even when he lost, because he is a catastrophic loser; his speaker is always on; ruins expensive shoes shuffling; never uses his quirk in public.
· CHOZEN — stutters when asked something suddenly; freezes in round one; buys absurd gifts on occasions that do not involve gifts; fitness-obsessed; has a contingency for a volcanic eruption.
· REN — never starts a conversation, always finishes one kindly; forgives everybody; eats only traditional food; reads; cannot work technology without help; veins burn yellow in control and white in rage.
· KAZAMA — kind or cruel depending on the day; always clean; close to his mum; answers any direct question about his scar, and nobody asks.
· IZUTO — maintains his own engines with a wrench like a motorbike; does group projects alone and asks for a review; cannot say thank you.
· HIRO — one emoji at a time, always half a second late; hand signs; holds a cup at every meal and never drinks.
· SAMITSU — arms grow out of the counter while he cooks, doing three jobs at once, and he never watches them.
· KIBI — flowers bloom in his vine-hair when he is happy. He will not discuss it.
· ISOKONO — her tail wraps around the nearest friend when she is scared, and wags when she is not.
· NOMI — small objects drift toward her when she is not paying attention.
· YOSHIBARA — her clone has exactly her personality, so two of her is simply more of everything.
· RAKUKA — announces his own moves and his own entrances; has named a doorframe Hiroshi.
· ANDO — sunglasses always on; off means he is genuinely shaken; afraid of the dark.
· SETAKA — writes physical thank-you cards after ordinary conversations.
· MASAHATA — the laminated chart; mentions his ranking whenever rankings come up.
· ICHITAKA — makes small holograms for no reason; corrects teachers, and is sometimes right.
· AIKAWA — organises things nobody asked her to; taps her claws on every surface.
· TAZATO — helps people, then constructs a reason it was efficient.
· NAKAYA — giggles, loves anything that sparks, and is always near whatever just went entertainingly wrong.

ADD YOURS HERE. When you improvise something at the table that the players love, write it on this page the same night. Toragi's one-liners started exactly like that.

appendix.heading: Clean Read, the market, and what it costs
appendix.body:
The reference page for Chapters 7 and 8. Everything here is legal, and that is the design.

THE SITE — cleanread.jp. Two years old, four employees, about ninety thousand subscribers, ¥4,000 a month, cancel any time. It sells quirk teardowns: calm, well-made, eleven-minute breakdowns of a named quirk user's mechanism, limit and weakness, assembled entirely from public broadcast footage and professional commentary. Pro-hero pages are the business; Sports Festival pages are the back catalogue. A search box, a grid of thumbnails, four hundred and six public source links, and a comments section that is closed.

WHY IT IS LAWFUL — the Sports Festival archive is public record under the Public Broadcast Licence, revised in 2019 as a transparency measure after agencies were caught hiding the records of heroes who hurt people. Clean Read never films, interviews or contacts a subject. It has never been sued. Its takedown policy covers copyrighted material and not facts.

KIRISHITA NOE — thirty-one, founder, a former broadcast researcher who worked on the festival commentary team for four years. Answers email within a day, will meet students in person if asked, thinks she is doing journalism, and can argue it well. She is not sorry and she is not a monster. She was on the team for the festival that catalogued Habara Jun, and she knows which lines were hers.

THE THUMBNAILS — chosen by an algorithm for being the frame where the subject's expression changes, which is usually the moment the commentary explains their weakness. Moshita Maro's page is still up, with MEMORIAL in small grey letters at the top, because somebody at Clean Read thought that was the decent thing to do.

THE SUBSCRIPTION, AS A RULE — a PC who subscribes (¥4,000 a month) and watches a teardown gains advantage on their first attack roll against that quirk user, once per fight. It works. It works on heroes, on Byakko, on anybody with a page. Half the table will want to cancel it and one player will not.

THE BROKER — EBATA KYŌSUKE, forty-five, Room 9 of a karaoke place off Shinjuku's east exit, after eight, cash only. A former fight analyst for a broadcaster's sports desk, made redundant in 2021. He buys the ¥4,000 page, reads it properly, writes a page of plain Japanese, and charges between ¥8,000 and ¥400,000 depending on the subject and the customer's means. His quirk is Legible — he reads footage faster than a person should. It is registered. Nobody has ever thought about it. He has never used it on anybody and has never been in a fight.

THE PRICES, WHICH THE PLAYERS SHOULD HEAR OUT LOUD
· ¥4,000 — the subscription. Anybody.
· ¥8,000–18,000 — a written page on a student. Most of his trade.
· ¥60,000 — a package for three people, co-ordinated.
· ¥400,000 — a pro. Forty minutes on Saki Hiyori has 2.3 million views and he will still charge you for reading it.

THE FOUR COMPETITORS — there are now four sites. One is in Osaka. One is in Korean. Ebata was first because he is good at it. Removing him removes nothing, and the laptop turned round in Room 9 is how the class find that out.

THE RIGHT OF REPLY — granted by the Standing Committee on Records and Licensing in Chapter 8. Any subject of the public archive may attach their own annotation to their own footage, permanently, and it plays first, and nobody else may edit it. Form 4B, field name SUBJECT'S STATEMENT, no character limit, because nobody had ever filled it in. Within a month of the class using it, four thousand people have, and Clean Read starts playing them, because it has to.

THE ONE RULE FOR THIS WHOLE STORYLINE — Clean Read did not help Sylar, nobody planned the archive as a trap, and no part of the second season is permitted to retroactively change what happened in Chapters 1 to 5. It is a consequence, not a revelation.

appendix.heading: Stat blocks — the market
appendix.body:
Chapter 7 and 8's human opposition. None of them are monsters and most of them are not even criminals until the moment they decide to be. All of them are in the encounter manager under "Supporting Cast."

EVERY ONE OF THESE HAS READ ABOUT YOU. Where a block has PREPARED FOR YOU or READ AHEAD, open the PC's sheet, find the limitation the Chapter 3 commentary flagged, and have the NPC say it out loud. That is the mechanic and it costs nothing but nerve.

MIYASHITA GŌ, "TENPIN" — CR 7
Fifty-one, a C-rank villain with nine previous convictions and a kinetic quirk that puts a standing target down and keeps it down. Has never beaten anybody good in his life. Subscribed to Clean Read in February and has beaten four licensed heroes since.
AC 15 · HP 110 · Speed 30 ft · Initiative +2 · Save DC 15
STR 18 · DEX 14 · CON 16 · INT 11 · WIS 12 · CHA 9
· MULTIATTACK — TWO STRIKES (+8) — 2d10+4 bludgeoning each. On a hit, STR DC 15 or knocked prone.
· SPLIT (recharge 5–6) — 30-ft cone of kinetic force: DEX DC 15, 5d10 bludgeoning and pushed 20 ft and prone; half and no push on a save.
· READ AHEAD (once per round) — he names one thing a target's quirk cannot do, accurately, from the video playing on the phone clipped to his jacket, and gains advantage on his next attack roll against them.
· KEEPS THEM DOWN — he has advantage on attacks against prone creatures and does not let them up.
· HOW TO RUN — Not clever and not fast, and he knows exactly what each of them cannot do. He surrenders the moment it goes badly and then talks, helpfully, at length, and gives the class Ebata Kyōsuke's name.

TOKIEDA MEI, FIRST YEAR — CR 1/2
Fifteen, 1-A, Replay. Enormously polite, relentless, and has built a fighting style entirely out of somebody else's footage. An ally and a liability, usually at once.
AC 13 · HP 25 · Speed 30 ft · Initiative +3 · Save DC 12
STR 11 · DEX 16 · CON 12 · INT 15 · WIS 13 · CHA 14
· BORROWED OPENING (+4) — 1d8+3, damage type as whatever she is copying.
· REPLAY — once per fight she repeats her own last action exactly, including the parts she does not understand.
· SHE FIGHTS LIKE SOMEBODY ELSE — she uses a PC's signature opening at the wrong moment, and it does not fit her body, and it will not, and she has not worked that out.
· WILL NOT GO DOWN — at 0 HP she is unconscious and stable, never dying; the module does not kill her.
· HOW TO RUN — In the car park she is up and losing and still going, because she copied somebody who does not stop. A PC who tells her to get out has to actually make her.

YUKA ŌBA — CR 1
Thirty-eight, a cardigan, a nine-page printout she paid ¥18,000 for, no combat training of any kind, and a real grievance about a real hero that nobody would look at. She is going to try.
AC 11 · HP 20 · Speed 30 ft · Initiative +0 · Save DC 11
STR 10 · DEX 10 · CON 11 · INT 13 · WIS 12 · CHA 14
· SHE HITS SOMEBODY WITH A BAG (+2) — 1d4 bludgeoning.
· WARP (3 per day) — her quirk moves a held object three feet to the left. It is on a form. It is useless. She has read nine pages about how to use it on a sixteen-year-old and one of the nine pages is right.
· SHE WILL NOT STOP — she has no save against being frightened and no interest in one.
· THE HARDEST FIGHT IN THE CHAPTER — because hitting her is monstrous, because she is correct about the hero, and because she came to a karaoke booth in Shinjuku since it was the only door that opened.
· HOW TO RUN — First customer in "The Market." Do not make her dangerous and do not make her ridiculous. Let the class work out that the problem is not her.

A CO-ORDINATED PACKAGE (THREE) — CR 5 each
¥60,000 bought three people one plan built around one real limitation, and they have rehearsed it, and they get to four minutes forty.
AC 15 · HP 65 · Speed 30 ft · Initiative +3 · Save DC 14
STR 15 · DEX 16 · CON 15 · INT 12 · WIS 12 · CHA 11
· MULTIATTACK — TWO STRIKES (+6) — 2d8+3, damage type to taste; give each one a different element.
· THE PLAN (while at least two of them are within 30 ft of each other) — each of them has advantage on attacks against the target the package was bought for.
· FOUR MINUTES FORTY — at the start of round five, if the fight is still going, they all gain 20 temporary HP and say so out loud.
· HOW TO RUN — In a stairwell at Nakano station, because the plan needs a corridor. Break up the trio and the plan collapses entirely.

THE LAST CUSTOMER — CR 10
She did not buy a teardown of a student. She bought forty minutes on Saki Hiyori, 2.3 million views, ¥400,000, and she is a professional with a three-year grudge, and four second-years are in the road.
AC 17 · HP 165 · Speed 35 ft · Initiative +5 · Save DC 17
STR 17 · DEX 20 · CON 17 · INT 14 · WIS 15 · CHA 13
· MULTIATTACK — THREE PRECISE STRIKES (+9) — 2d10+5 slashing each.
· PREPARED FOR HER, NOT FOR YOU — she has no teardown of any PC and does not want one. The class are an obstacle and she treats them as one, which means she will walk away from them if they let her.
· FORTY MINUTES OF HOMEWORK — against Saki Hiyori specifically she has advantage on all attacks and saves, and she knows the exact shape of Burst.
· DISENGAGE AS A BONUS ACTION — she is not here for a brawl.
· HOW TO RUN — Professional, unhurried, uninterested, and genuinely dangerous to a party at level 12 only because she is trying to get past them. If the table needs her, let Creed arrive at the end of round three, absolutely furious about the whole business.

EBATA KYŌSUKE — NOT A FIGHT
Forty-five, Room 9, a good coat, the free pickles, a laptop and a second phone face-down. Quirk: Legible — he reads footage faster than a person should. Registered. Unremarked.
AC 11 · HP 40 · no attacks, no tactics, no fight.
· HE DOES NOT DEFEND HIMSELF. If the class attack him he lets them, presses charges, and ends somebody's provisional licence, and Sugitsu will not be able to fix it.
· WHAT HE IS FOR — the scene in Chapter 7's aftermath and Chapter 8's "Ebata Kyōsuke." He orders them tea, explains the business, offers to be argued with, and turns the laptop round to show them the four competitors.
· WHAT HE GIVES THEM — "If you lot ever get to say something first, over the top of your own footage — say the thing the commentary got wrong. Not the weakness. The reason. Nobody's ever put a reason in the archive."
· HOW TO RUN — Courteous, unhurried, and not a sophist. He is a middle-aged man doing lawful work that hurts children, and he knows the second half of that and has decided it is not his half.

appendix.heading: The first-year cohort — five names and forty children
appendix.body:
Chapter 7 puts forty new first-years in the building and assigns each PC two of them. You need five names and the rest is improvisation. Hand two out per PC in "Second Years" and keep them all season.

· TOKIEDA MEI — Replay (Uncommon). Small, intense, enormously polite, holds a bow slightly too long. Repeats her own last action once, perfectly, including the parts she does not understand. She has watched one PC's festival footage four hundred times and built herself out of it, down to the back foot, and she has a forty-page notebook about them which she will show anybody who asks. She is not sinister, she is not a plant, and she is going to be a very good hero because of a document that got five people killed. Give her to the PC whose player most enjoyed the festival.
· ŌGAKI SHUN — Ballast (Rare). Cheerful, heavy, immovable, hero-worships Setaka Toko to an embarrassing degree and has started writing thank-you notes, badly, six pages long. He is the first-year who phones a PC when somebody does not come back.
· FUJIMORI NENE — Static (Rare). Furious at everything including herself, fastest in the cohort, and loses on purpose rather than be helped. She is Izuto Kutsu's arc in a smaller blazer and the PC who shares it is the one who can reach her.
· BABA TOSHIKI — Nine Lives (Uncommon). Cannot pass the obstacle course and will not stop attempting it. Everybody in the building already loves him and nobody has told him. He finishes it on the eleventh try and the only person who sees it is whoever was assigned to him.
· SHIRAKAWA AOI — Loudspeaker (Uncommon). The cohort's Masahata: already maintaining a ranking chart, already sure of it, already seeking quotes. Masahata Shikoji regards her existence as an act of war and will not discuss it.
· AND, IF THE CLASS DID THE SIDE QUEST — TOMO, fifteen, in the back row, who was on a crash barrier in Ikebukuro two years ago practising somebody's stance, and who has told absolutely everybody how he got here.

HOW TO USE THEM
· ONE SLOT PER WINDOW. A PC who spends a free-time slot on their assigned first-years gets Inspiration, and the DM gets to ask the player one question about their character that a fifteen-year-old would ask. Write the answers on the sheet; they are the best material in the second season.
· ONCE PER CHAPTER a first-year does something useful at exactly the wrong moment. That is also what they are for.
· THEY ARE THE ARCHIVE'S BEST ARGUMENT. Forty children are better at this than they would otherwise be because the commentary explains the weakness. Every scene in Chapters 7 and 8 that argues for taking the catalogue down is arguing against them, and the module never resolves that, and neither should you.
· DO NOT KILL ANY OF THEM. Chapter 7 hurts Tokieda Mei in a car park and that is the whole of the module's appetite for harming first-years. The second season is a school story with a market in it, not a horror campaign with a second cast to spend.

campaigns.title: After Hours: The City
campaigns.tagline: Everything Class 1-A does when nobody is hunting them. Weekends, odd jobs, a street gang that ranks you by who you have beaten, and four societies older than quirks.
campaigns.estimate: Reference — as much or as little as the table wants
campaigns.tone:
The companion volume to The Shortlist: After Hours, and all of it optional. The main volume is a school year with a killer in it. This one is the city around that year: the weekends, the evenings, the week after the festival when the class are famous and bored, and the summer afterwards when they are not being hunted by anybody.

It holds three things and a shop. FREE TIME is the structure — windows, slots, and the lists a player picks from when you ask what they do with a Saturday. BYAKKO are a street gang in the backstreets of west Tokyo with exactly one rule, which is that you hold the rank of the strongest person you have beaten, and who turns up next depends on a number on a strip of paper the players can see. THE UNDERGROUND is four societies hiding in plain sight — vampires, sun-priests, sorcerers and a civil service of death-gods — none of which anybody has noticed, because in a world where everybody has a quirk, every strange power gets mistaken for one.

None of it touches the main plot. All of it is there when the class have a Saturday off.

background.heading: How to use this volume
background.body:
This is the second half of The Shortlist: After Hours. The story — eight chapters, Appetite, the archive, the Sports Festival and the second season — is in the main volume on this page. This one is the city those fifteen-year-olds live in on their days off, and it is all reference: lists to look things up in during a session, not pages to read before one.

WHAT IS IN HERE
· FREE TIME — how a window and a slot work, and then the lists: side quests, odd jobs, hangouts, little things, and Tokyo ward by ward.
· BYAKKO — a street gang that ranks its members by who beat whom. The Stripe Law, the Heat track, Heat events, every named member from a Stray to the White Tiger, the turf economy, and the Cage floor by floor.
· THE UNDERGROUND — four societies whose powers are not quirks: the Scarlet Legion, the Astral Court, the Kuroshiki and the Ledger. Odd Nights, the five-rung discovery ladder, two rumour tables, and stat blocks for all of them.
· THE SHOP — what is new in it and what it is for.

WHEN YOU NEED IT — read "Free Time — How It Works" before the first free-time window, which the main volume puts in Chapter 2. Read "Byakko" when the class first wander into the backstreets. Do not read "The Underground" before Chapter 4, and do not read it to your players at all.

THE TWO RULES THAT GOVERN EVERYTHING IN HERE — free time never solves the main plot, and the main plot never happens in free time. Nothing in this volume is required, none of it touches the spine, and a table that never opens it has still played the whole campaign.

THERE ARE NO CHAPTERS IN THIS VOLUME, and that is deliberate. The city does not have a running order.

background.heading: Free Time — How It Works
background.body:
The spine of this campaign is a school year with a killer in it. Free time is everything else: the weekends, the evenings, the week after the festival when the class are famous and bored. It is optional, it is the players' to direct, and it is where most of this edition's new material lives.

THE WINDOW — between chapters, and at the points each chapter marks with a "Free Time" section, the class get a window. A window is a weekend, or a week of evenings, or a fortnight of summer.

THE SLOTS — in each window, every PC gets TWO free-time slots (THREE in Chapter 6). A slot is an afternoon or an evening. Go round the table and ask each player what they do with theirs. Resolve each one in a sentence, a roll or a short scene, and move on. A whole window should take fifteen to forty minutes of table time, not a session — unless a slot turns into something, in which case play the something.

WHAT A SLOT CAN BE SPENT ON
· A SIDE QUEST STEP — most side quests take two or three slots, spread over windows. See "Free Time — side quests."
· AN ODD JOB — civilian work for yen. Provisional students cannot be paid for hero work, but they can work a konbini till. See "Free Time — odd jobs."
· A HANGOUT — time with one classmate, teacher or NPC. It is worth exactly one honest conversation, and you should update the relationship tracker afterwards. Hangouts are the cheapest, best thing in this list.
· TRAINING — three training slots, in any order across any windows, earn one new named training benefit, on the same pattern as Chapter 3's. A teacher who is asked will always say yes.
· SHOPPING — the shop page is open whenever a PC has a slot and the yen. Some things in it are a lot more useful than they look.
· WANDERING — pick a ward and see what happens. Roll on the "little things" list, or let the player tell you what they are looking for. Wandering is how the class meets Byakko, and the only way anybody ever stumbles into the Underground.
· REST — a slot spent doing nothing at all clears one rank of exhaustion or one lingering condition. Bose will be disappointed. Help Woman will approve.

MONEY — every student starts on ¥20,000 and the shop, the arcade and the ramen stall all want some of it. Odd jobs pay ¥3,000–¥15,000 a slot. Byakko's Ring pays far more, is illegal, and raises Heat.

THE CHAPTER DECIDES THE MAP
· Chapter 1: none. They have not started yet.
· Chapter 2: the whole city, carefree. Byakko Heat cannot rise above 3.
· Chapter 3: the whole city, and from the festival onward they are recognised in it. Heat cap 5.
· Chapter 4: lockdown. Free time is inside the fence unless they sneak out, and every sneak-out is a choice with a cost. Heat cap 7.
· Chapter 5: none. Nine days of nothing. Say so.
· Chapter 6: summer, the whole city, three slots each, no caps on anything.

THE TWO RULES — free time never solves Appetite, and Appetite never happens in free time. If a player chases Case 9 on a Saturday, give them the honest dead end the Developments boxes already describe. If you want something to go wrong on a Saturday, that is what Byakko are for.

background.heading: Byakko
background.body:
Every teenager in west Tokyo has heard of Byakko and most of them have seen the tiger. It is sprayed on shutters from Ikebukuro to the Shinjuku west exit: a white tiger, mid-stride, sometimes with names under it.

WHAT THEY ARE — a street gang, and a fairly old one. They run protection on the backstreet shops, the illegal fight nights in a closed batting centre called the Cage, a dice den above a noodle bar, and a chop shop that will sell you a van with no questions asked. They are criminals. They are also, in their own neighbourhoods, the closest thing to law there is, and the old woman who runs the dice den has kept the same street quiet for thirty-one years.

THE STRIPE LAW — Byakko have one rule, and it is the whole gang: rank is power. You hold the rank of the strongest person you have beaten in front of witnesses. Anybody can challenge upward. Nobody runs from a challenge on their own street. The White Tiger — the boss, the title, the person — is simply whoever nobody can beat. Ranks are tattooed: one white stripe on the inside of the forearm for a Claw, two for a Fang, three for a Stripe, four for the Four Corners, and a whole pelt down the back for Byakko.

WHY THEY GET HARDER — because the Law makes them. Beat a Claw and the Claw's Fang hears about it. Beat a Fang in front of witnesses and a Stripe comes to see who did it. Every win the class rack up against Byakko is a reason for somebody stronger to come and look. Track it as Heat, on a strip of paper numbered 0 to 10, and let it decide who turns up next. See "Byakko — the Stripe Law and the Heat track."

WHY THEY ARE INTERESTED IN CLASS 1-A — the festival. Byakko watched it the way everybody did, and to people who rank each other by strength, a national broadcast of the strongest first-years in the country is a list of people worth fighting. The week the archive goes up, a white tiger appears on the wall opposite the U.A. west gate with the podium names under it. It is not a threat. It is an invitation, and that is worse, because the class are provisional students who are not allowed to use their quirks in a street fight and Byakko know it.

WHAT THEY ARE NOT — part of Appetite. Riddle bought a white van from a Byakko chop shop with cash in the spring, and the Stripe who sold it remembers a man who bled on the counter, and that is the entire connection. Byakko are the city's noise. Do not let them become its plot.

background.heading: The Underground — read this before Chapter 4, not before
background.body:
Nothing in this page appears in Chapters 1 to 3 except as a rumour, and nothing in it is required at all. It is here so that the city has a basement.

THE IDEA — eighty percent of the world has a quirk. Anything strange a person can do is assumed to be one, written on a form, and forgotten. That is the best hiding place there has ever been. Three groups in Tokyo have powers that are not quirks — no quirk factor, no registry entry, no Compendium page — and they have survived the quirk era simply by letting everybody assume.

THE SCARLET LEGION — vampires, in the Hellsing tradition: old, aristocratic, military, and appalling. They came to Japan with the foreign legations in 1868, and they run a members' club in Ginza, a private clinic in Minato and the night shipping at Kurogane Wharf. On paper they are old-money foreigners with no quirks. They feed on people nobody misses, which lately has meant Byakko.

THE ASTRAL COURT — a court of sun-priests older than the shogunate, who practise Sunbreath: a breathing art that carries sunlight through the blood. Its masters wake a second self called an Envoy, a figure that stands beside them and does one impossible thing. They are the Legion's oldest enemy. They are registered Quirkless and proud of it, and one of them teaches English at U.A.

KUROSHIKI — the black rite. Old families who pass down inherited techniques fuelled by Sumi, the ink of dread turned against itself, and use them to exorcise Kegare — things born out of human fear, invisible to everybody else. They hide their work behind Veils that cameras cannot see through. A city that has spent a year afraid of Case 9 is full of Kegare, and the Kuroshiki are badly overstretched.

HOW THE CLASS FIND THEM — by accident, and late. There is no scene in the spine that points at them. The class find them by being out after dark in the wrong place on a free-time slot, by noticing a teacher do something an acid quirk cannot do, or by losing somebody and then sleeping in a building full of that. Every faction sits on a five-rung ladder — Rumour, Trace, Witness, Contact, Invitation — and each rung needs a PC to choose to chase it. See "The Underground — Odd Nights and the discovery ladder."

THE HARD LIMITS — no faction reaches Contact before Chapter 6. None of them is behind Appetite, knows Appetite exists, or can solve it. And there is room for more: the fourth door is deliberately left unpainted. See "Room for more."

AND A FOURTH, IF YOUR CAMPAIGN GETS THAT FAR. THE LEDGER — a department. Death-gods in black uniforms who have collected this city's dead since the Heian court first wrote a date next to a name, and who do it in rounds, on a schedule, with forms. Their wardens carry a writ, which is a sword with a name; a soul they fail to collect on time becomes an Arrear and stands where it was told to stand until somebody comes. Nobody has noticed them because everybody has: they wear black, they are courteous, and they turn up at accidents. They are chronically understaffed, they are in arrears across two-thirds of Tokyo, and they collected four of the five Case 9 victims on time and closed the file. Their contact scene is in Chapter 8 and no faction reaches Contact before Chapter 6. See "The Ledger."

appendix.heading: Free Time — side quests, and where they are now
appendix.body:
All 42 side quests now live in the chapter that opens them, in the main volume, in a box at the end of the chapter. That is where a DM needs them: you are running Chapter 3, and the three quests that just became available are on the same page as the scene you are running, rather than forty pages away behind four other chapters' worth.

HOW A QUEST IS WRITTEN — a name, who brings it, what it costs in free-time slots, a line to say out loud to start it, what it is, and what it pays. Offer two or three per window, casually, as things classmates are doing. None of them is required and every one of them is better if a player raises it first.

WHAT IS WHERE
· CHAPTER 2, TEN PAIRS — 9 quests: HIRO'S SIGNS; A SONG FOR KINJI; WHOSE MILK IS IT; SAMITSU'S KITCHEN; REN'S PHONE; TORAGI'S GIFTS; THE ISOBAR TAPES; NAKATA'S GYM; THE ECHO TWINS.
· CHAPTER 3, THE SHORTLIST — 11 quests: KAZAMA'S MUM; IZUTO'S UNCLE; THE AGENCY LETTER; THE BYAKKO KID; YANAMI'S CREDIT; MADAME TSURU'S DIE; ADACHI WANTS IN; DOJIMA ON THE ROOF; HANA'S LESSONS; TOBE MIYU'S EXERCISE BOOKS; YANAGI'S SECOND ATTEMPT.
· CHAPTER 4, QUESTION ONE — 5 quests: THE PANDA'S PROBLEM SET; ROB JOESTAR'S DETENTION; THE ROOF AT NIGHT; THE GROUND-FLOOR DOOR; QUIET'S FOUR PATIENTS.
· CHAPTER 5, KEEPSAKE — 1 quest: THE SPEAKER.
· CHAPTER 6, AFTER HOURS — 7 quests: KUMA'S PAROLE; MOSHITA'S NOTEBOOK; NEXT YEAR'S CHART; THE GREY PEOPLE AT THE WHARF; THE OLD WOMAN IN THE COLD BATH; THE STAIRWELL IN OTA; THE KID WHO DIDN'T CLIMB.
· CHAPTER 7, THE TEACHING COPY — 5 quests: MEI'S NOTEBOOK; BABA TOSHIKI AND THE OBSTACLE COURSE; FUJIMORI NENE WILL NOT BE HELPED; SHIRAKAWA'S CHART; CANCEL THE SUBSCRIPTION.
· CHAPTER 8, RIGHT OF REPLY — 4 quests: YUKA ŌBA'S BROTHER; WHAT KAJIURA CANNOT DO; A PAGE WITH YOUR NAME ON IT; THE ANNOTATION.

THE RULES THAT APPLY TO ALL OF THEM — a quest costs free-time slots and most take two or three, spread across windows. A quest never solves the main plot. A quest left alone simply waits; nothing expires. And a player who invents their own is worth more than anything on this list — say yes, and charge them slots for it.

See "Free Time — How It Works" for windows and slots, and "Free Time — odd jobs," "hangouts" and "little things" for the other three ways to spend one.

appendix.heading: Free Time — odd jobs
appendix.body:
Provisional students cannot be paid for hero work. They can be paid for everything else. One slot, one check, one wage; a failed check halves the pay. Fame from Chapter 3 onwards opens the jobs marked ★.

· KONBINI NIGHT SHIFT — any. CON DC 10. ¥6,000. On a failure you are wrecked next session (no Inspiration). In Kōenji, your co-worker has a pompadour.
· RAMEN STALL — DEX or CHA DC 11. ¥5,000 and a free meal.
· TUTORING MIDDLE-SCHOOLERS — INT DC 12. ¥8,000. Ichitaka, Nomi and Chozen are naturals and know it.
· MOVING COMPANY — STR DC 13. ¥7,000, doubled for Setaka, Samitsu or Hiro, who carries a piano up four flights and shows 🙂 the whole way.
· BICYCLE DELIVERY — DEX DC 12. ¥6,000. Izuto earns double and gets a speeding warning.
· THE ANCHOR CAFÉ, KUROGANE WHARF — CHA DC 10. ¥5,000, and roll on the rumour table.
· SWING TOWN ATTENDANT — no check. ¥6,000. You work for a Byakko Fang. Heat neither rises nor falls; you learn the backstreets.
· NAKATA'S GYM, CLEANING — no check. ¥3,000 and half a training slot.
· FORGE'S LAB ASSISTANT — no check, no pay. After three slots she builds you something small, out of gratitude and rice.
· ★ EVENT SECURITY — WIS DC 12. ¥10,000. A civilian job; using a quirk on it is still an offence.
· ★ MODELLING OR A SPONSOR SHOOT — CHA DC 13. ¥15,000. Your face is on a billboard in Shibuya by Friday.
· THE RING (ILLEGAL) — a fight. Purse ¥25,000 to ¥85,000 for a win, nothing for a loss. Heat +2. Bose finds out.

THE SECOND BLOCK — second-years only (Chapter 7 onward), when the paperwork stops being a problem and the pay goes up. Same rules: one slot, one check, one wage, halved on a failure.
· DEMONSTRATION WORK AT AN OPEN DAY — CHA DC 12. ¥12,000. You stand in a gym and answer questions from forty parents. Three of them have seen your Clean Read page.
· SPARRING PARTNER AT A PRO AGENCY — CON DC 13. ¥18,000. Legal, supervised, and you will be used as a wall.
· CRAMMING-SCHOOL COACH FOR THE U.A. EXAM — INT DC 13. ¥14,000. Six fifteen-year-olds who all want to know what it was like.
· STAGEHAND ON A HERO VARIETY SHOW — DEX DC 12. ¥10,000, and you meet two people who are famous and one who is kind.
· COURIER WORK, NIGHT SHIFT — DEX DC 12. ¥9,000, and after midnight roll an Odd Night.
· ARCHIVE CLERK AT THE BROADCASTER — INT DC 14. ¥11,000. Filing the footage. Yours is in there. So is everybody's.
· TRANSLATING FOR A FOREIGN AGENCY — INT DC 15 (or free if a PC speaks the language). ¥20,000. The agency is in Ginza and the building next door has no sign.
· HOSPITAL PORTER, NIGHTS — CON DC 12. ¥10,000. You will see somebody in black by the bins, writing. (Ledger haunt.)
· SHOP WORK AT A YANAKA SWEET SHOP — no check. ¥4,000 and a bag of rice crackers. The owner is extremely cheerful and asks your name twice.
· ★ A SPONSOR'S SUMMER CAMPAIGN — CHA DC 14. ¥40,000, and a billboard, and a fortnight of being recognised everywhere.
· ★ CONSULTANT ON A CLEAN READ PAGE — CHA DC 13. ¥25,000. They will pay a subject to appear on their own teardown and correct it. It is the best-paid job on this list. Think about it properly.
· THE RING, STILL (ILLEGAL) — a fight. ¥25,000 to ¥85,000, Heat +2, Bose finds out. Second-years have more to lose.

appendix.heading: Free Time — hangouts, one scene each
appendix.body:
A hangout is one slot spent with one person, and it is worth exactly one honest conversation. The free-time rules call it the cheapest, best thing on the list and then give no list. This is the list: a line to open on, and the thing that comes out if a PC actually sits down. Update the relationship tracker afterwards.

HOW TO RUN ONE, IN FOUR STEPS — this is the whole technique and it takes ninety seconds to learn.
· OPEN ON THEM DOING SOMETHING. Never on them waiting to be talked to. Samitsu is already cooking. Masahata already has the chart out. Bose is already running. The PC has walked into the middle of something.
· SAY THE LINE. Each entry below has one. Say it and then stop, which is the hard part.
· ASK ONE QUESTION AND LET THE PLAYER ANSWER IT PROPERLY. Not "what do you do" — something only their character can answer. The best hangouts in this campaign have all been a player talking for two minutes while the DM says nothing.
· END IT EARLY. Finish on the good line, not on the natural end of the conversation. A hangout that stops a beat too soon is one a player will bring up again.

AND THE ONE RULE — a hangout is never a skill check. There is nothing to roll. If a player asks what they need to roll, the answer is nothing, and say it warmly.

THE CLASS
· AIKAWA SAKUME — "I made you a rota. You don't have to use it." A pause. "I just made one." She organises things nobody asked her to organise, because the alternative is noticing that nobody asked her to.
· ANDO IORAI — The sunglasses are already off when you get there, folded on the table, and he does not mention it. It is the second time all year. He does not explain, and he does not put them back on until you have gone.
· HIRO — He clears a space on the table, holds up both hands, and waits. 🙂. Four pages of hand signs, patiently, with a 🙂 every time you get one right. After Chapter 4 this is a conversation with Otowa Suzume, and both of you know it.
· ICHITAKA SHIJIME — "Teach me something I'll be bad at." He says it like a business proposal and means it like a favour. He has never once been allowed to be bad at anything in front of anybody.
· ISOKONO YOROMU — "Can I ask you something nobody's asked you?" He is crying by the time you answer and is not remotely embarrassed about it, and the question is one nobody else in the class would have thought of.
· KIBI KANKEI — He moves up one cushion so there is room, and then says nothing for an hour. It is the most restful hour of the term. The flowers come out.
· MASAHATA SHIKOJI — "Don't tell anyone I showed you this." It is the chart's working. It is meticulous, it is fair, and he has ranked himself honestly — and he would rather die than have that mentioned.
· NAKAYA EMARI — "D'you want to know how much I'm actually carrying?" She is still giggling when she asks it, and then she tells you, completely seriously, and tells you how long she thinks she has.
· NOMI IGISA — She listens for forty minutes. Then she says one sentence. It is about you, and it is correct.
· RAKUKA RIZO — "I know I announce everything." He says it perfectly cheerfully. "It's because of how quiet it got when my brother stopped." And then he announces something, and that is the end of it.
· SAMITSU HINSEI — "Sit down. Don't help." He takes offence at something tiny about twenty minutes in, gets over it out loud and in real time, and is a better friend by the end of the evening.
· SETAKA TOKO — He is writing something while you talk, and he will not say what. At the end he hands it over. It is a thank-you note for the conversation you are still having.
· KINJI HAMAKIDA — "Right. Headphones. All of it — it's forty-one minutes, don't make that face." Then he watches your face for forty-one minutes and says nothing at all. After Chapter 5 he will talk about Carlos Might, to one person, once.
· TAZATO TADAMAKI — "It was more efficient this way." It was not more efficient. It was enormously kind and he has built a reason for it, and if you point that out he leaves.
· TORAGI KAYO — He puts a wrapped box on the table, sits down, and does not say one word for twenty minutes. Out of a fight he cannot find any. It is one of the best scenes in the campaign and you have to let the silence run.
· YOSHIBARA HIYOKO — "Which one of those do you think is the real one?" Funny, then furious, then fine — and then she asks you that, seriously, and waits.
· CHOZEN, IZUTO, KAZAMA AND REN are PCs. Hangouts between two PCs are free, happen in the fiction, and the DM should get out of the way entirely.

THE STAFF
· NOBARA FORGE — "Right. Diagrams." She clears half the bench with one forearm and explains the pairing experiment properly, and it is better reasoning than the class ever assumed.
· SUGITSU JARVICHI — "Twelve minutes. Ask me anything and I'll answer it honestly, which you may regret." He does. One of the answers will keep somebody awake.
· BOSE — Ninety minutes of training and four words in total. All four are useful. Do not give him a fifth.
· HELP WOMAN — "Sit. I'm going to tell you something about your own body that you won't enjoy." She does, and she is right, and then she makes tea.
· SUPER PANDA — "Ah! Good. Sit, sit. Now — why do you think you noticed that?" Maths, then a genuinely profound aside about pattern-matching, then more maths.
· ROB JOESTAR — He loses his temper at a stapler and then apologises for four minutes. If anybody mentions the bathhouse he goes very quiet and changes the subject.
· SAKI HIYORI (CREED) — "I'm not talking about the loading yard." A pause. "I'll teach you how to stand in front of something instead." Which is not the same as being brave, and he will say so.
· CARLOS MIGHT — Never in the building. If a PC finds him anyway, that is a side quest, not a hangout.

OUTSIDE SCHOOL
· OTOWA SUZUME — Knock. "Come in." Everything after that belongs to the players, and the DM should have nothing prepared.
· NAKATA ISAMU — "Ten thousand a month. I pay it." He starts taping his hands. "D'you want to know why, or d'you want to hit something first?" No self-pity anywhere in it.
· OKABE FUMI (THE ANCHOR) — "Sit at the end. You hear more from the end." Coffee, and every rumour in the ward, and she will not tell you where a single one came from.
· INSPECTOR OKUMA — "Twenty minutes. And I'll tell you the truth about whatever you ask, including the parts that are my fault." She means all of that, including the last bit.
· MURASE KOTOHA (BYAKKO) — "This isn't happening. We're not talking." She is already talking. She will deny the whole thing afterwards and help again next time.
· YANAGI DAICHI (BYAKKO) — "You want to learn something? Now? Properly?" He is delighted and trying very hard not to show it, and he teaches it for free.
· TOKIEDA MEI (FIRST YEAR, CHAPTER 7+) — She puts the notebook on the table, turns it round so it faces you, opens it at the first page, and waits.

appendix.heading: Free Time — little things (d40)
appendix.body:
For a slot spent wandering, or when a player asks "what is there to do?" Roll a d40 or pick one. Each is a sentence, a smile, and a very small reward.

1 · Karaoke. Kinji takes the mic for forty minutes. At the very end Toragi sings one line, perfectly, and refuses to do it again. (¥1,500. Inspiration to whoever paid.)
2 · An Akihabara claw machine. Hiro empties it in ten minutes and the manager asks him, politely, to leave.
3 · Ramen in Shinjuku. Ren orders like a monk; the chef adores him and gives the table free gyoza.
4 · A cat café. A cat sits on whoever is most stressed, which is Chozen. He does not move for two hours. (Advantage on his next WIS save.)
5 · A public bathhouse. Clears one rank of exhaustion. In Kōenji, there is a very old woman sitting at the bottom of the cold pool. (Court haunt.)
6 · A two a.m. konbini run. Oden, a magazine, and a clerk with a magnificent pompadour.
7 · Swing Town batting cages. ¥600. A gentle giant gives you a tip about your stance. (Byakko turf.)
8 · A purikura photo booth. Hiro's emoji is a beat late in every single frame.
9 · Fishing at Kurogane Wharf with Nakata Isamu. You catch something; he tells you something.
10 · The Shibuya crossing, after the festival. You are mobbed. (Chapter 3+.)
11 · Odaiba beach. Samitsu builds a sandcastle with arms that grow out of the sand. (Chapter 6.)
12 · Ueno. Super Panda will not set foot in the zoo and will not say why.
13 · A six a.m. workout with Chozen, who has opinions about protein. (+1 on your next STR or CON check.)
14 · The Shijime family's private box at the Tokyo Dome. Ichitaka explains baseball wrongly with total confidence.
15 · Laundry duty. You find a sock that belongs to nobody, because Hiro does not wear socks.
16 · Study group. Nomi says one sentence and everybody's maths makes sense.
17 · Movie night. Kinji and Ando talk through the entire film. Vote on what to watch; lose.
18 · Write a letter home. The reply arrives next window, and the DM reads one line of it aloud.
19 · A phone call with family. The player describes it; the DM gives one line from the other end.
20 · A haircut. Ando's barber is a genius. Kibi needs a gardener.
21 · A fighting game at the arcade. Toragi is unbeatable and says nothing. Masahata starts a ranking.
22 · A second-hand bookshop in Jimbōchō. Ren buys a book about swords; in its margins, somebody has written about "the black rite." (Kuroshiki rumour.)
23 · Akihabara electronics. Izuto spends everything and builds something by Sunday. (+1 on his next TECH check.)
24 · A shrine fortune. Roll a d6: 1 curse, 2–3 small luck, 4–5 good luck, 6 great blessing. Kinji demands to draw twenty.
25 · A summer festival: yukata, goldfish scooping, fireworks. Rakuka announces every firework. (Chapter 6.)
26 · Hot pot night in the dorm. Samitsu presides; Tazato fixes the burner and says it was efficient.
27 · The roof at night. Somebody tells a PC a secret.
28 · An open sparring session at Nakata's Gym. (Half a training slot.)
29 · Coffee at The Anchor, Kurogane Wharf. Okabe Fumi hears everything. (A rumour.)
30 · Visiting 1-B's common room. Awkward, then warm. Hatashi Hamba has notes on you.
31 · Volunteering at a shelter. A civilian thanks a PC like they are already a hero. (Inspiration.)
32 · Getting lost in Shinjuku station for forty-five minutes. After dark, roll an Odd Night.
33 · A street performer doing your festival moves, badly. Tip or heckle.
34 · The konbini manga stand. Kinji's favourite series is about a gambler, and he will tell you all of it.
35 · A food challenge with Forge. She wins. It is not close.
36 · Bose's five a.m. run. Nobody else comes. He says nothing. (Advantage on your next training slot.)
37 · A check-up with Help Woman. She tells you something true about your body that you did not want to hear.
38 · A lost dog in the dorm courtyard. Super Panda translates; it would like some of Samitsu's cooking.
39 · Writing thank-you notes with Setaka. He gives you a card of your own.
40 · Doing absolutely nothing on the sofa with Kibi. Flowers bloom in his hair. (Clears one rank of exhaustion.)

appendix.heading: Free Time — little things, the second forty (d40)
appendix.body:
A second table for tables that wore out the first one, weighted a little older: these assume the class are second-years with money, a reputation and four factions in the city. Roll a d40 or pick one.

1 · A konbini at four in the morning with a first-year who could not sleep. (Inspiration.)
2 · The Clean Read account page, open, with the cancel button on it. Nobody else is in the room.
3 · Ueno at closing time. Super Panda is standing outside the zoo. He does not go in. He does not explain.
4 · A second-hand record shop in Kōenji. Kinji finds something on vinyl and loses his mind. (¥3,800.)
5 · Teaching an assigned first-year to use the good vending machine. Twenty minutes. Perfect.
6 · A Yanaka cemetery walk at dusk. Very quiet, very old, and somebody on a bicycle goes past twice. (Ledger haunt.)
7 · The Anchor café. Okabe Fumi has a rumour she has been saving for whichever of them came in. (Roll on the rumour tables.)
8 · Swing Town on a Friday, in the stands, not fighting. Imai Tatsuhiko quotes you odds on yourself.
9 · A sweet shop in Yanaka run by a very cheerful old man who sells you rice crackers and asks your name twice.
10 · Hot pot with 1-B. Hatashi Hamba makes a toast. It goes on a long time and it is lovely.
11 · A tailor in Ginza, for somebody's costume repair. The building next door has no sign and is open eleven till dawn. (Legion haunt.)
12 · The U.A. roof at five in the morning with Bose, who is already there and does not acknowledge you. (Advantage on your next training slot.)
13 · A baseball game. Ichitaka's box. He explains the rules wrongly, again, with total confidence, again.
14 · Nakata's Gym on a Monday. Hazama Ritsu is there now, in gloves, being taught properly.
15 · Reading the 2019 committee minutes at the library. Dry, and one paragraph is genuinely moving. (+2 on one hearing check.)
16 · A level crossing in Yanaka at midnight. The barriers come down for a train with nobody on it. (Ledger haunt.)
17 · A karaoke booth. Room 9 is occupied. The man in it offers you tea.
18 · Sparring with Yanagi Daichi for free, because he asked. (Half a training slot and a better stance.)
19 · Watching your own festival footage, alone, with the commentary on, all the way through.
20 · Watching your own festival footage with the person it is about to say something unkind about.
21 · A letter from Ikari Tomonobu's widow. It is three lines and the DM reads one of them.
22 · Odaiba in the rain. The giant robot. Nobody else there. Rakuka announces it anyway.
23 · A first-year asks you the question you have been avoiding all season. Give the player the question.
24 · Tsukiji at five, with Samitsu, who has entered another competition under another name.
25 · A school cultural-festival planning meeting. Aikawa has made a spreadsheet. It is forty tabs.
26 · The Shinjuku west-exit alleys. Fukami Ryōta buys you a coffee and is extremely nice to you.
27 · A hospital back entrance after visiting hours. Someone in black is standing by the bins, writing. (Ledger haunt.)
28 · Shopping for shoes with Kinji. It takes four hours. He buys the first pair he tried on.
29 · A bathhouse in Kōenji. The old woman is at the bottom of the cold pool again. She waves. (Court haunt.)
30 · Sorting the dorm's lost property. There is a pair of sunglasses nobody will claim.
31 · A phone call from Natsuki Kaori (Blazewatch) about a colleague who got beaten by a man with a printout.
32 · Super Panda's extra problem set, the hard one, voluntarily. (INT DC 16, Inspiration.)
33 · A quiet hour with Otowa Suzume's door open and the corridor light behaving perfectly normally.
34 · The wall opposite the west gate, repainted again. Count what is on it now.
35 · An arcade fighting game where somebody has uploaded a mod of your own moveset. It is accurate.
36 · Setaka's thank-you note workshop. Six people, good paper, two hours, total silence.
37 · A ramen stall at one in the morning. A very large white heteromorph is three seats down, eating. She nods.
38 · Forge's lab at midnight. She is asleep under the bench. There is a half-built speaker on it.
39 · A newspaper interview about the hearing. Twenty minutes, and they print four words of it.
40 · Doing nothing on the sofa while a first-year does their homework badly in the corner. (Clears one rank of exhaustion.)

appendix.heading: Free Time — Tokyo, ward by ward
appendix.body:
Where the class can go on a free afternoon, and what is there. Anything not listed exists; Tokyo is very large.

· SHIBUYA — agency storefronts, the rankings on the big screens, Blazewatch's headquarters, and the crossing, where after the festival you will be recognised.
· AKIHABARA — electronics, parts, claw machines, maid cafés, and the collector with the Isobar tapes.
· IKEBUKURO WEST — Byakko. Swing Town, Lucky Seven, the noodle bar (neutral ground), the chop shop, and the Cage.
· SHINJUKU — the station that eats people, the west-exit alleys (Byakko), and rooftop bars with fairy lights where the Vermilion Corner holds court.
· KŌENJI — second-hand shops, live music, the Matsu-no-Yu bathhouse, and a convenience store with a very polite night clerk. (Astral Court haunt.)
· GINZA — department stores, galleries, and the top floor of a building with no sign, open eleven till dawn. (Legion haunt.)
· MINATO — embassies, money, and the Hiruma Clinic, whose blood bank is always full. (Legion haunt.)
· KUROGANE WHARF — The Anchor café (Okabe Fumi), Nakata's Gym, Ryuto Hana's neighbourhood, and the docks after midnight. (Legion haunt.) Its own section.
· HACHIŌJI HILLS — hiking trails, a shrine nobody can find twice, and a "Shinto seminary" called the Kurama Rite School. A few miles from U.A. (Kuroshiki.)
· ADACHI AND OTA — ordinary wards with a car park and a stairwell in them that were on the news. Nothing for the spine. For the Kuroshiki, everything.
· ODAIBA — the beach, the giant robot statue, the summer.
· UENO — the park, the museums, and the zoo Super Panda will not enter.
· TSUKIJI OUTER MARKET — five in the morning, Samitsu, and the best breakfast in the city.
· JIMBŌCHŌ — bookshops, and things written in margins.

ADDED FOR THE SECOND SEASON
· YANAKA — the cemetery district: temples, cats, narrow lanes, a level crossing where the barriers come down for trains with nobody on them, and a sweet shop run by a very cheerful old man. The best-preserved old Tokyo in the city and the Ledger's haunt. There is also a teahouse here that nobody in this module has claimed.
· KASUMIGASEKI — ministries, committee rooms, strip lighting, carafes of water, and Room 4 of the Standing Committee on Records and Licensing. Nothing here can be punched and everything here decides things.
· NAKANO — Clean Read's rented office above a shop, and a station stairwell that three people with a package will use because the plan needs a corridor.
· NERIMA — ordinary, residential, and a multi-storey car park that the class will recognise the shape of before anybody says anything.
· SHINJUKU EAST — karaoke, third floor, Room 9, after eight. Cash only. He will order you tea.
· U.A. ITSELF, AGAIN — the first-year corridor, the good vending machine, the Tuesday classroom with the archive playing in it, and the wall opposite the west gate, which now has three or four things on it and one empty space.

appendix.heading: Byakko — the Stripe Law and the Heat track
appendix.body:
THE RANKS — Stray (no stripe, not a member) · Claw (one stripe) · Fang (two) · Stripe (three — holds a street) · the Four Corners (four — each holds a quarter of the turf, and each is named after one of the other guardian beasts as a boast) · the White Tiger (a full pelt down the back — whoever nobody can beat). Stripes are white tattoos on the inside of the left forearm.

THE LAW — you are what you have beaten. Anybody may climb. Nobody runs on their own street. Nobody touches the noodle bar (its own section, with Lucky Seven upstairs). The Tiger is whoever is left. And, newest: nobody fights a kid who has not got a stripe yet.

RANK IS INHERITED — a PC who beats a ranked member in front of witnesses holds that rank under the Law, wanted or not. See "The Rank You Didn't Ask For."

THE HEAT TRACK — 0 to 10, on a strip of paper the players can see.
· +1 every time the class beat a ranked Byakko member in front of witnesses. Strays do not count.
· +2 for a fight in the Ring.
· +1 at the start of each window while any PC holds a rank.
· −1 for each window with no Byakko contact at all. −1 for losing fairly to a Corner. −2 for losing a held rank.
· CAPS — 3 in Chapter 2, 5 in Chapter 3, 7 in Chapters 4 and 5, none in Chapter 6.

WHO SHOWS UP
· HEAT 0–1 — a knot of Strays, or Hazama Ritsu ("Ricochet").
· HEAT 2–3 — Claws; the Echo Twins.
· HEAT 4–5 — a Fang (Brick or Hairpin) with two Claws. From Heat 4, Hairpin has something standing behind her: an Astral Court trace.
· HEAT 6–7 — a Stripe (Three-Stripe Kō or Madame Tsuru) with an escort.
· HEAT 8–9 — a Corner. See "The Four Corners."
· HEAT 10 — a note on the Heights Alliance doormat, in white paint. See "The White Tiger."

OR DO NOT ROLL AT ALL — if the table would rather the backstreets were a story with a beginning, "Byakko — the straight line through it" puts everything in this appendix into a fixed nine-step order and sets Heat at each step instead of tracking it. The sandbox is still the default.

WHEN TO ROLL — a PC who wanders into Byakko turf rolls a d6 at the start of the slot: on 1–3, Byakko find them, at the current Heat. Outside the turf, once Heat is 4 or more, a 1 on a d6 means Byakko come to them.

THE RING — Friday nights: the back cage at Swing Town for small fights, the Cage itself for big ones. Swing Town has its own section and its own preset map; the week it sits in is in "The backstreets week." One on one, a circle of witnesses, a purse for the winner, a stripe for anybody who beats a member. Quirk use is an offence and everybody in the room is committing one.

THE ONLY APPETITE CONNECTION — in the spring, a man with a scar bought a white van from Byakko's chop shop with cash and bled on the counter. The Stripe who sold it, if the class ever ask, describes him exactly. That is all; it confirms what the spine already tells them, and it should never be more.

CARRIED INTO THE SECOND SEASON
· CAPS — none in Chapters 6, 7 or 8. Heat carries over from wherever Chapter 6 left it, including 0, and Heat 0 does not mean Byakko have stopped existing; it means they are being polite. See the Heat events list.
· HEAT EVENTS — at the start of each window, if Heat has not moved, something fires on its own without the class going anywhere. See "Byakko — Heat events, and the turf economy."
· THE SEVENTH RULE, IF A PC WROTE ONE. Chapter 7 puts a man with four stripes in front of the class who has beaten six people with a phone propped on a crate, and the Law has no answer for him. If the class add a rule — Madame Tsuru's suggested wording is "Seven. You climb with what's yours" — write it on the wall inside the Cage's front door in their handwriting, and expect a third of the gang to disagree with it loudly for a month.
· WHO SHOWS UP, EXTENDED. The middle of the gang is now named: see "Byakko — the middle ranks, and who holds what." At Heat 2–3, use Nagira, Ōkawachi or Tobe. At 4–5, Murase, Yanagi or Imai. At 6–7, Kōno, Fukami or Sawaguchi. From Chapter 7, Amano Keita can appear at any Heat at all, because he does not wait to be invited.

appendix.heading: Byakko — the middle ranks, and who holds what
appendix.body:
Chapter 6 gave you Byakko's top end and its bottom rung. This is the middle: eleven named members between a Stray on a crash barrier and a Corner, each with a street, a job and one reason to talk to a U.A. student. Use them to make the backstreets a place with staff rather than a Heat roll with a stat block attached.

THE SHAPE OF THE GANG — about three hundred people across two wards. Roughly two hundred Strays and hangers-on, sixty-odd Claws, twenty Fangs, a dozen Stripes, four Corners and a Tiger. Every single one of them holds their rank because of a specific fight that specific people watched, and most of them can tell you the date.

CLAWS — one stripe. They collect, they enforce, and they are the gang's teenagers.
· NAGIRA SOU, "PYLON" — seventeen, holds the laundrette corner, makes himself heavy enough to be immovable and hates every part of his job except that. Collects protection money apologetically. Will tell a PC anything if they buy him a drink, and then be upset with himself.
· TOBE MIYU, "TALLY" — sixteen, cannot fight at all and has one stripe because she hit a Stray with a chair in front of nine witnesses and the Law is the Law. She keeps the gang's books in three exercise books and a phone, and she is the single most valuable person in the backstreets to anybody investigating anything.
· ŌKAWACHI JIN, "DROPKICK" — eighteen, challenges upward constantly, loses constantly, is completely undeterred, and is the reason rule six exists, because he once challenged a twelve-year-old and the Tiger heard about it.

FANGS — two stripes. A Fang runs a block and wants a witness for everything.
