· MURASE KOTOHA, "NETTLE" — nineteen, holds the noodle bar's street, which means she personally enforces rule four and has broken two arms doing it. Kind to the unstriped kids and frightening to everybody else. She is the Byakko most likely to help the class, and she will deny it afterwards.
· YANAGI DAICHI, "HALF-STEP" — twenty-one, the best technician in the gang and the one who teaches the Claws. Failed the U.A. entrance exam twice at fifteen, and does not bring it up, and everybody knows. Bose would have him tomorrow. If a PC spars with him he will be better than they expect and happier about losing than anybody should be.
· IMAI TATSUHIKO, "SANDBAG" — twenty, runs the betting book on Ring nights out of Swing Town's back office. Knows exactly what every fighter in two wards is worth, to the yen, and will sell that information. He is also the first person in Byakko to start buying Clean Read pages, in Chapter 7, and the first to understand what that means.

STRIPES — three stripes, a street each, about a dozen of them. These are the three worth naming.
· KŌNO SAE, "HINGE" — twenty-four, holds the chop shop, opens any lock by touch, and is the Stripe who sold a man with a scar a white van for cash in the spring and watched him bleed on the counter. She remembers him exactly and will describe him precisely, once, to anybody who asks properly. That is the entire Appetite connection and it should never be more.
· FUKAMI RYŌTA, "LADDER" — twenty-six, holds the Shinjuku west-exit alleys, and recruits. He is the one who finds the fourteen-year-olds on the crash barriers and gives them something to belong to, and he is genuinely good at it, and he believes he is doing them a favour. He is the most dangerous person in the gang and he has never hurt anybody in his life.
· SAWAGUCHI HIDEMI, "QUIET" — thirty-three, holds the hospital street, never speaks above a murmur, and was a nurse for eleven years before the Law suited her better. She patches up every fighter in the backstreets and asks nothing. Since the spring she has been treating Claws who turn up grey, slow and missing a night, and she has stopped asking about that too, and she is the Scarlet Legion's loudest trace if anybody ever talks to her.

FOUR STRIPES, WHICH IS NOT A RANK AND NOW IS — AMANO KEITA, "FOOTNOTE," nineteen, who has beaten six people with a phone propped on a crate. See Chapter 7, "A Challenge, Bought and Paid For." Byakko have no rule for him and several of them have asked for one.

HOW TO USE THEM — one per Heat band is plenty. The useful trick is to give each PC a Byakko they know by name, so that "Byakko find you" stops meaning a stat block and starts meaning Nagira apologising on a laundrette corner. Tobe Miyu's exercise books, Yanagi Daichi's sparring and Murase Kotoha's grudging help are three standing threads that will run as long as the table wants them.

appendix.heading: Byakko — Heat events, and the turf economy
appendix.body:
Chapter 6 gave you the Heat track and who shows up on it. This gives Heat something to do when nobody is looking for a fight, and it gives the backstreets an economy the class can actually disrupt — or fail to.

HEAT EVENTS — at the start of each free-time window, if Heat has not moved since the last one, one of these fires on its own, without the class going anywhere. For the days in between, when nothing is scheduled and the class are simply in the ward, roll on "Byakko in public." Read it as a sentence and let the players decide whether it is their problem.
· HEAT 0–1 — a fourteen-year-old is sitting on the crash barrier outside the U.A. west gate. He has no stripes. He is practising a PC's stance badly and he has been there since before school started.
· HEAT 2–3 — the white tiger on the wall opposite the gate has been repainted, and this time one of the names under it has been circled.
· HEAT 4–5 — a shopkeeper the class have met asks them, very carefully, not to come back for a month. She is not angry. She has been told something.
· HEAT 6–7 — Tobe Miyu's exercise books go missing, and she turns up at U.A.'s gate at seven in the morning, in uniform, asking for the class by name, because she thinks they took them. They did not. Imai Tatsuhiko did.
· HEAT 8–9 — a Corner sends a date and a place, by hand, to a named PC, and the message is read out by whichever first-year or classmate was unlucky enough to answer the door.
· HEAT 10 — white paint on the Heights Alliance doormat. The class know what that means by now.
· AND AT ANY HEAT, ONCE PER SEASON — somebody from Byakko turns up injured at the U.A. gate, and the person who brought them is Sawaguchi Hidemi, who has run out of options and will not come inside.

THE TURF ECONOMY — what the gang actually lives on, roughly per month. Give the players these numbers if they ask; the whole point is that they are small.
· PROTECTION — about ninety shops across two wards, ¥5,000 to ¥20,000 each. Call it ¥700,000. This is the bulk of it and it is also the part that keeps those streets quiet, which the shopkeepers will say out loud if asked.
· THE RING — Friday nights at Swing Town and the Cage. Gate, bets and the house's cut: ¥400,000 on a good month. Imai's book is most of it.
· LUCKY SEVEN — Madame Tsuru's rake off the dice. ¥300,000, and thirty-one years of it, and she has never once been robbed.
· THE CHOP SHOP — vans, plates, no questions. ¥250,000, and extremely occasional, and the reason Appetite ever touched the backstreets at all.
· OUTGOINGS — nothing formal. Fighters are paid in rank. Sawaguchi's supplies come out of the Ring's gate. Nobody in Byakko is rich, including the Tiger, who eats at the same ramen stall every night because it is ¥900.

WHAT THE CLASS CAN ACTUALLY DISRUPT, AND WHAT IT COSTS
· THE RING — the easiest to kill and the most popular. One phone call to Okuma closes Swing Town's back cage for a season. Forty fighters lose their only income, Imai's book moves to a worse venue in Itabashi run by people with no rule four, and two of the Claws end up there.
· THE PROTECTION — the hardest, and the one the class will want most. The honest answer, and Nakata Isamu will give it to them: take Byakko off those ninety shops and something else arrives inside a month, and the something else does not have a rule about not touching the noodle bar. The real fix is the police, slowly, with witnesses, and it takes years, and Okuma will say so.
· THE CHOP SHOP — genuinely worth closing, genuinely criminal, and Kōno Sae will not resist arrest. Do it and the backstreets think better of the class, not worse. The room has its own section.
· LUCKY SEVEN — nobody will help the class with this. Nobody. Madame Tsuru has kept that street quiet for thirty-one years and the street knows it.
· OR THEY CAN HOLD THE TITLE. If a PC came off the roof of the Cage with the pelt, all of the above is theirs, including the ninety shops, including the decision about the Ring, including Fukami Ryōta's recruiting. That is the most interesting thing a second season can hand a group of sixteen-year-olds, and the campaign has no opinion about what they should do with it.

THE ONE RULE — Byakko are the city's noise, not its plot, and that does not change because they now have a balance sheet. Nothing in this appendix connects to Appetite except one van, and nothing in it should ever connect to Clean Read except Imai Tatsuhiko's subscription, which is quite enough.

appendix.heading: The Cage — floor by floor
appendix.body:
Byakko's heart, as a ladder you can run in one night if your table wants to. A dead six-storey batting centre in the Ikebukuro backstreets, every floor a ring of green netting under floodlights, lit up like a stadium at one in the morning.

HOW THE LADDER WORKS — one fight per floor, a stairwell between each one worth a short rest's worth of breathing, and Heat +1 per floor cleared. The crowd follows upward. Nobody has climbed it in one night in six years. Who is home depends on Heat; see "the Stripe Law and the Heat track."

THE FRONT DOOR — Genda Tetsuo, the Black Corner, in a folding chair beside a takoyaki cart with a paperback. He decides who comes in. He can be beaten or talked past and is open to both, and he would genuinely rather discuss load-bearing with Kazama, Setaka or Hiro.

GROUND FLOOR — THE CLAWS' RING. Netting, floodlights, about two hundred people, and a queue. Three fights available and all of them are kids: Hazama Ritsu will volunteer instantly, Ōkawachi Jin will challenge whoever looks most famous, and Nagira Sou will apologise before and after. On the wall by the door, the Stripe Law in white paint, six rules, the sixth in a different hand.

FIRST FLOOR — SWING TOWN'S OVERFLOW. Where the Ring's small fights go when the back cage is full. Imai Tatsuhiko's betting book is set up on a trestle table and he will happily quote odds on the PCs to their faces. A Fang fight, witnessed, with money on it.

SECOND FLOOR — THE TEACHING FLOOR. Yanagi Daichi's. Twenty Claws drilling footwork at one in the morning under a man who failed the U.A. entrance exam twice. This is the only floor of the Cage where nobody wants to fight the class, and the best scene in the building: he will offer to spar instead, properly, and he will be better than they expect.

THIRD FLOOR — THE STRIPES. Three-Stripe Kō with his notebook, or Kōno Sae if the chop shop is quiet, or — in Chapter 7 — Amano Keita with a phone propped on a crate. This is as far as the class can get at Heat 7 or below; above that the floor is a proper brawl, because a Stripe's escort stops watching the moment two PCs engage together.

FOURTH FLOOR — EMPTY, AND IT IS NOT A TRICK. Nobody holds the fourth floor. It is full of broken batting machines and a sofa, and three or four off-duty Fangs are usually on it eating convenience-store food, and they will not fight anybody climbing. One of them will tell the class what is on the roof. Give the table this floor as a breather and let it be funny and ordinary.

FIFTH FLOOR — THE CORNERS, WHEN THEY ARE HOME. At Heat 8 or more, one of Kuze, Hōjō or Kōga is up here, and the fight is the set piece from "The Four Corners" relocated. Kōga Rin is here most nights, because she is the Tiger's second and the Cage is her quarter.

THE ROOF — the White Tiger's. Floodlights, green netting on three sides, a view of the whole ward, an upturned crate, and a takeaway ramen bowl. The door is locked at Heat 9 or below. At Heat 10 it is open. If the class reach it early, she is not there, and there is a bowl of ramen cooling and a note, and the note is in the same white paint as the doormat.

IF THE CLASS BRING THE POLICE — the Cage is empty before anybody arrives and open again on Friday. Byakko have survived worse than a school calling the police, and Okuma knows it, and will tell them so without being asked twice.

appendix.heading: Byakko — the straight line through it
appendix.body:
The rest of this appendix is a sandbox: a Heat track, eleven named members and a six-storey building, all of it built so Byakko turn up when the dice say so and never hold the plot. That is still the default and still the better way to run them.

This is the same material in a fixed order, for a table that wants the backstreets to be a story with a beginning rather than a weather system. Nine steps, from a fourteen-year-old on a crash barrier to a roof in Ikebukuro, each one an hour or a session depending on how much the players talk, each one naming the preset to load and where Heat goes when it is done. Nothing here is new. Every fight, every name and every room is somewhere else in this appendix; the ladder only decides what order the class meet them in.

HEAT ON THE LADDER — set it, do not roll it. At the top of each step move Heat to the number the step gives, and ignore the −1 for a quiet window, because the ladder is the quiet window. Everything else on the track still applies, including the +1 at the start of every window while a PC holds a rank, which is the ladder's own accelerator and the reason step five changes the pace of everything after it.

IF YOU HAVE FOUR SESSIONS AND NOT NINE — steps one, four, seven and nine. The kid, the Ring, the Cage and the roof. That is the whole shape, and the four of them still answer each other.

• ONE — THE KID ON THE CRASH BARRIER. Heat 1, and no preset, because nobody fights. A fourteen-year-old is sitting outside the U.A. west gate with no stripes on his arm, practising a PC's stance badly, and he has been there since before school started. He will not say who told him about them. Fukami Ryōta did, because Fukami finds the ones on the crash barriers and gives them something to belong to, and he is genuinely good at it, and he believes he is doing the boy a favour. Let the class do whatever they like with him. The arc opens on this question and the roof closes on it.
• TWO — THE LAUNDRETTE CORNER. Heat 2. Load "Byakko shakedown" onto Hosu District. Nagira Sou is collecting protection money and apologising for it, which is how he collects it every week. The fight is available and so is a drink: Pylon will tell a PC anything over one and then be upset with himself. If it does come to a fight the two Claws commit, the Fang watches, and it is the Fang who reports it — so this is the first Heat the class earn rather than are handed.
• THREE — RULE FOUR. Heat 3. Load "Byakko market sweep" onto Night Market Street. Somebody is leaning on stalls he has no business leaning on: a Claw who has decided the noodle bar's street is negotiable. Murase Kotoha arrives to enforce rule four personally, as she has twice before, and she would much rather the class were not there to watch her do it. Play it straight and this is the step where the class learn that the Law protects people, which is what makes every step after it harder.
• FOUR — FRIDAY AT SWING TOWN. Heat 4. Load "Byakko cage night" onto Swing Town, which is a preset map of the building; "Swing Town — the hub, room by room" is the rest of it. The back cage, a circle of witnesses, a purse for the winner, and Imai Tatsuhiko quoting odds on the PCs to their faces from a trestle table. One on one, under the Law, with quirk use an offence that every single person in the room is committing. A PC who beats a ranked member here takes that rank whether they meant to or not, which is step five — and the reason this step is not optional if you want the arc to have a middle.
• FIVE — THE RANK YOU DIDN'T ASK FOR. Heat 5. No preset; the challengers come one at a time out of the encounter manager by name. The chapter section of that name, fired on purpose instead of by accident: the box of tribute on the doorstep, free food in ninety shops, a dozen teenagers running errands, the first challenger at a time and place of their choosing, and Sugitsu's office asking the only question that matters — what are you going to do with it. At Fang the challenger is Hazama Ritsu, who has climbed to two stripes and wants his first teacher. At Stripe it is Saeki Momo or Brick. At Corner it is a Stripe from another street, and then Kōga Rin, who simply wants to know.
• SIX — THE CHOP SHOP. Heat 6. Load "Byakko at the chop shop" onto The Chop Shop, which has its own section. Kōno Sae opens any lock by touch and sold a man with a scar a white van for cash in the spring, and watched him bleed on the counter. Ask her properly and she describes him exactly, once, and that is the entire Appetite connection and it should never be more. The chop shop is also the one thing in the turf economy genuinely worth closing, and Hinge will not resist arrest — so this is the step where the class decide whether they are heroes in the backstreets or simply the newest gang in them.
• SEVEN — THE CAGE, FLOOR BY FLOOR. Heat 7, then +1 for every floor cleared. Load "Byakko in the Claws' ring", then "Byakko on the Stripes' floor". Genda Tetsuo is in a folding chair by the takoyaki cart with a paperback, deciding who comes in, and he can be beaten or talked past and is open to both. Then the ladder as the Cage section lays it out: the Claws' ring and its queue of kids, Imai's book on the first floor, Yanagi Daichi's teaching floor — the only floor where nobody wants to fight the class, and the best scene in the building — the Stripes on the third, and the fourth floor, which is empty, and is not a trick. Clearing floors is what carries Heat from 7 to the Corners without another step being needed. If the table is in Chapter 7, Amano Keita is on the third floor with a phone propped on a crate, and the Law has no answer for him yet.
• EIGHT — TWO CORNERS. Heat 8 to 9. Load "Byakko — two Corners" onto Abandoned Factory, or run them on the Cage's fifth floor where they live. Play two of the four, never all of them in a session. Each asks for a classmate by festival name and the class do not have to give them who they ask for; a PC who turns up instead is accepted under the Law with visible disappointment. One as a duel and one as a brawl is the right pair, because the Law permits both and the players should be the ones who choose which fight they are in.
• NINE — THE ROOF. Heat 10. Load "Byakko — the White Tiger" onto Rooftop Chase. White paint on the Heights Alliance doormat, and the roof at one in the morning: floodlights, netting on three sides, an upturned crate and a cooling bowl of ramen. Hakuro Mitsuki has been undefeated for six years, wrote rule six herself, and is not a villain. The choice is the encounter and there are three ways through it — alone under the Law, as a pair ignoring it, or as a pair claiming it — and the third is this campaign's whole thesis paid out in the side plot. Do not cut the choice to get to the fight.

AFTER THE ROOF — whoever came down off it with the pelt holds ninety shops, the Ring, Lucky Seven's rake, Fukami Ryōta's recruiting, and the boy from step one, who is fifteen by now and has a stripe. The turf economy section is the bill for all of it, and the honest answer about the protection racket is in there too, and Nakata Isamu will give it to them out loud. The campaign has no opinion about what a group of sixteen-year-olds should do with a gang, and neither should the table's.

WHAT THE LADDER DOES NOT CHANGE — Byakko are still the city's noise and not its plot. In order they are a story about a gang that ranks children by who they have beaten; made into the plot they are the spine's oxygen spent on the side plot. If the class ignore the ladder for a month it waits exactly where it was. Nobody in Byakko is in a hurry.

appendix.heading: Swing Town — the hub, room by room
appendix.body:
Byakko's front door, and the one place in the backstreets where a U.A. student can stand around for an hour and nothing in particular happens. A working batting centre — nine cages under a net roof, a prize counter nobody has claimed anything from in years, a vending wall, and a back cage and a back office behind a door marked STAFF that everybody uses. Open until two. Dōmeki Daigo, "Brick," runs it, and the whole reason this place works is that he is the Fang most PCs meet first and he is gentle with the kids who come in to bat.

WHY IT IS THE HUB — neutral enough that students can be in it, Byakko enough that something is always going on at the back. Nobody fights in the front of house. That is not one of the six rules; it is Brick, who will take a fight outside with one hand on somebody's shoulder and no raised voice, and has never had to do it twice to the same person.

THE OPENER, IF A PC WALKS IN COLD — Brick, at the counter, with a bucket in one hand: "Six hundred for twenty. You want the slow machine, or the one that's broken?" The broken one throws about one in five at something absurd and is the most popular machine in the building.

THE FRONT — nine cages, ¥600 for twenty balls, a speed dial on each one that Brick has taped at the top end of three of them. On the wall by the counter, in chalk: the fastest machine anybody has cleared, with names, going back four years. There are two U.A. names on it already and neither of them is a hero course student. A PC who clears the top machine goes on the wall in Brick's handwriting, and it stays there, and that is worth more to the backstreets than anything they do in a cage out the back.

THE VENDING WALL — hot cans, cold cans, one machine that takes money and delivers nothing and has a biro note taped to it saying so. This is where everybody actually talks. If the class want to meet somebody in the backstreets without it meaning anything, it happens standing at this wall.

THE STANDS — four rows of plastic seats facing the back cage, which is where you watch from on a Friday if you are not fighting. Imai Tatsuhiko will find you in them.

THE BACK CAGE — the Ring's small fights, Friday nights, one on one, a circle of witnesses and a purse. On any other night of the week it is a cage with a ball machine in it that nobody has plugged in since spring.

THE BACK OFFICE — Imai Tatsuhiko's betting book, a kettle, a safe with ¥400,000-odd of other people's money in it on a Friday, and a wall of numbers in pencil. Imai will quote the PCs odds on themselves to their faces and enjoy it. He will also, for money, tell them what any fighter in two wards is worth, which is the single most useful thing anybody in Byakko sells.

WHAT A PC CAN ACTUALLY DO HERE, with nothing else going on
· Bat. ¥600. Get on the chalk wall, or get a tip about their stance from a man who has beaten sixty people.
· Take the attendant shift — ¥6,000 for the slot, from the odd jobs list, and the backstreets stop treating you as a visitor.
· Watch a Friday fight from the stands without being in one.
· Ask Imai what they are worth, and find out he has already worked it out.
· Catch Yanagi Daichi on a Tuesday and get taught something for free.
· Buy a fourteen-year-old a drink at the vending wall. Fukami Ryōta does this too, which is the entire argument about this gang in one gesture.
· Leave a message for anybody in Byakko. It arrives. It always arrives.

AS HEAT RISES — the building is the barometer, and the players should be able to read it without being told.
· HEAT 0–3 — nothing changes. Brick says hello by name once he has learned it.
· HEAT 4–5 — the vending wall conversation stops when they walk in and starts again a beat later.
· HEAT 6–7 — Brick asks them, politely, standing very close, not to come on a Friday. He is not threatening them. He is telling them that he cannot promise the room.
· HEAT 8–9 — the back cage is full on a Tuesday, and the people in it have three stripes.
· HEAT 10 — the front shutters are down at seven in the evening with every light in the building on.

IF THE CLASS CLOSE IT — one phone call to Okuma shuts the back cage for a season, and the turf economy appendix has the bill: forty fighters lose their only income, Imai's book moves to a worse room in Itabashi run by people with no rule four, and two Claws go with it. Add Brick to that list. He has no second job, he is twenty-four, and he will be at the front counter of a closed batting centre for a fortnight before he stops opening up.

appendix.heading: The noodle bar, and Lucky Seven above it
appendix.body:
One building, two floors, two completely different sets of rules, and thirty-one years of both. Downstairs is a six-stool counter noodle shop and the only neutral ground in the backstreets. Upstairs, past the kitchen and up a flight nobody guards, is Lucky Seven — Madame Tsuru's dice den, where every Byakko member in the room fights for her without being asked. The stairs are nine steps long and they are the most interesting nine steps in the ward.

Swing Town is the gang's front door and the Heat barometer. This place is the opposite of a barometer: nothing about the ground floor changes at Heat 10 that was not already true at Heat 0, and that is the whole point of it. There is a preset map, “The Noodle Bar & Lucky Seven” — the two floors side by side, the stairwell between them, the upper room marked one floor up.

DOWNSTAIRS — THE ONE PLACE NOBODY TOUCHES
Rule four of the Stripe Law is "nobody touches the noodle bar," it is the only rule about a building rather than about fighting, and no member can tell you who added it. Murase Kotoha holds this street, which means she enforces that rule personally and has broken two arms doing it.
· THE OPENER — whoever is behind the counter, without looking up: "Sit anywhere. Not that one, it's wobbly." Do not give them a name unless a player asks for it; this campaign has not needed one in six chapters and the moment they have a name they have a plot.
· ¥750 a bowl, ¥950 with the egg, and the noodles are genuinely excellent, which is the reason any of the rest of it holds.
· WHO IS IN — Claws, queueing like everybody else and paying. A Fang eating alone at the end of the counter and not wanting company. Two fourteen-year-olds who have been talked out of the Cage and into a bowl, which is what the good version of holding a rank looks like.
· ASKING AT THE COUNTER EARNS A RUMOUR. This is already how the Odd Nights ladder works: a PC who eats here and asks about the strange thing they saw gets one rung of one faction's ladder, flatly, from somebody who is not making a thing of it.
· WHAT HAPPENS IF SOMEBODY BREAKS RULE FOUR IN FRONT OF THE CLASS — Murase arrives. She does not negotiate, she is not grateful for help, and she will deny the entire incident afterwards. If the class handle it themselves before she gets there, she is annoyed about that for a month and then stops being annoyed.
· AND IF THE CLASS BREAK IT — the fastest way to lose the backstreets. Not a fight: a silence, and then nobody in two wards tells them anything for a season.

THE STAIRS — nine steps up from behind the kitchen, past the crates, with no door at the bottom and no door at the top. Anybody may go up. Nothing stops a sixteen-year-old going up. The Law does not come with them: rule four is a rule about this building's ground floor, and upstairs is the house.

UPSTAIRS — LUCKY SEVEN
Tsuruoka Fusae, "Madame Tsuru," sixty-eight, three stripes for thirty-one years because nobody has beaten her yet. About thirty people, a low table, dice, and one woman's voice keeping order without ever being raised. ¥300,000 a month in rake, thirty-one years of it, and she has never once been robbed — and the reason is in her stat block: inside this room every Byakko member present fights for her, without being asked, including the ones who are losing.
· THE GAME, SO A PLAYER CAN ACTUALLY SIT DOWN — two d6 against the house's two d6. Higher total takes the pot. A tie goes to the house, which is the rake, and Tsuru lifts ¥100 off every pot on top of that. Minimum stake ¥1,000, maximum ¥20,000, and a natural 7 beats everything except another 7. That is the entire game; it takes thirty seconds to run and the players will play it for an hour.
· WHY THE HOUSE WINS — ties and the hundred, and nothing else. There is no cheating anywhere in this room. Nobody has ever needed to.
· TSURU IS NOT A FIGHT. She is the best-informed person in the backstreets about where the gang's money goes, she will talk to anybody who is polite, and she adores Kinji's shoes and will say so within a minute of meeting him. A PC who wants to know what Byakko actually is should be sent up these stairs, not into a cage.
· AS HEAT RISES — the room gets quieter, not louder. At Heat 8 or more, the dice are still going and nobody is talking, and Tsuru says the class's names when they come in, which is the only warning anybody in this building will ever give them.
· IF THE CLASS TRY TO CLOSE IT — nobody will help them. Not Okuma, not Nakata, not the street, not the shopkeepers who pay protection and resent it. Thirty-one years of a quiet street is the argument, everybody on that street will make it, and the campaign does not have a counter-argument to hand them.

THE TWO FLOORS ARE THE SAME POINT TWICE — downstairs is what the Law protects, and upstairs is what the Law is for. Byakko put the only sanctuary in the backstreets directly underneath their most profitable room and have run both for three decades without anybody being hurt in either. The class are allowed to find that admirable and it is still a protection racket with a dice den over it, and nobody in this campaign is going to resolve that for them.

appendix.heading: The chop shop — vans, plates, no questions
appendix.body:
The fourth room in the backstreets, and the only one in the turf economy that is straightforwardly a crime. A two-bay lock-up in Ikebukuro West with a roller shutter, a pit between the bays, a bench down the back wall and a counter at the front. Vans, plates, no questions. ¥250,000 a month and extremely occasional, which means weeks of nothing and then a fortnight where the shutter is down in the daytime. There is a preset map, “The Chop Shop.”

KŌNO SAE, “HINGE,” holds it. Twenty-four, three stripes, and she opens any lock, door, restraint, panel or joint by touching it — which is why she runs this room and not a street.

THE OPENER — her legs sticking out from under a van, not coming out: “Door's open. It's always open. That's the joke.”

THE COUNTER AT THE FRONT is where a man with a scar bought a white van for cash in the spring and bled on it, and she watched him do it. Ask her properly — once, politely, without making it an interrogation — and she describes him exactly. That is the entire Appetite connection, it confirms only what the spine has already told the class, and it should never grow into anything. If a player pushes for more she has no more; she sold a van to a man who paid cash and she remembers the blood because she had to clean it.

THURSDAY is the chop shop's night, which is why Swing Town's back cage is free on a Thursday and the unranked kids get it for an hour.

THE TWO FACTS THAT ARE THE WHOLE CHARACTER
· No cell holds her and no handcuffs stay on. Hinge works on both, and her stat block says so in as many words.
· She will not resist arrest.
Those two together are the only interesting thing anybody in this gang does with a quirk. She can leave any room in Tokyo whenever she likes, and when the police finally come for the shop she will put her hands out and go, and the backstreets will know she did.

CLOSING IT — the one disruption in the turf economy with no sting in it. Genuinely criminal, genuinely worth doing, and the appendix already says what it costs: ¥250,000 off the gang's month and nothing else. The shopkeepers do not depend on it, no fighters lose their income, and the backstreets think better of the class rather than worse. If the table has been looking for a way to be heroes in the backstreets without making anything worse, this is the one, and it is the only one.
· WHAT HAPPENS AFTERWARDS — she is out inside a year and back under a van in a different lock-up, and she will say hello. Byakko do not punish her for it and nobody in the gang thinks the class were wrong.

IF THE CLASS WANT HER FOR SOMETHING ELSE — and they will, the first time a door in this campaign does not open. Her quirk is a key to every locked thing in it: a cold-store hatch, a cell, a panel, a set of restraints on somebody who should not be in them. She will help for a reason she finds sufficient and she will not take money for it. The price is that the class asked a criminal, in a lock-up full of stolen plates, and she is the one who decided it was reasonable.

AS HEAT RISES — nothing happens here, which is worth noticing. Kōno Sae is a technician, not a fighter, and the Heat track is about fighters. The shop is the same at Heat 8 as at Heat 2, except that at Heat 8 or more there is a second van in the far bay with the plates already off, and nobody in the room says whose it is or where it is going.

appendix.heading: Byakko in public (d20)
appendix.body:
What the gang is doing in daylight, in public, where anybody can see it. Roll a d20 or pick one when the class are in Ikebukuro West or Shinjuku and nothing is scheduled. None of these is a fight. Most of them are not even a scene — they are the backdrop being visible, which is the difference between a gang that exists and a gang that turns up.

1 · Nagira Sou on the laundrette corner, collecting, apologising while he does it, and apologising again on the way out.
2 · Two Claws queueing at the noodle bar like everybody else. They pay. One of them holds the door for whoever is behind them.
3 · The white tiger on the wall opposite the U.A. west gate, being repainted by three people who are not hiding.
4 · Tobe Miyu in a café window with three exercise books open and a phone on a calculator app, doing the gang's accounts in public because nobody has ever thought to stop her.
5 · A flyer taped to a lamp post: Friday's card at Swing Town, four names, in biro, with the odds already written next to two of them.
6 · Fukami Ryōta buying a drink for a kid on a crash barrier. He talks to him for ten minutes. He is kind, and he is good at it, and the kid is fourteen.
7 · Ōkawachi Jin challenging somebody outside a konbini, losing immediately, and buying them a drink about it.
8 · A Fang walking a shopkeeper's daughter home from the station, four paces behind, like a man doing his job.
9 · Sawaguchi Hidemi coming out of the hospital street with a carrier bag of dressings, moving like somebody who has been up all night.
10 · Three kids on the crash barrier outside the gate, running a PC's stance, badly, in sequence, like a drill.
11 · A chalked tally on a shutter — somebody's fights, somebody's wins — and a hand rubbing out one of the marks.
12 · A doorway open onto a back room where somebody is being inked, sitting very still, with four people watching the needle.
13 · Kōno Sae opening a shop's jammed shutter with one hand flat against it, for nothing, because she was walking past.
14 · Lucky Seven audible from the street: dice, and about thirty people, and one woman's voice keeping order without raising itself.
15 · A Claw steering a drunk away from the noodle bar's frontage with enormous patience and no violence whatsoever.
16 · Murase Kotoha standing in the middle of the street doing nothing at all, which is how that street stays quiet.
17 · Imai Tatsuhiko on the phone outside Swing Town, reading numbers off a notebook, saying the same four words over and over.
18 · Yanagi Daichi teaching footwork to three Claws in a car park at four in the afternoon, counting out loud.
19 · An envelope handed over on a shop counter in full view, taken without being counted, and the shopkeeper saying something that makes the collector laugh.
20 · Somebody in Byakko recognising a PC across the street and nodding at them. Just that. At Heat 6 or more, two of them nod, and neither of them moves.

HOW TO USE THESE — one, in passing, while the class are on their way to something else, and do not stop for it unless a player does. The whole effect is that Byakko are a going concern with staff and a Tuesday, and that effect is ruined by making each sighting a scene.

AND AT HEAT 8 OR MORE — roll twice and let both be true. The gang is not hiding at that point; they are waiting, and being seen is the point.

appendix.heading: The backstreets week — what is on, and when
appendix.body:
The backstreets run to a timetable, and almost nothing in this campaign depends on it — which is exactly why it is useful. A player who asks "what's happening tonight?" should get an answer, the same answer, every time they ask on the same day, until they have learned the week and can plan around it. That is what makes a place real rather than responsive.

MONDAY — collections, all day, two wards. Every named Claw in the middle-ranks appendix is out on their own corner. The backstreets are busier and more polite on a Monday than on any other day. Swing Town is nearly empty; Brick restrings the nets.

TUESDAY — Yanagi Daichi's night. Twenty Claws drilling footwork, in the Cage's second floor if the weather is bad and a car park if it is not, and Swing Town's back cage if Yanagi has decided somebody needs a net around them. Anybody may watch. Anybody may join. This is the single best night for a PC to be in the backstreets and the class will work that out for themselves.

WEDNESDAY — books. Tobe Miyu reconciles the week in a café window; Imai Tatsuhiko settles Friday's outstanding bets out of the back office, in cash, with a receipt nobody keeps. The quietest night, and the best one for asking somebody something.

THURSDAY — the chop shop's night, which means Kōno Sae is working and Swing Town's back cage is free, so the unranked kids get it for an hour. Fourteen-year-olds in a cage with nobody betting on them. It is harmless and it is also exactly how Fukami's recruiting works.

FRIDAY — the Ring. Small fights in Swing Town's back cage from nine, big ones at the Cage when there is a card worth the walk. Forty fighters, two hundred people, Imai's book on a trestle table, and the only night of the week when the whole gang is in one of two rooms. Heat +2 for a fight in it.

SATURDAY — families, daylight, and the market. The cages are full of children; the noodle bar has a queue down the street; the Claws are off, and in the market, spending. This is the day the class see the gang as the neighbourhood sees them, and it is the hardest day to be certain about anything.

SUNDAY — Brick cleans. The front is open, the back is shut, the machines are off, and he will talk to absolutely anybody for as long as they want, about anything, while he mops. Madame Tsuru's dice game runs all afternoon and nobody who has ever robbed it exists; the game itself is in "The noodle bar, and Lucky Seven above it," and a player can sit down at it.

WHAT THE TIMETABLE IS FOR
· A player who says "we'll go Tuesday" has learned something, and the DM should reward that by having Tuesday be Tuesday.
· It gives Heat somewhere to show. The same Tuesday at Heat 2 and at Heat 8 is two completely different evenings in the same room with the same people in it.
· It makes the gang's size legible. Three hundred people with jobs have a week; a stat block that appears when the dice say so does not.
· And it gives the class a thing to disrupt that is not a person. Closing the back cage does not remove Friday. It moves it to Itabashi, where there is no rule four, and the week carries on without them.

appendix.heading: Stat blocks — Byakko
appendix.body:
Every rank and every named member, from the crash barrier to the roof. All of them are in the encounter manager under "Byakko."

BYAKKO STRAY (UNRANKED) — CR 1/4
Not a member yet. Strays hang around the gang hoping to be noticed, in threes, in tracksuits, at volume.
AC 12 · HP 13 · Speed 30 ft · Initiative +1
STR 12 · DEX 12 · CON 11 · INT 9 · WIS 9 · CHA 10
· KNUCKLES (+3) — 1d6+1 bludgeoning.
· UNRANKED — beating Strays raises no Heat. Byakko do not count them, and neither should you.
· They run the moment the first one goes down.
· HOW TO RUN — Mob whoever looks smallest, shout a lot, scatter. Use them to show the players the street before the street is dangerous.

BYAKKO CLAW (ONE STRIPE) — CR 1
The bottom rung: one white stripe tattooed on the inside of the left forearm. Claws collect protection money and enforce it.
AC 13 · HP 25 · Speed 30 ft · Initiative +1 · Save DC 12
STR 13 · DEX 13 · CON 12 · INT 10 · WIS 10 · CHA 11
· TEKKO-KAGI (HAND CLAWS) (+4) — 2d6 slashing.
· ONE TRICK — every Claw has exactly one quirk trick. Pick one: a 15-ft shove (STR DC 12), a blinding flash (CON DC 12, blinded 1 round), or a 20-ft standing leap.
· HOW TO RUN — Fights to win, not to kill. Surrenders cleanly to anyone who beats them cleanly — and then goes and tells a Fang.

BYAKKO FANG (TWO STRIPES) — CR 3
Two stripes. A Fang runs a block and wants a witness for everything.
AC 14 · HP 45 · Speed 30 ft · Initiative +2 · Save DC 13
STR 15 · DEX 14 · CON 14 · INT 10 · WIS 11 · CHA 12
· MULTIATTACK — TWO CLAW STRIKES (+5) — 2d8+2 slashing each.
· SIGNATURE (recharge 5–6) — one real quirk move: 3d8 in a 15-ft cone (DEX DC 13 half), or a grab that restrains (STR DC 13 to escape).
· RING-WISE — advantage on saves against being knocked prone.
· HOW TO RUN — Will not fight in an empty alley. Walks you to a street with people in it, because a win nobody saw does not count.

BYAKKO STRIPE (THREE STRIPES) — CR 5
Three stripes. Holds a street. There are about a dozen of them, and each one got there by beating the last one.
AC 15 · HP 70 · Speed 30 ft · Initiative +2 · Save DC 14
STR 16 · DEX 15 · CON 15 · INT 11 · WIS 12 · CHA 14
· MULTIATTACK — TWO STRIKES (+6) — 3d8 each.
· TWO SIGNATURES — give a Stripe two real quirk moves on the Fang pattern, one of them a recharge.
· THE LAW — a Stripe fights one challenger at a time if they can. If two PCs engage together, every Byakko member watching stops being an audience and joins in.
· HOW TO RUN — Arrives with an escort of two Claws who do not fight unless the Law is broken. Offers the challenge by name.

HAZAMA RITSU, "RICOCHET" (CLAW) — CR 1
Sixteen, skinny, one stripe and desperate for a second. Picks the smallest-looking PC every single time and narrates the whole fight, badly, at volume.
AC 14 · HP 24 · Speed 35 ft · Initiative +3 · Save DC 12
STR 10 · DEX 16 · CON 12 · INT 10 · WIS 9 · CHA 13
· ELBOW (+5) — 2d6 bludgeoning.
· RUBBER JOINTS (reaction, once per round) — when hit in melee, he takes half damage and bounces 15 ft away without provoking.
· HOW TO RUN — Hit and bounce. Gives up the moment he is cornered — and then follows the PCs home to ask how they did that. A good first Byakko for any table.

KEI & REI OKITA, "THE ECHO TWINS" (CLAWS) — CR 1
One preset per twin — run two. Byakko's only pair, and the rest of the gang thinks they are a joke.
AC 13 · HP 22 · Speed 30 ft · Initiative +2 · Save DC 12
STR 12 · DEX 14 · CON 12 · INT 11 · WIS 10 · CHA 10
· TWIN BATONS (+4) — 1d8+2 bludgeoning.
· ECHO STEP — whatever one twin did on their last turn, the other may do on this one with +2 to hit, and the target has disadvantage on any save against it.
· PAIR — they have never met anybody else who fights as two.
· HOW TO RUN — The 2v2 bracket's mirror. Fought as a pair it is a fair, funny, excellent fight. Fought alone, they take you apart. Either way they will want to know who taught you.

DŌMEKI DAIGO, "BRICK" (FANG) — CR 3
Runs Swing Town, a batting centre in the Ikebukuro backstreets, and the Ring nights in its back cage. Twenty-four, gentle with the kids who come in to bat, and the Fang most PCs meet first.
AC 15 · HP 60 · Speed 30 ft · Initiative +0 · Save DC 13
STR 18 · DEX 10 · CON 16 · INT 9 · WIS 11 · CHA 10
· MULTIATTACK — TWO HAYMAKERS (+6) — 2d8+4 bludgeoning each.
· BRICKHIDE — resistance to bludgeoning damage.
· BRICK WALL (bonus action, recharge 5–6) — until his next turn he cannot be moved, knocked prone or grappled, and anything that hits him in melee takes 1d6.
· HOW TO RUN — Stands still and lets you hit him, because hitting him hurts. Respects anybody who works out that he hates being made to move.

SAEKI MOMO, "HAIRPIN" (FANG) — CR 3
Ex-sprinter, thrown off her school team for using her quirk on the track. Izuto Kutsu is everything she lost and she will want to race him.
AC 14 · HP 42 · Speed 40 ft · Initiative +4 · Save DC 13
STR 10 · DEX 18 · CON 12 · INT 12 · WIS 12 · CHA 13
· NEEDLE HAIR — TWO SHOTS (+6, 60/120 ft) — 2d6+2 piercing each.
· PINCUSHION (recharge 5–6) — 15-ft burst around her, DEX DC 13, 3d6 piercing, half on a save.
· TRACK LEGS — can Disengage as a bonus action.
· SOMETHING STANDING BEHIND HER (Heat 4+ only) — since spring there has been a figure at her shoulder that she cannot explain and her registry does not list. It is an Envoy, and it is the Astral Court's first trace. See "The Astral Court."
· HOW TO RUN — Kites. Never stands still. If a PC outruns her, she stops fighting and asks for a rematch on a track.

IBUKI KŌSUKE, "THREE-STRIPE KŌ" (STRIPE) — CR 5
Holds Ikebukuro North Alley. Cold, precise, honourable to the letter of the Law, and the owner of a notebook with the name of everyone he has ever beaten.
AC 15 · HP 75 · Speed 35 ft · Initiative +3 · Save DC 14
STR 14 · DEX 17 · CON 14 · INT 12 · WIS 13 · CHA 14
· MULTIATTACK — TWO CLAW STRIKES (+6) — 3d8 slashing each.
· AFTERIMAGE — begins each fight with two afterimages. While any remain, attacks against him have disadvantage, and any hit or area effect that would touch him pops one instead of dealing damage.
· THE COLLECTOR — he has watched the festival archive. He quotes the commentary at you, accurately, and he has read your weakness.
· HOW TO RUN — The first Byakko who has done his homework. Play the commentary-quoting lightly — it is a schoolyard echo of Appetite, not a scare.

TSURUOKA FUSAE, "MADAME TSURU" (STRIPE) — CR 5
Sixty-eight. Runs Lucky Seven, the dice den above a noodle shop, and has held three stripes for thirty-one years because nobody has beaten her yet. Adores Kinji's shoes.
AC 13 · HP 80 · Speed 25 ft · Initiative +0 · Save DC 15
STR 16 · DEX 10 · CON 16 · INT 14 · WIS 16 · CHA 16
· HEAVY HAND (+7) — 3d8+4 bludgeoning. Once per round, the target makes a CON DC 15 save or is stunned until the end of its next turn.
· SEEN IT ALL — advantage on saves against being frightened, charmed or tricked, and she cannot be surprised.
· THE HOUSE — inside Lucky Seven, every Byakko member present fights for her without being asked.
· HOW TO RUN — Does not start fights. Ends them, with one slap, and then offers you tea. Would very much like to see what Kinji's quirk does, and has a die she would like him to roll.

KUZE ASAGI, THE AZURE CORNER — CR 8
Holds the east. Twenty-two, a former national-level swimmer, calm to the point of boredom. Masahata Shikoji is the first person in years he has wanted to fight.
AC 16 · HP 125 · Speed 30 ft, swim 40 ft · Initiative +3 · Save DC 16
STR 14 · DEX 16 · CON 16 · INT 13 · WIS 14 · CHA 12
· MULTIATTACK — TWO RIPTIDE WHIPS (+8, 20 ft reach) — 4d8 bludgeoning each. A hit pulls the target 15 ft toward him.
· TIDECALL — pulls water out of drains, pipes and gutters. While he stands in water, +2 AC.
· FLOOD LANE (recharge 5–6) — 60-ft line, DEX DC 16 or 5d8 bludgeoning, knocked prone and pushed 20 ft; half and no push on a save. The line stays flooded.
· WEAKNESS — lightning in water. If he takes lightning damage while standing in water, he is stunned until the end of his next turn. Nakaya Emari will find this out.
· HOW TO RUN — Floods the street first and fights second. Every Corner is named for one of the other three guardian beasts, as a boast: the other gods are Byakko's doormen.

HŌJŌ AKANE, THE VERMILION CORNER — CR 8
Holds the south. Nineteen, theatrical, gorgeous, insufferable. Watched Tazato breathe fire at the festival and has been furious about the competition ever since. Rakuka thinks she is the coolest person he has ever seen.
AC 16 · HP 115 · Speed 30 ft, fly 40 ft · Initiative +4 · Save DC 16
STR 12 · DEX 18 · CON 14 · INT 12 · WIS 12 · CHA 18
· MULTIATTACK — TWO FLAME TALONS (+8) — 3d10 fire each.
· PYRE DIVE (recharge 5–6) — dives on a point within 40 ft: 10-ft radius, DEX DC 16, 6d10 fire, half on a save.
· REBIRTH (once per day) — at 0 HP she bursts into flame (3d10 fire to everything within 15 ft, no save) and stands back up with 40 HP.
· SHOWWOMAN — will not fight without an audience, and plays to it.
· HOW TO RUN — Opens from the air and never lands if she can help it. Hates being ignored more than being hit.

GENDA TETSUO, THE BLACK CORNER — CR 8
Holds the north and the front door of the Cage. Forty, enormous, sells takoyaki from a cart, reads philosophy between customers, and has not lost a fight in eleven years.
AC 18 · HP 160 · Speed 20 ft · Initiative -1 · Save DC 16
STR 22 · DEX 8 · CON 20 · INT 12 · WIS 15 · CHA 10
· SHELL SLAM (+9) — 4d10+6 bludgeoning.
· SHELL — if he has not moved this turn: AC 20 and resistance to all damage except psychic.
· IMMOVABLE — cannot be pushed, pulled, knocked prone or grappled by anything smaller than Huge.
· DOORMAN — to reach the White Tiger in the Cage, you go through him or you talk your way past him. He is open to both.
· HOW TO RUN — Plants himself and waits. Thinks Kazama, Setaka and Hiro are the most interesting things to happen to him in a decade, and will happily stop a fight to discuss load-bearing.

KŌGA RIN, THE YELLOW CORNER — CR 9
Holds the centre — the Cage itself — and is the White Tiger's second. Twenty-five, unsmiling, and the fastest thing in west Tokyo until the festival. She has watched Izuto Kutsu's obstacle course run forty times.
AC 17 · HP 120 · Speed 60 ft · Initiative +5 · Save DC 17
STR 14 · DEX 20 · CON 14 · INT 13 · WIS 14 · CHA 13
· MULTIATTACK — TWO THUNDERHOOF KICKS (+9) — 2d10+5 bludgeoning + 2d10 lightning each.
· STORM STRIDE — never provokes opportunity attacks.
· ARC STEP (bonus action) — teleports up to 30 ft along anything conductive: rail, wire, wet ground.
· OVERCHARGE — if she is soaked, her next kick deals its lightning damage to her as well.
· SECOND — if the White Tiger is in the fight, Rin acts immediately after her.
· HOW TO RUN — Izuto's rival whether he likes it or not, and Nakaya's too. Never stops moving; hates water.

HAKURO MITSUKI, THE WHITE TIGER — CR 12
Byakko. Twenty-seven, six foot four, a white-tiger heteromorph with black stripes down her arms and gold eyes, undefeated for six years. Eats at the same ramen stall at one in the morning every night. Watched the Sports Festival's paired tournament and thought it was cowardice.
AC 18 · HP 230 · Speed 40 ft · Initiative +4 · Save DC 18
STR 22 · DEX 18 · CON 20 · INT 13 · WIS 16 · CHA 18
· MULTIATTACK — TWO CLAWS (+11) — 3d10+6 slashing each.
· BITE (AFTER POUNCE ONLY) (+11) — 2d10+6 piercing.
· POUNCE — if she moves 20 ft straight at a creature and hits it with a claw, it makes a STR DC 18 save or is knocked prone, and she may bite it as a bonus action.
· ROAR (recharge 5–6) — 30-ft cone, WIS DC 18 or frightened for 1 minute (repeat the save at the end of each turn).
· APEX READ — after a creature hits her, she has advantage on her next attack against that creature.
· UNDEFEATED (2 per round, at the end of another creature's turn) — move up to half her speed without provoking, or make one claw attack.
· THE LAW IS THE LAW — she fights one challenger at a time. If a second U.A. student joins in, she steps back and declares the fight void. The way round this is in "The White Tiger," and it is the campaign's thesis.
· HOW TO RUN — Not a monster, not a villain in the Appetite sense — a champion. She wants the best fight in Tokyo and she thinks the festival winners might be it. Play her with total sincerity.

appendix.heading: Stat blocks — Byakko, the middle ranks
appendix.body:
The eleven named members between a Stray and a Corner, plus the one with four stripes. All of them are in the encounter manager under "Byakko." Where a block says it is not a fight, it is not a fight.

NAGIRA SOU, "PYLON" (CLAW) — CR 1
Seventeen, holds the laundrette corner, hates collecting and does it anyway. Apologises before and after.
AC 13 · HP 30 · Speed 25 ft · Initiative +0 · Save DC 12
STR 15 · DEX 11 · CON 15 · INT 10 · WIS 11 · CHA 12
· SHOULDER (+5) — 2d6+2 bludgeoning.
· DEADWEIGHT (bonus action) — until his next turn he cannot be moved, pushed or knocked prone by anything short of Huge, and his speed is 0.
· HOW TO RUN — Plants himself in a doorway so nobody can get past, which is the entire extent of his ambition. Will stand aside if asked nicely, and then be in trouble for it.

TOBE MIYU, "TALLY" (CLAW) — CR 1/4
Sixteen, one stripe, earned with a chair in front of nine witnesses. Keeps the gang's books in three exercise books and a phone.
AC 12 · HP 16 · Speed 30 ft · Initiative +2 · Save DC 11
STR 9 · DEX 14 · CON 10 · INT 16 · WIS 14 · CHA 13
· A CHAIR (+2) — 1d6 bludgeoning. She is not a fighter and the stat block is a formality.
· THE BOOKS — she knows what every member of Byakko is owed, owes, and is worth, and where the money goes, and she has never shown anybody. She is the most useful NOT A FIGHT in the backstreets.
· HOW TO RUN — Talk to her. Everything in "the turf economy" is in her exercise books, and she will trade it for help with a problem that has nothing to do with the gang.

ŌKAWACHI JIN, "DROPKICK" (CLAW) — CR 1
Eighteen, challenges upward constantly, loses constantly, undeterred. The reason rule six exists.
AC 13 · HP 28 · Speed 35 ft · Initiative +2 · Save DC 12
STR 14 · DEX 15 · CON 13 · INT 8 · WIS 8 · CHA 14
· FLYING KICK (+4) — 2d8+2 bludgeoning. If he moved 20 ft first, add 1d8 and he lands prone, every time, without fail.
· UNDETERRED — he fights until he is unconscious and is cheerful about it the next day.
· HOW TO RUN — Announce him. Have him challenge the most famous PC in the street in front of everybody, lose in two rounds, and come back next window.

MURASE KOTOHA, "NETTLE" (FANG) — CR 3
Nineteen, holds the noodle bar's street, personally enforces rule four. Kind to the unstriped kids and frightening to everybody else.
AC 15 · HP 48 · Speed 30 ft · Initiative +3 · Save DC 13
STR 14 · DEX 16 · CON 14 · INT 11 · WIS 14 · CHA 12
· MULTIATTACK — TWO STING STRIKES (+6) — 2d6+3 slashing + 1d6 poison each.
· NETTLE (recharge 5–6) — 15-ft radius, CON DC 13, 3d6 poison and poisoned until the end of its next turn; half and no condition on a save.
· RULE FOUR — anybody who threatens the noodle bar or an unstriped kid in her presence gets her full attention and nothing else does.
· HOW TO RUN — The Byakko most likely to end up helping the class, which she will deny. Fight her once and she is a contact for the rest of the campaign.

YANAGI DAICHI, "HALF-STEP" (FANG) — CR 4
Twenty-one, the gang's teacher, and the best pure technician in two wards. Failed the U.A. entrance exam twice at fifteen and never mentions it.
AC 16 · HP 55 · Speed 30 ft · Initiative +4 · Save DC 14
STR 15 · DEX 18 · CON 14 · INT 13 · WIS 15 · CHA 13
· MULTIATTACK — THREE PALM STRIKES (+7) — 1d10+4 bludgeoning each.
· HALF-STEP — once per round, as a reaction to being targeted by a melee attack, he moves 5 ft and the attack misses.
· HE HAS WATCHED YOUR MATCH, AND NOT ON CLEAN READ — he watched the broadcast, twice, because he loves it. He will tell a PC what they did well, specifically, and he will be right.
· HOW TO RUN — A spar, not a fight. Honourable, delighted, and the most generous opponent in the campaign. Bose would have him tomorrow and the table should feel that.

IMAI TATSUHIKO, "SANDBAG" (FANG) — CR 3
Twenty, runs the Ring's betting book out of Swing Town's back office. Knows what everybody is worth to the yen.
AC 14 · HP 50 · Speed 30 ft · Initiative +1 · Save DC 13
STR 16 · DEX 12 · CON 16 · INT 15 · WIS 12 · CHA 15
· MULTIATTACK — TWO BODY BLOWS (+6) — 2d8+3 bludgeoning each.
· SOAK — the first 10 damage from each attack against him is reduced to half. He has been hit for a living for four years.
· THE BOOK — he will quote odds on the PCs to their faces, sell information about any fighter in two wards, and in Chapter 7 he is the first member of Byakko to buy a Clean Read page. He is also the first to work out what the site means for the Law, and he is frightened by it, and he is right to be.
· HOW TO RUN — A businessman who can take a punch. Would much rather have the class's custom than their blood.

KŌNO SAE, "HINGE" (STRIPE) — CR 5
Twenty-four, holds the chop shop, opens any lock by touch. Sold a man with a scar a white van for cash in the spring.
AC 15 · HP 72 · Speed 30 ft · Initiative +3 · Save DC 14
STR 13 · DEX 17 · CON 15 · INT 14 · WIS 13 · CHA 12
· MULTIATTACK — TWO JIMMY STRIKES (+6) — 3d6+3 piercing each.
· HINGE (action) — she touches any lock, door, restraint, panel or joint and it opens. Any of them. Including a cell, a cold-store hatch, or a set of handcuffs on somebody else.
· UNHINGE (recharge 5–6) — one creature within 5 ft wearing armour or carrying a weapon: STR DC 14 or it comes apart and falls to the ground.
· THE VAN — she remembers him exactly: the scar, the height, the way he did not haggle, and the blood on her counter. She will describe him once, properly, to anybody who asks properly. That is all there has ever been.
· HOW TO RUN — Professional, bored, and completely willing to be arrested, which nobody expects. She will not resist.

FUKAMI RYŌTA, "LADDER" (STRIPE) — CR 5
Twenty-six, holds the Shinjuku west-exit alleys, and recruits. Finds the fourteen-year-olds on the crash barriers and gives them somewhere to belong.
AC 15 · HP 78 · Speed 30 ft · Initiative +2 · Save DC 15
STR 16 · DEX 14 · CON 16 · INT 13 · WIS 14 · CHA 18
· MULTIATTACK — TWO HOOKS (+6) — 3d8+3 bludgeoning each.
· CLIMB WITH ME (action, once per fight) — one creature within 30 ft that can hear him: WIS DC 15 or it cannot attack him until the end of its next turn. He is not charming them. He is telling them, sincerely, that they are better than this street and that he can see it.
· THE MOST DANGEROUS MAN IN BYAKKO — and he has never hurt anybody in his life, and he believes he is doing those kids a favour, and for about a third of them he is.
· HOW TO RUN — Warm. Genuinely warm. Every single thing he says to an unstriped fourteen-year-old is something U.A. said to the class in Chapter 1.

SAWAGUCHI HIDEMI, "QUIET" (STRIPE) — CR 5
Thirty-three, holds the hospital street, murmurs, patches up every fighter in the backstreets and asks nothing. A nurse for eleven years first.
AC 14 · HP 85 · Speed 30 ft · Initiative +1 · Save DC 15
STR 14 · DEX 13 · CON 17 · INT 15 · WIS 18 · CHA 13
· MULTIATTACK — TWO PRESSURE STRIKES (+6) — 2d8+2 bludgeoning, and the target makes a CON DC 15 save or has disadvantage on its next attack.
· FIELD DRESSING (action, 3 per day) — one creature within 5 ft regains 4d8 HP. She will use these on the PCs, in a fight, without being asked, if somebody is badly hurt.
· THE GREY ONES — since spring she has treated four Claws who turned up pale, slow and missing a night, with two neat marks on the neck, and she stopped asking. She is the Scarlet Legion's loudest trace in the city and nobody has ever talked to her.
· HOW TO RUN — Barely a fight at all; she would rather treat than hit. If the class are kind to her once, she is the Underground's best doorway and does not know it.

AMANO KEITA, "FOOTNOTE" (FOUR STRIPES) — CR 6
Nineteen. Eight months ago he was a Stray. His quirk, Second Wind, lets him stand up once. He has beaten a Claw, two Fangs, Three-Stripe Kō and Saeki Momo, every one of them by knowing exactly what they could not do.
AC 15 · HP 80 · Speed 30 ft · Initiative +3 · Save DC 14
STR 14 · DEX 16 · CON 16 · INT 16 · WIS 15 · CHA 11
· MULTIATTACK — TWO PLAIN STRIKES (+7) — 2d8+3 bludgeoning each. No quirk in them at all.
· PREPARED FOR YOU (once per round) — he names, out loud and accurately, one thing a target's quirk cannot do, read off a teardown he watched before the fight, and gains advantage on his next attack roll against them. Say the actual limitation from the PC's sheet.
· SECOND WIND — the first time he drops to 0 HP, he stands back up with 25.
· FOOTWORK, NOTHING ELSE — he has no signature move. Any creature that uses a technique, training benefit or Underground gift that has never been filmed strips Prepared For You for the rest of the fight, against everybody. Do not tell the players this.
· HOW TO RUN — Polite, apologetic, and genuinely puzzled that anybody minds. He did not break the Law; he read it. See Chapter 7, "A Challenge, Bought and Paid For."

appendix.heading: Kurogane Wharf — the gym, the café, and the docks after midnight
appendix.body:
The class's half of the map. Byakko's rooms are where the gang is; this is where the class go when they want to train, to hear something, or to sit on a bollard with a line in the water. Three things in a hundred metres — a gym, a café and a stretch of dock — and after midnight the third one belongs to the Scarlet Legion, which is the entire trick of the place: the party will have been here in daylight first.

NAKATA'S GYM
Nakata Isamu pays Byakko ¥10,000 a month and will tell anybody who asks, with no self-pity anywhere in it. There is a preset map, “Nakata's Gym” — a ring, four bags, mats, and an office with the month's envelope on the desk — and nobody has ever fought in that building for real.
· THE OPENER — he is already taping his hands. "Ten thousand a month. I pay it." Then: "D'you want to know why, or d'you want to hit something first?" Either answer is the right one and he respects both.
· WHAT A PC CAN DO — an open sparring session, which is half a training slot; the cleaning shift, which is ¥3,000 and half a training slot; or ask him the honest question about the protection racket and get the honest answer, which is that taking Byakko off those ninety shops puts something worse on them inside a month and the real fix is the police, slowly, with witnesses, and years.
· ON A MONDAY, HAZAMA RITSU IS THERE. In gloves. Being taught properly, by a man who pays protection to the gang that boy belongs to, and neither of them finds this strange. If one scene in this campaign explains the backstreets, it is that one, and it is already on the little-things table.
· HE IS THE ADULT WHO IS NOT STAFF. No lesson, no agenda, no self-pity, and no interest in being anybody's mentor. A PC who wants an answer about the world and does not want it from a teacher comes here.
· IF A PC HOLDS THE STREET AND ENDS THE GYM'S PAYMENT — he does not thank them. He points out, without heat, that it lasts exactly as long as they hold the rank, and he is right, and the rank section says so too. Then he tapes his hands.

THE ANCHOR
Okabe Fumi's café, and the ward's early warning system. Coffee, a counter, and every rumour in two wards.
· THE OPENER — "Sit at the end. You hear more from the end."
· SHE HAS ONE SAVED for whoever walks in, and it is the one she thought they would want. Roll on the rumour table or pick; she delivers it flatly and she will not tell anybody where it came from, ever, including under pressure, including from the police.
· SHE NEVER SAYS WHETHER IT IS TRUE. The rumour tables mark that for the DM and for nobody else. Half of what she hands over is wrong, she knows that, and she passes it on anyway because sorting it is not her job.
· THE SHIFT BEHIND THE COUNTER — CHA DC 10, ¥5,000, and a roll on the rumour table, which is the cheapest information in the campaign.
· DO NOT TURN HER INTO A SHOP. She gives one rumour, warmly, for nothing. The moment she has a price list the ward has lost the only person in it who talks for free.

THE DOCKS AFTER MIDNIGHT
The same hundred metres, and a Scarlet Legion haunt — at a haunt the Odd Night band widens to 01–10, which makes this the most likely place in Tokyo for the class to meet the Underground by accident.
· WHAT IS OUT THERE — six Thralls at a time, out of the dark, and the horror is in the stat block rather than in the description: they are slow and they do not stop. Load "Thralls on the wharf" onto Dockside Container Yard.
· AND ONE FIGURE IN A GOOD COAT, watching them, who does not run and does not explain. That is the Legion's witness rung and it is worth saving.
· THE RUMOUR IS TRUE — "there are grey people at Kurogane Wharf after midnight, they walk like they've forgotten how" is the first entry on the rumour table and it is marked TRUE, and Okabe Fumi is the one who hands it over, two hundred metres from where it happens, in the afternoon, with a coffee.

THE DAY, SHORT VERSION — the boats are in before five, the Anchor opens at six and Okabe is behind the counter all morning, the gym fills after school, Hazama is there on a Monday, the café shuts at seven, and nothing on the dock itself is worth looking at until about half past midnight.

THE ONE RULE — daylight here is a gym and a café and a man who pays his ten thousand a month, and the campaign should spend three or four free-time windows making that completely ordinary before anything grey walks out of the dark at the end of the same street.

appendix.heading: The Underground — Odd Nights and the discovery ladder
appendix.body:
The full ladder for each faction: what each rung looks like, so you can deliver it flatly when the dice or the players get there. The rules for rolling are in Chapter 6, "Odd Nights."

THE SCARLET LEGION
· RUMOUR — "grey people at the wharf after midnight"; "a club in Ginza with no sign"; "a clinic in Minato that buys blood."
· TRACE — a Byakko Claw found asleep in a doorway, pale, with two neat marks on his neck, alive and remembering nothing; a blood bank that is always full and never has night patients; a guest at the dorm door who will not step over the threshold until somebody says "come in."
· WITNESS — six slow grey shapes on the docks and one figure in a good coat watching them ("Thralls on the wharf," on Dockside Container Yard); or a tall pale man reflected in a shop window, who is not on the street when you turn round. (Alucard is a placed trace; use him once.)
· CONTACT — "A Party That Ends at Dawn."
· INVITATION — an alliance, a favour, a war, or Alucard's black card.

THE ASTRAL COURT
· RUMOUR — "the old woman in the cold bath can stay under ten minutes"; "a kid in Kōenji folded a car in half"; "Mr Joestar's acid has a ghost in it."
· TRACE — Saeki Momo's Envoy at the gate; Whitesnake picking up a pen; a Byakko fighter with a power that is not on any registry.
· WITNESS — Hōshō Kaito, at three in the morning in a Kōenji car park, folding a car flat with a figure made of paper — and seeing that you saw.
· CONTACT — "Matsu-no-Yu."
· INVITATION — Sunbreath, the hunt for Saotome Shin's stolen arrowhead, and Rob Joestar's confession.

KUROSHIKI
· RUMOUR — "something counts in the stairwell where Backdraft died"; "a seminary in the hills you can only find if they want you to."
· TRACE — a security camera in Adachi showing an empty street while three people watch a fight in it (a Veil); a Case 9 site where the air feels watched; after Chapter 5, the ground-floor corridor light clicking off, and on, and off. (The light is a placed trace; use it once.)
· WITNESS — a sleepy boy in a black high-collared uniform presses an inked thumb to a PC's eyelids, and for one minute they see what is in the stairwell.
· CONTACT — "The Thing in the Laundry Room."
· INVITATION — the Kurama Rite School, a lesson in Pacts, a pair of ink-lens glasses, and Shirasagi Rei's "huh."

THE LEDGER
· RUMOUR — "somebody in black turns up at every accident in this ward before the ambulance does"; "there's a thing standing under the barrier at the Yanaka crossing and it's been there since winter"; "the sweet shop by the cemetery sells more than sweets."
· TRACE — a hospital's back entrance at midnight where somebody in a black uniform is standing by the bins, writing; a security recording of a crash in which a figure in black is a smudge that nobody can focus on; a notice, correctly addressed, delivered to the Heights Alliance pigeonholes by bicycle, for a student who does not exist on any register. (The notice is a placed trace; use it once.)
· WITNESS — the barriers come down at the Yanaka crossing for a train with nobody on it, and there are two people standing on the wrong side of them, and one of them is licking the end of a pencil and counting.
· CONTACT — "Nobody Signed For It" (Chapter 8).
· INVITATION — a Mark, a countersignature forged in a sweet shop, and one true answer from the First Desk at the price of a page.

ODD NIGHT BANDS, WITH FOUR FACTIONS. Chapters 7 and 8: 01–02 Legion, 03–04 Court, 05–06 Kuroshiki, 07–08 the Ledger, 09–14 a rumour. The Ledger's haunts — Yanaka, any hospital, any level crossing after midnight, and every Case 9 site — overlap the Kuroshiki's almost exactly, which is why those two cannot be in a room together.

appendix.heading: The Underground — rumours (d20)
appendix.body:
Roll a d20 when a rumour comes up, or pick one. True and false rumours are told the same way, by the same kind of person, in the same tone. Only you know which is which. Pin each on the rumour board when it is heard.

1 · "There are grey people at Kurogane Wharf after midnight. They walk like they've forgotten how." — TRUE, Legion.
2 · "The White Tiger is three people in a costume." — FALSE.
3 · "The old woman in the cold bath at Matsu-no-Yu can stay under for ten minutes." — TRUE, Court (it is twelve).
4 · "Something counts, in the stairwell in Ota where Backdraft was found." — TRUE, Kuroshiki.
5 · "Super Panda is an actual panda." — nobody at U.A. will confirm or deny this.
6 · "There's a club in Ginza with no sign. Eleven till dawn. Nobody eats." — TRUE, Legion.
7 · "Byakko work for Appetite." — FALSE, and somebody should say so quickly.
8 · "A kid at a Kōenji konbini folded a car in half." — TRUE, Court.
9 · "There's a seminary above Hachiōji you can only find if they want you to." — TRUE, Kuroshiki.
10 · "They're taking the festival archive down." — FALSE.
11 · "A tall pale man in black turns up in crowds and isn't there when you look again. He's been seen at U.A." — TRUE, Legion (Alucard).
12 · "Mr Joestar's acid has a ghost in it." — TRUE, Court.
13 · "Madame Tsuru never loses because she's psychic." — FALSE. She hits very hard.
14 · "A camera in Adachi recorded an empty street while three people watched a fight in it." — TRUE, Kuroshiki.
15 · "Hiro is three first-years in a robot suit." — FALSE, and nearer the truth than the person saying it knows.
16 · "The Hiruma Clinic in Minato buys blood. Pays well. Doesn't ask." — TRUE, Legion.
17 · "There's a floor in the Cage above the top floor." — TRUE, sort of: it is the roof.
18 · "Since spring, some Byakko fighters have something standing behind them." — TRUE, Court.
19 · "The light on the ground floor of the U.A. dorm goes off at eleven. And on. And off." — TRUE, Kuroshiki (Chapter 6 only).
20 · "A fishmonger at Tsukiji hasn't aged a day since 1964." — UNCLAIMED. See "Room for more."

THE SECOND TWENTY (d20) — for Chapters 6 onward, or when the first table is used up. Same rules: told the same way, by the same kind of person, in the same tone.

1 · "Somebody in black gets to every accident in this ward before the ambulance." — TRUE, the Ledger.
2 · "There's a thing standing under the barrier at the Yanaka crossing. It's been there since winter." — TRUE, the Ledger.
3 · "The sweet shop by the Yanaka cemetery sells more than sweets." — TRUE, the Ledger.
4 · "A fishmonger at Tsukiji hasn't aged a day since 1964." — UNCLAIMED. Still. See "Room for more."
5 · "There's a teahouse in Yanaka where you can buy a dream. The price is one of yours." — UNCLAIMED, and three streets from a Ledger haunt, which is a coincidence unless you want it not to be.
6 · "Byakko have got a bloke with four stripes who hasn't won a fight on his own." — TRUE. See Chapter 7.
7 · "You can pay a man in Shinjuku four hundred thousand yen and he'll tell you how to beat a pro." — TRUE, and his name is in Chapter 8.
8 · "The nurse on the hospital street has been patching up Claws who come in grey." — TRUE, Legion.
9 · "The Commission are sealing the festival archive." — FALSE until Chapter 8, and then it depends entirely on what the class did in Room 4.
10 · "Clean Read's got a page on Super Panda." — TRUE. It is eleven minutes long and it is about maths.
11 · "A kid in the new first-year class fights exactly like one of 2-A." — TRUE, and she will tell you so herself.
12 · "There's a floor of the Cage nobody holds." — TRUE. It is the fourth and there is a sofa on it.
13 · "Three of the Four Corners have been beaten by school kids." — TRUE, if they were.
14 · "The old man at the sweet shop used to run something." — TRUE, and he will not say which.
15 · "They never caught everyone who was with Appetite." — FALSE. Do not reopen it.
16 · "Mr Joestar went back to the bathhouse." — the DM decides, and the class will never be told.
17 · "Hiro's got a speaker in him now." — TRUE if Otowa said yes, and nobody outside 2-A knows which.
18 · "There's a page in a book in Yanaka with your name on it and no date." — TRUE for any PC who signed for something.
19 · "Byakko are finished. It's all going to be whoever reads fastest." — TRUE, and it is Imai Tatsuhiko saying it, and he is right.
20 · "Somebody wrote on the front of their own festival footage." — TRUE from Chapter 8 onward, and within a month four thousand people have.

appendix.heading: The Scarlet Legion
appendix.body:
THE SCARLET LEGION — vampires, after Hellsing: gothic, courteous, military, monstrous.

WHO THEY ARE — a vampire order that arrived in Yokohama with the foreign legations in 1868 and has fed quietly in Tokyo ever since. About forty true vampires and many more Thralls. They own the Crimson Room (a members' club on the top floor of an unsigned Ginza building, open eleven till dawn), the Hiruma Clinic in Minato (a private hospital with an always-full blood bank), and the night shipping at Kurogane Wharf.

WHY NOBODY KNOWS — a vampire has no quirk factor. On paper the Legion are old-money foreign residents, Quirkless, with very good lawyers. Their code forbids feeding anywhere it will be noticed, turning anybody without the Legate's leave, or touching anybody on the hero register. They have kept that code for a hundred and fifty years.

WHAT HAS CHANGED — Case 9 put Commission eyes on the backstreets, and the Legion has lately been feeding on Byakko, because nobody misses gang members. They also recruit strong Byakko fighters as Legionaries: the Legion, too, believes in a ladder of power. And Alucard Chosoji has been in Tokyo all year.

RANKS — Thrall (fed on, not finished, mindless) · Legionary · Centurion · Tribune · Legate.

HOW A LEGION VAMPIRE WORKS — Regeneration every turn, a charming Gaze, Mist once a night, and a bite that heals them. Elites fight sealed, and release their restriction in stages — Level Three, Two, One — growing stronger and stranger each time; the Legate has a Level Zero, and you do not want to see it.

WEAKNESSES — sunlight (no regeneration, radiant damage every turn, disadvantage on everything); radiant damage and silver (vulnerable); a threshold (they cannot enter a private home uninvited, and Heights Alliance is a home); running water (they cannot cross it unaided). REN SUZUKI'S BEAM IS RADIANT. The Legion will notice this before he does.

PEOPLE — LADY AKABANE SERAPHINE, the Legate: four hundred years old, looks thirty, a negotiation, never a fight. MINA TODA, Centurion: looks nineteen, has since 1923; the diplomat, and the first one a PC will meet. CAPTAIN GRAU, Centurion: seven feet, grey greatcoat, has not spoken since 1945. DR HIRUMA SHŌGO: runs the clinic, makes the Thralls, keeps meticulous records of who they were. ALUCARD CHOSOJI: not a member. A deserter, the oldest vampire in the city, and the thing the Legion fears most.

WHAT A PC CAN EARN — a Legion favour (once, anything money and four centuries can do; it will be repaid with interest); Alucard's black card (burned at midnight, it brings him once); or a silvered weapon, made for them by Alucard's contacts, which deals an extra 1d6 to Legion vampires and stops their Regeneration for a round. None of these are in the shop.

THE OTHER SIDE — the Astral Court has been at war with the Legion since 1868. Anybody who finds one should, eventually, hear about the other.

appendix.heading: The Astral Court
appendix.body:
THE ASTRAL COURT — sun-priests and spirit-bearers, after JoJo's Bizarre Adventure: a breathing art, a war with vampires, and a great deal of style.

WHO THEY ARE — a court of sun-priests that traces itself to the Heian period. Its art is SUNBREATH: a way of breathing that carries sunlight through the blood, so that a strike burns like noon, a palm on water holds your weight, and a touch can heal — or, to a vampire, scorch. Its masters can wake an ENVOY: a second self that stands beside them and does one impossible thing.

WHY NOBODY KNOWS — Sunbreath is a skill, not a quirk, and an Envoy standing behind a person looks, to everyone in a world of quirks, like part of their quirk. Most Courtiers are registered Quirkless and proud of it. When quirks appeared, the Court simply went quiet, because in a world where everybody has powers, a breathing art is invisible.

WHAT HAS CHANGED — in spring, a former Courtier, Saotome Shin, stole one of the Court's seven arrowheads — meteorite shards that wake Envoys in whoever survives a cut from them. He has been cutting Byakko fighters with it. Some died. Some, like Saeki Momo, woke something they do not understand, and are climbing the Cage faster than they should.

RANKS — Daybreak (initiates, Sunbreath only) · Morning (Courtiers) · Noon (Envoy-bearers) · Zenith (elders) · the Throne, which has been empty since 1945.

HOW SUNBREATH WORKS — a pool of uses per short rest. Spend one on a hit for extra radiant damage; or to walk on water or up a wall for a turn; or to heal by touch (which burns a Legion vampire instead). It stops working if you cannot breathe.

HOW AN ENVOY WORKS — each has a name (Court tradition: the name of a song, chosen by its bearer), a card of six grades from A to E (Power, Speed, Range, Durability, Precision, Potential), one impossible ability, and one rule: an Envoy can only be hurt by another Envoy or by radiant damage, and anything that hurts it hurts its bearer instead. So hit the bearer.

PEOPLE — GRANDMOTHER HINATA SAE, the Zenith elder: eighty-one, runs Matsu-no-Yu in Kōenji, holds her breath for twelve minutes, never took an Envoy, has buried three students who did. HŌSHŌ KAITO: seventeen, night clerk, pompadour, Envoy PAPER PLANES (anything it punches folds like paper). SAOTOME SHIN: the arrowhead thief, Envoy BAD MOON (an Eclipse in which no light and no Sunbreath works). ROB JOESTAR: U.A.'s English teacher, Hinata's student until he was twenty-two, whose "acid quirk" has always had an Envoy standing behind it called WHITESNAKE. It comes when he is angry, and it carries a gun.

WHAT A PC CAN EARN — SUNBREATH, after the Invitation and three training slots at Matsu-no-Yu (CON DC 12 each, in the cold pool): proficiency-bonus uses per short rest; on a hit, +1d6 radiant (2d6 from level 9); or, as a bonus action, walk on liquid and up walls until the end of the turn; or, as an action, heal 1d8 by touch (a Legion vampire takes 2d8 radiant instead). Works only while you can breathe freely. An ENVOY, only by the arrowhead, only at real risk (CON DC 16 or drop to 0 HP and begin dying), and only if the player truly wants one; let them name it after a song.

THE OTHER SIDE — the Court's whole history is a war with the Scarlet Legion. Ren Suzuki's beam is radiant, and Hinata will want to look at it very closely.

appendix.heading: Kuroshiki
appendix.body:
KUROSHIKI — the black rite, after Jujutsu Kaisen: curses born from fear, inherited techniques, barriers nobody can see through.

WHO THEY ARE — a handful of old families, descended from Heian court diviners, who exorcise KEGARE: knots of human dread that have learned to move, invisible to almost everybody. They fight with SUMI — the ink of dread turned against itself — and with an INHERITED TECHNIQUE, a power that passes down a bloodline and is the family's real name. They train at the Kurama Rite School, a "Shinto seminary" in the hills above Hachiōji, a few miles from U.A.

WHY NOBODY KNOWS — Kegare cannot be seen without Sumi and do not show on cameras, and the Kuroshiki fight behind VEILS: black domes that, from outside, show an empty street. On the registry, sorcerers are Quirkless or claim small, dull quirks. One person in the Commission knows. The campaign never says who.

WHAT HAS CHANGED — Case 9. A city that has spent a year afraid breeds Kegare faster than three families can clear them.
